detail.faq:
q: Is 5-Amino-1MQ FDA-approved?
a: No. 5-Amino-1MQ is not FDA-approved for any indication. It is a preclinical research compound. It is not available by prescription.
q: Has 5-Amino-1MQ been tested in humans?
a: No published human clinical trials of 5-Amino-1MQ exist as of September 2026. All reported effects ,  on body composition, glucose tolerance, and adipocyte biology ,  come from animal and cell studies. Preclinical findings in rodents do not reliably predict human outcomes.
q: What does 5-Amino-1MQ do in preclinical adipose tissue studies?
a: In diet-induced obese mice, 5-Amino-1MQ reduced white fat mass and adipocyte size without changing food intake, and a later mouse study found it improved oral glucose tolerance. The proposed mechanism is NNMT inhibition: by preserving SAM in fat cells and blocking the methylation drain, the compound shifts adipose tissue toward greater energy expenditure. Whether this effect occurs in humans has not been studied.
q: Is 5-Amino-1MQ a peptide?
a: No. 5-Amino-1MQ is a methylquinolinium salt ,  a small synthetic organic molecule, not a peptide. It is often found in the same gray-market channels as peptide compounds and is sometimes searched for alongside peptides, but its chemistry is categorically different.
q: How does 5-Amino-1MQ compare to semaglutide or tirzepatide?
a: They operate through entirely different mechanisms. Semaglutide and tirzepatide are GLP-1 receptor agonists (and GIP agonist in tirzepatide's case) with extensive human trial data and FDA approval for specific indications. 5-Amino-1MQ is an NNMT inhibitor with preclinical animal data only. No human comparison exists. Extrapolating from rodent efficacy data to compare these compounds would be methodologically unsound.
q: What is the difference between 5-Amino-1MQ and NR or NMN?
a: NR and NMN are NAD+ precursors that increase cellular NAD+ levels by supplying additional substrate for the salvage pathway. 5-Amino-1MQ inhibits NNMT, the enzyme that diverts nicotinamide away from NAD+ synthesis while also depleting SAM. In principle, the compounds work on adjacent but distinct nodes of the same pathway; 5-Amino-1MQ also addresses the methylation axis that NR and NMN do not. In practice, both NR and NMN have reached small human RCTs, with little metabolic benefit so far: eight NMN trials showed no significant benefit on glucose or lipid markers, and NR did not improve insulin sensitivity in obese men. 5-Amino-1MQ has no human data at all.
q: Can I get 5-Amino-1MQ from a compounding pharmacy?
a: No. 5-Amino-1MQ is not available by prescription and has no established safety or efficacy profile in humans. Gray-market vendors sell it as a research chemical; those products are not manufactured under pharmaceutical GMP standards and are not subject to regulatory oversight.
q: What are the risks of using 5-Amino-1MQ?
a: The human risk profile is unknown because no human safety studies have been conducted. Theoretical concerns include off-target effects of sustained SAM elevation on methylation biology and unknown drug interactions. Long-term effects ,  including any implications for cancer biology, given NNMT's roles in various cancers ,  have not been characterized. Gray-market products carry additional risks related to undetermined purity, dose accuracy, and contamination.
detail.sections:
title: What is 5-Amino-1MQ?
text: 5-Amino-1MQ (5-amino-1-methylquinolinium) is a small synthetic molecule that inhibits an enzyme called nicotinamide N-methyltransferase, or NNMT. It is not a peptide. Peptides are short chains of amino acids, whereas 5-Amino-1MQ is a small-molecule methylquinolinium compound. It is often grouped with research peptides, but it belongs to a different chemical class.
title: How does 5-Amino-1MQ work?
text: NNMT is an enzyme that becomes more active in fat tissue in obesity. In cell studies, inhibiting it increases NAD+ and SAM and suppresses fat production in fat cells. In diet-induced obese mice, a potent NNMT inhibitor reduced body weight and fat mass without changing how much the animals ate. These findings come from animal and cell studies, not from humans.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No. 5-Amino-1MQ has never been approved by the FDA for any use and, unlike an approved drug, it has not gone through completed human trials.
title: What does the research show?
text: The research is almost entirely preclinical. The main evidence comes from animal and cell work, including these two studies:
Study | Model | Finding
Foundational NNMT-inhibitor study | Mice | First showed NNMT inhibitors reduce obesity
2022 study | Obese mice | NNMT inhibition combined with a low-fat diet reduced body weight and adiposity
There are no completed randomized controlled human trials, so its effects and safety in people remain unknown.
detail.sources_note: Sources: preclinical studies cited above are indexed on PubMed and cited by DOI where used, including the 2017 NNMT-inhibitor study in Biochemical Pharmacology (DOI: 10.1016/j.bcp.2017.11.007) and a 2022 study in Scientific Reports (DOI: 10.1038/s41598-021-03670-5). This document is educational research and does not constitute medical advice, a health claim, or an offer to sell; 5-Amino-1MQ is not approved by the FDA, and its safety and effectiveness in humans have not been established.

peptides.name: Abaloparatide
peptides.fda_status: FDA-approved peptide injection
peptides.evidence_note: It is approved by the FDA for osteoporosis in postmenopausal women and men at high fracture risk, backed by the pivotal ACTIVE double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.
peptides.what_it_is:
Abaloparatide is a synthetic 34-amino acid peptide modeled on a signaling molecule your body already makes, called parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrP). Abaloparatide isn't a receptor itself; it instead binds to PTH1R, a G-protein-coupled receptor sitting on the surface of your bone-building cells.
Once attached, it triggers a pathway that instructs those cells to create new bone. This can increase the density of bones, improving their strength and reducing the likelihood of bone fractures.
It is given as a daily subcutaneous injection for postmenopausal women who are experiencing osteoporosis. It can also be prescribed for others, including men, who have either not responded well to or tolerated other osteoporosis medications.
peptides.research_at_a_glance: In the pivotal placebo-controlled study, abaloparatide reduced vertebral and nonvertebral fractures in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis. This does not establish blanket superiority over teriparatide.
peptides.key_takeaway: Abaloparatide is a synthetic 34-amino acid analog of parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrP) that activates the PTH1 receptor to stimulate new bone formation. FDA-approved in 2017 as Tymlos, it is a daily injection for postmenopausal women and men with osteoporosis at high fracture risk, and it is capped at two years of use. In the pivotal ACTIVE trial, it cut the risk of new spine fractures by about 86% versus placebo.
peptides.mechanism:
Bone is constantly being torn down (resorption) and rebuilt (formation). Abaloparatide ramps up the build-up faster than the tear-down so that new bone is created quicker than old bone is removed. This creates what's called an anabolic window, the stretch where bone formation outpaces bone resorption.
Abaloparatide also influences the calcium and phosphate balance in the body, both of which are minerals that contribute to bone health. In trials, abaloparatide reduced the risk of major fractures; in the spine, the relative risk reduction for new fractures was 86%, and in nonvertebral fractures it was 43%.
In addition to reducing fractures, abaloparatide increases bone mineral density, which measures the amount of calcium and other minerals in your bones to determine the bones’ strength and fracture risk. In a large trial abbreviated ACTIVE, it had a statistically significant impact on the hip, lower spine, and femoral neck (the bone that connects the femur to the hip). In comparison to the placebo, bone mineral density increased at each site as follows:
Site | Bone mineral density increase vs placebo
Hip | 4.25%
Lower spine | 10.37%
Femoral neck | 4.01%
Strong results were seen as soon as six months. Abaloparatide is used for at maximum two years.

Teriparatide (Forteo) was considered first-in-class as it was FDA-approved in 2002, 15 years before abaloparatide. Both are daily injections, anabolic drugs that build new bone through the same receptor (PTH1R), and are capped at two years of lifetime use. However, teriparatide is a fragment of parathyroid hormone (PTH) itself while abaloparatide is synthetically modeled on PTHrP. That difference is how abaloparatide is a more bone-building, less bone-dissolving drug
There is no study that has a direct comparison between the two drugs, but rather trials compare them to placebo groups where teriparatide serves as the active control group. The best evidence comes from the ACTIVE trial, which included both drugs:
- Spine fractures were roughly comparable: Abaloparatide cut new vertebral fractures by 86% and teriparatide by 80% versus placebo. Neither was shown to beat the other here.
- Nonvertebral fractures: Abaloparatide showed a statistically significant 43% reduction, while teriparatide’s 28% reduction didn’t reach significance in this trial.
- Major osteoporotic fractures: Abaloparatide beat teriparatide significantly with a 55% lower risk.
- Bone density: There were similar increases at the spine, but abaloparatide produced significantly greater increases at the hip and femoral neck.
- Hypercalcemia was less common with abaloparatide (3.4%) than with teriparatide (6.4%).
peptides.side_effects_safety: Tymlos lists the potential side effects as: - Dizziness - Nausea - Headache - Fast heartbeat - Fatigue - Vertigo - Redness, swelling, and/or bruising at injection site - Joint and/or bone pain - Abdominal bloating or pain - Diarrhea - Nausea Serious side effects can include: - Increased blood calcium (hypercalcemia) - Increased urine calcium (hypercalciuria), which may cause kidney stones

title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: Yes, abaloparatide has been FDA-approved since 2017 under the brand names Tymlos and Eladynos.
title: What is abaloparatide prescribed for?
text: Estrogen is one of the body’s natural brakes on bone breakdown. When estrogen levels fall during menopause, that brake comes off: bone resorption speeds up, outpaces formation, and many women lose bone density rapidly in the years right afterward, especially with the spine and hip. (These bones are highly load-bearing structures that are the easiest places to identify bone density.) Abaloparatide works directly against that imbalance.
Rather than only slowing the accelerated breakdown (as many osteoporosis drugs do), it helps actively rebuilds bone, helping to recover some of what was lost and restore strength in the areas where postmenopausal bone loss does the most damage.
Because abaloparatide actively builds new bone rather than just slowing bone loss, it makes it a heavier hitter than most osteoporosis drugs. For that reason, it’s generally reserved for people whose fracture risk is high enough to justify it, i.e. someone who has already broken a bone, whose bone-density scores are very low, or who has several risk factors. It's also approved for men with osteoporosis at high fracture risk, too, not just postmenopausal women.
Doctors typically don’t prescribe it to people with a higher baseline risk of bone cancer, including Paget’s disease of bone, a history of bone cancer or radiation to the skeleton, or unexplained elevated alkaline phosphatase on bloodwork. It’s also generally avoided in people who already run high on blood calcium or who are prone to calcium-based kidney stones.

- Headache

- Fatigue
- Vertigo
- Redness, swelling, and/or bruising at injection site
- Joint and/or bone pain
- Abdominal bloating or pain
- Diarrhea
- Nausea
Serious side effects can include:
- Increased blood calcium (hypercalcemia)
- Increased urine calcium (hypercalciuria), which may cause kidney stones

peptides.name: Acetyl hexapeptide-8
peptides.fda_status: Cosmetic ingredient rather than a drug, so does not require FDA approval
peptides.evidence_note: It has human trial evidence, including a 2013 randomized, placebo-controlled study, but that evidence is limited, since the studies are small, often manufacturer-associated, and complicated by real questions about how well the peptide penetrates the skin.
peptides.what_it_is: Synthetic peptide used in anti-aging skincare, best known by the trade name Argireline
peptides.key_takeaway: Acetyl hexapeptide-8, sold in skincare as Argireline, is a synthetic peptide modeled on the nerve protein SNAP-25 and marketed as a topical, "Botox-like" way to soften the appearance of expression lines. In lab and small clinical studies it interferes with the SNARE complex that nerves use to trigger muscle contraction, and a 2013 randomized study found it reduced the appearance of peri-orbital wrinkles over four weeks. It is a cosmetic ingredient rather than a drug, so it does not require FDA approval, and its evidence is rated Moderate.
peptides.mechanism: Acetyl hexapeptide-8 softens the look of expression lines by reducing the small muscle contractions that create them. Nerves trigger those contractions by releasing a chemical signal, and that release depends on a group of proteins called the SNARE complex, of which SNAP-25 is a part. In laboratory studies, acetyl hexapeptide-8 mimics the end of SNAP-25 and competes with it, which interferes with SNARE complex formation and reduces the release of the signal that tells the muscle to contract. This is the same broad target as Botox, but acetyl hexapeptide-8 is applied topically and is far milder, not an injection that blocks the nerve. One important limit is delivery. Because it is a relatively large, water-loving peptide, how well it crosses the skin barrier to reach the nerves underneath is debated, and that penetration question is a major reason its effect is modest.
peptides.human_study_findings: The main controlled evidence is a 2013 randomized, placebo-controlled study in 60 people, in which a topical argireline product reduced the appearance of peri-orbital wrinkles over four weeks compared with placebo. A 2025 review and other small studies report similar modest improvements, while noting that many studies are small or manufacturer-associated and that skin penetration is a genuine question. The research supports a modest cosmetic benefit, not a result like injectable Botox.
peptides.side_effects_safety:
Topical acetyl hexapeptide-8 is generally well tolerated, and a cosmetic-industry safety review assessed it as safe as used in cosmetics. As with any skincare ingredient, some people can still experience:
- Mild redness
- Irritation
- An allergic reaction
For that reason, a patch test before regular use is sensible. Because the peptide is applied to the skin rather than injected, its safety considerations are those of a typical cosmetic ingredient.
Is argireline safe to use? Across published studies, argireline has shown a low-irritation profile. Early testing found no primary irritation at high doses, and no allergic reactions were reported in a 26-patient case series or a small 2023 double-blind study. The CIR Expert Panel formally assessed acetyl hexapeptide-8 amide as safe for cosmetic use at concentrations up to 0.005% in its 2025 assessment. The safety profile is one of argireline's genuine strengths relative to injected botulinum toxin, which carries risks including eyelid ptosis and headache.

detail.mechanism:
Acetyl hexapeptide-8 softens the look of expression lines by reducing the small muscle contractions that create them. Nerves trigger those contractions by releasing a chemical signal, and that release depends on a group of proteins called the SNARE complex, of which SNAP-25 is a part. detail.research_findings: The main controlled evidence is a 2013 randomized, placebo-controlled study in 60 people, in which a topical argireline product reduced the appearance of peri-orbital wrinkles over four weeks compared with placebo. The research supports a modest cosmetic benefit, not a result like injectable Botox.
detail.safety_side_effects:
Topical acetyl hexapeptide-8 is generally well tolerated, and a cosmetic-industry safety review assessed it as safe as used in cosmetics. As with any skincare ingredient, some people can still experience:
- Mild redness
- Irritation
- An allergic reaction
For that reason, a patch test before regular use is sensible. Because the peptide is applied to the skin rather than injected, its safety considerations are those of a typical cosmetic ingredient.
Is argireline safe to use? Across published studies, argireline has shown a low-irritation profile. Early testing found no primary irritation at high doses, and no allergic reactions were reported in a 26-patient case series or a small 2023 double-blind study. The CIR Expert Panel formally assessed acetyl hexapeptide-8 amide as safe for cosmetic use at concentrations up to 0.005% in its 2025 assessment. detail.faq:
q: Is argireline the same as Botox?
a: No. Botulinum toxin A is injected directly into the target muscle, where it enzymatically cleaves SNAP-25 and produces a true, long-lasting neuromuscular blockade that reverses only slowly as nerve connections to the muscle recover. Argireline is a topical cosmetic peptide that, according to its proposed mechanism, interferes with SNARE complex assembly. The mechanisms are fundamentally different, and whether argireline reaches neuromuscular junctions in meaningful concentrations through topical application is debated. Marketing argireline as "topical Botox" overstates what the evidence supports.
q: Does argireline actually work for wrinkles?
a: The evidence is mixed. A randomized, placebo-controlled trial published in 2013 found significant improvements in periorbital wrinkles after 28 days of twice-daily argireline application in 60 subjects. An independent 2023 split-face study of 19 women using objective Visia analysis found no significant wrinkle reduction. No large, long-duration, independently conducted RCT has confirmed efficacy. Modest effects under specific formulation conditions are plausible given the mechanistic data; established efficacy equivalent to retinoids or injected botulinum toxin is not supported by the current evidence base.
q: Why doesn't argireline penetrate the skin effectively?
a: Argireline is a hydrophilic peptide with a molecular weight of approximately 889 daltons. The stratum corneum is a lipid-rich barrier that preferentially impedes the passage of large, polar, water-soluble molecules. In laboratory penetration tests on human cadaver and guinea pig skin, most applied argireline washed off the surface, the portion that penetrated stayed mostly in the stratum corneum, only about 0.01% reached the epidermis, and no peptide was detected in the dermis. Reaching neuromuscular junctions, which are located in muscle tissue beneath the dermis, would require substantially greater tissue penetration than has been demonstrated.
q: What concentration of argireline do commercial products contain?
a: Commercial cosmetics typically contain argireline at low concentrations. The Cosmetic Ingredient Review Expert Panel, in a 2025 assessment, found argireline safe at concentrations up to 0.005% in present practices of use. Some efficacy studies describe formulations containing 10% of the hexapeptide, which is orders of magnitude higher. A 2021 analysis of commercial creams and serums detected argireline alongside its oxidized form, because its methionine residue can oxidize, which raises questions about product stability. The gap between clinical trial concentrations and typical commercial use concentrations is relevant to evaluating real-world product claims.
q: Is argireline safe to use?
a: Across published studies, argireline has shown a low-irritation profile. Early testing found no primary irritation at high doses, and no allergic reactions were reported in a 26-patient case series or a small 2023 double-blind study. The CIR Expert Panel formally assessed acetyl hexapeptide-8 amide as safe for cosmetic use at concentrations up to 0.005% in its 2025 assessment. The safety profile is one of argireline's genuine strengths relative to injected botulinum toxin, which carries risks including eyelid ptosis and headache.
q: How does argireline compare to Matrixyl (palmitoyl pentapeptide)?
a: Matrixyl (pal-KTTKS) is a signal peptide designed to stimulate collagen production in the dermis. Argireline is a neurotransmitter-inhibitor peptide that attempts to modulate SNARE complex assembly and reduce muscle contraction signals. The mechanisms are entirely different. Both face the skin penetration barrier, but signal peptides targeting dermal fibroblasts have a less extreme distance to travel than peptides attempting to reach neuromuscular junctions in underlying muscle. A 2005 placebo-controlled, split-face trial in 93 women found statistically significant wrinkle reductions with pal-KTTKS, though that evidence base is similarly small-scale and requires independent replication. Neither ingredient has an evidence base comparable to topical retinoids.
q: Can formulation improvements help argireline penetrate the skin?
a: Possibly. In pig-skin experiments, water-in-oil-in-water multiple emulsions significantly increased argireline skin penetration compared to simpler emulsion types. A 2018 study showed that molecular modifications to argireline analogs can improve human skin permeation in vitro, with one modified variant reducing glutamate release by 43% in a neural cell model. As of September 2026, no modified or delivery-enhanced argireline formulation has completed a placebo-controlled clinical trial demonstrating superior efficacy to standard commercial formulations. Formulation science is the active frontier for this ingredient.
detail.sections:
title: What is acetyl hexapeptide-8?
text: Acetyl hexapeptide-8 is a synthetic six-amino acid peptide used as a cosmetic ingredient, best known by the trade name Argireline. It is also called acetyl hexapeptide-3, an older name for the same molecule. Its sequence is patterned on the end of SNAP-25, a protein that nerves use to release the signals that make muscles contract.
It is sold in serums and creams marketed for anti-aging, and it is applied topically to the skin.
title: How does it work?
text: Acetyl hexapeptide-8 softens the look of expression lines by reducing the small muscle contractions that create them. Nerves trigger those contractions by releasing a chemical signal, and that release depends on a group of proteins called the SNARE complex, of which SNAP-25 is a part. In laboratory studies, acetyl hexapeptide-8 mimics the end of SNAP-25 and competes with it, which interferes with SNARE complex formation and reduces the release of the signal that tells the muscle to contract. This is the same broad target as Botox, but acetyl hexapeptide-8 is applied topically and is far milder, not an injection that blocks the nerve.
One important limit is delivery. Because it is a relatively large, water-loving peptide, how well it crosses the skin barrier to reach the nerves underneath is debated, and that penetration question is a major reason its effect is modest.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No, and it does not need to be. The FDA does not approve cosmetics or most cosmetic ingredients before they go on the market. Cosmetics are regulated and must be safe when used as directed and properly labeled, but there is no pre-market approval step the way there is for drugs, so no anti-aging peptide in a serum is "FDA-approved."
The line that actually matters for an ingredient like this is the difference between a cosmetic and a drug. A product is a cosmetic when it is intended to improve appearance, but if it claims to change the structure or function of the skin, such as a claim to paralyze muscles, the FDA can regulate it as an unapproved drug. This is why skincare claims are written around the appearance of lines rather than a promised physiological change.
title: What is it used for?
text: Acetyl hexapeptide-8 is used almost entirely in topical anti-aging products. It is included to soften the appearance of expression lines and wrinkles, especially forehead lines and the crow's feet around the eyes. It is one of the most common peptide ingredients in over-the-counter skincare.
title: What does the research show?
text: The main controlled evidence is a 2013 randomized, placebo-controlled study in 60 people, in which a topical argireline product reduced the appearance of peri-orbital wrinkles over four weeks compared with placebo. A 2025 review and other small studies report similar modest improvements, while noting that many studies are small or manufacturer-associated and that skin penetration is a genuine question. The research supports a modest cosmetic benefit, not a result like injectable Botox.
title: What are the side effects?
text: Topical acetyl hexapeptide-8 is generally well tolerated, and a cosmetic-industry safety review assessed it as safe as used in cosmetics. As with any skincare ingredient, some people can still experience:
- Mild redness
- Irritation
- An allergic reaction
For that reason, a patch test before regular use is sensible. Because the peptide is applied to the skin rather than injected, its safety considerations are those of a typical cosmetic ingredient.

peptides.what_it_is: Synthetic peptide used in anti-aging and eye-care skincare, best known by the trade name Eyeseryl
peptides.key_takeaway: Acetyl tetrapeptide-5, sold in skincare as Eyeseryl, is a synthetic four-amino acid peptide used in eye creams to soften the look of under-eye bags and puffiness. It is thought to work in two ways, by easing the fluid buildup that makes the under-eye area look swollen and by limiting the glycation that stiffens collagen, though its published evidence comes almost entirely from the manufacturer. It is a cosmetic ingredient rather than a drug, so it does not require FDA approval, and its evidence is rated Low.
peptides.mechanism: Acetyl tetrapeptide-5 is thought to reduce the appearance of under-eye bags through two proposed actions: - An anti-edema effect. Puffiness under the eyes is partly caused by fluid pooling in the tissue, and in the manufacturer's testing the peptide reduced that fluid buildup, in part by lowering the leakiness of small blood vessels, their vascular permeability, so that less fluid escapes into the surrounding skin. - An effect on glycation, the process in which sugars bind to and stiffen collagen. By limiting glycation, the peptide is proposed to help the thin skin under the eyes stay more elastic and less prone to the slackening that deepens the look of bags. Both of these are findings from laboratory and manufacturer studies rather than independent clinical research. As with any topical peptide, how much of it actually crosses the skin barrier to reach the tissue underneath is uncertain, and that places a ceiling on how strong the effect can be.
peptides.human_study_findings: The published evidence for acetyl tetrapeptide-5 is thin and comes mostly from its manufacturer. Lipotec's own panel studies report a visible reduction in the appearance of under-eye bags and puffiness in volunteers who used a formulation containing the peptide, but those results have not been reproduced in independent, peer-reviewed clinical trials. So while the proposed mechanism is reasonable and the manufacturer data is encouraging, the cosmetic benefit rests largely on the company's own testing rather than on strong outside evidence.
peptides.side_effects_safety: Topical acetyl tetrapeptide-5 is generally considered well tolerated, with the low potential for irritation typical of cosmetic peptides, and it is used on the especially delicate skin around the eyes. As with any skincare ingredient, some people can still experience mild redness, stinging, or an allergic reaction, so patch testing before regular use and keeping the product out of the eyes themselves is sensible.

detail.mechanism:
Acetyl tetrapeptide-5 is thought to reduce the appearance of under-eye bags through two proposed actions:
- An anti-edema effect. Puffiness under the eyes is partly caused by fluid pooling in the tissue, and in the manufacturer's testing the peptide reduced that fluid buildup, in part by lowering the leakiness of small blood vessels, their vascular permeability, so that less fluid escapes into the surrounding skin.
- An effect on glycation, the process in which sugars bind to and stiffen collagen. By limiting glycation, the peptide is proposed to help the thin skin under the eyes stay more elastic and less prone to the slackening that deepens the look of bags.

detail.research_findings: The published evidence for acetyl tetrapeptide-5 is thin and comes mostly from its manufacturer. Lipotec's own panel studies report a visible reduction in the appearance of under-eye bags and puffiness in volunteers who used a formulation containing the peptide, but those results have not been reproduced in independent, peer-reviewed clinical trials. So while the proposed mechanism is reasonable and the manufacturer data is encouraging, the cosmetic benefit rests largely on the company's own testing rather than on strong outside evidence.
detail.safety_side_effects: Topical acetyl tetrapeptide-5 is generally considered well tolerated, with the low potential for irritation typical of cosmetic peptides, and it is used on the especially delicate skin around the eyes. detail.sections:
title: What is acetyl tetrapeptide-5?
text: Acetyl tetrapeptide-5 is a synthetic peptide of four amino acids used as a cosmetic ingredient, best known by the trade name Eyeseryl, developed by the ingredient maker Lipotec, now part of Lubrizol. It is a small "signal" peptide, meaning it is designed to interact with skin biology rather than simply sit on the surface, and it is sold almost exclusively in products aimed at the under-eye area.
It is applied topically, usually in eye creams, serums, and gels marketed to reduce the look of puffiness and bags.
title: How does it work?
text: Acetyl tetrapeptide-5 is thought to reduce the appearance of under-eye bags through two proposed actions:
- An anti-edema effect. Puffiness under the eyes is partly caused by fluid pooling in the tissue, and in the manufacturer's testing the peptide reduced that fluid buildup, in part by lowering the leakiness of small blood vessels, their vascular permeability, so that less fluid escapes into the surrounding skin.
- An effect on glycation, the process in which sugars bind to and stiffen collagen. By limiting glycation, the peptide is proposed to help the thin skin under the eyes stay more elastic and less prone to the slackening that deepens the look of bags.
Both of these are findings from laboratory and manufacturer studies rather than independent clinical research. As with any topical peptide, how much of it actually crosses the skin barrier to reach the tissue underneath is uncertain, and that places a ceiling on how strong the effect can be.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No, and it does not need to be. The FDA does not approve cosmetics or most cosmetic ingredients before they go on the market. Cosmetics must be safe when used as directed and properly labeled, but there is no pre-market approval step the way there is for drugs, so no de-puffing or anti-aging peptide in a serum is "FDA-approved."
The distinction that matters for an ingredient like this is the line between a cosmetic and a drug. A product is a cosmetic when it is intended to improve appearance, but if it claims to change the structure or function of the body, the FDA can regulate it as an unapproved drug. This is why de-puffing claims are written around the appearance of the under-eye area rather than a promised physiological change.
title: What is it used for?
text: Acetyl tetrapeptide-5 is used almost entirely in topical eye-care products, where it is included to reduce the appearance of under-eye puffiness, bags, and swelling. It often appears alongside ingredients such as caffeine or hyaluronic acid in eye creams, serums, and gels, and some formulas also position it as helping the under-eye skin look firmer and smoother.
title: What does the research show?
text: The published evidence for acetyl tetrapeptide-5 is thin and comes mostly from its manufacturer. Lipotec's own panel studies report a visible reduction in the appearance of under-eye bags and puffiness in volunteers who used a formulation containing the peptide, but those results have not been reproduced in independent, peer-reviewed clinical trials. So while the proposed mechanism is reasonable and the manufacturer data is encouraging, the cosmetic benefit rests largely on the company's own testing rather than on strong outside evidence.
title: What are the side effects?
text: Topical acetyl tetrapeptide-5 is generally considered well tolerated, with the low potential for irritation typical of cosmetic peptides, and it is used on the especially delicate skin around the eyes. As with any skincare ingredient, some people can still experience mild redness, stinging, or an allergic reaction, so patch testing before regular use and keeping the product out of the eyes themselves is sensible.

peptides.name: Afamelanotide
peptides.fda_status: FDA-approved peptide, sold as Scenesse, given as a subcutaneous implant
peptides.evidence_note: It is approved by the FDA for erythropoietic protoporphyria, backed by two multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials showing increased pain-free light exposure.
peptides.what_it_is:
Afamelanotide is a synthetic peptide that mimics alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (α-MSH), the natural hormone that controls skin pigmentation. It is an analog engineered to be more potent and far longer-lasting than natural α-MSH, and it is also known by the research names Melanotan I and NDP-MSH. It is made by Clinuvel Pharmaceuticals and sold as Scenesse.
Rather than a daily injection, it is given as a small dissolvable implant placed just under the skin by a healthcare provider, which releases the drug slowly over several days.
peptides.key_takeaway: Afamelanotide is a synthetic, longer-lasting analog of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (α-MSH) that activates the MC1R receptor on pigment cells to boost the skin's own protective eumelanin. The FDA approved it in 2019 as Scenesse, a subcutaneous implant for adults with erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP), a rare light-sensitivity disorder. In the pivotal 2015 placebo-controlled trials, U.S. patients (94) logged a median 69.4 pain-free hours in direct sunlight versus 40.8 on placebo (P = 0.04). EU patients (74) logged 6.0 versus 0.8 hours (P = 0.005).
peptides.mechanism:
Afamelanotide works by switching on the skin's own pigment system to build a protective layer of melanin. It is a potent agonist of the melanocortin-1 receptor, or MC1-R, which sits on melanocytes, the pigment-producing cells of the skin.
Activating MC1R drives those cells to make more eumelanin, the dark form of melanin that acts as the body's natural sunscreen, absorbing and scattering light and neutralizing the reactive oxygen species that light can generate in the skin. Because the drug triggers this through the receptor rather than through sun exposure, it raises eumelanin without requiring the UV damage that normally produces a tan.
In erythropoietic protoporphyria, that extra pigment matters for a specific reason. People with EPP build up a molecule called protoporphyrin IX, which reacts with visible light to produce bursts of reactive oxygen that damage tissue and cause severe burning pain after even brief light exposure. By increasing eumelanin, afamelanotide reduces how much light reaches and reacts in the skin, which lengthens the time a person can spend in the light before pain begins.
The pharmacology explains the delivery form. The peptide is far more stable than natural α-MSH, so it is delivered as a bioresorbable implant that releases it over days.
Two placebo-controlled pivotal trials, reported together in 2015, enrolled 168 adults with EPP. The table shows their results beside a later real-world cohort:
Study | Patients | Result
U.S. pivotal trial | 94 | Median pain-free time in direct sunlight 69.4 hours with afamelanotide versus 40.8 hours with placebo (P = 0.04)
EU pivotal trial | 74 | Median 6.0 hours versus 0.8 hours (P = 0.005), with 77 phototoxic reactions versus 146
Dutch real-world cohort | 117 patients | 98% stayed on treatment over a median 2.0 years of follow-up
The most common adverse events in the pivotal trials were headache, nausea, nasopharyngitis, and back pain, and quality of life improved in both studies.
peptides.side_effects_safety: According to the prescribing information, the most common side effects are: - Implant-site reactions - Nausea - Throat pain and cough - Fatigue - Skin hyperpigmentation and darkening of existing moles - Dizziness or drowsiness - Respiratory tract infection - Skin irritation The label also warns that serious hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported with postmarket use. Because afamelanotide increases skin pigmentation, the label calls for regular full-body skin exams so that moles and any suspicious lesions can be monitored over time.

detail.sections:
title: What is afamelanotide?
text: Afamelanotide is a synthetic peptide that mimics alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (α-MSH), the natural hormone that controls skin pigmentation. It is an analog engineered to be more potent and far longer-lasting than natural α-MSH, and it is also known by the research names Melanotan I and NDP-MSH. It is made by Clinuvel Pharmaceuticals and sold as Scenesse.
Rather than a daily injection, it is given as a small dissolvable implant placed just under the skin by a healthcare provider, which releases the drug slowly over several days.
title: The history of afamelanotide
text: Afamelanotide began as an attempt to bottle a sunless tan. In the 1980s, researchers Mac Hadley and Victor Hruby at the University of Arizona set out to design a synthetic version of α-MSH that could darken skin without sun exposure, reasoning that a drug-induced protective tan might lower skin cancer risk in a sun-drenched state like Arizona. Natural α-MSH breaks down too quickly to be practical, so they built a more stable, more potent analog and called it Melanotan.
The Arizona program actually produced two related compounds. Melanotan I, the linear analog, is what became afamelanotide. A second, cyclic analog called Melanotan II was pursued separately and eventually led to a different drug for sexual dysfunction.
The program then shifted from a cosmetic tanning agent to a medical photoprotectant for people with serious light-sensitivity disorders. That path led, over roughly two decades, to approval for erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP), in the European Union in 2014 and the United States in 2019.
The original tanning idea never fully went away. Unapproved "Melanotan I" and "Melanotan II" peptides are still sold online as injectable tanning products, and regulators have repeatedly warned against them, because they are not approved, not quality-controlled, and not the same as the regulated implant.
title: How does afamelanotide work?
text: Afamelanotide works by switching on the skin's own pigment system to build a protective layer of melanin. It is a potent agonist of the melanocortin-1 receptor, or MC1-R, which sits on melanocytes, the pigment-producing cells of the skin.
Activating MC1R drives those cells to make more eumelanin, the dark form of melanin that acts as the body's natural sunscreen, absorbing and scattering light and neutralizing the reactive oxygen species that light can generate in the skin. Because the drug triggers this through the receptor rather than through sun exposure, it raises eumelanin without requiring the UV damage that normally produces a tan.
In erythropoietic protoporphyria, that extra pigment matters for a specific reason. People with EPP build up a molecule called protoporphyrin IX, which reacts with visible light to produce bursts of reactive oxygen that damage tissue and cause severe burning pain after even brief light exposure. By increasing eumelanin, afamelanotide reduces how much light reaches and reacts in the skin, which lengthens the time a person can spend in the light before pain begins.
The pharmacology explains the delivery form. The peptide is far more stable than natural α-MSH, so it is delivered as a bioresorbable implant that releases it over days.
Two placebo-controlled pivotal trials, reported together in 2015, enrolled 168 adults with EPP. The table shows their results beside a later real-world cohort:
Study | Patients | Result
U.S. pivotal trial | 94 | Median pain-free time in direct sunlight 69.4 hours with afamelanotide versus 40.8 hours with placebo (P = 0.04)
EU pivotal trial | 74 | Median 6.0 hours versus 0.8 hours (P = 0.005), with 77 phototoxic reactions versus 146
Dutch real-world cohort | 117 patients | 98% stayed on treatment over a median 2.0 years of follow-up
The most common adverse events in the pivotal trials were headache, nausea, nasopharyngitis, and back pain, and quality of life improved in both studies.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: Yes. The FDA approved afamelanotide in October 2019 as Scenesse, the first treatment in the United States shown to increase pain-free light exposure in adults with a history of phototoxic reactions from erythropoietic protoporphyria. It had already been approved in the European Union in 2014. It remains the only FDA-approved drug that works by stimulating melanin for photoprotection.
title: What is afamelanotide prescribed for?
text: Afamelanotide is prescribed for adults with erythropoietic protoporphyria to increase the amount of time they can spend in the light without pain. EPP is a rare inherited disorder in which light exposure causes severe burning pain in the skin, which sharply limits daily life. Consensus guidelines from 2023 recommend afamelanotide for preventing phototoxic symptoms in EPP. It is not a cosmetic tanning product and is not approved for tanning or for any other condition.
Because it is an implant, it is administered by a healthcare provider rather than self-injected. The label advises a full-body skin examination twice a year, since the drug increases pigmentation and can darken existing moles, which makes routine skin monitoring important.
title: What are the side effects?
text: According to the prescribing information, the most common side effects are:
- Implant-site reactions
- Nausea
- Throat pain and cough
- Fatigue
- Skin hyperpigmentation and darkening of existing moles
- Dizziness or drowsiness
- Respiratory tract infection
- Skin irritation
The label also warns that serious hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported with postmarket use.
Because afamelanotide increases skin pigmentation, the label calls for regular full-body skin exams so that moles and any suspicious lesions can be monitored over time.

peptides.what_it_is:
Albiglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist, a peptide that mimics the natural gut hormone GLP-1. It was engineered by fusing two GLP-1 analog chains to human albumin, the most abundant protein in blood, which extended its lifespan enough for once-weekly dosing.

Despite that, GSK withdrew it from the market in 2018 for commercial reasons, so it remains FDA-approved but is no longer available.
peptides.mechanism: Albiglutide lowers blood sugar by activating the GLP-1 receptor, mimicking a gut hormone the body releases after eating. In the HARMONY OUTCOMES trial, albiglutide reduced major cardiovascular events in people with type 2 diabetes and established heart disease.

- Lowers glucagon

- Nausea

- Upper respiratory infection

- Severe allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis
- Low blood sugar, especially when combined with insulin or a sulfonylurea

detail.sections:
title: What is amycretin?
text: Amycretin, also known as zenagamtide, is an experimental drug that combines two hormone actions in one molecule: it activates the GLP-1 receptor and the amylin receptor at the same time. It is being developed by Novo Nordisk for weight management, in a once-weekly subcutaneous form and a once-daily oral form. It is investigational and has not been approved for any use.
title: How does it work?
text: Amycretin combines two appetite-signaling actions in one molecule. The first is activation of the GLP-1 receptor, the same incretin target as drugs like semaglutide. Switching it on:
- Raises insulin release when blood sugar is high
- Slows how fast the stomach empties
- Reduces appetite
The second is activation of the amylin receptor, which responds to amylin, a pancreatic hormone that promotes a feeling of fullness.
Each pathway curbs eating on its own, and the reason for building both into a single drug is that the two fullness signals may add together to reduce food intake more than either does alone. This is the proposed mechanism; whether it produces lasting benefit is what clinical trials are meant to establish.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No. Amycretin is investigational and not approved by the FDA or any other regulator. According to Novo Nordisk, both the subcutaneous and oral forms are advancing into Phase 3 development for weight management after early-phase results. The Phase 3 trial AMAZE 1 began recruiting in February 2026.

First-in-human trial of the oral form | 12 weeks | Focused mainly on safety and drug levels, with exploratory weight-change signals
These are small, short studies; no Phase 3 efficacy data are available yet, so amycretin's longer-term effect and tolerability remain unproven.

peptides.name: Angiotensin II
peptides.fda_status: FDA-approved peptide, sold as Giapreza, given as an intravenous infusion in intensive care
peptides.evidence_note: It is approved by the FDA for septic or other distributive shock, supported by the randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled ATHOS-3 trial.
peptides.what_it_is:
Angiotensin II is a peptide hormone made of eight amino acids that the body uses to control blood pressure, and a synthetic form of it is used as a drug. It is the main active molecule of the renin-angiotensin system, the hormone cascade that regulates blood pressure and fluid balance.
As a medicine, it is a laboratory-made copy of the human hormone, developed by La Jolla Pharmaceutical, now part of Innoviva, and sold as Giapreza. It is given only as a continuous intravenous infusion in a hospital, not as an injection a person takes at home.
peptides.key_takeaway: Angiotensin II is a natural peptide hormone and the main active signal of the renin-angiotensin system, which the body uses to raise blood pressure by tightening blood vessels. A synthetic version is FDA-approved as Giapreza, an intravenous drug given in intensive care to raise dangerously low blood pressure in adults with septic or other distributive shock. In its pivotal ATHOS-3 trial it raised blood pressure in about 70% of patients compared with 23% on placebo, though it also carries a risk of blood clots.
peptides.mechanism:
Angiotensin II raises blood pressure by binding to receptors on the muscle lining the blood vessels and making them tighten. It acts mainly through the AT1 receptor on vascular smooth muscle, and activating it constricts the vessels, which raises blood pressure quickly. This is the final active step of the renin-angiotensin system: the kidney releases renin, which starts a chain that produces angiotensin I, and an enzyme called ACE converts that into angiotensin II, the potent form.
Beyond directly tightening vessels, angiotensin II signals the adrenal glands to release aldosterone, a hormone that makes the body hold on to sodium and water, and it promotes the release of vasopressin, another blood-pressure hormone. In shock, this matters because it gives clinicians a way to raise blood pressure through a pathway separate from the standard catecholamine drugs such as norepinephrine, which helps when those drugs alone are not enough.
In the pivotal ATHOS-3 trial of patients with vasodilatory shock who were already on high-dose vasopressors, adding angiotensin II raised blood pressure to the target in 69.9% of patients, compared with 23.4% on placebo. It is given as a continuous infusion and adjusted to blood pressure, and because the peptide is cleared from the blood within about a minute, its effect can be dialed up or down quickly.
peptides.side_effects_safety: The most important safety concern is a risk of blood clots. In its trial, angiotensin II was associated with thrombotic events, including deep vein thrombosis, and the label recommends giving clot-prevention treatment (venous thromboembolism prophylaxis) while a patient is receiving it. According to the prescribing information, other reported effects included: - Low platelet counts - A fast heart rate - Fungal infection - Delirium - Acidosis - High blood sugar - Reduced blood flow to the hands and feet Because it is used only in intensive care, patients receiving it are already under close monitoring.

detail.sections:
title: What is angiotensin II?
text: Angiotensin II is a peptide hormone made of eight amino acids that the body uses to control blood pressure, and a synthetic form of it is used as a drug. It is the main active molecule of the renin-angiotensin system, the hormone cascade that regulates blood pressure and fluid balance.
As a medicine, it is a laboratory-made copy of the human hormone, developed by La Jolla Pharmaceutical, now part of Innoviva, and sold as Giapreza. It is given only as a continuous intravenous infusion in a hospital, not as an injection a person takes at home.
title: The history of angiotensin II
text: Angiotensin II was discovered twice at once, and that is how it got its name. The table below traces it from discovery to approval.
Period | Event
Late 1930s and early 1940s | Two research groups independently isolated the same blood-pressure-raising substance from the kidney's renin pathway. A team led by Irvine Page in the United States called it angiotonin, while a group led by Eduardo Braun-Menéndez in Argentina called it hypertensin. For years the literature carried both names.
1958 | The two camps compromised and blended their terms into a single word, angiotensin, which is still used today
2017 | Approved by the FDA as an intravenous drug for shock, more than seven decades after its discovery
For most of the following decades, the molecule was studied as a hormone and as a target to block, since many common blood-pressure medicines (ACE inhibitors and ARBs) work by reducing its activity. Using the hormone itself as a treatment came much later, when it was developed as an intravenous drug for shock.
title: How does angiotensin II work?
text: Angiotensin II raises blood pressure by binding to receptors on the muscle lining the blood vessels and making them tighten. It acts mainly through the AT1 receptor on vascular smooth muscle, and activating it constricts the vessels, which raises blood pressure quickly. This is the final active step of the renin-angiotensin system: the kidney releases renin, which starts a chain that produces angiotensin I, and an enzyme called ACE converts that into angiotensin II, the potent form.
Beyond directly tightening vessels, angiotensin II signals the adrenal glands to release aldosterone, a hormone that makes the body hold on to sodium and water, and it promotes the release of vasopressin, another blood-pressure hormone. In shock, this matters because it gives clinicians a way to raise blood pressure through a pathway separate from the standard catecholamine drugs such as norepinephrine, which helps when those drugs alone are not enough.
In the pivotal ATHOS-3 trial of patients with vasodilatory shock who were already on high-dose vasopressors, adding angiotensin II raised blood pressure to the target in 69.9% of patients, compared with 23.4% on placebo. It is given as a continuous infusion and adjusted to blood pressure, and because the peptide is cleared from the blood within about a minute, its effect can be dialed up or down quickly.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: Yes. The FDA approved angiotensin II as Giapreza in December 2017 to increase blood pressure in adults with septic or other distributive shock. It was a notable approval because it introduced a new type of vasopressor, giving intensive care teams a hormone-based option to add when standard drugs are not controlling dangerously low blood pressure.
title: What is angiotensin II prescribed for?
text: Angiotensin II is prescribed in the intensive care unit to raise blood pressure in adults whose blood pressure is dangerously low from septic or other distributive shock, a state in which the blood vessels lose their tone and dilate. It is typically added on top of standard vasopressors such as norepinephrine and vasopressin for patients who are not responding adequately to those alone, rather than used first. It is a short-term, closely monitored hospital treatment, not an outpatient medication.
title: What are the side effects?
text: The most important safety concern is a risk of blood clots. In its trial, angiotensin II was associated with thrombotic events, including deep vein thrombosis, and the label recommends giving clot-prevention treatment (venous thromboembolism prophylaxis) while a patient is receiving it. According to the prescribing information, other reported effects included:
- Low platelet counts
- A fast heart rate
- Fungal infection
- Delirium
- Acidosis
- High blood sugar
- Reduced blood flow to the hands and feet
Because it is used only in intensive care, patients receiving it are already under close monitoring.

This document is educational and does not constitute medical advice.

peptides.fda_status: Non-FDA-approved peptide

peptides.what_it_is: Modified fragment of the growth hormone molecule, studied for fat loss
peptides.research_at_a_glance: Human obesity trials did not beat placebo, and development was discontinued
peptides.key_takeaway: AOD-9604 is a modified fragment of the tail end of human growth hormone, developed as a fat-loss drug. Its human obesity trials failed to beat placebo, and development for obesity was halted. As of 2026 it is not FDA-approved and is banned in sport.
peptides.mechanism: The proposed idea is that the tail region of growth hormone carries its fat-burning activity without the rest of the hormone's effects. In animal and cell studies, AOD-9604 increased both fat breakdown and fat oxidation while it reduced fat storage, reportedly without activating the growth hormone receptor or causing growth or insulin-resistance effects. In rodents, it also raised markers of fat metabolism (here and here). These are animal and laboratory findings; the human trials below tested whether they translate.
peptides.human_study_findings: Unusually for a wellness peptide, AOD-9604 was tested in real human trials, and they were negative. A 24-week Phase 2b obesity trial of 536 participants did not produce significant weight loss versus placebo, and development for obesity was terminated in 2007; an earlier, smaller signal did not replicate. The supporting mechanism data remain animal and cell-based. So the best human evidence does not support the marketed fat-loss use; it argues against it.

detail.faq:
q: Does AOD-9604 actually help with fat loss?
a: The most rigorous human evidence ,  the Phase 2b obesity trial conducted by Metabolic Pharmaceuticals ,  did not demonstrate weight-loss efficacy versus placebo at 24 weeks. Preclinical rodent data consistently showed fat-mass reduction and increased fat oxidation, but those findings did not replicate in the larger human trial. Misra documented in a 2013 review in Current Cardiology Reviews that development was terminated in 2007 after a 24-week, 536-subject Phase 2b trial failed to induce significant weight loss. The claim that AOD-9604 is an effective fat-loss compound in humans is not supported by the available clinical evidence.
q: Is AOD-9604 the same as HGH?
a: No. AOD-9604 is a synthetic peptide corresponding to amino acids 177 to 191 of the growth hormone C-terminus, with an added N-terminal tyrosine for stability ,  16 amino acids total, not the 191 amino acids of full-length hGH. The two compounds have distinct molecular structures, different receptor interactions, and different evidence bases. Orlovius and colleagues published evidence in 2013 that AOD-9604 does not register on the WADA hGH isoform immunoassay.
q: Is AOD-9604 FDA-approved?
a: No. AOD-9604 has never received FDA approval for any indication. Its history includes an attempt to position it as a food/supplement ingredient. Its nomination for the 503A bulks list was withdrawn, FDA lists it among substances that may present significant safety risks, and as of September 2026 it is not eligible for 503A compounding.
q: Is AOD-9604 legal to buy in 2026?
a: As of September 2026, AOD-9604 is not eligible for compounding under Section 503A. Products sold as AOD-9604 through online vendors operate outside FDA oversight and lack pharmaceutical-grade manufacturing standards. The compound is not legally available by prescription through U.S. compounding pharmacies under the current regulatory framework.
q: Is AOD-9604 banned in sports?
a: Yes. AOD-9604 appears on the WADA Prohibited List and is prohibited at all times. Cox and colleagues confirmed its WADA-banned status and described a stable metabolite that may extend the detection window in a 2015 paper in Drug Testing and Analysis. Competitive athletes subject to anti-doping testing should not use products containing AOD-9604.
q: Can a doctor still prescribe AOD-9604?
a: As of September 2026, AOD-9604 is not eligible for compounding under Section 503A, meaning it is not available through the licensed compounding pharmacy pathway. There is no FDA-approved drug formulation of AOD-9604 that a licensed prescriber can prescribe.
q: What happened to the FDA Category 2 peptide list, and will these compounds become available again?
a: FDA's 503A Category 2 list covers bulk substances that raise significant safety risks, and as of September 2026 it holds only a handful of substances, not AOD-9604. FDA removed peptides from the list in April 2026 after the nominations were withdrawn, which was not a finding that they are safe. A withdrawn substance is not eligible for 503A compounding unless FDA adds it to the 503A bulks list through rulemaking or places it in Category 1, and no timeline for that exists for AOD-9604.
q: What is the difference between AOD-9604 and tesamorelin?
a: These are structurally unrelated compounds that target fat metabolism through different mechanisms. Tesamorelin is a stabilized GHRH analog that stimulates the pituitary to release endogenous growth hormone. AOD-9604 is a synthetic C-terminal fragment of hGH itself, proposed to act on adipose tissue directly without stimulating pituitary GH release. Tesamorelin has FDA approval to reduce excess abdominal fat in adults with HIV-associated lipodystrophy, supported by two randomized controlled trials including the Falutz and colleagues 2007 NEJM study. AOD-9604 has no FDA-approved indication and failed its Phase 2b obesity trial. This comparison is for scientific context only. These compounds have fundamentally different regulatory statuses and evidence bases.
detail.sections:
title: What is AOD-9604?
text: AOD-9604 is a synthetic peptide based on the C-terminal (tail) region of human growth hormone, with an added amino acid to stabilize it. The name stands for "Advanced Obesity Drug," reflecting its original development by Metabolic Pharmaceuticals as a weight-loss candidate. It is sold on the wellness and "research peptide" market for fat loss, often under the broader "hGH fragment 176-191" label, though it is a modified version of that fragment rather than the bare fragment.
title: How does it work?
text: The proposed idea is that the tail region of growth hormone carries its fat-burning activity without the rest of the hormone's effects. In animal and cell studies, AOD-9604 increased both fat breakdown and fat oxidation while it reduced fat storage, reportedly without activating the growth hormone receptor or causing growth or insulin-resistance effects. In rodents, it also raised markers of fat metabolism (here and here). These are animal and laboratory findings; the human trials below tested whether they translate.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No. AOD-9604's regulatory status covers several points:
- Not approved by the FDA for any use, and never reached market as a drug
- A history that includes an attempt to position it as a food/supplement ingredient
- Not an approved compounding substance
- Prohibited at all times in sport under the WADA list, which covers growth hormone fragments including AOD-9604
title: What does the research show?
text: Unusually for a wellness peptide, AOD-9604 was tested in real human trials, and they were negative. A 24-week Phase 2b obesity trial of 536 participants did not produce significant weight loss versus placebo, and development for obesity was terminated in 2007; an earlier, smaller signal did not replicate. The supporting mechanism data remain animal and cell-based. So the best human evidence does not support the marketed fat-loss use; it argues against it.

detail.sections:
title: What is apraglutide?
text: Apraglutide is an experimental analog of glucagon-like peptide-2 (GLP-2), a hormone that helps the intestine grow and absorb nutrients. It is designed to last long enough for once-weekly injection and is being developed by Ironwood Pharmaceuticals (development code FE 203799) for short bowel syndrome with intestinal failure, where people rely on long-term intravenous, meaning parenteral, nutrition. It is investigational and not approved.
title: How does it work?
text: Apraglutide activates the GLP-2 receptor in the gut. GLP-2 signaling has these effects:
- Promotes growth and adaptation of the intestinal lining
- Slows how fast the stomach empties and food transits
- Increases absorption of fluid and nutrients
In short bowel syndrome, the goal is to help the remaining intestine absorb more so that patients can reduce their dependence on intravenous feeding. This describes the mechanism, separate from the trial outcomes below.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No. Apraglutide is investigational and not approved. Ironwood began a rolling submission to the FDA, but according to company disclosures the FDA communicated that an additional confirmatory Phase 3 trial is needed before approval can be sought, and the company also disclosed a drug-exposure issue in the pivotal trial.
title: What does the research show?
text: The main evidence is one Phase 3 trial, with a supporting Phase 2 study. According to PubMed, the two studies found:
Study | Phase and population | Result
STARS trial | Phase 3, adults with short bowel syndrome | Met its primary endpoint, with a greater reduction in weekly intravenous support volume on apraglutide than placebo, and more participants achieving at least 1 day per week off intravenous support
Supporting study | Phase 2 | Reported improved absorption and reduced parenteral support over a year
The evidence is from a single pivotal trial that has not been replicated, and the FDA has asked for a confirmatory study.

peptides.name: Aviptadil
peptides.fda_status: Investigational drug, not approved by the FDA for any use; studied mainly for severe respiratory failure in COVID-19
peptides.evidence_note: Although it has been tested in randomized controlled human trials, the results do not support a benefit. Since the largest independent trial found no significant improvement and was stopped for futility, there is no sound human evidence that it works for its studied uses.
peptides.what_it_is: Synthetic version of vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), also known by the development code RLF-100 and the name Zyesami
peptides.research_at_a_glance: Mixed human evidence: the largest independent randomized trial found no significant benefit and was halted early for futility
peptides.key_takeaway: Aviptadil is a synthetic form of vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), a signaling molecule that acts on lung receptors, and it has been studied mainly for severe COVID-19 respiratory failure. In the NIH-funded TESICO trial of 461 patients, aviptadil did not beat placebo on the 90-day recovery scale (odds ratio 1.11, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.55, p = 0.54). Ninety-day mortality was 38% with aviptadil versus 36% with placebo (p = 0.78), and the trial stopped early for futility. As of 2026 it is not FDA-approved for any use.
peptides.mechanism:
Aviptadil works by mimicking vasoactive intestinal peptide, the natural signaling molecule the body uses to relax blood vessels and calm inflammation, particularly in the lungs. VIP binds to two receptors, VPAC1 and VPAC2, that are common on lung tissue, and activating them relaxes the smooth muscle in blood vessels and airways and triggers signals that lower inflammation.
Those receptors are not limited to the lungs. VPAC1 and VPAC2 sit on T cells and macrophages, and VPAC1 receptors couple to adenylyl cyclase, the enzyme that makes the signaling molecule cAMP.
A 2013 review of VIP's immune effects describes work in mice, where VIP:
- Inhibited TNF, IL-6, and IL-12 and raised IL-10
- Blocked NF-κB movement into the nucleus
- Induced Foxp3-positive regulatory T cells through tolerogenic dendritic cells
These are animal findings, and they do not show the same effects in patients.
Much of the therapeutic rationale centers on a specific lung cell. In laboratory studies, VIP helps protect the alveolar type II cells that produce surfactant, the substance that keeps the tiny air sacs of the lungs open, and it reduces the release of inflammatory molecules. The theory tested in trials was that supplying extra VIP might help shield the lungs during the severe inflammation of ARDS. This describes the proposed mechanism and the underlying biology; whether aviptadil actually improves outcomes in patients is a separate question, addressed next.
peptides.human_study_findings: The strongest research shows that aviptadil has not been proven to work for the condition it was most studied in. It was tested primarily in critically ill COVID-19 patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure. The companies developing it reported favorable early findings from a company-sponsored phase 2b/3 study in 2021, but the pivotal independent test was the NIH-funded TESICO trial, a randomized, placebo-controlled study of 461 patients. According to PubMed, that trial found that aviptadil did not significantly improve a patient's clinical status at 90 days, showed no reduction in mortality, and was stopped early for futility on the recommendation of its independent safety monitoring board. TESICO's two headline results, up to day 90, were: Outcome | Aviptadil vs placebo | Significance Better category on the primary 90-day recovery scale | Odds ratio 1.11 (95% CI 0.80 to 1.55) | p = 0.54 Death up to day 90 | 38% of patients on aviptadil died versus 36% on placebo (hazard ratio 1.04) | p = 0.78 In short, the human evidence is real but conflicting, and the best-designed independent study did not confirm a benefit. Outside the respiratory-failure setting, published human evidence is limited. Aviptadil is best understood as an investigational compound whose effectiveness for its studied uses has not been established.

detail.sections:
title: What is aviptadil?
text: Aviptadil is a synthetic copy of vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), a 28-amino acid signaling molecule that occurs naturally in the human body. It has been developed and tested as a drug, most prominently as a candidate treatment for acute respiratory failure. It is also known by the research code RLF-100 and the trade name Zyesami.
VIP itself is concentrated in the lungs and the gut, where it acts as a messenger between nerves and tissue. Aviptadil is a manufactured version of that same molecule, intended to be given in larger amounts than the body makes on its own.
title: The history of aviptadil
text: Aviptadil's story runs from basic physiology to a high-profile pandemic trial. Vasoactive intestinal peptide was first isolated from the small intestine in 1970 by Said and Mutt, and Sami Said later focused on its protective role in the lungs. Because VIP is concentrated in lung tissue and helps regulate inflammation and blood flow there, it was proposed as a candidate for acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), a form of severe lung injury.
Interest surged during the COVID-19 pandemic. A synthetic VIP, aviptadil, was taken into clinical trials for critically ill COVID-19 patients with respiratory failure by the companies NRx Pharmaceuticals and Relief Therapeutics, under the names RLF-100 and Zyesami. The program drew wide attention when the companies reported encouraging early results in 2021. Independent testing followed, and it was found that it’s not effective, as described below.
title: How does aviptadil work?
text: Aviptadil works by mimicking vasoactive intestinal peptide, the natural signaling molecule the body uses to relax blood vessels and calm inflammation, particularly in the lungs. VIP binds to two receptors, VPAC1 and VPAC2, that are common on lung tissue, and activating them relaxes the smooth muscle in blood vessels and airways and triggers signals that lower inflammation.
Those receptors are not limited to the lungs. VPAC1 and VPAC2 sit on T cells and macrophages, and VPAC1 receptors couple to adenylyl cyclase, the enzyme that makes the signaling molecule cAMP.
A 2013 review of VIP's immune effects describes work in mice, where VIP:
- Inhibited TNF, IL-6, and IL-12 and raised IL-10
- Blocked NF-κB movement into the nucleus
- Induced Foxp3-positive regulatory T cells through tolerogenic dendritic cells
These are animal findings, and they do not show the same effects in patients.
Much of the therapeutic rationale centers on a specific lung cell. In laboratory studies, VIP helps protect the alveolar type II cells that produce surfactant, the substance that keeps the tiny air sacs of the lungs open, and it reduces the release of inflammatory molecules. The theory tested in trials was that supplying extra VIP might help shield the lungs during the severe inflammation of ARDS. This describes the proposed mechanism and the underlying biology; whether aviptadil actually improves outcomes in patients is a separate question, addressed next.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No. Aviptadil is not approved by the FDA for any use and remains an investigational drug in the United States. During the pandemic it was studied under FDA oversight and received expedited review designations, but the FDA declined to authorize it for emergency use in COVID-19, and it has not been approved since.
The FDA granted aviptadil Fast Track Designation for respiratory distress in COVID-19 in 2020, which speeds review but does not signal approval. Later, the agency declined the company's request for Breakthrough Therapy Designation in November 2021, according to the sponsor's quarterly filing.
One nuance is worth noting for accuracy. A separate combination product that pairs aviptadil with phentolamine, sold as Invicorp, is approved in some other countries, including in Europe, as an injection for erectile dysfunction. That is a different formulation and a different use, and it does not carry over to the United States, where aviptadil has no FDA approval for any indication.
title: What does the research show?
text: The strongest research shows that aviptadil has not been proven to work for the condition it was most studied in. It was tested primarily in critically ill COVID-19 patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure. The companies developing it reported favorable early findings from a company-sponsored phase 2b/3 study in 2021, but the pivotal independent test was the NIH-funded TESICO trial, a randomized, placebo-controlled study of 461 patients. According to PubMed, that trial found that aviptadil did not significantly improve a patient's clinical status at 90 days, showed no reduction in mortality, and was stopped early for futility on the recommendation of its independent safety monitoring board.
TESICO's two headline results, up to day 90, were:
Outcome | Aviptadil vs placebo | Significance
Better category on the primary 90-day recovery scale | Odds ratio 1.11 (95% CI 0.80 to 1.55) | p = 0.54
Death up to day 90 | 38% of patients on aviptadil died versus 36% on placebo (hazard ratio 1.04) | p = 0.78
In short, the human evidence is real but conflicting, and the best-designed independent study did not confirm a benefit. Outside the respiratory-failure setting, published human evidence is limited. peptides.name: Bacitracin
peptides.fda_status: FDA-approved polypeptide antibiotic, sold over the counter as a topical ointment for minor wounds
peptides.evidence_note: It is approved by the FDA as a topical antibiotic for preventing infection in minor skin wounds and is sold over the counter, with decades of clinical use behind it.
peptides.what_it_is:
Bacitracin is an antibiotic that is actually a mixture of closely related cyclic polypeptides, produced by bacteria in the Bacillus subtilis group. It is a peptide antibiotic rather than a small-molecule drug, and its main component, bacitracin A, is the most active.
It is used almost entirely on the skin. In the United States, it is widely available over the counter as an ointment for minor wound care, both on its own and combined with other topical antibiotics.
peptides.key_takeaway: Bacitracin is a cyclic polypeptide antibiotic produced by Bacillus bacteria that kills gram-positive bacteria by blocking the construction of their cell wall. It is best known as an over-the-counter topical ointment for preventing infection in minor cuts, scrapes, and burns, often combined with neomycin and polymyxin B in "triple antibiotic" products. It is widely available over the counter, but it is also a common cause of allergic skin reactions, and its injectable form was withdrawn over kidney-toxicity concerns.
peptides.mechanism: Bacitracin kills bacteria by blocking the construction of their cell wall. It interferes with a recycling step in wall-building: A lipid carrier molecule (C55 or undecaprenyl pyrophosphate) ferries the building blocks of the wall across the bacterial membrane, and it must shed a phosphate to be reused. Bacitracin binds that carrier and prevents its dephosphorylation, so the carrier is pulled out of circulation and new cell-wall material can no longer be delivered. Because this target matters most in gram-positive bacteria, bacitracin's activity is strongest against organisms such as staphylococci and streptococci. It is poorly absorbed through the skin, which is part of why it works well as a surface antibiotic but is not used orally for body-wide infection.
peptides.side_effects_safety: The most notable side effect of bacitracin is allergy. Its main risks are: - Allergic contact dermatitis: it is a well-recognized cause of this itchy, red, sometimes blistering rash where it is applied, and in 2003, the American Contact Dermatitis Society named it "Allergen of the Year." - Anaphylaxis: more rarely, topical bacitracin has triggered anaphylaxis, a severe whole-body allergic reaction, which is unusual for an over-the-counter ointment. - Kidney damage: when given by injection, bacitracin can cause serious kidney damage, which is why that form was taken off the U.S. market. Applied topically to small areas, it is generally well tolerated apart from the allergy risk.
peptides.summary_es: Antibiótico peptídico utilizado en productos tópicos para determinadas infecciones superficiales; puede producir dermatitis de contacto.

title: How does bacitracin work?
text: Bacitracin kills bacteria by blocking the construction of their cell wall. It interferes with a recycling step in wall-building: A lipid carrier molecule (C55 or undecaprenyl pyrophosphate) ferries the building blocks of the wall across the bacterial membrane, and it must shed a phosphate to be reused. Bacitracin binds that carrier and prevents its dephosphorylation, so the carrier is pulled out of circulation and new cell-wall material can no longer be delivered.
Because this target matters most in gram-positive bacteria, bacitracin's activity is strongest against organisms such as staphylococci and streptococci. It is poorly absorbed through the skin, which is part of why it works well as a surface antibiotic but is not used orally for body-wide infection.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: Yes, and much of it is sold without a prescription. Its status depends on the form, and the injectable form is the exception:
Form | Status | Detail
Topical | Over-the-counter drug | Prevents infection in minor cuts, scrapes, and burns
Ophthalmic (eye) ointment | Prescription | Available in prescription eye ointments
Injection | Approval withdrawn in 2020 | The FDA withdrew approval because of the risk of serious kidney damage, so the systemic version is no longer marketed in the United States
title: What is bacitracin used for?
text: Bacitracin is used to prevent infection in minor skin wounds such as cuts, scrapes, and burns, and it is a common ingredient in first-aid ointments. It is frequently combined with neomycin and polymyxin B in "triple antibiotic" products to broaden the range of bacteria covered.
One nuance is worth knowing: for clean minor wounds, antibiotic ointment is not clearly better than plain petroleum jelly. In a randomized trial of 922 dermatologic-surgery patients, white petrolatum and bacitracin produced comparable, low infection rates, while only the bacitracin group had cases of allergic contact dermatitis. That has led many clinicians to favor plain petrolatum for routine wound care.
title: What are the side effects?
text: The most notable side effect of bacitracin is allergy. Its main risks are:
- Allergic contact dermatitis: it is a well-recognized cause of this itchy, red, sometimes blistering rash where it is applied, and in 2003, the American Contact Dermatitis Society named it "Allergen of the Year."
- Anaphylaxis: more rarely, topical bacitracin has triggered anaphylaxis, a severe whole-body allergic reaction, which is unusual for an over-the-counter ointment.
- Kidney damage: when given by injection, bacitracin can cause serious kidney damage, which is why that form was taken off the U.S. market.
Applied topically to small areas, it is generally well tolerated apart from the allergy risk.
