detail.sections:
title: What is balixafortide?
text: Balixafortide is an experimental peptide that blocks CXCR4, a receptor involved in how cells move through the body and interact with their surroundings. It was developed by Polyphor (later Spexis) and studied intravenously together with the chemotherapy drug eribulin for HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer. It is investigational and not approved, and its development has effectively ended. It is also known as POL6326.
title: How does it work?
text: Balixafortide blocks the CXCR4 receptor and interrupts its signaling with a partner molecule called CXCL12 (SDF-1α). This pathway influences the trafficking of tumor cells, the tumor's surrounding environment, and immune cell behavior. In laboratory work, blocking CXCR4 was proposed to make tumors more responsive to chemotherapy, which is the rationale for combining it with eribulin. This describes the proposed mechanism, separate from the patient outcomes below.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No. Balixafortide is investigational and not approved, and the program is effectively discontinued after its pivotal trial.
title: What does the research show?
text: The decisive evidence is negative. Two trials tested balixafortide plus eribulin in metastatic breast cancer:
Trial | Design | Result
Phase 1 trial, according to PubMed | Early single-arm study in heavily pretreated metastatic breast cancer | Partial responses in about 30% of evaluable patients, encouraging for an uncontrolled study
Phase 3 FORTRESS trial, reported by the company in 2021 | Randomized, compared with eribulin alone | Did not meet its primary endpoint; response and clinical-benefit rates were similar to eribulin alone, showing no meaningful improvement from adding balixafortide
The controlled evidence does not support a benefit.

peptides.name: Bivalirudin
peptides.fda_status: FDA-approved peptide anticoagulant, sold as Angiomax, given intravenously in the hospital
peptides.evidence_note: It is approved by the FDA as an anticoagulant for coronary procedures, supported by large randomized controlled trials including HORIZONS-AMI.
peptides.what_it_is:
Bivalirudin is a synthetic peptide of 20 amino acids that works as an anticoagulant, or blood thinner. It belongs to a class called direct thrombin inhibitors, meaning it blocks thrombin, the enzyme that drives the final step of clot formation, by binding to it directly. It is made by chemical synthesis and sold under the brand name Angiomax (and as Angiox outside the United States).
It is given only by intravenous infusion in a hospital, typically in a cardiac catheterization lab, and is not an oral or at-home medication.
peptides.key_takeaway: Bivalirudin is a synthetic 20-amino acid peptide anticoagulant, derived in design from the leech protein hirudin, that directly and reversibly blocks thrombin, the central enzyme in blood clotting. Sold as Angiomax, it is given intravenously during coronary procedures such as angioplasty and stenting to prevent clots, including in people who cannot receive heparin. In a large trial of heart-attack patients, using it instead of heparin plus a second blood thinner reduced major bleeding and lowered 30-day death rates.
peptides.mechanism:
Bivalirudin works by directly binding and blocking thrombin, the enzyme at the center of blood clotting. Thrombin converts fibrinogen into the fibrin mesh that holds a clot together and also activates platelets, and by occupying thrombin, bivalirudin stops both. It is a bivalent inhibitor: one end binds thrombin's active (catalytic) site, and the other binds a separate docking region, called exosite 1, that normally grips fibrinogen. Because it latches on at two points, it blocks thrombin that is free in the blood as well as thrombin already bound inside a clot, which heparin does less well.
Its action is also reversible and short-lived. Thrombin slowly cleaves the bound drug and recovers its function, so the effect fades within roughly 25 minutes of stopping the infusion, which makes it predictable to use during a procedure.
In the HORIZONS-AMI trial of 3,602 heart-attack patients undergoing angioplasty, bivalirudin alone reduced 30-day major bleeding and lowered death from cardiac causes compared with heparin plus a glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor.
Outcome in HORIZONS-AMI | Bivalirudin alone | Heparin plus a glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor
30-day major bleeding | 4.9% | 8.3%
Death from cardiac causes | 1.8% | 2.9%
peptides.side_effects_safety: The main risk of bivalirudin, as with any anticoagulant, is bleeding, though in trials it caused less major bleeding than heparin-based regimens. Other effects reported during treatment include: - Back pain - Nausea - Low blood pressure - Headache One specific signal from the HORIZONS-AMI trial was a higher rate of acute stent thrombosis, a clot forming on the new stent, in the first 24 hours; this did not persist at 30 days and is managed by ensuring adequate antiplatelet therapy. Because it is used only in monitored hospital settings, its dosing is carefully controlled.

detail.sections:
title: What is bivalirudin?
text: Bivalirudin is a synthetic peptide of 20 amino acids that works as an anticoagulant, or blood thinner. It belongs to a class called direct thrombin inhibitors, meaning it blocks thrombin, the enzyme that drives the final step of clot formation, by binding to it directly. It is made by chemical synthesis and sold under the brand name Angiomax (and as Angiox outside the United States).
It is given only by intravenous infusion in a hospital, typically in a cardiac catheterization lab, and is not an oral or at-home medication.
title: The history of bivalirudin
text: Bivalirudin traces back to the leech. The medicinal leech makes a natural anticoagulant protein called hirudin, which is why a leech can feed without the blood clotting, and hirudin became the template for a family of direct thrombin inhibitors. Bivalirudin is a short synthetic analog built from that model, engineered to bind thrombin at two sites at once, which makes it a bivalent inhibitor.
It was developed as a more predictable, shorter-acting alternative to heparin for use during heart procedures, and the FDA approved it in 2000. Unlike the leech protein it was modeled on, its effect is reversible and brief, which suited the controlled setting of angioplasty.
title: How does bivalirudin work?
text: Bivalirudin works by directly binding and blocking thrombin, the enzyme at the center of blood clotting. Thrombin converts fibrinogen into the fibrin mesh that holds a clot together and also activates platelets, and by occupying thrombin, bivalirudin stops both. It is a bivalent inhibitor: one end binds thrombin's active (catalytic) site, and the other binds a separate docking region, called exosite 1, that normally grips fibrinogen. Because it latches on at two points, it blocks thrombin that is free in the blood as well as thrombin already bound inside a clot, which heparin does less well.
Its action is also reversible and short-lived. Thrombin slowly cleaves the bound drug and recovers its function, so the effect fades within roughly 25 minutes of stopping the infusion, which makes it predictable to use during a procedure.
In the HORIZONS-AMI trial of 3,602 heart-attack patients undergoing angioplasty, bivalirudin alone reduced 30-day major bleeding and lowered death from cardiac causes compared with heparin plus a glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor.
Outcome in HORIZONS-AMI | Bivalirudin alone | Heparin plus a glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor
30-day major bleeding | 4.9% | 8.3%
Death from cardiac causes | 1.8% | 2.9%
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: Yes. The FDA approved bivalirudin (Angiomax) in 2000 as an anticoagulant for use during coronary angioplasty, and its labeling later covered patients with or at risk of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia undergoing PCI. It is an established, guideline-recognized option for anticoagulation during these procedures.
title: What is bivalirudin prescribed for?
text: Bivalirudin is used as the anticoagulant during percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), the catheter-based procedures (angioplasty and stent placement) that open blocked heart arteries. It is given to prevent clots from forming on the catheter and the freshly treated artery during the procedure. It is especially valuable for patients with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT), a serious immune reaction to heparin, because it provides anticoagulation without using heparin at all. It is administered and monitored by the medical team, not self-administered.
title: What are the side effects?
text: The main risk of bivalirudin, as with any anticoagulant, is bleeding, though in trials it caused less major bleeding than heparin-based regimens. Other effects reported during treatment include:
- Back pain
- Nausea
- Low blood pressure
- Headache
One specific signal from the HORIZONS-AMI trial was a higher rate of acute stent thrombosis, a clot forming on the new stent, in the first 24 hours; this did not persist at 30 days and is managed by ensuring adequate antiplatelet therapy. Because it is used only in monitored hospital settings, its dosing is carefully controlled.

peptides.name: BPC-157
peptides.fda_status: Not approved by the FDA for any use
peptides.evidence_note: Its human evidence is limited to a single small retrospective report (12 patients with chronic knee pain), while the rest of the literature, including all 35 studies in the 2025 systematic review, is preclinical animal or lab work.
peptides.what_it_is: Synthetic peptide made of 15 amino acids, based on a protein found in gastric juice
peptides.research_at_a_glance: Almost all done in animals rather than in humans
peptides.key_takeaway: BPC-157 is a synthetic 15-amino-acid peptide studied for tissue and gut repair, and 35 of the 36 studies in a 2025 systematic review were animal or lab work. The one human report, a retrospective series of 12 patients with chronic knee pain, found that seven (58%) described relief lasting more than 6 months. It had no control group, effect size, or safety data. BPC-157 is not FDA-approved, is prohibited in sport, and remains unsettled in FDA compounding review.
peptides.mechanism: The proposed mechanisms come almost entirely from animal and cell studies. The most consistent finding is that BPC-157 promotes angiogenesis, the growth of new blood vessels, mainly through the VEGFR2-Akt-eNOS pathway and by influencing the nitric oxide system, which helps regulate blood flow and vascular health. In laboratory models, researchers have also reported that BPC-157 increases collagen production, activates fibroblasts, reduces inflammatory signaling, and affects pain pathways. In tendon cells, it has been shown to increase expression of the growth hormone receptor. Across rodent studies, it has been associated with faster healing of muscle, tendon, ligament, bone, and gastrointestinal tissue. In animal data, BPC-157 is metabolized in the liver, cleared by the kidneys, and has a short half-life of under 30 minutes. None of these findings have been confirmed in controlled human studies.
peptides.human_study_findings: The research on BPC-157 is overwhelmingly preclinical. The 2025 systematic review in orthopedic sports medicine screened the literature and included 36 studies, of which 35 were preclinical (animal or laboratory) and only one involved humans. There are no completed randomized controlled human trials, and there is no long-term human data. A 2019 review reached a similar conclusion, describing consistent healing effects in rodents while noting that efficacy is “yet to be confirmed in humans.” The animal research is broad and fairly consistent, but the human research needed to draw firm conclusions has not been done. The most replicated animal findings involve tendons. In rats with a cut Achilles tendon, BPC-157 improved tendon strength, elasticity, and function and shrank the defect by day 14. The one human report is a retrospective, uncontrolled series of 12 patients with chronic knee pain. After a single knee injection, seven of them (58%) reported relief lasting more than 6 months. The report published no effect size or safety data.

detail.faq:
q: Is BPC-157 FDA-approved?
a: No. BPC-157 is not FDA-approved for any indication. As of September 2026, it is not eligible for 503A compounding: FDA removed it from Category 2 in April 2026 after the nomination was withdrawn, but it is not on the 503A bulks list or in Category 1, so licensed compounding pharmacies in the United States still cannot legally use it.
q: Is BPC-157 legal in the United States?
a: BPC-157 cannot be legally compounded or dispensed by a licensed pharmacy in the United States because it is not on the 503A bulks list or in Category 1, even after FDA removed it from Category 2 in April 2026. Products sold as BPC-157 for human use through online vendors or research chemical suppliers operate outside the regulated pharmaceutical system. Obtaining and using an unregulated compound with no pharmaceutical oversight carries both legal and safety risks.
q: Can BPC-157 be prescribed by a doctor?
a: No. Because BPC-157 is not on the 503A bulks list or in Category 1, licensed compounding pharmacies cannot compound it for patient use. A physician cannot legally prescribe a compound that a licensed pharmacy cannot dispense. Any product a prescriber attempts to order through regulated channels would not be fillable.
q: What is BPC-157 used for in research?
a: BPC-157 has been studied in preclinical (animal) models for gastrointestinal mucosal protection, tendon and ligament healing, wound repair, and vascular biology. The 2025 systematic review by Vasireddi, Hahamyan, Salata, and colleagues in HSS Journal synthesized 36 studies (35 preclinical, 1 retrospective human study) and found that all controlled efficacy work remains in animal models, with no completed controlled human trials published. Research interest centers on its proposed anti-inflammatory, pro-angiogenic, and connective tissue repair mechanisms.
q: What is the difference between BPC-157 and TB-500?
a: TB-500 is a synthetic fragment of thymosin beta-4, a protein involved in actin regulation and cell migration. BPC-157 is a synthetic fragment derived from human gastric juice protein. The two compounds have different sequences, different proposed mechanisms, and different research backgrounds. Both are unapproved for human use, both appear on the WADA Prohibited List (BPC-157 under S0, Non-Approved Substances, and TB-500 under S2, Peptide Hormones, Growth Factors, Related Substances, and Mimetics), and neither has completed controlled human efficacy trials. They are sometimes discussed together in recovery and sports contexts, but they are distinct compounds with distinct pharmacological profiles.
q: What does WADA's ban on BPC-157 mean for athletes?
a: Under the 2026 WADA Prohibited List, BPC-157 is prohibited at all times under Section S0 (Non-Approved Substances). An athlete who tests positive for BPC-157 faces an anti-doping rule violation, as with any other prohibited substance. Athletes subject to anti-doping testing should regard any product containing or potentially contaminated with BPC-157 as a prohibited substance.
q: Is BPC-157 the same as a compounded medication?
a: No. A compounded medication under section 503A is a preparation made by a state-licensed pharmacist or physician using only bulk ingredients the law allows: ones with a USP monograph, ones in an FDA-approved drug, or ones on FDA's 503A bulks list. BPC-157 is not on the 503A bulks list or in Category 1, so no pathway currently covers its use in compounding. Products sold as "compounded BPC-157" are not legally compounded medications. They are unregulated products produced outside the pharmaceutical regulatory system.
detail.sections:
title: What is BPC-157?
text: BPC-157, short for “Body Protection Compound-157,” is a synthetic pentadecapeptide, a chain of 15 amino acids (sequence GEPPPGKPADDAGLV). It is a lab-made fragment modeled on a larger protective protein that occurs naturally in human gastric juice, the acidic fluid the stomach uses to break down food.
Unlike a hormone such as insulin, BPC-157 does not appear to act on a single, well-defined receptor. Researchers instead describe it as a “cytoprotective” agent, meaning a molecule associated with protecting and maintaining the integrity of cells and tissue in laboratory and animal models.
BPC-157 has never been approved as a medicine through the FDA.
title: The history of BPC-157
text: The idea behind BPC-157 dates to 1975, when a Croatian medical student named Predrag Sikiric attended a lecture on the body’s stress response at the University of Zagreb. He reasoned that if stress can damage the stomach, the stomach might also produce its own protective substance.
By 1983, Sikiric had assembled a team that collected human and animal gastric juice from hospitals, emergency rooms, and slaughterhouses to search for the active ingredient. In 1989, the group isolated a 15 amino acid peptide called BPC-157. The name and number carried personal and patriotic meaning for Sikiric during a turbulent period in Croatia’s history, as described in a 2026 STAT News profile of the researcher.
From 1993, the Zagreb pharmaceutical company PLIVA, later working with Parke-Davis, developed the peptide and ran early animal studies along with two small human trials for ulcerative colitis in the early 2000s. The second of those trials reported a positive effect that did not reach statistical significance. After GlaxoSmithKline acquired PLIVA’s research institute in 2006, the program was shelved, and the rights returned to Sikiric in 2009.
Without a pharmaceutical company continuing its development, BPC-157 followed an unusual path. Around 2010, it spread through online forums and Sikiric’s published papers, and suppliers began selling it directly. It has circulated as a research chemical ever since. Most of the underlying studies still come from Sikiric’s own laboratory. A 2025 systematic review identified 544 BPC-157 articles published between 1993 and 2024, most of them from a small number of research groups.
The only registered interventional human trial of BPC-157 was a small Phase I safety study of oral tablets (NCT02637284) run in Tijuana, Mexico around 2015 and 2016. It was never completed to publication and remains listed with an “unknown” status and no posted results, so even its basic safety findings in humans were never independently reported.
title: How does BPC-157 work?
text: The proposed mechanisms come almost entirely from animal and cell studies. The most consistent finding is that BPC-157 promotes angiogenesis, the growth of new blood vessels, mainly through the VEGFR2-Akt-eNOS pathway and by influencing the nitric oxide system, which helps regulate blood flow and vascular health.
In laboratory models, researchers have also reported that BPC-157 increases collagen production, activates fibroblasts, reduces inflammatory signaling, and affects pain pathways. In tendon cells, it has been shown to increase expression of the growth hormone receptor. Across rodent studies, it has been associated with faster healing of muscle, tendon, ligament, bone, and gastrointestinal tissue.
In animal data, BPC-157 is metabolized in the liver, cleared by the kidneys, and has a short half-life of under 30 minutes. None of these findings have been confirmed in controlled human studies.
title: Is BPC-157 FDA-approved?
text: No, BPC-157 has never been approved by the FDA, or any comparable regulator, for any condition, and it has not completed the controlled human trials that approval requires.
Its regulatory status has also changed several times:
- 2023: The FDA placed BPC-157 in Category 2 of its interim 503A bulk drug substances list, the category for substances that may present significant safety risks, which restricted compounding pharmacies from making it.
- April 2026: The FDA removed BPC-157 from that category because the nominators withdrew their nominations. BPC-157 is still not on the 503A bulks list or in Category 1.
- July 23, 2026: Its Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee voted in favor of allowing the peptide to be compounded, meaning prepared for individual patients by licensed compounding pharmacies rather than mass-produced and sold as a standardized, FDA-approved drug.
That vote is a recommendation only. The FDA still has to write and finalize a rule, so BPC-157 is not currently cleared for compounding and remains unapproved. Being permitted for compounding would also not be the same as FDA approval.
BPC-157 is also prohibited at all times in sport under the World Anti-Doping Agency’s S0 category for non-approved substances.
title: What does the research show?
text: The research on BPC-157 is overwhelmingly preclinical. The 2025 systematic review in orthopedic sports medicine screened the literature and included 36 studies, of which 35 were preclinical (animal or laboratory) and only one involved humans. There are no completed randomized controlled human trials, and there is no long-term human data.
A 2019 review reached a similar conclusion, describing consistent healing effects in rodents while noting that efficacy is “yet to be confirmed in humans.” The animal research is broad and fairly consistent, but the human research needed to draw firm conclusions has not been done.
The most replicated animal findings involve tendons. In rats with a cut Achilles tendon, BPC-157 improved tendon strength, elasticity, and function and shrank the defect by day 14.
The one human report is a retrospective, uncontrolled series of 12 patients with chronic knee pain. After a single knee injection, seven of them (58%) reported relief lasting more than 6 months. The report published no effect size or safety data.
title: What is the difference between BPC-157 and TB-500?
text: BPC-157 is often mentioned alongside TB-500, a synthetic fragment of the protein thymosin beta-4. The two share several features. Both are peptides, unapproved by the FDA, prohibited in sports, and have been studied mainly in animals rather than in humans.
The differences are largely mechanistic:
Feature | BPC-157 | TB-500
Origin | Derived from a gastric protein | Synthetic fragment of thymosin beta-4
Proposed action | Broad cytoprotective agent | Acts mainly by regulating actin, a structural protein involved in cell movement
Animal research emphasis | Gastrointestinal tissue | Wound and cardiac tissue
Neither has controlled human evidence.

This document is educational research and does not constitute medical advice, a health claim, or an offer to sell; BPC-157 is not approved by the FDA, and its regulatory status should be re-verified before publication, as the FDA compounding review is ongoing.

peptides.name: Bremelanotide
peptides.fda_status: FDA-approved peptide, sold by prescription as Vyleesi, given as a self-injection
peptides.evidence_note: It is approved by the FDA for hypoactive sexual desire disorder in premenopausal women, supported by the two randomized, placebo-controlled RECONNECT phase 3 trials, which showed a modest but statistically significant benefit.
peptides.what_it_is:
Bremelanotide is a synthetic peptide of seven amino acids that acts as a melanocortin receptor agonist, a drug that switches on a family of brain receptors involved in appetite, pigmentation, and sexual response. Its FDA-approved form is sold as Vyleesi and treats low sexual desire in certain women.
It is given as a small subcutaneous (under-the-skin) self-injection in the thigh or abdomen. Its research name, still widely used online, is PT-141.
peptides.key_takeaway: Bremelanotide is a synthetic seven-amino acid peptide that activates melanocortin receptors in the brain to increase sexual desire, unlike blood-flow drugs such as sildenafil. In the two RECONNECT phase 3 trials of 1,267 premenopausal women with hypoactive sexual desire disorder (HSDD), it raised the desire score 0.35 points more than placebo and reduced desire-related distress 0.33 points more (both P<.001) over 24 weeks. It is FDA-approved as Vyleesi, a prescription self-injection for acquired, generalized HSDD. Versions sold online as PT-141 are not the FDA-approved product and are not quality-controlled.
peptides.mechanism:
Bremelanotide works in the brain rather than on the genitals. It activates melanocortin receptors, chiefly the MC4 receptor, in regions of the central nervous system that help regulate sexual desire. By stimulating this pathway it is thought to shift the balance of brain signals toward excitation, which can increase desire. This is a different mechanism from erectile dysfunction drugs such as sildenafil, which increase blood flow; bremelanotide targets desire itself.
It is used on demand rather than daily. In its pivotal RECONNECT trials, two phase 3 studies of 1,267 randomized premenopausal women with HSDD, bremelanotide produced a small but statistically significant gain on both outcomes over 24 weeks (P<.001 for both):
Outcome | Change vs placebo
Desire score | Raised 0.35 points more
Desire-related distress | Cut 0.33 points more
An independent reanalysis of the RECONNECT data judged the benefit statistically modest, and found little evidence that the desire and distress scales used as outcomes are valid in women with HSDD.
peptides.side_effects_safety: The most common side effect is nausea, which was frequent in trials and sometimes required anti-nausea treatment. Other common effects include flushing, headache, vomiting, and injection-site reactions. Two effects deserve specific mention: Bremelanotide causes a transient rise in blood pressure and a brief drop in heart rate after each dose, which is why it is avoided in people with cardiovascular risk, and repeated use can cause focal hyperpigmentation, darkened patches of skin or gums, more likely with frequent dosing and in people with darker skin.

detail.sections:
title: What is bremelanotide?
text: Bremelanotide is a synthetic peptide of seven amino acids that acts as a melanocortin receptor agonist, a drug that switches on a family of brain receptors involved in appetite, pigmentation, and sexual response. Its FDA-approved form is sold as Vyleesi and treats low sexual desire in certain women.
It is given as a small subcutaneous (under-the-skin) self-injection in the thigh or abdomen. Its research name, still widely used online, is PT-141.
title: The history of bremelanotide
text: Bremelanotide came out of research on a tanning drug. It descends from Melanotan II, a melanocortin peptide developed from University of Arizona work on synthetic hormones that darken skin. During testing, Melanotan II was noticed to cause sexual arousal as a side effect, which led researchers to pursue the melanocortin pathway for sexual dysfunction, and the resulting compound, originally called PT-141, became bremelanotide.
It was developed by Palatin Technologies, tested first for erectile dysfunction and later for low desire in women, and the FDA approved it as Vyleesi in 2019. Its cousin from the same tanning research, afamelanotide, took a different path and became a treatment for a rare light-sensitivity disorder.
title: How does bremelanotide work?
text: Bremelanotide works in the brain rather than on the genitals. It activates melanocortin receptors, chiefly the MC4 receptor, in regions of the central nervous system that help regulate sexual desire. By stimulating this pathway it is thought to shift the balance of brain signals toward excitation, which can increase desire. This is a different mechanism from erectile dysfunction drugs such as sildenafil, which increase blood flow; bremelanotide targets desire itself.
It is used on demand rather than daily. In its pivotal RECONNECT trials, two phase 3 studies of 1,267 randomized premenopausal women with HSDD, bremelanotide produced a small but statistically significant gain on both outcomes over 24 weeks (P<.001 for both):
Outcome | Change vs placebo
Desire score | Raised 0.35 points more
Desire-related distress | Cut 0.33 points more
An independent reanalysis of the RECONNECT data judged the benefit statistically modest, and found little evidence that the desire and distress scales used as outcomes are valid in women with HSDD.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: Yes, in one specific form and use. The FDA approved bremelanotide as Vyleesi in 2019 for acquired, generalized hypoactive sexual desire disorder in premenopausal women. "Acquired" means the low desire developed after a period of normal function, and "generalized" means it is not limited to a certain partner or situation. Because the drug can briefly raise blood pressure, it is contraindicated in people with uncontrolled high blood pressure or known cardiovascular disease, and it is not approved for postmenopausal women or for men.
title: What is bremelanotide prescribed for?
text: Bremelanotide (Vyleesi) is prescribed for premenopausal women who have hypoactive sexual desire disorder, meaning persistent, distressing low sexual desire that is not better explained by another medical or psychiatric condition, relationship problems, or a medication. Its label advises stopping it when a woman reports no improvement. It is prescribed and monitored by a clinician.
title: What are the side effects?
text: The most common side effect is nausea, which was frequent in trials and sometimes required anti-nausea treatment. Other common effects include flushing, headache, vomiting, and injection-site reactions. Two effects deserve specific mention: Bremelanotide causes a transient rise in blood pressure and a brief drop in heart rate after each dose, which is why it is avoided in people with cardiovascular risk, and repeated use can cause focal hyperpigmentation, darkened patches of skin or gums, more likely with frequent dosing and in people with darker skin.
title: What about "PT-141" sold online?
text: Bremelanotide is sold widely online under its research name, PT-141, and this is not the same as the FDA-approved product. The only version the FDA has approved is Vyleesi, a prescription autoinjector for premenopausal women with HSDD. The PT-141 sold through "research chemical" vendors, and the vials and nasal sprays marketed for do-it-yourself use, are not FDA-approved medicines, and they are often labeled "not for human use" to sidestep regulation.
Several concerns follow from that:
- These products are not quality-controlled, so the actual identity, dose, purity, and sterility are not guaranteed, and contamination or incorrect dosing is a real risk.
- They are frequently marketed for uses the drug was never approved for, including in men and as a nasal spray, where it has not been tested to an approval standard.
- Because bremelanotide raises blood pressure and can affect heart rate, using an unregulated version without medical screening removes an important safety check.
Compounded bremelanotide, prescribed through some telehealth clinics, is a separate category: Compounded drugs are also not FDA-approved, and their quality depends heavily on the specific pharmacy. In short, the approved product is the only form that has been tested and regulated for safety, quality, and a defined use, while the versions sold online are neither approved nor quality-assured.

detail.faq:
q: Is cagrilintide FDA-approved?
a: No. As of September 2026, cagrilintide is not FDA-approved for any indication. It is an investigational compound under development by Novo Nordisk, is not available by prescription, and cannot be used in compounding under federal law. The furthest-advanced regulatory pathway is CagriSema, the combination of cagrilintide and semaglutide.
q: Can a doctor prescribe cagrilintide?
a: No. Cagrilintide is not FDA-approved, and it cannot be used in compounding under federal law, so there is no approved or compounded form for a provider to prescribe. Access is limited to enrollment in a Novo Nordisk clinical trial.
q: What is the difference between cagrilintide and pramlintide?
a: Both are amylin analogs that activate amylin receptors to reduce food intake, slow gastric emptying, and suppress postprandial glucagon. Pramlintide (Symlin) is FDA-approved as an adjunct to mealtime insulin in type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Cagrilintide is engineered for once-weekly dosing and achieved up to 10.8% weight loss at its highest dose in a 26-week Phase 2 monotherapy trial. This comparison is for scientific context only; these compounds have different regulatory statuses and evidence bases.
q: What is the difference between cagrilintide and CagriSema?
a: Cagrilintide is the amylin component of the CagriSema regimen. CagriSema refers to the co-administration of cagrilintide and semaglutide. The Phase 3 REDEFINE 1 trial of CagriSema showed 20.4% mean weight loss over 68 weeks in adults with overweight or obesity without diabetes. This page covers cagrilintide as the amylin component in isolation; the CagriSema article covers the combination's Phase 3 data and regulatory status.
q: Is cagrilintide being developed as a standalone drug?
a: Partly. Most of its late-stage development is as part of CagriSema, but Novo Nordisk has also started a standalone Phase 3 trial, RENEW 1, comparing cagrilintide alone with placebo in people with overweight or obesity. In separate trials, the Phase 2 monotherapy data showed up to 10.8% weight loss at 26 weeks, below the 14.9% shown by semaglutide 2.4 mg alone in the STEP 1 trial and the 20.9% shown by tirzepatide 15 mg in SURMOUNT-1. The combination of cagrilintide with semaglutide 2.4 mg produced 17.1% weight loss at 20 weeks in a Phase 1b trial and 20.4% in the REDEFINE 1 Phase 3 trial. Novo Nordisk is also developing amycretin, a single-molecule GLP-1 and amylin receptor agonist.
q: What are the side effects of cagrilintide?
a: In the 26-week Phase 2 trial, which assigned 706 participants to cagrilintide, the most common adverse events were gastrointestinal: 41% to 63% of cagrilintide-treated participants had a gastrointestinal event depending on dose, mainly nausea, versus 32% in the placebo group. A 2024 thorough QT cardiac safety study enrolled 105 healthy participants and found no clinically relevant QTcF prolongation at any measured time point after the final 4.5 mg dose. Long-term safety data beyond 26 weeks for cagrilintide monotherapy is limited.
q: How does cagrilintide compare to eloralintide?
a: Eloralintide is Lilly's once-weekly selective amylin receptor agonist. Its 48-week Phase 2 trial showed dose-dependent weight reductions ranging from about 9% to 20% depending on dose. These results come from a separate trial of a different length, so they cannot be ranked against cagrilintide's 26-week monotherapy result. This comparison is for scientific context only; these compounds have different regulatory statuses and evidence bases.
q: Will cagrilintide become available through compounding pharmacies?
a: Not under current federal law. FDA states that cagrilintide cannot be used in compounding and is not a component of any FDA-approved drug. It is an investigational Novo Nordisk compound, and the nearest approval pathway is CagriSema, which Novo Nordisk has submitted to the FDA for review.

detail.faq:
q: Is cagrisema FDA-approved?
a: No. As of September 2026, cagrisema is not FDA-approved for any indication. Novo Nordisk filed a US new drug application in the fourth quarter of 2025 and expects the review to finish around the turn of 2026 to 2027. No approval has been issued; the timeline depends on the outcome of the FDA's NDA review. Cagrisema is not available outside of enrolled clinical trials in the United States.
q: Can a doctor prescribe cagrisema now?
a: No. Cagrisema has not received FDA approval and cannot be prescribed as a medication in the United States as of September 2026. Its cagrilintide component cannot be used in compounding under federal law, and it is not legally marketed. The only current legal pathway for access is enrollment in an active, registered clinical trial; see clinicaltrials.gov for enrollment information.
q: How does cagrisema work differently from semaglutide alone?
a: Semaglutide activates the GLP-1 receptor, which enhances glucose-dependent insulin release, slows gastric emptying, and reduces appetite. Cagrisema adds cagrilintide, which mimics the hormone amylin and adds a separate satiety signal through a different receptor pathway. The combination targets two complementary appetite pathways at once. This comparison is for scientific context only; these compounds have different regulatory statuses and evidence bases.
q: How does cagrisema compare to tirzepatide for weight loss?
a: Cross-trial comparisons are unreliable due to differences in study populations, duration, and design. In REDEFINE-1, cagrisema produced mean weight loss of 20.4% at 68 weeks. In SURMOUNT-1, tirzepatide 15 mg produced 20.9% at 72 weeks. These figures come from different trials. Novo Nordisk has reported topline results from a head-to-head trial. In REDEFINE 4, cagrisema did not meet its goal of showing non-inferiority to tirzepatide 15 mg at 84 weeks (23.0% versus 25.5% among participants who stayed on treatment). Brand-name tirzepatide is FDA-approved, and cagrisema is under FDA review.
q: What was the '22.7%' result that appeared in news coverage?
a: On December 20, 2024, Novo Nordisk disclosed topline REDEFINE-1 results before the trial was peer-reviewed. The 22.7% figure assumed all participants stayed on treatment; the same announcement reported 20.4% when counting everyone regardless of adherence. The result landed below the roughly 25% that markets had anticipated. The peer-reviewed REDEFINE-1 publication is the authoritative source; its mean body weight change was -20.4% versus -3.0% with placebo at 68 weeks. The two figures differ because they answer different questions, not because of rounding.
q: What are the main side effects of cagrisema?
a: In REDEFINE-1 and REDEFINE-2, gastrointestinal adverse events were the most common, affecting 72.5% to 79.6% of CagriSema-treated participants. These included nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation; most were described as transient and mild to moderate in severity. The semaglutide component's label warns of acute gallbladder disease, including gallstones, and acute pancreatitis, and carries a boxed warning about thyroid C-cell tumors seen in rodents; it is not used in people with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma. In a 2024 thorough QT study in healthy participants, cagrilintide showed no clinically relevant QTc prolongation.
q: Does cagrisema cause lean mass loss?
a: The main REDEFINE-1 and REDEFINE-2 results do not report lean mass. Across GLP-1-based therapies generally, reported lean mass reductions range from about 15% or less to 40% to 60% of total weight lost, depending on the population and compound. Based on MRI studies, skeletal muscle changes with these treatments appear largely adaptive, in line with the amount of weight lost.

detail.sections:
title: What is calcitonin-salmon?
text: Calcitonin-salmon is a lab-made copy of calcitonin, a hormone that helps regulate how much calcium is in the blood and how bone is maintained. The version used in medicine is modeled on the calcitonin found in salmon rather than the human form because the salmon hormone is more potent and longer-lasting in the body. It is approved by the FDA and has been used in clinical practice for decades under the brand names Miacalcin and Fortical.
title: How does it work?
text: It works by putting a brake on the cells that break down bone. Bone is constantly being remodeled: cells called osteoclasts dissolve old bone while others build new bone. Calcitonin-salmon binds to calcitonin receptors on osteoclasts and quiets their activity, which slows the release of calcium from bone into the blood. It also nudges the kidneys to pass more calcium in the urine. Together these effects lower blood calcium and can modestly protect bone.
title: What is it used for?
text: Calcitonin-salmon is approved for three main situations:
- In postmenopausal osteoporosis, it is used to help reduce the risk of spinal fractures in women who are more than five years past menopause and who cannot use other treatments.
- In Paget's disease of bone, a disorder in which bone is remodeled too quickly and becomes weak or misshapen, it helps bring that overactive turnover back toward normal.
- In hypercalcemia, a dangerous rise in blood calcium, the injection can be used for its rapid calcium-lowering effect.
title: How is calcitonin-salmon taken?
text: There are two main ways to use calcitonin-salmon, and the right one depends on the condition.
The nasal spray is the more convenient, needle-free option and is used for postmenopausal osteoporosis. It is delivered as a single spray into one nostril each day, alternating nostrils from day to day. Because it avoids injections, many people find it easier to stay on long term.
The injection is given either under the skin (subcutaneously) or into a muscle (intramuscularly). This form is used for Paget's disease and for hypercalcemia, and it can also be used for osteoporosis when the spray is not suitable. For hypercalcemia in particular, the injection is preferred because it lowers blood calcium quickly. People who need the injection long term are sometimes taught to give it to themselves at home, similar to how insulin is self-administered.
title: What does the research say?
text: The strongest evidence comes from a large trial of the nasal spray in osteoporosis. According to PubMed, the five-year PROOF study of 1,255 postmenopausal women found that the 200 IU daily nasal dose reduced the risk of new spinal fractures by about 33% compared with placebo. The result was statistically significant, but the effect was modest and, notably, the higher and lower doses tested did not show the same clear benefit, which left some uncertainty about how robust the finding was.
title: Safety and the cancer-risk review
text: The most important safety development came years after approval. In 2013, a reassessment by European regulators, echoed by an FDA advisory committee, pooled data across trials and found a small but consistent increase in cancer rates among people treated with calcitonin over long periods. Regulators concluded that the modest benefit no longer clearly outweighed this risk for routine, long-term osteoporosis use.
As a result, the nasal spray's role in osteoporosis was narrowed, and calcitonin-salmon is now generally reserved for people who cannot take other, better-established bone treatments. More common, milder side effects include nasal irritation with the spray and nausea or flushing with the injection. The injection's label also warns of serious allergic reactions and low blood calcium.
detail.sources_note: Sources: Drugs.com calcitonin-salmon monograph; DrugBank (calcitonin salmon); the PROOF Study (Chesnut et al., The American Journal of Medicine, 2000, DOI: 10.1016/s0002-9343(00)00490-3), indexed on PubMed; and the European Medicines Agency calcitonin referral and cancer-risk review. This document is educational and does not constitute medical advice.

peptides.name: Carnosine
peptides.fda_status: Cosmetic ingredient rather than a drug, so does not require FDA approval
peptides.evidence_note: The case for topical carnosine rests on antioxidant and anti-glycation activity seen in laboratory and ex-vivo skin studies, with no sound standalone human trial showing an appearance benefit.
peptides.what_it_is: Cosmetic ingredient, a naturally occurring dipeptide used for its antioxidant properties
peptides.research_at_a_glance: Lab and ex-vivo studies point to antioxidant and anti-glycation activity; standalone human appearance trials are limited
peptides.key_takeaway: Carnosine is a naturally occurring dipeptide, made of the amino acids beta-alanine and histidine, used in skincare as an antioxidant ingredient. Laboratory and ex-vivo skin studies suggest it can neutralize reactive oxygen species and limit glycation, a process in which sugars stiffen skin proteins, which is the rationale for using it in products aimed at the appearance of aging skin. As of 2026, the evidence for topical carnosine is largely from lab and ex-vivo studies rather than large human appearance trials.
peptides.mechanism: Laboratory studies suggest carnosine acts mainly as an antioxidant and an anti-glycation agent. As an antioxidant, it can neutralize reactive oxygen species, the unstable molecules generated by UV light and pollution that are associated with the visible signs of skin aging. In an ex-vivo human skin study, topical carnosine reduced markers of UV-induced oxidative stress. Its second proposed role is limiting glycation, a reaction in which sugar molecules bind to proteins such as collagen and form advanced glycation end-products that make those proteins stiff and dysfunctional. By slowing that reaction in laboratory models, carnosine is thought to help skin keep the appearance of suppleness. These are study findings; the benefit in finished cosmetics is described in appearance terms, such as supporting the look of firmness and a brighter, more even tone.
peptides.human_study_findings: Most of the evidence is from laboratory and ex-vivo skin experiments rather than large human trials. According to PubMed, an ex-vivo human skin study found that topical carnosine lowered UV-induced reactive oxygen species and glycation markers. Independent, well-controlled trials of carnosine alone measuring wrinkle or firmness outcomes in people are lacking, and several studies that include carnosine test it inside multi-ingredient formulas, so its individual contribution is hard to isolate.
peptides.side_effects_safety: Carnosine is generally considered well tolerated on the skin, with a low potential for irritation at cosmetic use levels. As with any new skincare ingredient, people with sensitive or reactive skin may want to patch test first, since individual reactions vary.

detail.sections:
title: What is carnosine?
text: Carnosine is a small peptide made of two amino acids, beta-alanine and histidine, that occurs naturally in the human body, especially in muscle and brain tissue. In skincare it is used as an antioxidant ingredient, often in products positioned for the appearance of aging or environmentally stressed skin. It is a cosmetic ingredient, not a drug, and is usually listed plainly as "carnosine" on ingredient labels.
title: How does it work?
text: Laboratory studies suggest carnosine acts mainly as an antioxidant and an anti-glycation agent. As an antioxidant, it can neutralize reactive oxygen species, the unstable molecules generated by UV light and pollution that are associated with the visible signs of skin aging. In an ex-vivo human skin study, topical carnosine reduced markers of UV-induced oxidative stress.
Its second proposed role is limiting glycation, a reaction in which sugar molecules bind to proteins such as collagen and form advanced glycation end-products that make those proteins stiff and dysfunctional. By slowing that reaction in laboratory models, carnosine is thought to help skin keep the appearance of suppleness. These are study findings; the benefit in finished cosmetics is described in appearance terms, such as supporting the look of firmness and a brighter, more even tone.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No, and it does not need to be. The FDA does not pre-approve cosmetic ingredients or products the way it approves drugs. A cosmetic may describe how it affects the look and feel of skin, but a claim that a product changes the structure or function of the body would make it a drug in the eyes of regulators. Carnosine is used within that cosmetic boundary, for the appearance of the skin.
title: What is it used for?
text: Carnosine is used in antioxidant and "anti-aging" skincare, typically serums and moisturizers. The appearance goals are protection against the dullness and uneven tone associated with oxidative stress, and support for the look of firm, smooth skin. It is often combined with other antioxidants.
title: What does the research show?
text: Most of the evidence is from laboratory and ex-vivo skin experiments rather than large human trials. According to PubMed, an ex-vivo human skin study found that topical carnosine lowered UV-induced reactive oxygen species and glycation markers. Independent, well-controlled trials of carnosine alone measuring wrinkle or firmness outcomes in people are lacking, and several studies that include carnosine test it inside multi-ingredient formulas, so its individual contribution is hard to isolate.
title: What are the side effects?
text: Carnosine is generally considered well tolerated on the skin, with a low potential for irritation at cosmetic use levels. As with any new skincare ingredient, people with sensitive or reactive skin may want to patch test first, since individual reactions vary.
detail.sources_note: Sources: an ex-vivo human skin study of topical carnosine and UV-induced oxidative stress (Girardi et al., Photochemistry and Photobiology, 2023, DOI: 10.1111/php.13850), indexed on PubMed; and cosmetic ingredient reference data on carnosine. This document is educational and does not constitute medical advice.

detail.faq:
q: Is Cerebrolysin FDA-approved?
a: No. As of September 2026, Cerebrolysin is not approved by the FDA for any indication. It is used clinically in more than 50 countries, but no US pharmaceutical channel exists for Cerebrolysin.
q: Is Cerebrolysin legal in the United States?
a: Cerebrolysin is not legally marketed for human use in the United States. There is no FDA-approved product and no compounding pathway for this proprietary porcine-derived preparation. Importation for personal use carries legal and safety risk. Access outside of a registered clinical trial is not authorized.
q: Can a doctor prescribe Cerebrolysin in the US?
a: No US-licensed physician can prescribe Cerebrolysin within any legal framework, because the compound is neither FDA-approved nor eligible for compounding under US law. Physicians cannot prescribe or dispense it in the United States.
q: Does Cerebrolysin actually work?
a: The human evidence does not establish a clear benefit. Manufacturer-funded trials such as CARS reported better arm function after stroke, and the CAPTAIN trial series reported a small-to-medium benefit after traumatic brain injury. Independent Cochrane reviews, most recently updated in 2023, have found moderate-certainty evidence of no beneficial effect on death in acute ischemic stroke, with a possible increase in non-fatal serious adverse events. The two bodies of evidence measured different outcomes, and the Cochrane authors rated much of the stroke trial evidence at unclear or high risk of bias.
q: What is the difference between Cerebrolysin and a peptide supplement?
a: Cerebrolysin is a proprietary injectable pharmaceutical extract manufactured by a single company (EVER Neuro Pharma, Austria) and used in clinical settings in countries where it is approved. It is not a dietary supplement. Oral peptide supplements sold over the counter are chemically, regulatorily, and clinically distinct from Cerebrolysin.
q: What did the Cochrane review find about Cerebrolysin?
a: The 2023 Cochrane systematic review pooled seven RCTs including 1,773 participants with acute ischemic stroke (one trial tested a similar agent, Cortexin). It found moderate-certainty evidence of no beneficial effect on all-cause death (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.41) and a possible increase in non-fatal serious adverse events (RR 2.39, 95% CI 1.10 to 5.23; 3 trials, 1,335 participants). It updates a review first published in 2010 and last updated in 2020.
q: Why is Cerebrolysin approved in so many countries if the evidence is uncertain?
a: International regulatory approvals were granted at different points in time and under different evidentiary standards than current FDA requirements. Many approvals predate the 2023 Cochrane findings. Regulatory bodies in different jurisdictions weigh the available evidence differently, particularly for conditions with limited therapeutic options. International approval does not constitute FDA endorsement and does not resolve the methodological concerns independent reviewers have raised.
detail.sections:
title: What is cerebrolysin?
text: Cerebrolysin is a preparation of low-molecular-weight peptides and free amino acids produced from pig brain tissue. Cerebrolysin is also known as Cere and FPF-1070. It is not a single peptide but a mixture, and its exact composition is not fully defined. It is approved and used as an injectable in several countries for conditions such as stroke, dementia, and traumatic brain injury, and it is marketed more broadly for cognition. It is not approved in the United States.
title: How does it work?
text: Cerebrolysin is proposed to act like the brain's own neurotrophic factors, the signals that support the survival and function of nerve cells. In laboratory and animal models it has shown these effects:
- Neuroprotective
- Anti-apoptotic
- Anti-excitotoxic
Because the preparation is a complex mixture, its precise active components and mechanism are not fully characterized. This describes the proposed mechanism, separate from whether it improves outcomes in people.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No, not in the United States. Cerebrolysin is not approved by the FDA and is not an FDA-recognized compounding substance. It is used clinically in more than 50 countries, including parts of Europe, Russia and the CIS, China, and South Korea, for stroke, dementia, and brain-injury indications.
title: What does the research show?
text: It has genuine human trials, and the pooled results are largely unfavorable. The main reviews reached these conclusions:
Review | Finding | Certainty
Cochrane systematic review of acute ischemic stroke, according to PubMed | No beneficial effect on death, with a possible increase in non-fatal serious adverse events; many trials were manufacturer-supported | Moderate-certainty evidence
Separate Cochrane review in vascular dementia | A cognition and global-function signal, but any effect may be too small to be clinically meaningful | Very low quality evidence
Independent analysis of brain-derived nootropics | Similar modest conclusions | Low certainty
So despite extensive testing, the human evidence does not establish a clear benefit.

detail.sections:
title: What is cetrorelix?
text: Cetrorelix is a synthetic peptide made of ten amino acids that acts as a GnRH antagonist, a drug that blocks the receptor for gonadotropin-releasing hormone in the pituitary gland. Its FDA-approved form is sold as Cetrotide and is used during in vitro fertilization (IVF).
It is given as a small subcutaneous (under-the-skin) injection, usually in the abdomen, during the stimulation phase of an IVF cycle. Its job is narrow and practical: to keep the body from ovulating too early so that the growing eggs can be retrieved at the right time.
title: The history of cetrorelix
text: Cetrorelix came out of a long effort to improve how IVF controls ovulation. For years the standard approach used GnRH agonists, drugs that first overstimulate the pituitary and then, after about two weeks, exhaust and quiet it. That worked, but it was slow and caused an initial hormone "flare" and estrogen-withdrawal side effects. Researchers wanted a drug that would switch the signal off directly and immediately.
GnRH antagonists were the answer, and cetrorelix was among the first to reach the clinic for fertility care. The FDA approved Cetrotide in 2000, giving IVF a shorter, simpler way to prevent premature ovulation. The antagonist approach has since become a mainstream option for ovarian stimulation.
title: How does cetrorelix work?
text: Cetrorelix works by blocking the pituitary receptor that normally triggers ovulation. Gonadotropin-releasing hormone is released in pulses from the hypothalamus and tells the pituitary to secrete luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). During IVF, as stimulated follicles grow and estrogen climbs, the body can launch a premature LH surge that makes the ovaries release their eggs too early and ruins the cycle. Cetrorelix is a decapeptide that competes with natural GnRH for its receptor and occupies it, which rapidly suppresses LH and FSH release.
The key difference from GnRH agonists is timing:
Feature | GnRH agonists | Cetrorelix (GnRH antagonist)
First effect on the pituitary | Stimulate it, causing a temporary surge | No initial flare
Suppression | Downregulate it over a couple of weeks | Immediate, dose-dependent, and reversible
That is why cetrorelix can be started later in the stimulation cycle and used for only a few days. It is given as a 0.25 mg dose injected daily. A single 3 mg dose was also studied, but only the 0.25 mg product is sold in the U.S.
The effect is reliable. According to PubMed, in a multicenter randomized trial a single 3 mg dose of cetrorelix prevented an LH surge in every patient studied, with shorter stimulation and fewer gonadotropin ampules than the long agonist protocol.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: Yes. The FDA approved cetrorelix (Cetrotide) in 2000 for the inhibition of premature LH surges in women undergoing controlled ovarian stimulation. It is a prescription product used under the supervision of a fertility specialist, and it is approved specifically for this fertility use rather than as a general hormone treatment.
title: What is cetrorelix prescribed for?
text: Cetrorelix is prescribed to prevent premature ovulation during an IVF cycle. After a woman begins gonadotropin injections to grow multiple follicles, cetrorelix is added to hold back the LH surge until the eggs are mature, at which point a separate trigger shot is given and the eggs are retrieved. It is not a fertility drug in the sense of stimulating egg growth; it is the brake that keeps the timing under the clinic's control. It is contraindicated in:
- Pregnancy
- Women with severe kidney impairment
- Women with known hypersensitivity to the drug or to other GnRH analogs
Cetrorelix is used only within a monitored treatment cycle.
title: What are the side effects?
text: The most common effects are mild and local. They include:
- Injection-site reactions such as redness, itching, or swelling
- Nausea
- Headache
Serious effects are uncommon but worth knowing:
- Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), a risk of the overall IVF stimulation; according to PubMed, a Cochrane review found that antagonist protocols reduced OHSS compared with the long agonist protocol, with no conclusive difference in live birth rate
- Allergic or hypersensitivity reactions, which can rarely be severe

peptides.name: CJC-1295
peptides.fda_status: Non-FDA-approved peptide sold in the wellness/gray market, not an approved medicine
peptides.evidence_note: Human data are limited to short studies of hormone levels, with no controlled trials showing a benefit for the marketed muscle, fat-loss, recovery, or anti-aging uses.
peptides.what_it_is: GHRH analog ("growth hormone secretagogue"); a longer-acting "DAC" version and a short-acting "no-DAC" (modified GRF 1-29) version are both sold
peptides.research_at_a_glance: Human data limited to short studies of hormone levels; benefit for muscle, fat, or anti-aging is unproven
peptides.key_takeaway: CJC-1295 is a synthetic long-acting analog of growth-hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH). In two placebo-controlled trials of healthy adults aged 21 to 61 (Teichman, 2006), a single injection raised mean growth hormone 2- to 10-fold for 6 days or more. Mean IGF-1 rose 1.5- to 3-fold, but no controlled human trial shows benefit for muscle, fat loss, recovery, or anti-aging. CJC-1295 is not FDA-approved, it is not eligible for routine pharmacy compounding, and it is banned in sport.
peptides.mechanism:
The proposed mechanism is indirect. GHRH is the hypothalamic signal that tells the pituitary gland to release growth hormone in pulses. As a GHRH-receptor agonist, CJC-1295 is intended to amplify those pulses, raising growth hormone and, downstream, IGF-1. The marketed effects on body composition and recovery are inferred from that hormone rise rather than demonstrated directly. This describes the proposed pharmacology; whether it produces the claimed results in people is a separate question that controlled trials have not answered.
The best-characterized human data come from two randomized, placebo-controlled trials in healthy adults aged 21 to 61 (Teichman, 2006) and a follow-up analysis of healthy men aged 20 to 40.
Measure | Study group | Finding
Mean growth hormone after one injection | Healthy adults aged 21 to 61 | Rose 2- to 10-fold for 6 days or more
Mean IGF-1 after one injection | Healthy adults aged 21 to 61 | Rose 1.5- to 3-fold
IGF-1 after repeat injections | Healthy adults aged 21 to 61 | Stayed elevated up to 28 days
Growth hormone pattern after a single injection | Healthy men aged 20 to 40 | Kept its pulsatile pattern
Trough levels over the same period | Healthy men aged 20 to 40 | Rose 7.5-fold
peptides.human_study_findings: The human evidence is limited to short pharmacology studies of hormone levels, not outcomes. According to PubMed, a Phase 1 study found CJC-1295 produced sustained, dose-dependent increases in growth hormone and IGF-1 and was described as well tolerated over the short term. A related long-acting GHRH study reported similar hormone rises along with some impairment of glucose tolerance in older adults. These measure hormone levels, not muscle, fat, or recovery, and the short-acting "no-DAC" product sold online is largely uncharacterized in controlled human trials. There is no sound human evidence that it delivers the marketed wellness benefits. CJC-1295 is often paired with ipamorelin, which acts at a separate receptor that growth hormone-releasing peptides (GHRPs) engage. No published human randomized controlled trial tests that combination as of September 2026.
peptides.side_effects_safety: What are the side effects of CJC-1295? In short human studies, CJC-1295 was generally well tolerated, with mild local and systemic effects, and no serious adverse reactions were reported. FDA has separately identified serious adverse events, including increased heart rate and a systemic vasodilatory reaction. A related long-acting GHRH study reported some impairment of glucose tolerance in older adults. No long-term safety data are available.

detail.safety_side_effects: What are the side effects of CJC-1295? In short human studies, CJC-1295 was generally well tolerated, with mild local and systemic effects, and no serious adverse reactions were reported. detail.faq:
q: What is the difference between CJC-1295 with DAC and without DAC?
a: The difference is plasma half-life and GH release pattern. CJC-1295 with DAC contains a maleimidopropionyl linker that covalently bonds to circulating albumin after injection, extending plasma half-life to approximately 6 to 8 days and producing sustained IGF-1 elevation lasting up to 11 days after a single dose. CJC-1295 without DAC (modified GRF 1-29) lacks this linker; its half-life has not been reported in human studies, and it is thought to produce only a transient GH rise. The two variants produce different GH secretion patterns. They are not interchangeable.
q: Is CJC-1295 FDA-approved?
a: No. CJC-1295 is not FDA-approved for any indication. As of September 2026, it is not eligible for 503A compounding by licensed pharmacies in the United States: it had been in FDA's Category 2 before its nomination was withdrawn, and FDA now lists it among bulk drug substances nominated but withdrawn. It differs from tesamorelin, an FDA-approved GHRH analog that is approved specifically to reduce excess abdominal fat in HIV-associated lipodystrophy.
q: How long does CJC-1295 take to raise IGF-1?
a: In the Phase 1 trial, a single subcutaneous injection of CJC-1295 with DAC kept IGF-1 raised for 9 to 11 days, and a separate study in healthy young men found IGF-1 about 45% higher one week after injection. The timeline for modified GRF 1-29 (without DAC) is not established, because the no-DAC product is largely uncharacterized in controlled human trials.
q: What are the side effects of CJC-1295?
a: In short human studies, CJC-1295 was generally well tolerated, with mild local and systemic effects, and no serious adverse reactions were reported. FDA has separately identified serious adverse events, including increased heart rate and a systemic vasodilatory reaction. A related long-acting GHRH study reported some impairment of glucose tolerance in older adults. No long-term safety data are available.
q: Can you get CJC-1295 without a prescription?
a: Not legally in the United States. CJC-1295 is not an approved drug, and it cannot be compounded by licensed 503A pharmacies as of September 2026, because it is not on the 503A bulks list or in Category 1. It is not available over the counter in any formulation. Products sold without a prescription or through unregulated channels are not FDA-approved drugs and have no FDA quality oversight.
q: What changed in the FDA peptide category list and how does it affect CJC-1295?
a: CJC-1295 sat in FDA's 503A Category 2 until its nomination was withdrawn, and FDA now lists it among bulk drug substances nominated but withdrawn. It was already off Category 2 before April 2026, when FDA moved a group of other peptides, such as BPC-157, to that withdrawn list. Withdrawal was not an FDA finding that the peptide is safe; FDA still lists potential safety risks for it. A withdrawn substance is not eligible for 503A compounding unless FDA adds it to the 503A bulks list through notice-and-comment rulemaking or places it in Category 1, and neither has happened for CJC-1295. Licensed pharmacies cannot legally compound it under 503A, regardless of whether a patient has a prescription.
q: Is CJC-1295 the same as sermorelin?
a: No. Both are GHRH analogs that bind the same pituitary receptor, but their structures and pharmacokinetics differ substantially. Sermorelin is the native 29-residue GHRH fragment, with an intravenous disappearance half-time of about 4 minutes in healthy men. CJC-1295 incorporates four amino acid substitutions that confer protease resistance, and the DAC formulation additionally conjugates to albumin for a half-life of 6 to 8 days. The practical difference is how long each one stimulates the GH axis.

peptides.name: Tesamorelin
peptides.fda_status: FDA-approved as Egrifta, but only for HIV-associated lipodystrophy
peptides.evidence_note: The approved HIV-lipodystrophy use has strong randomized-trial support, but the off-label wellness and anti-aging use in people without HIV is not established by dedicated trials and reverses off treatment.
peptides.what_it_is: Tesamorelin is a synthetic analog of growth-hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH). It is FDA-approved and sold as Egrifta for reducing excess visceral (abdominal) fat in people with HIV-associated lipodystrophy. In wellness settings it is used off-label for body composition and anti-aging in people without HIV; that use is the subject of this entry and is not an approved indication.
peptides.key_takeaway: Tesamorelin is an FDA-approved growth-hormone-releasing peptide, sold as Egrifta, for excess abdominal fat in HIV-associated lipodystrophy. In a randomized trial of 404 people with HIV (Falutz 2010), visceral fat fell 10.9% on tesamorelin versus 0.6% on placebo over 6 months. Its off-label use for body composition and anti-aging in people without HIV is not an approved indication and lacks dedicated trials. It is banned in sport.
peptides.mechanism: Tesamorelin binds pituitary GHRH receptors and stimulates the body's own growth hormone release, which raises IGF-1 and, in its approved population, reduces visceral fat. This mechanism is well established and underlies the approved use. This describes how it works, separate from whether the off-label wellness use is supported. The label describes growth hormone released this way as both anabolic and lipolytic, meaning it also drives fat breakdown, and visceral fat is the depot the HIV trials measured. Visceral fat changed as follows in the largest trial: Group | Time point | Visceral fat change Tesamorelin | 6-month phase | Fell 10.9% Placebo | 6-month phase | Fell 0.6% Tesamorelin, continued | 12 months | Fell by about 18%
peptides.human_study_findings: For the approved use, the evidence is strong; for the wellness use, it is extrapolated. According to PubMed, a randomized, placebo-controlled trial of 404 people with HIV-associated fat accumulation found tesamorelin significantly reduced visceral fat and raised IGF-1, with no change in glucose parameters. A 52-week extension found it generally well tolerated, and the lost visceral fat returned once treatment stopped. However, there are no dedicated controlled trials of the off-label body-composition or anti-aging use in people without HIV; that use is an extrapolation from the HIV population, and growth hormone-axis stimulation carries class considerations such as IGF-1 elevation and effects on glucose.
peptides.summary_es: Análogo de GHRH con una indicación específica para exceso de grasa abdominal asociado a lipodistrofia por VIH. Su uso para adelgazar o rejuvenecer fuera de ese contexto no debe presentarse como aprobado.

- Active malignancy

peptides.name: Copper tripeptide-1
peptides.fda_status: Cosmetic ingredient rather than a drug, so does not require FDA approval
peptides.evidence_note: It has a large body of laboratory and animal data plus manufacturer-associated human studies pointing to appearance benefits, but the one independent controlled human trial found no clear objective effect, so the human evidence remains limited.
peptides.what_it_is: Cosmetic ingredient (GHK-Cu), a copper-bound peptide used in "anti-aging" and repair products
peptides.research_at_a_glance: Deep laboratory and wound-healing support; independent human appearance evidence is mixed
peptides.key_takeaway: Copper tripeptide-1, often called GHK-Cu, is a three-amino acid peptide (glycine-histidine-lysine) bound to a copper ion and used in skincare for its proposed role in skin renewal. Laboratory and animal studies show it can signal cells to make collagen and other matrix components. Independent human evidence is thin. In a randomized trial of 13 patients after CO2 laser resurfacing, GHK-Cu skincare showed no significant difference in redness or skin quality in blinded evaluations, though patients rated their overall skin quality higher (p = 0.04). As of 2026 it is a cosmetic ingredient, not an FDA-approved drug.
peptides.mechanism:
Laboratory studies suggest copper tripeptide-1 acts as a signal that tells skin cells to rebuild the supporting matrix. In cell and animal studies, GHK-Cu:
- Stimulates fibroblasts to produce collagen, elastin, and glycosaminoglycans, the molecules that give skin its structure and cushioning
- Helps regulate the enzymes that break that matrix down
- Delivers copper, a mineral involved in tissue repair
- Has been shown to act as an antioxidant and to support wound healing in animal models
Reviews of laboratory work describe further activity, mostly studied in cells and animals rather than in skin products. In gene-expression analyses, the GHK peptide shows anti-inflammatory activity, increased blood-vessel formation, and changes in many genes tied to repair. These are systemic, preclinical findings, separate from the topical cosmetic use this page covers.
Because of this activity, it is used in cosmetics with the aim of improving the appearance of firm, smooth, and evenly textured skin. These are laboratory and animal findings describing how the peptide behaves; in finished products the benefit is described in appearance terms rather than as a medical repair claim.
peptides.human_study_findings: The research is deep on mechanism but thinner on independent human appearance outcomes. According to PubMed, review articles summarize extensive laboratory and animal evidence that GHK-Cu promotes matrix synthesis and wound healing, though many of those studies are associated with the ingredient's commercial developers. An independent randomized trial of 13 patients used GHK-Cu skincare after CO2 laser resurfacing. Blinded evaluators found no statistically significant difference in redness or skin quality, although patients rated their overall skin quality higher (p = 0.04). In short, the mechanism is well characterized, but strong independent proof of a cosmetic appearance benefit is still limited. Separately, a small set of animal studies tested GHK-Cu given by injection, and these findings are systemic and preclinical: Model | Finding Rats after knee ligament reconstruction | Weekly joint injections for 4 weeks led to a smaller knee laxity difference than saline at 6 weeks (p = 0.009), but the difference was not significant at 12 weeks Mice with lipopolysaccharide-induced acute lung injury | GHK-Cu lowered TNF-alpha and IL-6 through NF-κB p65 and p38 MAPK suppression Because both studies are in animals, they do not show an effect of systemic use in people.
peptides.side_effects_safety: Copper tripeptide-1 is generally well tolerated on the skin. Potential concerns are mostly practical: very high copper concentrations could be irritating, and the ingredient can be destabilized when layered with strong acids such as high-strength vitamin C or certain exfoliants, which is a formulation consideration rather than a safety hazard. Sensitive skin may react to any new product, so a patch test is reasonable.

detail.sections:
title: What is copper tripeptide-1?
text: Copper tripeptide-1 is a peptide made of three amino acids, glycine, histidine, and lysine, joined to a copper ion. The peptide part, known as GHK, occurs naturally in the body and declines with age. In its copper-bound form, GHK-Cu, it is one of the longest-studied "copper peptides" in skincare and is used in products marketed for skin renewal and repair. It is a cosmetic ingredient, not a drug.
title: How does it work?
text: Laboratory studies suggest copper tripeptide-1 acts as a signal that tells skin cells to rebuild the supporting matrix. In cell and animal studies, GHK-Cu:
- Stimulates fibroblasts to produce collagen, elastin, and glycosaminoglycans, the molecules that give skin its structure and cushioning

- Delivers copper, a mineral involved in tissue repair
- Has been shown to act as an antioxidant and to support wound healing in animal models

In gene-expression analyses, the GHK peptide shows anti-inflammatory activity, increased blood-vessel formation, and changes in many genes tied to repair. These are systemic, preclinical findings, separate from the topical cosmetic use this page covers.
Because of this activity, it is used in cosmetics with the aim of improving the appearance of firm, smooth, and evenly textured skin. These are laboratory and animal findings describing how the peptide behaves; in finished products the benefit is described in appearance terms rather than as a medical repair claim.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No, and it does not need to be. The FDA does not pre-approve cosmetic ingredients. Cosmetics may describe effects on the look and feel of skin, while claims to change the body's structure or function would place a product in the drug category. Copper tripeptide-1 is used as a cosmetic ingredient, for the appearance of the skin.
title: What is it used for?
text: Copper tripeptide-1 is used in "anti-aging" serums, creams, and post-procedure products, and also in some hair and scalp products. The appearance goals are the look of firmer, denser skin, a reduction in the appearance of fine lines, and smoother texture, as well as a soothed look after cosmetic procedures.
title: What does the research show?
text: The research is deep on mechanism but thinner on independent human appearance outcomes. According to PubMed, review articles summarize extensive laboratory and animal evidence that GHK-Cu promotes matrix synthesis and wound healing, though many of those studies are associated with the ingredient's commercial developers.
An independent randomized trial of 13 patients used GHK-Cu skincare after CO2 laser resurfacing. title: What are the side effects?
text: Copper tripeptide-1 is generally well tolerated on the skin. Sensitive skin may react to any new product, so a patch test is reasonable.

peptides.key_takeaway: Cosyntropin (sold as Cortrosyn) is a synthetic fragment of adrenocorticotropic hormone used as a diagnostic agent to test whether the adrenal glands are working. A dose is given and the resulting rise in cortisol shows how well the adrenals respond. It has long been FDA-approved in the U.S. and is given as a single injection during the test.
peptides.mechanism: Cosyntropin binds the melanocortin-2 receptor on the adrenal cortex, the same receptor as natural ACTH, and stimulates the adrenal glands to release cortisol. In the diagnostic test, a baseline cortisol level is measured, a dose of cosyntropin is given, and cortisol is measured again after a set interval. A healthy adrenal gland responds with a clear rise in cortisol; a blunted or absent rise points to adrenal insufficiency. Because the value of the test lies in the measured response, cosyntropin is given as a single dose under controlled conditions. Studies comparing test protocols have examined lower and standard doses; a meta-analysis found the low-dose test was better than the standard dose at detecting chronic adrenal insufficiency caused by the pituitary or hypothalamus. The test helps distinguish primary adrenal failure from other causes of low cortisol.
