title: What is cosyntropin?
text: Cosyntropin, sold under the brand Cortrosyn, is a synthetic peptide made of the first 24 amino acids of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). Those 24 amino acids carry the full hormone's ability to stimulate the adrenal glands, so cosyntropin acts like natural ACTH but is simpler to manufacture and standardize. It is used not as a treatment but as a diagnostic agent. It is also known by the generic name tetracosactide. It has been FDA-approved for many years.
title: How does cosyntropin work?
text: Cosyntropin binds the melanocortin-2 receptor on the adrenal cortex, the same receptor as natural ACTH, and stimulates the adrenal glands to release cortisol. In the diagnostic test, a baseline cortisol level is measured, a dose of cosyntropin is given, and cortisol is measured again after a set interval. A healthy adrenal gland responds with a clear rise in cortisol; a blunted or absent rise points to adrenal insufficiency.
Because the value of the test lies in the measured response, cosyntropin is given as a single dose under controlled conditions. Studies comparing test protocols have examined lower and standard doses; a meta-analysis found the low-dose test was better than the standard dose at detecting chronic adrenal insufficiency caused by the pituitary or hypothalamus. The test helps distinguish primary adrenal failure from other causes of low cortisol.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: Yes. Cosyntropin (Cortrosyn) has long been FDA-approved as a diagnostic agent for screening adrenocortical insufficiency. It is given as a single injection, with cortisol measured before and after.
title: What is cosyntropin prescribed for?
text: Cosyntropin is used for the ACTH stimulation test, to evaluate whether the adrenal glands can produce cortisol normally. It is a diagnostic tool used by clinicians, not an ongoing therapy.
title: What are the side effects?
text: According to the prescribing information, reported side effects include:
- Slow or fast heart rate
- High blood pressure
- Swelling in the hands or feet
- Rash
More serious considerations include:
- Allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis

peptides.what_it_is: A calcineurin-inhibitor immunosuppressant, a cyclic 11-amino-acid peptide of fungal origin
peptides.key_takeaway: Cyclosporine (also spelled ciclosporin; brands include Sandimmune, Neoral, and the eye drop Restasis) is a cyclic peptide from a fungus that suppresses the immune system, and it transformed organ transplantation when it arrived in the 1980s. It works by blocking the activation of T cells. It has been FDA-approved in the U.S. since 1983, is available in oral, intravenous, and eye-drop forms, and carries boxed warnings for the systemic versions.
peptides.mechanism: Cyclosporine enters T cells and binds a protein called cyclophilin, and the resulting complex blocks an enzyme called calcineurin. Calcineurin normally activates a transcription factor (NFAT) that switches on the gene for interleukin-2 and other signals T cells need to multiply and mount an immune response. By inhibiting calcineurin, cyclosporine prevents that activation, so the immune attack on a transplanted organ, or the overactive immune response in autoimmune disease, is suppressed. That targeted suppression of T-cell activation is what made it so valuable in transplantation. In the landmark Canadian multicenter trial, cyclosporine improved one-year kidney graft survival compared with the older azathioprine-based regimen. The same mechanism underlies its use in autoimmune conditions and, at low local doses in Restasis, in reducing the inflammation of chronic dry eye.
peptides.side_effects_safety: According to the prescribing information, common side effects of systemic use include: - High blood pressure - Kidney impairment with rising creatinine - Tremor - Excess hair growth and gum overgrowth More serious considerations include: - Boxed warnings for kidney toxicity and for increased risk of serious infections and cancers, including lymphoma and skin cancer - The need for blood-level monitoring and attention to many drug interactions - Restasis, acting locally, mainly causes eye burning or stinging and does not carry these systemic warnings

detail.sections:
title: What is cyclosporine?
text: Cyclosporine, also spelled ciclosporin and known as cyclosporin A, is an immunosuppressant drug derived from a soil fungus. Chemically it is an unusual cyclic peptide, a ring of 11 amino acids including some that do not appear in ordinary proteins, which makes it fat-soluble and distinct from typical linear peptides. It is sold as Sandimmune, the microemulsion Neoral, and Gengraf for systemic use, and as the Restasis emulsion for the eyes. It was approved in the United States in 1983.
title: The history of cyclosporine
text: Cyclosporine changed the course of modern medicine. It was isolated from a fungus in the 1970s and found to suppress the immune system in a highly selective way, acting on the T cells that drive transplant rejection without broadly wiping out the bone marrow. Its approval in 1983 dramatically improved the survival of transplanted organs and helped make heart, liver, and other transplants routine rather than experimental. It remains a reference point for the calcineurin-inhibitor class.
title: How does cyclosporine work?
text: Cyclosporine enters T cells and binds a protein called cyclophilin, and the resulting complex blocks an enzyme called calcineurin. Calcineurin normally activates a transcription factor (NFAT) that switches on the gene for interleukin-2 and other signals T cells need to multiply and mount an immune response. By inhibiting calcineurin, cyclosporine prevents that activation, so the immune attack on a transplanted organ, or the overactive immune response in autoimmune disease, is suppressed.
That targeted suppression of T-cell activation is what made it so valuable in transplantation. In the landmark Canadian multicenter trial, cyclosporine improved one-year kidney graft survival compared with the older azathioprine-based regimen. The same mechanism underlies its use in autoimmune conditions and, at low local doses in Restasis, in reducing the inflammation of chronic dry eye.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: Yes. The FDA approved cyclosporine and two later formulations on this timeline:
Year | FDA approval
1983 | Cyclosporine, for transplant rejection
1995 | Neoral microemulsion
2002 | Restasis eye drop
The systemic formulations carry boxed warnings, including for kidney toxicity and for the increased risk of serious infections and malignancies (especially lymphoma and skin cancer) that comes with immunosuppression.
title: What is cyclosporine prescribed for?
text: Systemic cyclosporine is prescribed to prevent rejection in kidney, liver, and heart transplants, and for severe rheumatoid arthritis and severe plaque psoriasis that have not responded to other treatment. Restasis is prescribed to increase tear production in chronic dry eye associated with inflammation. The different oral products are not freely interchangeable and require monitoring.
title: What are the side effects?
text: According to the prescribing information, common side effects of systemic use include:
- High blood pressure
- Kidney impairment with rising creatinine
- Tremor
- Excess hair growth and gum overgrowth
More serious considerations include:
- Boxed warnings for kidney toxicity and for increased risk of serious infections and cancers, including lymphoma and skin cancer
- The need for blood-level monitoring and attention to many drug interactions
- Restasis, acting locally, mainly causes eye burning or stinging and does not carry these systemic warnings

peptides.what_it_is: Lipoglycopeptide antibiotics derived from the glycopeptide class, active against Gram-positive bacteria including MRSA
peptides.key_takeaway: Dalbavancin, oritavancin, and telavancin (sold as Dalvance, Orbactiv, and Vibativ) are lipoglycopeptide antibiotics, semi-synthetic relatives of vancomycin that treat Gram-positive infections, including MRSA. Dalbavancin's half-life of roughly two weeks and oritavancin's single-infusion course allow very infrequent dosing for a skin infection, while telavancin is dosed daily. All three are FDA-approved in the U.S., and they are given intravenously.
peptides.mechanism: Like vancomycin, these drugs block bacterial cell-wall synthesis by binding the D-alanyl-D-alanine end of the wall's building blocks, preventing the cross-linking that gives the wall strength. The lipid tail anchors them in the bacterial membrane, which both prolongs their activity and, in the case of oritavancin and telavancin, lets them also disrupt the membrane itself, a second bactericidal mechanism. All are bactericidal against Gram-positive bacteria including MRSA. The standout practical feature is duration. Dalbavancin's half-life of roughly two weeks allows a once-weekly or even single-dose regimen, and oritavancin treats a skin infection with a single infusion. In its pivotal program, once-weekly dalbavancin was non-inferior to a conventional vancomycin-to-linezolid course for skin infections. Telavancin is dosed daily and has a broader approved role that includes some pneumonia.
peptides.side_effects_safety: According to the prescribing information, common side effects include: - Nausea, headache, and diarrhea - Rises in liver enzymes (dalbavancin) - Taste disturbance and foamy urine (telavancin) More serious considerations include: - Telavancin's boxed warnings for kidney toxicity (with higher mortality in pneumonia patients who already have moderate-to-severe kidney impairment) and for fetal harm - Oritavancin interferes with some blood-clotting tests and should not be used with intravenous unfractionated heparin for a period after dosing - Infusion-related reactions

peptides.what_it_is: A cyclic lipopeptide antibiotic active against Gram-positive bacteria
peptides.key_takeaway: Daptomycin (sold as Cubicin) is a cyclic lipopeptide antibiotic that kills Gram-positive bacteria, including MRSA, by puncturing their cell membrane. It is used for serious skin infections and for Staphylococcus aureus bloodstream infections, but notably not for pneumonia. It has been FDA-approved in the U.S. since 2003 and is given intravenously.
peptides.mechanism: Daptomycin works at the bacterial cell membrane rather than the cell wall. In the presence of calcium, its lipid tail inserts into the Gram-positive membrane, where multiple molecules cluster to form channels. These channels let potassium and other ions leak out, rapidly collapsing the membrane's electrical charge. Without that charge the bacterium cannot sustain DNA, RNA, and protein synthesis, and it dies quickly, without bursting open. That membrane mechanism gives concentration-dependent, rapid killing. One important limitation follows from its chemistry: daptomycin is inactivated by lung surfactant, so it does not work for pneumonia and is not used there. In the pivotal trial for bloodstream infection, daptomycin was non-inferior to standard therapy for S. aureus bacteremia and right-sided endocarditis, with less kidney dysfunction.
peptides.side_effects_safety: According to the prescribing information, common side effects include: - Diarrhea, headache, and dizziness - Rash - Abnormal liver tests and rises in the muscle enzyme CPK - Urinary tract infections - Low blood pressure and shortness of breath More serious considerations include: - Muscle injury (myopathy and rarely rhabdomyolysis), so CPK is monitored and statins may be paused - Eosinophilic pneumonia, an uncommon lung reaction - Peripheral neuropathy - Serious allergic reactions, including a severe drug reaction called DRESS - Kidney inflammation (tubulointerstitial nephritis)

peptides.what_it_is: A glucagon analog peptide engineered for stability in a ready-to-use liquid
peptides.key_takeaway: Dasiglucagon (sold as Zegalogue) is a stable glucagon analog formulated as a ready-to-use injection for the emergency treatment of severe low blood sugar. Because it stays stable in solution, it comes premixed in an autoinjector or prefilled syringe, with no reconstitution needed. It has been FDA-approved in the U.S. since 2021 and is now approved for adults and children with diabetes who weigh at least 20 kg.
peptides.mechanism: Dasiglucagon activates the same liver glucagon receptor as native glucagon, triggering glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis so the liver releases glucose and blood sugar rises quickly. Its structural changes do not alter what it does at the receptor; they make the molecule stable enough to be stored as a ready-to-use liquid, which matters in an emergency where every step of mixing and preparation costs time. That practical advantage is the point of the drug. In its phase 3 trial in adults with type 1 diabetes, dasiglucagon produced a median time to plasma-glucose recovery of 10 minutes versus 40 minutes with placebo, with nearly all patients recovering within 15 minutes. A separate pediatric trial supported its use in children.

detail.sections:
title: What is dasiglucagon?
text: Dasiglucagon, sold under the brand Zegalogue, is a modified version of glucagon designed to remain stable in a water-based solution. Native glucagon is unstable once dissolved, which is why traditional emergency kits require mixing a powder with liquid at the moment of a crisis; dasiglucagon's amino-acid changes let it be supplied premixed and ready to use. It is an emergency rescue treatment for severe hypoglycemia. It was developed under the codes ZP4207 and ZP-GA-1 and approved in the United States in 2021.

That practical advantage is the point of the drug. In its phase 3 trial in adults with type 1 diabetes, dasiglucagon produced a median time to plasma-glucose recovery of 10 minutes versus 40 minutes with placebo, with nearly all patients recovering within 15 minutes. A separate pediatric trial supported its use in children.

title: What is davunetide?

peptides.what_it_is: A GnRH receptor antagonist peptide that suppresses testosterone without a flare
peptides.key_takeaway: Degarelix (sold as Firmagon) is a synthetic decapeptide that blocks the gonadotropin-releasing hormone receptor, dropping testosterone to castrate levels within a few days and without the initial surge seen with older hormone drugs. It is used to treat advanced prostate cancer and lowers testosterone to castrate levels faster than the agonist leuprolide. It has been FDA-approved in the U.S. since 2008 and is given as a monthly subcutaneous injection.

peptides.fda_status: Desirudin was approved by the FDA in 2003 for the prevention of deep vein thrombosis in patients undergoing elective hip replacement surgery. The only brand, Iprivask, has since been discontinued in the U.S., and no generic is sold.

peptides.what_it_is: A recombinant hirudin analog that directly inhibits thrombin
peptides.key_takeaway: Desirudin (formerly sold as Iprivask) is a recombinant form of hirudin, the natural anticoagulant from the medicinal leech, that was used to prevent blood clots after hip replacement surgery. It directly and specifically blocks thrombin, the central enzyme of the clotting cascade. It was FDA-approved in the U.S. in 2003, but Iprivask has since been discontinued and no desirudin product is currently sold in the U.S.
peptides.mechanism: Desirudin is a direct thrombin inhibitor. Thrombin is the key enzyme at the end of the clotting cascade, responsible for converting fibrinogen into the fibrin that forms a clot and for further activating platelets. Desirudin binds thrombin tightly at two sites at once, both its active site and the region it uses to grip fibrinogen, essentially clamping the enzyme shut. Unlike heparin, it does not need the body's antithrombin to work and it can inhibit thrombin that is already bound within a clot. That direct, antithrombin-independent action is useful for preventing the venous clots that can form after hip replacement, when immobility and surgical injury raise the risk. In its pivotal trial in elective hip replacement, desirudin reduced confirmed deep vein thrombosis compared with unfractionated heparin, without an increase in bleeding. It is given as a subcutaneous injection around the time of surgery.
peptides.side_effects_safety: Common side effects include: - Bleeding - Injection-site reactions - Anemia and nausea More serious considerations include: - Hemorrhage, the principal risk - A warning that spinal or epidural anesthesia carries a risk of spinal bleeding and paralysis, a caution shared across anticoagulants - Caution in kidney impairment, and the possible formation of antibodies to hirudin

title: What is desirudin?
text: Desirudin, formerly sold under the brand Iprivask, is a recombinant version of hirudin, the anticoagulant protein that medicinal leeches use to keep blood flowing while they feed. Made in yeast rather than extracted from leeches, it is a highly specific thrombin inhibitor used to prevent blood clots in the legs after major orthopedic surgery. It was developed under the code CGP 39393 and approved in the United States in 2003.

peptides.name: Desmopressin
peptides.fda_status: Yes. Desmopressin was first approved by the FDA in 1978, with later products including the Noctiva nasal spray (2017) and the Nocdurna sublingual tablet (2018) for nocturia. Noctiva and the Stimate nasal spray have since been discontinued in the U.S. Nocdurna carries a boxed warning about the risk of low blood sodium (hyponatremia), as Noctiva did.
peptides.evidence_note: Desmopressin is FDA-approved for diabetes insipidus, enuresis, nocturia, and certain bleeding disorders, supported by decades of clinical use and registration trials.
peptides.what_it_is: A synthetic vasopressin analog that selectively activates the V2 (antidiuretic) receptor
peptides.key_takeaway: Desmopressin (desmopressin acetate; brands include DDAVP and Nocdurna) is a synthetic version of the antidiuretic hormone vasopressin, engineered to concentrate urine without raising blood pressure. It treats central diabetes insipidus, bedwetting, nighttime urination, and certain bleeding disorders. It has been FDA-approved in the U.S. since 1978 and comes as tablets, a sublingual form, nasal spray, and injection.
peptides.mechanism:
Desmopressin selectively activates the V2 vasopressin receptor in the kidney's collecting ducts, where it increases the number of water channels (aquaporin-2) that reabsorb water back into the body. The result is more concentrated urine and less urine volume. Because the chemical changes that give desmopressin this selectivity also remove its activity at the V1 receptors on blood vessels, it does not cause the vasoconstriction that vasopressin does.
This makes it useful across several conditions. Desmopressin also has a second action unrelated to the kidney: it prompts the release of clotting factor VIII and von Willebrand factor from storage sites in blood-vessel walls. The table shows which action each use draws on:
Condition | What desmopressin does
Central diabetes insipidus, where the body lacks vasopressin | Restores normal water conservation
Bedwetting and nighttime urination | Reduces overnight urine production
Mild hemophilia A and type 1 von Willebrand disease | Releases stored clotting factor VIII and von Willebrand factor, which is why higher doses are used to manage bleeding
The main hazard of over-concentrating urine is dilutional low blood sodium.
peptides.side_effects_safety: Common side effects include: - Headache - Nausea - Nasal discomfort with the spray - Flushing More serious considerations include: - Low blood sodium (hyponatremia), which can cause seizures if severe, the reason fluid intake is restricted and the basis of the Nocdurna boxed warning - Caution in people at risk of fluid overload or with heart or kidney disease

peptides.fda_status: Yes. Difelikefalin was approved by the FDA in 2021 for moderate-to-severe pruritus associated with chronic kidney disease in adults on hemodialysis. It is given as an intravenous bolus into the venous line of the dialysis circuit at the end of each session, three times a week.

peptides.what_it_is: A peripherally restricted kappa-opioid receptor agonist peptide
peptides.key_takeaway: Difelikefalin (sold as Korsuva) is a peptide that activates kappa-opioid receptors to relieve the intense itching that affects many people on dialysis. Because it barely enters the brain, it eases itch without the typical opioid effects on mood or breathing. It has been FDA-approved in the U.S. since 2021 and is given intravenously during hemodialysis.
peptides.mechanism: Difelikefalin selectively activates kappa-opioid receptors, which are found on peripheral sensory nerves and on immune cells. The table below shows what activating each set of receptors does. Where the kappa receptors sit | Effect of activating them Itch-sensing peripheral sensory nerves | Dampens the transmission of itch signals Immune cells | May reduce the release of itch-promoting and inflammatory mediators The net effect is reduced itch. Its design is central to its profile: as a peripherally restricted peptide, it reaches these peripheral kappa receptors but has minimal entry into the brain, so it avoids the euphoria, dependence, and respiratory depression associated with classic opioids that act on mu receptors. In the KALM-1 trial, a significantly larger share of patients on difelikefalin than on placebo achieved a meaningful improvement in itch intensity over 12 weeks, with better itch-related quality of life.

It was developed under the codes CR845 and FE 202845 and approved in the United States in 2021.

title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: Yes. Difelikefalin was approved by the FDA in 2021 for moderate-to-severe pruritus associated with chronic kidney disease in adults on hemodialysis. It is given as an intravenous bolus into the venous line of the dialysis circuit at the end of each session, three times a week.
title: What is difelikefalin prescribed for?
text: Difelikefalin is prescribed for the itch of chronic kidney disease in adults undergoing hemodialysis. It is not a general anti-itch drug and is tied to the dialysis setting, which makes its intravenous dosing practical.
title: What are the side effects?
text: According to the prescribing information, common side effects include:
- Diarrhea
- Dizziness and nausea
- High potassium
- Headache
More serious considerations include:
- Dizziness, drowsiness, and changes in mental status or gait, which can raise the risk of falls, especially with sedating medicines
- Caution when combined with other central nervous system depressants

detail.faq:
q: Is dihexa FDA-approved?
a: No. As of September 2026, dihexa is not FDA-approved for any human indication. It is not eligible for 503A compounding: FDA removed it from Category 2 in April 2026, but it is not on the 503A bulks list or in Category 1. There is no legal prescription pathway for dihexa in the United States.
q: Is dihexa legal in the United States?
a: Dihexa is not FDA-approved and is not approved for human use. It is distributed through gray-market channels under "research use only" labeling, which does not confer legality for human consumption. The precise legal status as a consumer product involves regulatory nuances best addressed by a qualified regulatory attorney. Superpower does not offer legal or regulatory guidance on obtaining gray-market research chemicals.
q: Can a doctor prescribe dihexa?
a: No licensed provider can prescribe dihexa under 503A compounding law because it is not on the FDA's 503A bulks list or in Category 1. It cannot be compounded by a licensed pharmacy for a patient-specific prescription. Any provider offering to prescribe it is doing so outside established legal and regulatory frameworks.
q: What is the '10 million times more potent than BDNF' claim based on?
a: The comparison does not appear in the two main published dihexa papers. Those studies report that dihexa induced new synapses at picomolar concentrations in rat hippocampal neurons, and the paper tying that effect to HGF/c-Met has since been retracted. Higher potency at one narrow in vitro endpoint would not predict clinical cognitive efficacy in humans. BDNF's pharmacology, receptor interactions, and signaling pleiotropy make a simple molar comparison uninformative as a guide to real-world cognitive effects.
q: Was a key dihexa paper retracted?
a: Yes, two papers. A 2012 paper, which originally framed dihexa-class molecules as HGF-dimerization mimetics, was formally retracted in April 2025 following a 2021 expression of concern. A 2014 paper in the same journal, which proposed that angiotensin IV-derived peptides produce their procognitive and synaptogenic effects via HGF/c-Met activation, was also retracted in April 2025 after a 2021 expression of concern. The 2013 paper reporting oral cognitive restoration in rats carries a 2021 expression of concern but has not been formally retracted. The combined effect is that both the foundational biochemical characterization of dihexa and its primary mechanistic framing through HGF/c-Met have been called into question in the published record.
q: Is dihexa safe?
a: No human safety data exist for dihexa as of September 2026, and no human exposure data on dihexa products have been identified. No human Phase 1 dose-escalation study, pharmacokinetic profile, or systematic adverse-event characterization has been published. The compound's proposed c-Met agonist mechanism raises a specific theoretical oncogenic concern, because c-Met signaling is linked to tumor proliferation, invasion, and metastasis in several cancer types. This is not a minor caveat. It is a major safety unknown for a compound being circulated in consumer nootropic markets with no clinical oversight.
q: Is there human evidence for dihexa?
a: No. All published cognition data for dihexa comes from rodent models. No human efficacy or safety trial has been completed, and no trial is registered on ClinicalTrials.gov as of September 2026. The preclinical signal has been partially replicated by an independent laboratory in mice; whether any of it translates to humans is unknown.
q: What is the difference between dihexa and other nootropic peptides?
a: Dihexa is structurally a small peptidomimetic derived from angiotensin IV, with proposed oral bioavailability and blood-brain barrier penetration in rodents, properties that distinguish it from most injectable research peptides. Its proposed mechanism through the HGF/c-Met receptor system is distinct from peptides acting on growth hormone secretagogue receptors, BDNF pathways, or acetylcholine systems. Its most notable distinguishing feature in the current literature is the combination of preclinical cognitive signal, retracted foundational biochemistry paper, zero human data, and a theoretical oncogenic concern that remains uncharacterized.

peptides.fda_status: Cosmetic ingredient rather than a drug, so does not require FDA approval
peptides.evidence_note: The mechanism is supported by laboratory work, but there is no sound human trial of the isolated peptide showing an appearance benefit; the available human study tested it only within a multi-ingredient formula.
peptides.what_it_is: Cosmetic ingredient (SYN-AKE), a synthetic venom-mimic peptide
peptides.research_at_a_glance: Mechanism based on laboratory work; human evidence comes from combination formulas, not the isolated peptide
peptides.key_takeaway: Dipeptide diaminobutyroyl benzylamide diacetate, sold under the trade name SYN-AKE, is a synthetic peptide modeled on a component of temple viper venom, used in skincare as a "needle-free" alternative aimed at expression lines. Laboratory work suggests it mimics a venom peptide that blocks the muscle receptor for acetylcholine, which is the rationale for marketing it to soften the look of dynamic wrinkles. As of 2026, the evidence is mainly laboratory and manufacturer data, with human testing done inside multi-ingredient formulas rather than on the peptide alone.
peptides.mechanism: Laboratory studies suggest the peptide works by quieting the signal that makes facial muscles contract. Normally the neurotransmitter acetylcholine binds to receptors on muscle, called nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, to trigger contraction. The venom peptide it is modeled on reversibly blocks that receptor, and the synthetic version is proposed to do the same, so the small muscles that create "expression lines" contract less and the overlying skin looks smoother. This is the same general idea marketed for other "expression line" peptides, and it is why SYN-AKE is sometimes described as a topical alternative to muscle-relaxing injections. It is important to frame this accurately: The mechanism is demonstrated in laboratory settings, and a topical cosmetic does not reach or paralyze muscle the way an injection does. In finished products the goal is described in appearance terms, the look of fewer or softer dynamic lines.
peptides.human_study_findings: The direct evidence for the isolated peptide is limited. According to PubMed, a 2026 ex-vivo and clinical study tested a serum that contained dipeptide diaminobutyroyl benzylamide diacetate together with acetyl hexapeptide-8, niacinamide, and other actives, and reported improvements in the appearance of wrinkles and skin quality. That evidence has three limits: - Because the peptide was one of several active ingredients, that result cannot be attributed to it alone. - No independent trial of SYN-AKE by itself measuring appearance outcomes was found. - Much of the supporting data is laboratory or manufacturer-based.
peptides.side_effects_safety: The peptide is generally reported as well tolerated on the skin, with low irritation potential at cosmetic use levels, and topical application is not known to produce a systemic muscle effect. As with any new skincare product, people with sensitive skin may want to patch test, since individual reactions vary.

detail.sections:
title: What is dipeptide diaminobutyroyl benzylamide diacetate?
text: Dipeptide diaminobutyroyl benzylamide diacetate is a synthetic peptide marketed in skincare under the trade name SYN-AKE, developed by Pentapharm (now part of dsm-firmenich). It is designed to imitate waglerin-1, a small peptide found in the venom of the temple viper. Despite that origin, the cosmetic ingredient is made synthetically and contains no actual venom. It is a cosmetic ingredient, not a drug, and is used in products positioned as a gentler, topical approach to the look of expression lines.
title: The history of SYN-AKE
text: SYN-AKE grew out of snake venom research. It is modeled on waglerin-1, a peptide found in the venom of the temple viper (Tropidolaemus wagleri), a snake native to Southeast Asia. In the viper, that venom component briefly interrupts the nerve-to-muscle signal; scientists recreated a stable, synthetic version of its active region for use on skin, containing none of the venom itself.
The ingredient was developed by Pentapharm, a Swiss company known for venom-derived compounds, which introduced it as an anti-wrinkle active around 2005, and later became part of DSM. SYN-AKE went on to become one of the better-known snake venom skincare stories of the late 2000s, when creams built around it were marketed as a needle-free alternative to muscle-relaxing injections.
title: How does it work?
text: Laboratory studies suggest the peptide works by quieting the signal that makes facial muscles contract. Normally the neurotransmitter acetylcholine binds to receptors on muscle, called nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, to trigger contraction. The venom peptide it is modeled on reversibly blocks that receptor, and the synthetic version is proposed to do the same, so the small muscles that create "expression lines" contract less and the overlying skin looks smoother.
This is the same general idea marketed for other "expression line" peptides, and it is why SYN-AKE is sometimes described as a topical alternative to muscle-relaxing injections. It is important to frame this accurately: The mechanism is demonstrated in laboratory settings, and a topical cosmetic does not reach or paralyze muscle the way an injection does. In finished products the goal is described in appearance terms, the look of fewer or softer dynamic lines.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No, and it does not need to be. The FDA does not pre-approve cosmetic ingredients. A cosmetic may make claims about the appearance of skin, while a claim to relax muscles or otherwise change the body's function would make a product a drug. SYN-AKE is used as a cosmetic ingredient, for the appearance of the skin.
title: What is it used for?
text: It is used in "anti-aging" serums and creams aimed at dynamic or expression lines, such as forehead lines and crow's-feet around the eyes. The appearance goal is smoother-looking skin and a reduction in the look of lines that deepen with facial movement. It is frequently combined with other peptides and humectants.
title: What does the research show?
text: The direct evidence for the isolated peptide is limited. According to PubMed, a 2026 ex-vivo and clinical study tested a serum that contained dipeptide diaminobutyroyl benzylamide diacetate together with acetyl hexapeptide-8, niacinamide, and other actives, and reported improvements in the appearance of wrinkles and skin quality. That evidence has three limits:
- Because the peptide was one of several active ingredients, that result cannot be attributed to it alone.
- No independent trial of SYN-AKE by itself measuring appearance outcomes was found.
- Much of the supporting data is laboratory or manufacturer-based.
title: What are the side effects?
text: The peptide is generally reported as well tolerated on the skin, with low irritation potential at cosmetic use levels, and topical application is not known to produce a systemic muscle effect. As with any new skincare product, people with sensitive skin may want to patch test, since individual reactions vary.
detail.sources_note: Sources: an ex-vivo and clinical study of a multi-ingredient serum containing the peptide (Zhu et al., International Journal of Cosmetic Science, 2026, DOI: 10.1111/ics.70087), indexed on PubMed; and manufacturer and cosmetic ingredient reference data on SYN-AKE. This document is educational and does not constitute medical advice.

detail.sections:
title: What is DSIP?
text: DSIP, delta sleep-inducing peptide, is a naturally occurring nine-amino acid peptide first isolated decades ago from the blood of sleeping rabbits. It is sold through wellness and "research peptide" channels for sleep and stress, though its role in the body is still not well understood. It is not an approved medicine.
title: What is the history of DSIP?
text: DSIP was discovered in the 1970s out of a long-standing question in sleep science: whether sleep is driven by a chemical that circulates in the blood. Working in Switzerland, the physiologist Marcel Monnier and colleagues ran cross-circulation experiments in rabbits, electrically stimulating a sleep-related region of the brain in one animal and passing its blood to a second, which then showed the slow, high-amplitude "delta" brain waves of deep sleep. That pointed to a sleep-promoting substance carried in the blood.
In 1977, Guido Schoenenberger, Monnier, and their co-workers isolated and synthesized that substance, a nine-amino-acid peptide they named delta sleep-inducing peptide after the delta-wave sleep it was linked to. Having a synthetic version made the peptide available for wider study.
Over the following decades, researchers looked beyond sleep, exploring possible roles in stress, body temperature, pain, and antioxidant activity, but the findings never converged into a validated mechanism or an approved therapy. DSIP was later shown to occur naturally in humans as well as animals. Despite nearly fifty years of study, it remains an experimental compound rather than a medicine, sold today through wellness and "research peptide" channels.
title: How does it work?
text: DSIP has been proposed to play roles in:
- Regulating sleep
- Modulating the body's stress (HPA-axis) responses
- Acting as an antioxidant
It has no validated receptor or defined mechanism. The sleep association that gave it its name comes from early animal work that has not resolved into a clear understanding of how, or whether, it influences human sleep. This describes a proposed mechanism, separate from any demonstrated benefit.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No. DSIP is not approved by the FDA and is not approved as a drug in any country; it is sold only through research and gray-market channels and is not on FDA compounding lists. As a neutral regulatory note, a related sleep compound was reviewed at a 2026 FDA compounding advisory meeting and received an unfavorable vote.
title: What does the research show?
text: The human evidence is thin and old. A small number of studies from the 1980s and 1990s examined DSIP in insomnia, chronic pain, and withdrawal states and reported inconsistent findings; most were small and uncontrolled, and no modern, well-conducted trials have established a reproducible benefit. There is no sound human evidence that DSIP improves sleep or stress.

detail.sections:
title: What is ecallantide?
text: Ecallantide, sold under the brand Kalbitor, is a recombinant 60-amino-acid protein that inhibits plasma kallikrein, an enzyme central to the swelling of hereditary angioedema (HAE). It is used to treat acute HAE attacks. Because it can cause anaphylaxis, it is given by a healthcare professional rather than self-administered. It was developed under the code DX-88 and approved in the United States in 2009.
title: How does ecallantide work?
text: Ecallantide blocks plasma kallikrein, an enzyme that cleaves a protein called high-molecular-weight kininogen to release bradykinin. Bradykinin is the mediator that causes the blood vessels to leak and the tissues to swell in hereditary angioedema. By inhibiting kallikrein, ecallantide reduces the generation of bradykinin and thereby controls the acute attack.
This upstream action distinguishes it from drugs that block the bradykinin receptor directly. In the EDEMA3 trial, ecallantide significantly improved both symptom-severity and treatment-outcome scores compared with placebo. Because the molecule can provoke severe allergic reactions that may resemble an HAE attack, administration in a supervised setting is required.

peptides.key_takeaway: The echinocandins (caspofungin, micafungin, and anidulafungin; sold as Cancidas, Mycamine, and Eraxis) are antifungal lipopeptides that attack the fungal cell wall, a structure human cells lack. They are a preferred option for invasive Candida infections and are generally well tolerated. All three have been FDA-approved in the U.S. since the 2000s, a fourth (rezafungin, sold as Rezzayo) was approved in 2023, and all are given intravenously.
peptides.mechanism: Echinocandins target the fungal cell wall, specifically the enzyme 1,3-beta-D-glucan synthase. This enzyme builds 1,3-beta-D-glucan, a structural sugar polymer that gives the fungal wall its integrity. By blocking it, echinocandins weaken the wall until the fungal cell can no longer withstand internal pressure and ruptures. They are fungicidal against most Candida species and fungistatic against Aspergillus. A key advantage is selectivity: human cells have no cell wall and no equivalent of this enzyme, so echinocandins cause relatively little direct toxicity to the patient. Caspofungin, micafungin, and anidulafungin are given intravenously once daily, and rezafungin once weekly. In its pivotal trial, caspofungin was at least as effective as amphotericin B for invasive candidiasis while causing fewer adverse effects, and anidulafungin outperformed fluconazole on the primary measure in its own trial.

detail.sections:
title: What are the echinocandins?
text: The echinocandins are a class of antifungal drugs, semi-synthetic cyclic lipopeptides, that includes caspofungin (Cancidas), micafungin (Mycamine), and anidulafungin (Eraxis). They are used mainly for serious Candida infections and have become a preferred option because they combine strong activity with a clean safety profile. Caspofungin, the first in the class, was approved in the United States in 2001, followed by micafungin in 2005 and anidulafungin in 2006. A newer member of the class, rezafungin (Rezzayo), was approved in 2023 and is given once a week.
title: How do they work?
text: Echinocandins target the fungal cell wall, specifically the enzyme 1,3-beta-D-glucan synthase. This enzyme builds 1,3-beta-D-glucan, a structural sugar polymer that gives the fungal wall its integrity. By blocking it, echinocandins weaken the wall until the fungal cell can no longer withstand internal pressure and ruptures. They are fungicidal against most Candida species and fungistatic against Aspergillus.
A key advantage is selectivity: human cells have no cell wall and no equivalent of this enzyme, so echinocandins cause relatively little direct toxicity to the patient. Caspofungin, micafungin, and anidulafungin are given intravenously once daily, and rezafungin once weekly. In its pivotal trial, caspofungin was at least as effective as amphotericin B for invasive candidiasis while causing fewer adverse effects, and anidulafungin outperformed fluconazole on the primary measure in its own trial.

text: Yes. Caspofungin, micafungin, and anidulafungin are all FDA-approved, as is rezafungin; the table shows each one's approval year and approved uses.
Drug | FDA approval | Approved uses include
Caspofungin | 2001 | Candidemia, invasive candidiasis, and esophageal candidiasis; additionally, empiric therapy in febrile neutropenia and invasive aspergillosis refractory to or intolerant of other therapy
Micafungin | 2005 | Candidemia, invasive candidiasis, and esophageal candidiasis; additionally, Candida prophylaxis in stem-cell transplant recipients
Anidulafungin | 2006 | Candidemia, invasive candidiasis, and esophageal candidiasis
Rezafungin | 2023 | Candidemia and invasive candidiasis in adults with limited or no other treatment options
None carry a boxed warning.
title: What are they prescribed for?
text: Echinocandins are prescribed for invasive Candida infections, including candidemia, and for esophageal candidiasis. Caspofungin is also used for suspected fungal infection in neutropenic fever and for certain Aspergillus infections, and micafungin for preventing Candida infection during stem-cell transplantation.

peptides.key_takeaway: Efpeglenatide is an investigational long-acting GLP-1 receptor agonist, originally developed by Hanmi Pharmaceutical, given as a once-weekly injection for type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular risk. In a large Phase 3 outcomes trial it reduced major cardiovascular events in people with type 2 diabetes. As of 2026, it has not reached approval in major markets.
peptides.mechanism: Efpeglenatide activates the GLP-1 receptor, the same incretin target as drugs such as semaglutide and dulaglutide. Activation of the receptor: - Enhances glucose-dependent insulin secretion - Suppresses glucagon - Slows gastric emptying - Reduces appetite In people with type 2 diabetes these effects lower blood sugar and body weight, and GLP-1 agonists as a class have also shown cardiovascular benefits. This describes the mechanism, separate from the trial outcomes below.

title: What is efpeglenatide?
text: Efpeglenatide is an experimental GLP-1 receptor agonist built on an exendin-based peptide with a half-life-extension technology that allows once-weekly injection. It was developed by Hanmi Pharmaceutical and was previously licensed to Sanofi, which later returned the rights. It has been studied for type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular and kidney risk, and it is investigational, not approved in major markets.
title: How does it work?
text: Efpeglenatide activates the GLP-1 receptor, the same incretin target as drugs such as semaglutide and dulaglutide. Activation of the receptor:

text: No. Efpeglenatide is investigational and not approved by the FDA or EMA. After Sanofi returned development rights, Hanmi took the program back in-house and has pursued regional licensing arrangements, but no major-market approval exists.

peptides.fda_status:
Yes, for one use, through the accelerated pathway. The FDA granted elamipretide accelerated approval on September 19, 2025, as Forzinity, to improve muscle strength in adults and children with Barth syndrome who weigh at least 30 kg. It is the first approved treatment for the condition. The regulatory path was contentious:
- An earlier submission was turned down after the drug missed a walking-distance endpoint.
- The approval was ultimately based on a knee-extensor muscle-strength measure.
- A confirmatory randomized trial was required after approval.
Its other studied uses are not approved.
peptides.evidence_note: It is approved (accelerated approval) for Barth syndrome, though that approval rests on a muscle-strength surrogate and small open-label data, with the randomized trial having missed its primary endpoints and a confirmatory trial still pending; its non-Barth uses remain unproven.
peptides.what_it_is: A mitochondria-targeting tetrapeptide, sold as Forzinity
peptides.key_takeaway: Elamipretide is a mitochondria-targeting peptide that binds cardiolipin, a key molecule in the energy-producing inner membrane of mitochondria, developed by Stealth BioTherapeutics. It received FDA accelerated approval in 2025 as Forzinity for Barth syndrome, a rare genetic disorder of cardiolipin, making it the first approved treatment for that condition. Its approval rests on a muscle-strength surrogate measure with a confirmatory trial still required, and its other studied uses remain investigational.
peptides.mechanism: Elamipretide binds cardiolipin in the inner mitochondrial membrane and helps stabilize the folded structure (cristae) where energy production takes place. By supporting that architecture, it is intended to improve the efficiency of the electron transport chain that generates ATP and to reduce harmful reactive oxygen species. In Barth syndrome, which is caused by mutations in the TAFAZZIN gene that disrupt cardiolipin remodeling, this mechanism is the rationale for treatment. Mechanism describes how the drug is thought to act, separate from the clinical outcomes that trials measure.

detail.sections:
title: What is elamipretide?
text: Elamipretide is a small peptide designed to concentrate inside mitochondria, the energy-producing structures of cells, where it binds a membrane lipid called cardiolipin. It is developed by Stealth BioTherapeutics and is given by subcutaneous injection. Its approved use is Barth syndrome, a rare genetic disorder of cardiolipin that affects the heart, muscles, and immune system; it has also been studied in other mitochondrial and eye diseases, where it remains investigational.
title: How does elamipretide work?
text: Elamipretide binds cardiolipin in the inner mitochondrial membrane and helps stabilize the folded structure (cristae) where energy production takes place. By supporting that architecture, it is intended to improve the efficiency of the electron transport chain that generates ATP and to reduce harmful reactive oxygen species. In Barth syndrome, which is caused by mutations in the TAFAZZIN gene that disrupt cardiolipin remodeling, this mechanism is the rationale for treatment. Mechanism describes how the drug is thought to act, separate from the clinical outcomes that trials measure.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: Yes, for one use, through the accelerated pathway. The FDA granted elamipretide accelerated approval on September 19, 2025, as Forzinity, to improve muscle strength in adults and children with Barth syndrome who weigh at least 30 kg. It is the first approved treatment for the condition. The regulatory path was contentious:
- An earlier submission was turned down after the drug missed a walking-distance endpoint.
- The approval was ultimately based on a knee-extensor muscle-strength measure.
- A confirmatory randomized trial was required after approval.
Its other studied uses are not approved.
title: What is elamipretide prescribed for?
text: Elamipretide is prescribed to improve muscle strength in adults and children with Barth syndrome who weigh at least 30 kg, under specialist care. It is not approved for the other conditions in which it has been studied, such as dry age-related macular degeneration or primary mitochondrial myopathy, where trials did not lead to approval.
title: What are the side effects?
text: According to the prescribing information, the most common side effects are:
- Injection-site reactions such as redness, pain, hardening, itching, bruising, and hives
More serious considerations include:
- Serious allergic reactions
- A benzyl alcohol preservative, so it is not approved for newborns

peptides.name: Enfuvirtide
peptides.fda_status: Enfuvirtide was approved by the FDA in 2003 for HIV-1 infection in treatment-experienced patients with ongoing viral replication despite antiretroviral therapy. Its maker discontinued Fuzeon in the U.S. on February 28, 2025, citing reduced need as newer treatments became available.
peptides.evidence_note: Enfuvirtide is FDA-approved for treatment-experienced HIV-1 infection, supported by the randomized TORO trials showing greater viral-load reduction.
peptides.what_it_is: An HIV-1 fusion (entry) inhibitor, a 36-amino-acid peptide
peptides.key_takeaway: Enfuvirtide (formerly sold as Fuzeon) is a peptide HIV drug that blocks the virus from entering CD4 immune cells, the first of the so-called fusion inhibitors. It was used in treatment-experienced patients whose virus is no longer controlled by other antiretrovirals. It was FDA-approved in the U.S. in 2003, but Fuzeon was discontinued there in February 2025.
peptides.mechanism: Enfuvirtide blocks the step where HIV fuses its envelope with the membrane of a CD4 immune cell to get inside. The viral surface protein gp41 must fold on itself, forming a hairpin-like structure, to pull the two membranes together. Enfuvirtide mimics a segment of gp41 and binds the region the protein needs to grip, preventing that folding. Without it, the virus cannot complete fusion and cannot enter the cell. Because it works outside the cell at the point of entry, its mechanism is entirely different from the drugs that act inside the cell on reverse transcriptase, protease, or integrase, which is why it retains activity against virus resistant to those classes. In the TORO trials, adding enfuvirtide to an optimized background regimen produced a significantly greater reduction in HIV-1 RNA than the background regimen alone. It must be injected twice daily, which, with frequent injection-site reactions, limits its use to situations where other options are exhausted.
peptides.side_effects_safety: Common side effects include: - Injection-site reactions such as pain, hardened lumps, redness, and cysts, which occur in nearly all patients - Diarrhea and nausea - Fatigue More serious considerations include: - An increased rate of bacterial pneumonia - Hypersensitivity reactions, which can recur if the drug is restarted

detail.sections:
title: What is enfuvirtide?
text: Enfuvirtide, formerly sold under the brand Fuzeon, is a 36-amino-acid synthetic peptide that blocks HIV from entering host cells. It was the first in a class called fusion inhibitors (or entry inhibitors) and is used in people whose HIV has become resistant to multiple other drugs. It was developed under the code T-20 and approved in the United States in 2003.
title: How does enfuvirtide work?
text: Enfuvirtide blocks the step where HIV fuses its envelope with the membrane of a CD4 immune cell to get inside. The viral surface protein gp41 must fold on itself, forming a hairpin-like structure, to pull the two membranes together. Enfuvirtide mimics a segment of gp41 and binds the region the protein needs to grip, preventing that folding. Without it, the virus cannot complete fusion and cannot enter the cell.
Because it works outside the cell at the point of entry, its mechanism is entirely different from the drugs that act inside the cell on reverse transcriptase, protease, or integrase, which is why it retains activity against virus resistant to those classes. In the TORO trials, adding enfuvirtide to an optimized background regimen produced a significantly greater reduction in HIV-1 RNA than the background regimen alone. It must be injected twice daily, which, with frequent injection-site reactions, limits its use to situations where other options are exhausted.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: Enfuvirtide was approved by the FDA in 2003 for HIV-1 infection in treatment-experienced patients with ongoing viral replication despite antiretroviral therapy. Its maker discontinued Fuzeon in the U.S. on February 28, 2025, citing reduced need as newer treatments became available.
title: What is enfuvirtide prescribed for?
text: Enfuvirtide was prescribed, in combination with other antiretrovirals, for HIV-1 infection in treatment-experienced patients whose virus was replicating despite current therapy. It was generally reserved for people with multidrug-resistant HIV because of the twice-daily injections.
title: What are the side effects?
text: Common side effects include:
- Injection-site reactions such as pain, hardened lumps, redness, and cysts, which occur in nearly all patients
- Diarrhea and nausea
- Fatigue
More serious considerations include:
- An increased rate of bacterial pneumonia
- Hypersensitivity reactions, which can recur if the drug is restarted

peptides.fda_status: FDA-approved oral PCSK9 inhibitor, sold as Lipfendra, taken as a once-daily tablet
peptides.evidence_note: It is approved by the FDA to lower LDL cholesterol, supported by multiple large, positive Phase 3 trials showing LDL reductions comparable to injectable PCSK9 antibodies.
peptides.what_it_is: Macrocyclic peptide that blocks PCSK9, the first oral drug in a class previously limited to injections
peptides.research_at_a_glance: In Phase 3 trials, lowered LDL cholesterol by about 60%
peptides.key_takeaway: Enlicitide is an oral PCSK9 inhibitor, the first in its class that can be taken as a once-daily tablet rather than an injection, developed by Merck to lower LDL ("bad") cholesterol. In large Phase 3 trials it lowered LDL cholesterol by roughly 60%, comparable to injectable PCSK9 antibodies. It was approved by the FDA in 2026 under the brand name Lipfendra.
peptides.mechanism: Enlicitide binds circulating PCSK9 and stops it from attaching to the LDL receptor on liver cells. Normally PCSK9 marks those receptors for destruction, so blocking it lets more LDL receptors return to the cell surface and recycle. With more receptors available, the liver pulls more LDL cholesterol out of the blood, lowering LDL levels. Achieving this with a peptide small and stable enough to survive oral dosing is what distinguishes enlicitide from the injectable drugs in its class.
peptides.side_effects_safety: In the larger Phase 3 trial, CORALreef Lipids, side effects occurred at similar rates with enlicitide and placebo. In the trial of adults with HeFH, the most common side effects reported more often than with placebo were: - Dizziness (9% with enlicitide, 4% with placebo) - Diarrhea (7% with enlicitide, 2% with placebo) In both trials, similar proportions of people in the enlicitide and placebo groups stopped treatment because of a side effect. The prescribing information advises stopping enlicitide when pregnancy is recognized unless the benefits of treatment outweigh the potential risks to the fetus. It has the full safety details, and people should review their individual risks and other medications with their prescriber.

detail.sections:
title: What is enlicitide?
text: Enlicitide (development code MK-0616) is a cholesterol-lowering drug that blocks PCSK9, a protein that controls how the liver clears LDL cholesterol from the blood. It is notable as the first oral PCSK9 inhibitor: earlier drugs against this target are injectable antibodies or an injectable RNA therapy, while enlicitide is a specially engineered peptide taken as a once-daily tablet. It is made by Merck and sold under the brand name Lipfendra.
title: How does it work?
text: Enlicitide binds circulating PCSK9 and stops it from attaching to the LDL receptor on liver cells. Normally PCSK9 marks those receptors for destruction, so blocking it lets more LDL receptors return to the cell surface and recycle. With more receptors available, the liver pulls more LDL cholesterol out of the blood, lowering LDL levels. Achieving this with a peptide small and stable enough to survive oral dosing is what distinguishes enlicitide from the injectable drugs in its class.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: Yes. The FDA approved enlicitide in 2026 as Lipfendra, a once-daily oral PCSK9 inhibitor to reduce LDL cholesterol in adults with high cholesterol. A cardiovascular outcomes trial, testing whether the LDL lowering translates into fewer heart attacks and strokes, was reported to be ongoing at approval.
title: What is it prescribed for?
text: Enlicitide is prescribed, alongside diet and exercise, to lower LDL cholesterol in adults with hypercholesterolemia, including heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HeFH), an inherited form of high cholesterol. In its pivotal trials it was added to existing cholesterol-lowering treatment, usually a statin, in people who still needed further lowering. It offers an oral option for people who would otherwise need an injectable PCSK9 inhibitor to reach their LDL goals. It is taken under the direction of a clinician as part of overall cardiovascular risk management.
title: What are the side effects?
text: In the larger Phase 3 trial, CORALreef Lipids, side effects occurred at similar rates with enlicitide and placebo. In the trial of adults with HeFH, the most common side effects reported more often than with placebo were:
- Dizziness (9% with enlicitide, 4% with placebo)
- Diarrhea (7% with enlicitide, 2% with placebo)
In both trials, similar proportions of people in the enlicitide and placebo groups stopped treatment because of a side effect. The prescribing information advises stopping enlicitide when pregnancy is recognized unless the benefits of treatment outweigh the potential risks to the fetus. It has the full safety details, and people should review their individual risks and other medications with their prescriber.

detail.faq:
q: What is Epitalon?
a: Epitalon (also spelled Epithalon) is a synthetic tetrapeptide with the amino acid sequence alanine-glutamic acid-aspartic acid-glycine (AEDG). It was developed by Vladimir Khavinson's laboratory at the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology as a synthetic peptide designed from Epithalamin, a bovine pineal extract. Published research has examined putative effects on telomerase activity, circadian gene expression, and survival endpoints in animal models. It is not FDA-approved for any use in humans.
q: Does Epitalon activate telomerase in humans?
a: Epitalon has been shown to activate telomerase and elongate telomeres in human cell cultures, including a 2025 independent replication at Brunel University London. Whether this in-vitro effect translates to telomerase activation in living human tissues has not been established. No completed human clinical trial has measured telomere length before and after Epitalon administration under controlled conditions. The cell culture findings are meaningful as mechanistic evidence, but they do not confirm that Epitalon extends telomeres or activates telomerase in the bodies of people who use it.
q: Is Epitalon the same as Epithalamin?
a: No. Epithalamin is a polypeptide complex extracted from bovine pineal glands and studied by Russian researchers for decades. Epitalon is a synthetic tetrapeptide (AEDG) considered the putative active component of Epithalamin, designed from its amino acid composition. The human observational studies on longevity and cardiovascular aging that are often cited as evidence for Epitalon were conducted using Epithalamin, not synthetic AEDG. The two compounds are related but not identical, and the human data from Epithalamin trials cannot be directly attributed to synthetic Epitalon.
q: What does the human longevity data actually show?
a: The most-cited human longevity data for this compound family is a 6-8 year follow-up of 266 elderly persons treated with thymic and pineal peptide preparations (including Epithalamin), published by Khavinson and Morozov in 2003 in Neuroendocrinology Letters and available at PubMed. The reported mortality reduction ranged from 1.6- to 4.1-fold versus controls, depending on regimen. Although PubMed indexes it as a randomized clinical trial, the abstract describes no blinding or placebo arm and reports no p-values; the study used the parent pineal extract rather than synthetic Epitalon, was conducted by the same group that developed the compound, and has not been independently replicated. These are significant methodological limitations that prevent the data from being treated as established clinical evidence.
q: Is Epitalon legal to buy in the United States?
a: As of September 2026, Epitalon is not a federally controlled substance. It cannot legally be sold or marketed as a drug for human use without FDA approval. FDA removed Epitalon from its Category 2 list in April 2026 after the nomination was withdrawn, but it is not on the 503A bulks list or in FDA's Category 1, so it is not eligible for 503A compounding. FDA's advisory committee voted 7-4 on July 24, 2026 to recommend adding it for insomnia, the only use FDA evaluated, a non-binding vote that still requires rulemaking. Research chemical vendors sell Epitalon without prescription; these products are not FDA-approved, so no FDA review has assessed their quality.
q: Are there side effects associated with Epitalon?
a: No clinical safety studies of Epitalon in humans have been identified in the published literature. The Russian observational cohort studies and animal studies do not document significant adverse events at the doses studied. The absence of reported harms does not establish safety; it reflects the absence of adequately controlled human safety data. The long-term effects of Epitalon administration in humans, including effects on cell proliferation and oncogenesis given its telomerase-activating mechanism, have not been systematically studied.
q: How does Epitalon compare to other longevity peptides?
a: Epitalon's published evidence base is heavily concentrated within a single Russian research network. MOTS-c, humanin, and related mitochondrial-derived peptides are encoded in mitochondrial DNA and have a different mechanism of action. None of these compounds has completed a large-scale randomized controlled trial in humans demonstrating lifespan extension or reliable biological aging reversal. Comparing them based on current evidence would require treating animal and small in-vitro data as clinically equivalent, which they are not.
detail.sections:
title: What is epitalon?
text: Epitalon (also spelled epithalon) is a synthetic four-amino acid peptide derived from epithalamin, a natural extract of the pineal gland. It is sold through wellness and "research peptide" channels for anti-aging, longevity, and sleep, often described as a "peptide bioregulator." It is not an approved medicine.
title: How does it work?
text: Epitalon is proposed to:
- Help restore the body's melatonin rhythm
- Act as an antioxidant
- Influence gene expression, including claims of activating telomerase (an enzyme linked to cellular aging)
These mechanistic claims rest on cell-culture and animal work, with the telomerase findings coming from laboratory systems. This describes the proposed mechanism, separate from demonstrated benefit in people.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No. Epitalon is not approved by the FDA for any use. In July 2026 the FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee gave epitalon a narrow, non-binding favorable vote toward the 503A compounding list. Because that vote is only a recommendation and the FDA has not completed formal rulemaking, epitalon is not currently on the list and cannot be legally compounded by U.S. pharmacies on that basis.
title: What does the research show?
text: The human evidence is limited and single-source. The main human reports come from one Russian research group and include older studies on melatonin rhythm and age-related conditions; these are generally small, largely non-English, and not independently replicated with modern randomization and blinding. No independent, large, modern trial establishes a longevity or wellness benefit. The telomerase and lifespan claims rest mainly on laboratory and animal work.

peptides.what_it_is: A platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor antagonist, a cyclic heptapeptide antiplatelet drug
peptides.key_takeaway: Eptifibatide (sold as Integrilin) is a small cyclic peptide, modeled on a molecule from rattlesnake venom, that blocks the final step of platelet clumping to prevent dangerous clots during heart attacks and stenting. It is given intravenously in acute coronary syndrome and during coronary procedures. It has been FDA-approved in the U.S. since 1998, and its main risk is bleeding.
peptides.mechanism: Eptifibatide blocks the glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor on platelets, the receptor that represents the final common step in platelet aggregation. Normally, when platelets are activated, this receptor binds fibrinogen and links platelets together into a clot. Eptifibatide occupies the receptor and prevents that cross-linking, so platelets cannot aggregate even if they have been activated. The effect is potent but rapidly reversible once the infusion stops, because the drug binds the receptor reversibly. That makes it useful in the acute setting of a heart attack or a coronary stent procedure, where fresh clot formation on a disrupted plaque or a new stent is the danger. In the PURSUIT trial, eptifibatide reduced the combined rate of death or nonfatal heart attack at 30 days in acute coronary syndrome, at the cost of more bleeding. It is cleared by the kidneys, so dosing is reduced in kidney impairment.

text: Eptifibatide, sold under the brand Integrilin, is a cyclic seven-amino-acid peptide antiplatelet drug. It is used in heart attacks and during coronary stenting to prevent clots. It was approved in the United States in 1998.

peptides.fda_status: Yes. Etelcalcetide was approved by the FDA in 2017 for secondary hyperparathyroidism in adults on hemodialysis. It is administered as an intravenous bolus at the end of each dialysis session, three times a week.
peptides.evidence_note: Etelcalcetide is FDA-approved for secondary hyperparathyroidism in dialysis patients, supported by randomized trials including a head-to-head comparison with cinacalcet.
peptides.what_it_is: A peptide calcimimetic that activates the calcium-sensing receptor
peptides.key_takeaway: Etelcalcetide (sold as Parsabiv) is a peptide that activates the calcium-sensing receptor to lower parathyroid hormone, used for secondary hyperparathyroidism in people on dialysis for kidney disease. Unlike parathyroid hormone replacement, it suppresses an overactive parathyroid signal, and it is given intravenously at the end of each dialysis session. It has been FDA-approved in the U.S. since 2017.
peptides.mechanism: Etelcalcetide binds and activates the calcium-sensing receptor on the parathyroid glands, increasing the receptor's sensitivity to calcium. The glands interpret this as a signal that calcium is adequate and reduce their secretion of parathyroid hormone, which in turn lowers the high calcium and phosphate turnover that drives bone and cardiovascular problems in dialysis patients. This is the opposite approach to parathyroid hormone replacement: etelcalcetide turns the hormone down rather than supplying it. Because it is a peptide given intravenously into the dialysis circuit, it does not depend on a patient taking a daily pill, which can improve adherence. In a head-to-head randomized trial, intravenous etelcalcetide lowered parathyroid hormone at least as effectively as oral cinacalcet, with a greater proportion of patients achieving large reductions.

detail.sections:
title: What is etelcalcetide?
text: Etelcalcetide, sold under the brand Parsabiv, is a synthetic peptide "calcimimetic," a drug that makes the parathyroid glands behave as if blood calcium were higher than it is, so they release less parathyroid hormone. It is used in secondary hyperparathyroidism, a common complication of advanced kidney disease in which the parathyroid glands become overactive. It was developed under the codes AMG 416 and velcalcetide and approved in the United States in 2017.
title: How does etelcalcetide work?
text: Etelcalcetide binds and activates the calcium-sensing receptor on the parathyroid glands, increasing the receptor's sensitivity to calcium. The glands interpret this as a signal that calcium is adequate and reduce their secretion of parathyroid hormone, which in turn lowers the high calcium and phosphate turnover that drives bone and cardiovascular problems in dialysis patients. This is the opposite approach to parathyroid hormone replacement: etelcalcetide turns the hormone down rather than supplying it.
Because it is a peptide given intravenously into the dialysis circuit, it does not depend on a patient taking a daily pill, which can improve adherence. In a head-to-head randomized trial, intravenous etelcalcetide lowered parathyroid hormone at least as effectively as oral cinacalcet, with a greater proportion of patients achieving large reductions.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: Yes. Etelcalcetide was approved by the FDA in 2017 for secondary hyperparathyroidism in adults on hemodialysis. It is administered as an intravenous bolus at the end of each dialysis session, three times a week.
title: What is etelcalcetide prescribed for?
text: Etelcalcetide is prescribed for secondary hyperparathyroidism in adults with chronic kidney disease who are on hemodialysis. It is not recommended for people with kidney disease who are not on dialysis, or for primary hyperparathyroidism.
title: What are the side effects?
text: According to the prescribing information, common side effects include:
- Low blood calcium
- Muscle spasms
- Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea
- Headache
More serious considerations include:
- Serious low calcium, which can cause seizures or heart-rhythm changes, so calcium is monitored
- Worsening heart failure in some patients
- Upper gastrointestinal bleeding

peptides.fda_status: FDA-approved GLP-1 peptide, formerly sold as Byetta (twice-daily) and Bydureon (once-weekly) for type 2 diabetes
peptides.evidence_note: It is approved by the FDA for type 2 diabetes and was the first medicine in the GLP-1 class, supported by its randomized controlled trial program.
peptides.what_it_is:
Exenatide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist, a peptide that mimics the natural gut hormone GLP-1. It is a synthetic copy of exendin-4, a molecule first found in the venom of the Gila monster, a large venomous lizard native to the southwestern United States.
It was developed by Amylin Pharmaceuticals and Eli Lilly, later marketed by AstraZeneca, and sold as Byetta (a twice-daily injection) and Bydureon BCise (a once-weekly injection).
peptides.key_takeaway: Exenatide is the first GLP-1 receptor agonist ever approved, a synthetic copy of exendin-4 originally found in Gila monster venom, dosed twice daily as Byetta or once weekly as Bydureon. Approved in 2005, it launched the entire GLP-1 class and delivered modest reductions in blood sugar and weight. AstraZeneca discontinued both U.S. brands in 2024, and a generic of the twice-daily form has been sold since 2025.
peptides.mechanism:
Exenatide lowers blood sugar by activating the GLP-1 receptor, mimicking a gut hormone the body releases after meals. Through that receptor it triggers glucose-dependent insulin release, which keeps the risk of hypoglycemia low on its own, while lowering glucagon, slowing the rate at which the stomach empties, and reducing appetite.
Because it is based on the lizard peptide exendin-4 rather than human GLP-1, it resists the enzyme that rapidly breaks down natural GLP-1, so it lasts long enough to be dosed twice daily. The extended-release Bydureon formulation encases the peptide in tiny microspheres that release it slowly, allowing once-weekly dosing. In its trials it produced moderate reductions in A1c along with some weight loss.

Exenatide is the original GLP-1 drug, and the medicines that followed have largely surpassed it on both effectiveness and convenience.
The clearest difference is potency, especially for weight. Exenatide produces relatively modest reductions in blood sugar and weight. The newer drugs reached larger average weight loss in their weight-management trials:
Drug | Average weight loss
Liraglutide, a once-daily drug based on human GLP-1 | About 8%
Once-weekly semaglutide | About 15%
Tirzepatide | Up to about 22.5%
These figures come from separate trials rather than direct head-to-head studies, but the trend is consistent: the newer agents lower weight and blood sugar more.
Mechanism is part of the story. Exenatide, liraglutide, and semaglutide all act only on the GLP-1 receptor, while tirzepatide activates a second gut-hormone receptor, GIP, as well, which is thought to contribute to its larger effect. Exenatide is also distinctive in its origin, since it is based on the lizard peptide exendin-4, whereas liraglutide and semaglutide are engineered from human GLP-1.
Convenience shifted too. Exenatide started as a twice-daily injection, with a later once-weekly version, while liraglutide is once-daily and both semaglutide and tirzepatide are once-weekly, and semaglutide additionally comes as a daily pill.
Finally, the class has moved well beyond blood sugar. Liraglutide and semaglutide carry cardiovascular indications, semaglutide is also approved for chronic kidney disease and fatty liver disease, and tirzepatide is approved for obstructive sleep apnea. Exenatide's brands, by contrast, were discontinued in the U.S. in 2024, and it is effectively a first-generation drug that the newer options have replaced.

detail.safety_side_effects:
The most common side effects are gastrointestinal, with nausea especially common:
- Nausea
- Vomiting
- Diarrhea
- Feeling jittery
- Dizziness
- Headache
- Decreased appetite
Less common but more serious risks include:
- Pancreatitis, or inflammation of the pancreas
- Low blood sugar, especially when combined with a sulfonylurea
- Acute kidney injury, usually from dehydration caused by vomiting or diarrhea
- Gallbladder problems, including gallstones
- Injection-site lumps with the extended-release form

detail.sections:
title: What is exenatide?
text: Exenatide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist, a peptide that mimics the natural gut hormone GLP-1. It is a synthetic copy of exendin-4, a molecule first found in the venom of the Gila monster, a large venomous lizard native to the southwestern United States.
It was developed by Amylin Pharmaceuticals and Eli Lilly, later marketed by AstraZeneca, and sold as Byetta (a twice-daily injection) and Bydureon BCise (a once-weekly injection).
title: The history of exenatide
text: Exenatide began with a lizard. In the early 1990s, the endocrinologist John Eng studied the venom of the Gila monster and identified a hormone-like peptide, exendin-4, that closely resembled human GLP-1 but lasted far longer in the body. Human GLP-1 breaks down within minutes, but the lizard version persisted for hours, which made it a practical drug candidate.
That discovery became exenatide, and in 2005, Byetta became the first GLP-1 drug approved by the FDA, launching the entire class that now includes liraglutide, semaglutide, and tirzepatide. A once-weekly version, Bydureon, followed in 2012. In 2024, AstraZeneca discontinued both Byetta and Bydureon BCise in the U.S. for business reasons. A generic version of Byetta launched in May 2025, so twice-daily exenatide is still available.
title: How does it work?
text: Exenatide lowers blood sugar by activating the GLP-1 receptor, mimicking a gut hormone the body releases after meals. Through that receptor it triggers glucose-dependent insulin release, which keeps the risk of hypoglycemia low on its own, while lowering glucagon, slowing the rate at which the stomach empties, and reducing appetite.
Because it is based on the lizard peptide exendin-4 rather than human GLP-1, it resists the enzyme that rapidly breaks down natural GLP-1, so it lasts long enough to be dosed twice daily. The extended-release Bydureon formulation encases the peptide in tiny microspheres that release it slowly, allowing once-weekly dosing. In its trials it produced moderate reductions in A1c along with some weight loss.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: Yes. Byetta was approved in 2005 as the first GLP-1 drug, and the once-weekly Bydureon followed in 2012. AstraZeneca discontinued both in the U.S. market in 2024 for commercial reasons, not because of a safety problem. A generic version of twice-daily exenatide is now sold.
title: What is exenatide prescribed for?
text: Exenatide is prescribed to improve blood sugar control in adults with type 2 diabetes, alongside diet and exercise. It is not a treatment for type 1 diabetes. For the long-acting Bydureon form, it should not be used by people with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2.
title: What are the side effects?
text: The most common side effects are gastrointestinal, with nausea especially common:
- Nausea
- Vomiting
- Diarrhea
- Feeling jittery
- Dizziness
- Headache
- Decreased appetite
Less common but more serious risks include:
- Pancreatitis, or inflammation of the pancreas
- Low blood sugar, especially when combined with a sulfonylurea
- Acute kidney injury, usually from dehydration caused by vomiting or diarrhea
- Gallbladder problems, including gallstones
- Injection-site lumps with the extended-release form
- For the extended-release Bydureon form, a boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumors based on rodent studies, which is not carried by the twice-daily Byetta
