peptides.name: Follistatin-344
peptides.fda_status: Non-FDA-approved peptide sold as a research chemical/performance drug
peptides.evidence_note: The myostatin-inhibition rationale is strong in animals, but there is no human efficacy evidence for the injectable peptide; the only human data come from small gene-therapy disease trials that do not transfer to the wellness use.
peptides.what_it_is: Myostatin-binding protein, marketed to remove a natural brake on muscle growth
peptides.research_at_a_glance: Human data come only from small gene-therapy disease trials, not the injectable peptide
peptides.key_takeaway: Follistatin-344 is a form of the natural protein follistatin that blocks myostatin, a brake on muscle growth, sold as a "research chemical" in the performance market for muscle gain. The strongest human data come from gene therapy, not the injectable peptide. In a small 2017 trial, six patients with sporadic inclusion body myositis gained a median 56.0 m per year on the 6-minute walk test after follistatin gene therapy, versus a 25.8 m decline in eight matched untreated controls (p = 0.01). It is not FDA-approved and is banned in sport.
peptides.mechanism: Myostatin normally limits how much muscle the body builds. By binding and neutralizing myostatin, follistatin is proposed to release that brake and allow greater muscle growth. This pathway is well supported in animal models, where disrupting myostatin signaling produces pronounced muscle growth. This describes the proposed mechanism, which comes from animal work, separate from proven outcomes in people using the injectable peptide.
peptides.human_study_findings: The human evidence belongs to gene therapy, not the peptide. According to PubMed, a small Phase 1/2a trial used a gene therapy delivering the follistatin (FS344) gene in six patients with Becker muscular dystrophy, reporting some walking improvements and muscle changes; follow-up reported ambulation data. This is a disease population and a gene-therapy delivery, not the injectable follistatin peptide sold for wellness, and it does not establish efficacy or safety of that peptide in healthy people. There are no controlled human trials of the injectable peptide. Two small studies of this gene therapy report walking results: Study | Patients | Design | Result Phase 1/2a trial in Becker muscular dystrophy | 6 treated | No placebo group | 4 of the 6 walked farther on the 6-minute walk test, by 29 m to 125 m; muscle biopsies showed less fibrosis Study in sporadic inclusion body myositis, an inflammatory muscle disease, published in 2017 | 6 treated, versus 8 matched, untreated controls | Same gene therapy alongside an exercise regimen; controls not randomized | Treated patients gained a median 56.0 m per year on the 6-minute walk test, versus a 25.8 m decline in controls (p = 0.01), with individual changes of 5 to 153 m The 2017 sample was tiny and the controls were not randomized, so that result is hypothesis-generating.

detail.sections:
title: What is follistatin-344?
text: Follistatin is a natural protein that binds and neutralizes myostatin and related factors. Follistatin-344 (FS344) refers to a specific 344-amino acid form used in research and gene-therapy work. In the performance market, an injectable "follistatin peptide" is sold for muscle growth, though it is a different, uncharacterized product from the gene-therapy material. It is not an approved medicine.
title: How does it work?
text: Myostatin normally limits how much muscle the body builds. By binding and neutralizing myostatin, follistatin is proposed to release that brake and allow greater muscle growth. This pathway is well supported in animal models, where disrupting myostatin signaling produces pronounced muscle growth. This describes the proposed mechanism, which comes from animal work, separate from proven outcomes in people using the injectable peptide.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No. Follistatin-344 is not approved by the FDA as a drug. Its status by form and setting:
- Injectable peptide: a research chemical and performance-enhancing drug with no recognized compounding status
- Gene therapy: remains investigational
- Sport: myostatin-binding proteins including follistatin are prohibited at all times under the WADA list
title: What does the research show?
text: The human evidence belongs to gene therapy, not the peptide. According to PubMed, a small Phase 1/2a trial used a gene therapy delivering the follistatin (FS344) gene in six patients with Becker muscular dystrophy, reporting some walking improvements and muscle changes; follow-up reported ambulation data. This is a disease population and a gene-therapy delivery, not the injectable follistatin peptide sold for wellness, and it does not establish efficacy or safety of that peptide in healthy people. There are no controlled human trials of the injectable peptide.
Two small studies of this gene therapy report walking results:
Study | Patients | Design | Result
Phase 1/2a trial in Becker muscular dystrophy | 6 treated | No placebo group | 4 of the 6 walked farther on the 6-minute walk test, by 29 m to 125 m; muscle biopsies showed less fibrosis
Study in sporadic inclusion body myositis, an inflammatory muscle disease, published in 2017 | 6 treated, versus 8 matched, untreated controls | Same gene therapy alongside an exercise regimen; controls not randomized | Treated patients gained a median 56.0 m per year on the 6-minute walk test, versus a 25.8 m decline in controls (p = 0.01), with individual changes of 5 to 153 m
The 2017 sample was tiny and the controls were not randomized, so that result is hypothesis-generating.

peptides.name: Fragment 176-191
peptides.fda_status: Non-FDA-approved peptide sold in the wellness/gray market
peptides.evidence_note: The fat-metabolism rationale is supported only by animal and laboratory work, there is no human efficacy evidence for the fragment itself, and its optimized cousin failed in human trials.
peptides.what_it_is: C-terminal fragment of the growth hormone molecule, marketed for fat loss
peptides.research_at_a_glance: Evidence is animal and laboratory only; its optimized cousin AOD-9604 failed human trials
peptides.key_takeaway: Fragment 176-191 is the unmodified tail piece of human growth hormone, sold on the wellness market as a fat-loss "research peptide." Its evidence is limited to animal and laboratory work. In rat fat-pad experiments, a close relative (hGH 177-191) matched whole growth hormone's antilipogenic activity but showed no significant lipolytic effect (Wu and Ng, 1993). Its modified cousin, AOD-9604, failed in human obesity trials. As of 2026 the fragment is not FDA-approved and is banned in sport.
peptides.mechanism:
The proposed theory is that the fat-related activity of growth hormone is concentrated in this tail fragment, so the fragment alone might reduce fat storage without the hormone's growth or glucose effects. In rat studies, the fragment was shown to carry the anti-fat-storage activity of the parent hormone, localizing that function to the C-terminal region. The tested peptide was hGH 177-191, a close relative of this fragment, and it showed no significant lipolytic effect in rat fat pads. These are animal and cell findings. This describes the proposed mechanism, separate from proven outcomes.
The more detailed mechanism data belong to AOD-9604, the modified version, and not to the bare fragment. In obese Zucker rats, AOD-9604 cut weight gain over 50% in 19 days and raised lipolytic activity in adipose tissue, without the insulin-sensitivity harm seen with intact growth hormone. In obese mice, AOD-9604 increased fat oxidation and plasma glycerol, a marker of fat breakdown, and it did not compete for the growth hormone receptor or drive cell proliferation.
peptides.human_study_findings: The evidence is preclinical. Animal work localized the anti-lipogenic activity of growth hormone to this C-terminal fragment, and the closest human data belong to its modified version, AOD-9604, whose obesity trials failed to beat placebo. There are no controlled human trials of the bare fragment for fat loss, so its marketed benefit is unproven. The human data belong to AOD-9604, as reported in a review of obesity drug development. AOD-9604 trial | Result 12-week trial | AOD-9604 recipients lost 2.6 kg against 0.8 kg on placebo 24-week trial of 536 people | Failed to produce significant weight loss, which ended the obesity program Those results do not describe the bare fragment, which has not been tested in controlled human trials.

detail.sections:
title: What is Fragment 176-191?
text: Fragment 176-191 is the C-terminal (tail) fragment of human growth hormone, sold on the "research peptide" market for fat loss. It is closely related to AOD-9604, which is this fragment with an added stabilizing amino acid; the two are often conflated and sold interchangeably, but AOD-9604 is the engineered, better-studied version. Much of what vendors label "176-191" is pharmacologically the same fat-metabolism concept.
title: How does it work?
text: The proposed theory is that the fat-related activity of growth hormone is concentrated in this tail fragment, so the fragment alone might reduce fat storage without the hormone's growth or glucose effects. In rat studies, the fragment was shown to carry the anti-fat-storage activity of the parent hormone, localizing that function to the C-terminal region. The tested peptide was hGH 177-191, a close relative of this fragment, and it showed no significant lipolytic effect in rat fat pads. These are animal and cell findings. This describes the proposed mechanism, separate from proven outcomes.
The more detailed mechanism data belong to AOD-9604, the modified version, and not to the bare fragment. In obese Zucker rats, AOD-9604 cut weight gain over 50% in 19 days and raised lipolytic activity in adipose tissue, without the insulin-sensitivity harm seen with intact growth hormone. In obese mice, AOD-9604 increased fat oxidation and plasma glycerol, a marker of fat breakdown, and it did not compete for the growth hormone receptor or drive cell proliferation.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No. Fragment 176-191 is not approved by the FDA; it is a "research chemical" with no approved drug or recognized compounding status, sold through gray-market channels. AOD-9604, the modified version, was developed by Metabolic Pharmaceuticals as an obesity drug, but its development was terminated in 2007 after it failed to show efficacy. In sport, growth hormone fragments including "hGH 176-191" are prohibited at all times under the WADA list.
title: What does the research show?
text: The evidence is preclinical. Animal work localized the anti-lipogenic activity of growth hormone to this C-terminal fragment, and the closest human data belong to its modified version, AOD-9604, whose obesity trials failed to beat placebo. There are no controlled human trials of the bare fragment for fat loss, so its marketed benefit is unproven.
The human data belong to AOD-9604, as reported in a review of obesity drug development.

24-week trial of 536 people | Failed to produce significant weight loss, which ended the obesity program
Those results do not describe the bare fragment, which has not been tested in controlled human trials.

detail.sections:
title: What is gallium Ga-68 dotatate?
text: Gallium Ga-68 dotatate, sold under the brand NETSPOT, is a diagnostic radiopharmaceutical: a somatostatin analog (dotatate) chemically linked to the radioactive isotope gallium-68, which emits positrons that a PET scanner can detect. It is used to find neuroendocrine tumors, which often carry large numbers of somatostatin receptors on their surface. It was approved in the United States in 2016.
title: How does gallium Ga-68 dotatate work?
text: The dotatate portion of the molecule binds with high affinity to somatostatin receptor subtype 2, which is overexpressed on well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor cells. When injected, the tracer concentrates wherever those receptors are abundant, and the attached gallium-68 emits positrons that produce a signal on a PET scan. The result is a map that highlights tumor sites throughout the body, including small lesions that other imaging can miss.
This receptor-targeted approach is more sensitive than the older somatostatin imaging agents. In a prospective study, gallium-68 dotatate PET/CT performed at least as well as, and often better than, the earlier indium-111 agent and changed management in about a third of patients. It is a diagnostic tool and is not itself a treatment, though its target is the same one used by the companion therapy lutetium Lu-177 dotatate.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: Yes. Gallium Ga-68 dotatate (NETSPOT) was approved by the FDA in 2016 for the localization of somatostatin-receptor-positive neuroendocrine tumors by PET in adult and pediatric patients. It is given as a single intravenous injection before the scan.
title: What is gallium Ga-68 dotatate used for?
text: It is used to locate and help stage neuroendocrine tumors that express somatostatin receptors, and to help select patients for somatostatin-targeted treatment. Long-acting somatostatin analog medications can interfere with tracer uptake, so their timing around the scan is considered.
title: What are the side effects?
text: No serious adverse reactions were identified in its clinical studies, according to the prescribing information. Side effects reported since approval include:
- Pain or a burning sensation at the injection site
- Nausea and vomiting
More serious considerations include:
- Radiation exposure, inherent to any radiopharmaceutical, kept as low as reasonably achievable
- Hypersensitivity reactions, mostly rash and itching, and less often swelling or anaphylaxis-like reactions

peptides.fda_status: Yes. Ganirelix, developed by Organon, was approved by the FDA in 1999. It is approved as a 0.25 mg once-daily subcutaneous injection for use during controlled ovarian stimulation. The Antagon brand name is no longer used in the U.S., where the product is now sold as ganirelix acetate injection and as Fyremadel.

peptides.what_it_is: A GnRH receptor antagonist peptide used in assisted reproduction
peptides.key_takeaway: Ganirelix (originally approved as Antagon) is a synthetic decapeptide that blocks the gonadotropin-releasing hormone receptor, used during fertility treatment to stop an egg from being released too early. Given once daily during ovarian stimulation, it prevents the premature luteinizing hormone surge that could otherwise disrupt an IVF cycle. It has been FDA-approved in the U.S. since 1999 and is given as a small daily subcutaneous injection.
peptides.mechanism: Ganirelix competitively blocks GnRH receptors on the pituitary, rapidly suppressing the release of luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone. During an IVF cycle, the ovaries are stimulated with injectable hormones to grow multiple follicles; if the body's own luteinizing hormone surges before those follicles are ready, ovulation can happen too early and the cycle can be lost. Giving ganirelix during stimulation holds that surge in check so eggs can be retrieved at the planned time. Because it is an antagonist, its effect is immediate and reversible, which allows a shorter, more flexible protocol than the older agonist-based approach that first had to suppress the pituitary over days. In a North American phase 3 trial, ganirelix compared with a long leuprolide protocol as follows: Outcome | Ganirelix vs long leuprolide protocol Ongoing pregnancy rates | Comparable Number of injections | Fewer Injection-site reactions | Fewer

peptides.side_effects_safety: According to the prescribing information, common side effects include: - Injection-site reactions - Headache - Nausea - Abdominal or pelvic discomfort More serious considerations include: - Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, a risk of the overall stimulation cycle rather than of ganirelix specifically - Hypersensitivity reactions Ganirelix is contraindicated in pregnancy.

detail.sections:
title: What is ganirelix?
text: Ganirelix, known generically as ganirelix acetate and originally approved under the brand Antagon (marketed in some regions as Orgalutran), is a synthetic ten-amino-acid peptide that antagonizes the gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) receptor. It is used specifically in assisted reproductive technology to control the timing of ovulation. It was developed under the code Org 37462 and approved in the United States in 1999. In the U.S. it is now sold as ganirelix acetate injection and under the brand Fyremadel.
title: How does ganirelix work?
text: Ganirelix competitively blocks GnRH receptors on the pituitary, rapidly suppressing the release of luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone. During an IVF cycle, the ovaries are stimulated with injectable hormones to grow multiple follicles; if the body's own luteinizing hormone surges before those follicles are ready, ovulation can happen too early and the cycle can be lost. Giving ganirelix during stimulation holds that surge in check so eggs can be retrieved at the planned time.
Because it is an antagonist, its effect is immediate and reversible, which allows a shorter, more flexible protocol than the older agonist-based approach that first had to suppress the pituitary over days. In a North American phase 3 trial, ganirelix compared with a long leuprolide protocol as follows:

Number of injections | Fewer

text: Ganirelix is prescribed to inhibit premature luteinizing hormone surges in women undergoing controlled ovarian stimulation as part of assisted reproduction. It is used only during the stimulation phase of a treatment cycle, not on an ongoing basis.

detail.faq:
q: What is GHK-Cu and how does it work in the body?
a: GHK-Cu is a naturally occurring copper-binding tripeptide consisting of glycine, histidine, and lysine complexed with a copper(II) ion, first identified in human plasma in the 1970s. Plasma concentrations decline with age, falling from approximately 200 ng/mL at age 20 to around 80 ng/mL by age 60. In lab and animal studies, GHK-Cu is proposed to act as a copper complex that modulates matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) and their inhibitors, and it affects genes involved in anti-inflammatory and antioxidant defense. Rather than operating through a single pathway, GHK-Cu appears to play a broad regulatory role across multiple biological processes.
q: What does the research show about GHK-Cu and collagen production?
a: Preclinical and early clinical research shows GHK-Cu is associated with increased collagen type I and III synthesis, starting at very low concentrations. In cultured fibroblasts, GHK-Cu stimulated collagen synthesis beginning between 10⁻¹² and 10⁻¹¹ M, with peak effect at 10⁻⁹ M, independent of cell number changes. In a rat wound-chamber study, GHK-Cu raised collagen content in a concentration-dependent way compared with saline controls, increased type I and III collagen mRNA without increasing TGF-beta mRNA, and stimulated collagen synthesis twice as much as non-collagen protein synthesis. Gene-expression data from the Broad Institute's Connectivity Map suggest GHK alters 31.2% of human genes at a ≥50% threshold, and in a thigh-skin biopsy study, collagen production increased in 70% of GHK-Cu-treated women versus 50% with vitamin C cream and 40% with retinoic acid. Most collagen evidence remains in vitro, and human data are essentially limited to topical cosmetic contexts.
q: How does GHK-Cu affect wound healing?
a: GHK-Cu has a relatively well-documented research record in wound repair, with animal studies showing accelerated wound closure and reduced inflammatory markers. In a rat study, topical application of 2% GHK-Cu gel (Iamin) to full-thickness ischemic wounds in 24 Sprague-Dawley rats resulted in 64.5% wound area reduction at day 13, compared to 45.6% for vehicle control and 28.2% for untreated controls. The treated wounds also showed significantly lower concentrations of TNF-alpha and matrix metalloproteinases MMP-2 and MMP-9. However, human clinical data on wound healing remains limited, with most evidence derived from in vitro and animal studies.
q: Can GHK-Cu help with hair thinning or hair loss?
a: Animal and lab studies suggest copper peptides may support hair follicle activity, though human clinical data are limited. In fuzzy rats, a copper-binding peptide called PC1031 enlarged hair follicles similarly to topical minoxidil. In an ex vivo study, AHK-Cu, a related copper tripeptide, stimulated elongation of human hair follicles, apparently by promoting dermal papilla cell proliferation and limiting their cell death, while an earlier mouse study reported hair follicle-stimulating properties of peptide copper complexes. However, human randomized controlled trial data for GHK-Cu specifically are lacking.
q: How does GHK-Cu compare to retinol for skin aging?
a: GHK-Cu and retinoids address skin aging through distinct mechanisms and carry different tolerability profiles. Retinoids, including retinol and prescription tretinoin, act through nuclear retinoic acid receptors, and irritation is a known trade-off. In a 48-week randomized controlled trial of 99 people with photoaging, 0.1% and 0.025% tretinoin improved photoaging similarly, but erythema and scaling were significantly greater with the 0.1% strength. GHK-Cu is proposed to work through copper delivery and gene regulation. Three 12-week topical GHK-Cu studies, described as placebo-controlled and enrolling 41 to 71 women each, reported improvements in skin laxity, clarity, firmness, and fine lines. Retinoids benefit from a larger evidence base and an FDA-approved prescription form, tretinoin. Cross-study comparisons require caution given different formulations, populations, and study designs.
q: What anti-inflammatory effects does GHK-Cu have?
a: GHK-Cu modulates NF-κB signaling and is associated with downregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines in tissue studies. In a mouse lung-injury study, it lowered TNF-alpha and IL-6 by suppressing NF-κB signaling, and in rat ischemic wounds it lowered TNF-alpha. A 2012 review of Broad Institute Connectivity Map data from PC3 and MCF7 cells (GHK at 1 μM) reported 268 genes with increased expression and 167 suppressed. In rat wound tissue, GHK also raised superoxide dismutase and catalase levels, and across the 13,424 genes in the Connectivity Map data it stimulated 14 antioxidant genes. Among genes GHK changed by at least 50%, 59% were upregulated and 41% suppressed. However, this evidence is primarily at the local/tissue level; elevated CRP and systemic inflammatory markers are not direct targets, and clinical systemic anti-inflammatory effects have not been established.

title: What is GHK-Cu?
text: GHK-Cu is the tripeptide glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine bound to copper. It occurs naturally in the body and declines with age, and it is one of the most studied "copper peptides." This entry concerns the systemic, injectable wellness use for skin, hair, and tissue repair; the topical cosmetic form is cataloged separately under its ingredient name, Copper tripeptide-1. The injectable use is not an approved medicine.
title: How does it work?
text: In laboratory and animal models, GHK-Cu is described as a signal for tissue remodeling. It is reported to:
- Influence the extracellular matrix
- Deliver copper
- Act as an antioxidant and anti-inflammatory
- Support new blood-vessel formation
- Switch on gene programs linked to repair
These are cell and animal findings. This describes the proposed mechanism, separate from demonstrated benefit from systemic use in people.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No, not for systemic use. Injectable or systemic GHK-Cu is not an FDA-approved drug. Copper peptides sit in the contested peptide-compounding space; the FDA advisory committee reviewed several peptides in 2026, but those recommendations are non-binding and no additions to the compounding list have been finalized, so lawful compounding remains unsettled. (Topical cosmetic use is regulated separately as a cosmetic ingredient.)
title: What does the research show?
text: For systemic use, the evidence is preclinical. The table sets out what has been studied in each model, with both animal studies drawn from PubMed:
Model | Finding
Rat | Injected GHK-Cu transiently improved ligament-graft healing
Mouse | GHK-Cu reduced acute lung injury
Human | Data essentially limited to topical cosmetic and wound contexts; no robust human trials establish efficacy or safety of injected GHK-Cu for skin, hair, or tissue repair
The systemic benefit is therefore an extrapolation from cell and animal work.
detail.sources_note: Sources: a rat ligament-healing study (Journal of Orthopaedic Research, 2015, DOI: 10.1002/jor.22831) and a mouse lung-injury study (Oncotarget, 2016, DOI: 10.18632/oncotarget.11168), indexed on PubMed. This document is educational, is not medical advice or a health claim, and is not an offer to sell any product.

peptides.fda_status: Non-FDA-approved peptide (also known as pralmorelin) sold in the wellness/gray market

peptides.what_it_is: Ghrelin-receptor agonist/growth hormone-releasing peptide
peptides.key_takeaway: GHRP-2 (pralmorelin) is a synthetic ghrelin-mimic peptide that prompts the pituitary to release growth hormone, sold in the wellness market for muscle, recovery, and appetite. Its only genuine validated use is as a diagnostic test of growth hormone capacity (approved in Japan), not as a treatment, and there are no controlled trials supporting the marketed wellness benefits. As of 2026 it is not FDA-approved and is banned in sport.
peptides.mechanism: GHRP-2 activates the growth hormone secretagogue receptor (the ghrelin receptor) on the pituitary. Activating it has three reported effects: - It triggers a pulse of growth hormone, and growth hormone pulses raise IGF-1 downstream. - It tends to modestly raise other hormones such as cortisol and prolactin. - Like other ghrelin mimics, it can stimulate appetite. The marketed muscle and recovery claims are extrapolated from this hormone effect rather than demonstrated. This describes the proposed mechanism, separate from proven outcomes.
peptides.human_study_findings: The validated human data concern diagnosis, not treatment. According to PubMed, GHRP-2 is used to probe pituitary growth hormone reserve, as in a study of the growth hormone response, which is a diagnostic application rather than a wellness-outcome trial. There are no controlled human trials showing that GHRP-2 improves muscle, fat, recovery, or aging. The marketed uses rest on its ability to raise growth hormone, not on demonstrated benefit.

detail.sections:
title: What is GHRP-2?
text: GHRP-2, with the generic name pralmorelin, is a synthetic six-amino acid peptide that imitates ghrelin to stimulate growth hormone release. It is sold through wellness and "research peptide" channels and promoted for muscle gain, recovery, and increased appetite. Unlike most unapproved peptides, it has a narrow legitimate role: it is approved in Japan as a diagnostic agent to test the pituitary's growth hormone capacity.
title: How does it work?
text: GHRP-2 activates the growth hormone secretagogue receptor (the ghrelin receptor) on the pituitary. Activating it has three reported effects:
- It triggers a pulse of growth hormone, and growth hormone pulses raise IGF-1 downstream.
- It tends to modestly raise other hormones such as cortisol and prolactin.
- Like other ghrelin mimics, it can stimulate appetite.
The marketed muscle and recovery claims are extrapolated from this hormone effect rather than demonstrated. This describes the proposed mechanism, separate from proven outcomes.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No. GHRP-2 is not approved by the FDA; its only regulatory approval is as a diagnostic agent in Japan. The table below sets out its status with each regulator.
Regulator | Status
FDA | Not approved, with no approved product in the U.S., and not approved for performance or anti-aging
U.S. compounding rules | Treated as not eligible for routine 503A compounding
Japan | Approved as a diagnostic agent
WADA | Growth hormone-releasing peptides including GHRP-2 are prohibited in sport at all times under the WADA list
title: What does the research show?
text: The validated human data concern diagnosis, not treatment. According to PubMed, GHRP-2 is used to probe pituitary growth hormone reserve, as in a study of the growth hormone response, which is a diagnostic application rather than a wellness-outcome trial. There are no controlled human trials showing that GHRP-2 improves muscle, fat, recovery, or aging. The marketed uses rest on its ability to raise growth hormone, not on demonstrated benefit.
detail.sources_note: Sources: a study of GHRP-2 and the growth hormone response (Teramoto et al., Growth Hormone & IGF Research, 2023, DOI: 10.1016/j.ghir.2023.101545), indexed on PubMed; and the WADA Prohibited List. This document is educational, is not medical advice or a health claim, and is not an offer to sell any product.

peptides.name: GHRP-6
peptides.fda_status: Non-FDA-approved peptide sold in the wellness/gray market
peptides.evidence_note: Human data are limited to short studies of growth hormone release, with the marketed wellness benefits resting on animal and laboratory work.
peptides.what_it_is: Ghrelin-receptor agonist / growth hormone-releasing peptide that markedly increases appetite
peptides.research_at_a_glance: Human data are limited to short pharmacology studies; the marketed benefits are unproven
peptides.key_takeaway: GHRP-6 is one of the original synthetic ghrelin-mimic peptides, sold in the wellness market to raise the body's own growth hormone and stimulate appetite. Human data are limited to short studies of growth hormone release, with no controlled trials proving the marketed muscle, recovery, or anti-aging benefits. As of 2026 it is not FDA-approved and is banned in sport.
peptides.mechanism: GHRP-6 activates the growth hormone secretagogue receptor (the ghrelin receptor), prompting the pituitary to release growth hormone, and it is proposed to act partly by blunting the body's growth-hormone "brake," somatostatin. Compared with newer peptides it is less selective, notably: - Increasing appetite - Modestly raising cortisol - Modestly raising prolactin Laboratory work also describes growth hormone secretagogue receptors in heart and blood-vessel tissue, which is the basis for preclinical interest in other effects. The marketed benefits are extrapolated from the growth hormone rise. This describes the proposed mechanism, separate from proven outcomes.
peptides.human_study_findings: The human evidence is short pharmacology. According to PubMed, an infusion study in healthy men found GHRP-6 raised growth hormone and IGF-1 while the pituitary remained responsive, a hormone-level result rather than a clinical outcome. Cardiovascular and cell-protective effects are described mainly in preclinical work and reviews. No controlled human trials support the marketed muscle, fat, recovery, or anti-aging uses.

title: What is GHRP-6?
text: GHRP-6 is a synthetic six-amino acid peptide and one of the first growth hormone-releasing peptides developed. It is sold through wellness and "research peptide" channels and promoted for muscle gain, recovery, and appetite stimulation. It was never marketed as an approved drug.
title: How does it work?
text: GHRP-6 activates the growth hormone secretagogue receptor (the ghrelin receptor), prompting the pituitary to release growth hormone, and it is proposed to act partly by blunting the body's growth-hormone "brake," somatostatin.
Compared with newer peptides it is less selective, notably:
- Increasing appetite
- Modestly raising cortisol
- Modestly raising prolactin
Laboratory work also describes growth hormone secretagogue receptors in heart and blood-vessel tissue, which is the basis for preclinical interest in other effects. The marketed benefits are extrapolated from the growth hormone rise. This describes the proposed mechanism, separate from proven outcomes.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No. GHRP-6 is not approved by the FDA and has no approved product. It has been treated as not eligible for routine 503A compounding in the U.S. and is not approved for performance or anti-aging. In sport, growth hormone-releasing peptides including GHRP-6 are prohibited at all times under the WADA list.
title: What does the research show?

detail.sections:
title: What is glepaglutide?
text: Glepaglutide is an experimental analog of glucagon-like peptide-2 (GLP-2), the hormone that supports intestinal growth and absorption. It is developed by Zealand Pharma under the code ZP1848 and is given by subcutaneous injection for short bowel syndrome with intestinal failure, where people depend on intravenous nutrition. It is in the same drug class as apraglutide and the approved GLP-2 drug teduglutide, and it is investigational and not approved.
title: How does it work?
text: Glepaglutide activates the GLP-2 receptor in the intestine. This signaling promotes growth and adaptation of the intestinal lining and increases nutrient and fluid absorption, with the goal of reducing dependence on intravenous feeding in short bowel syndrome. This describes the mechanism, separate from the trial results below.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No. Glepaglutide is investigational and not approved. According to company disclosures, the FDA issued a Complete Response Letter in December 2024, stating the application did not establish efficacy and safety of the intended dose, since the pivotal trial's once-weekly arm was not positive. Zealand has said it will run an additional Phase 3 trial.
title: What does the research show?
text: The main evidence is one Phase 3 trial with a mixed result. According to PubMed, the two studies found:
Study | Design | Result
EASE trial | Phase 3, testing glepaglutide twice weekly, once weekly, or placebo | The twice-weekly regimen met the primary endpoint, reducing weekly intravenous support volume versus placebo and improving key secondary measures, but the once-weekly regimen did not reach significance
Smaller study | Phase 3b | Reported increased energy absorption and reduced parenteral support over a year
The evidence rests on a single pivotal trial in which one of the two tested regimens was negative.
detail.sources_note: Sources: the EASE Phase 3 trial (Jeppesen et al., Gastroenterology, 2025, DOI: 10.1053/j.gastro.2024.11.023) and a Phase 3b metabolic-balance study (Pinar et al., Clinical Nutrition ESPEN, 2025, DOI: 10.1016/j.clnesp.2025.08.006), both indexed on PubMed; and Zealand Pharma regulatory updates. This document is educational, is not medical advice or a health claim, and is not an offer to sell any product.

peptides.name: Glucagon
peptides.fda_status: Yes. Glucagon is approved for severe hypoglycemia and as a diagnostic aid for gastrointestinal imaging. The table shows when each product was approved: Product | Type | FDA approval Glucagon for injection, including the recombinant GlucaGen | Injection | Approved for decades Gvoke | Newer ready-to-use injector | 2019 Baqsimi | Newer ready-to-use nasal powder | 2019
peptides.evidence_note: Glucagon is FDA-approved for severe hypoglycemia and as a diagnostic aid, supported by long clinical use and trials of its injectable and nasal forms.
peptides.what_it_is: A pancreatic peptide hormone that raises blood glucose (counter-regulatory to insulin)
peptides.key_takeaway: Glucagon (brands include Gvoke and the nasal powder Baqsimi) is a pancreatic hormone that raises blood sugar fast, used as emergency treatment for severe low blood sugar in people with diabetes. It signals the liver to release stored glucose. Glucagon products have long been FDA-approved in the U.S., and modern forms include ready-to-use injectors and a needle-free nasal powder.
peptides.mechanism: Glucagon binds glucagon receptors on liver cells and switches on the pathways that release glucose. It stimulates glycogenolysis, the breakdown of stored glycogen into glucose, and gluconeogenesis, the making of new glucose, so the liver pushes glucose into the bloodstream and blood sugar rises within minutes. This is why it works as a rescue treatment when someone with hypoglycemia is unable to eat or drink. Because the effect depends on the liver having glucose stores to release, glucagon can be less effective when those stores are depleted, such as in prolonged fasting or starvation. Glucagon also relaxes the smooth muscle of the gastrointestinal tract, which is the basis of its separate use as a diagnostic aid during certain imaging studies. In a trial in adults with type 1 diabetes, a nasal powder formulation raised blood glucose about as effectively as injected glucagon, with the practical advantage of needing no injection or mixing in an emergency.
peptides.side_effects_safety: According to the injectable and nasal powder labels, common side effects include: - Nausea and vomiting - Headache - Injection-site reactions, or nasal and eye symptoms with the nasal powder More serious considerations include: - A sharp rise in blood pressure in people with pheochromocytoma - Low blood sugar rebound in people with insulinoma - Rare allergic reactions
peptides.summary_es: Hormona utilizada para rescate de hipoglucemia grave y determinados procedimientos diagnósticos según producto.

detail.sections:
title: What is glucagon?
text: Glucagon is a 29-amino-acid hormone made by the pancreas that works opposite to insulin: when blood sugar drops, glucagon raises it. As a medicine it is the emergency rescue treatment for severe hypoglycemia, the dangerous low-blood-sugar episodes that can occur in people with diabetes, especially those on insulin. It is sold as the ready-to-use Gvoke injector and Baqsimi, a nasal powder, among other products. The GlucaGen HypoKit emergency kit was discontinued in the U.S. in 2024.
title: How does glucagon work?

It stimulates glycogenolysis, the breakdown of stored glycogen into glucose, and gluconeogenesis, the making of new glucose, so the liver pushes glucose into the bloodstream and blood sugar rises within minutes. This is why it works as a rescue treatment when someone with hypoglycemia is unable to eat or drink.
Because the effect depends on the liver having glucose stores to release, glucagon can be less effective when those stores are depleted, such as in prolonged fasting or starvation. Glucagon also relaxes the smooth muscle of the gastrointestinal tract, which is the basis of its separate use as a diagnostic aid during certain imaging studies. In a trial in adults with type 1 diabetes, a nasal powder formulation raised blood glucose about as effectively as injected glucagon, with the practical advantage of needing no injection or mixing in an emergency.

title: What is glucagon prescribed for?
text: Glucagon is prescribed as emergency treatment for severe hypoglycemia in people with diabetes, typically given by a caregiver when the person cannot safely take sugar by mouth. Injectable forms are also used to relax the gut during radiologic procedures. It is contraindicated in pheochromocytoma (a catecholamine-producing tumor) and in insulinoma.
title: What are the side effects?
text: According to the injectable and nasal powder labels, common side effects include:
- Nausea and vomiting
- Headache
- Injection-site reactions, or nasal and eye symptoms with the nasal powder
More serious considerations include:
- A sharp rise in blood pressure in people with pheochromocytoma
- Low blood sugar rebound in people with insulinoma
- Rare allergic reactions

detail.sections:
title: What is glutathione?
text: Glutathione is a naturally occurring three-amino acid peptide (often abbreviated GSH) that serves as a major antioxidant inside cells. It is sold as an oral dietary supplement and, in wellness settings, as an intravenous, injectable, or inhaled product, promoted for skin-lightening and general antioxidant and wellness support. As a drug it is not FDA-approved.
title: How does it work?
text: Glutathione's biochemical role as a major intracellular antioxidant and detoxifier is well established; it neutralizes reactive molecules through enzyme systems. For skin-lightening, the proposed mechanism is inhibition of the pigment enzyme tyrosinase and a shift in pigment production toward lighter melanin. This describes the mechanism; the human evidence below tests whether supplementation produces the marketed effects.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No, not as a drug. Oral glutathione is sold as a dietary supplement, and IV, injectable, and inhaled forms are compounded rather than FDA-approved. The FDA has issued a safety alert warning against using dietary-ingredient glutathione powder to compound sterile injectables, citing adverse events and contamination concerns. Compounded IV and inhaled glutathione therefore carry specific FDA safety warnings.
On the FDA's May 14, 2026 list of 503A bulk drug substances, glutathione sits in category 1, under evaluation.
title: What does the research show?
text: There are several small human trials, with modest and mixed results. The skin results below are as reported on PubMed:
Study | Area | Result
4-week trial of oral glutathione | Skin | Small reductions in skin pigment versus placebo
12-week trial of an oral combination | Skin | Reported skin lightening
Systematic review | Skin | Skin-whitening evidence is inconclusive due to study quality and bioavailability concerns
Randomized pilot of IV glutathione | Parkinson's disease | No significant benefit over placebo
Meta-analysis | Parkinson's disease | Only a small motor-score improvement
6-month trial of oral glutathione in 54 non-smoking adults | Glutathione levels | Red blood cell, plasma, and lymphocyte glutathione rose 30% to 35% at the higher amount; levels returned to baseline after a 1-month washout
6-month randomized trial of inhaled glutathione in 153 people with cystic fibrosis | Lung function | FEV1 did not differ from placebo (p = 0.180), and oxidation markers did not change
Overall the human evidence is real but modest, short-term, and inconsistent.

This document is educational, is not medical advice or a health claim, and is not an offer to sell any product.

peptides.key_takeaway: Goserelin (goserelin acetate, sold as Zoladex) is a synthetic decapeptide agonist of gonadotropin-releasing hormone delivered as a small implant that suppresses the body's production of testosterone and estrogen. It is used across prostate cancer, breast cancer, and endometriosis, and in one long-term breast-cancer trial it matched standard chemotherapy for survival in certain premenopausal women. It has been FDA-approved in the U.S. since 1989 and is given as a monthly or three-month depot implant.
peptides.mechanism:
Goserelin binds the GnRH receptor on pituitary cells. A first dose briefly stimulates the pituitary, causing a transient rise in luteinizing hormone and sex hormones known as the flare. Because the implant then delivers drug continuously rather than in natural pulses, the receptors downregulate and desensitize, and within a few weeks luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone fall. Testosterone in men, or estrogen in women, drops to castrate or postmenopausal levels.
Lowering those hormones is the point of treatment:
Condition | Hormone lowered | Why it matters
Prostate cancer | Testosterone | Hormone-sensitive tumors depend on it
Premenopausal breast cancer | Ovarian estrogen | It can fuel estrogen-receptor-positive disease
Endometriosis | Estrogen, inducing a reversible low-estrogen state | The low-estrogen state shrinks lesions
In the long-term ZEBRA trial, goserelin was equivalent to standard CMF chemotherapy for disease-free and overall survival in premenopausal women with estrogen-receptor-positive, node-positive early breast cancer, without chemotherapy's acute toxicity.

detail.sections:
title: What is goserelin?
text: Goserelin, known generically as goserelin acetate and sold under the brand Zoladex, is a synthetic ten-amino-acid analog of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH, also called LHRH). GnRH is the hypothalamic signal that drives the pituitary to release luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone, which in turn stimulate the testes and ovaries. Goserelin is a longer-acting, more potent version of that signal, formulated as a wax-like cylinder that is placed under the skin of the abdomen and releases drug slowly. It was first developed under the code ICI-118630 and approved in the United States in 1989.
title: How does goserelin work?
text: Goserelin binds the GnRH receptor on pituitary cells. A first dose briefly stimulates the pituitary, causing a transient rise in luteinizing hormone and sex hormones known as the flare. Because the implant then delivers drug continuously rather than in natural pulses, the receptors downregulate and desensitize, and within a few weeks luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone fall. Testosterone in men, or estrogen in women, drops to castrate or postmenopausal levels.
Lowering those hormones is the point of treatment:
Condition | Hormone lowered | Why it matters
Prostate cancer | Testosterone | Hormone-sensitive tumors depend on it
Premenopausal breast cancer | Ovarian estrogen | It can fuel estrogen-receptor-positive disease
Endometriosis | Estrogen, inducing a reversible low-estrogen state | The low-estrogen state shrinks lesions
In the long-term ZEBRA trial, goserelin was equivalent to standard CMF chemotherapy for disease-free and overall survival in premenopausal women with estrogen-receptor-positive, node-positive early breast cancer, without chemotherapy's acute toxicity.

text: Yes. Goserelin, originally developed by ICI Pharmaceuticals (later Zeneca, now AstraZeneca), was approved by the FDA in 1989. The implant is available in a 3.6 mg monthly strength and a 10.8 mg three-month strength, and the approved indications have broadened over time across oncology and gynecology.
title: What is goserelin prescribed for?
text: Goserelin is prescribed for:
- Advanced prostate cancer (alone or with radiotherapy or an anti-androgen)
- Advanced breast cancer in pre- and perimenopausal women
- Endometriosis
- Thinning of the endometrial lining before surgical ablation for heavy uterine bleeding
It is contraindicated in pregnancy because of its hormonal effects.
title: What are the side effects?
text: According to the prescribing information, common side effects reflect reduced sex-hormone levels:
- Hot flashes and sweating
- Sexual dysfunction and vaginal dryness
- Headache
- Injection-site reactions
- Bone-density loss with long-term use

- Disease "flare" early in prostate-cancer treatment, sometimes managed with an anti-androgen
- Increased risk of hyperglycemia and cardiovascular events with long-term androgen deprivation
- Rare pituitary apoplexy

peptides.name: Hexapeptide-9
peptides.fda_status: As a cosmetic ingredient rather than a drug, does not require FDA approval
peptides.evidence_note: The ingredient's rationale rests on laboratory and manufacturer data, and the only controlled human study tested a modified version rather than standard hexapeptide-9, so there is no sound human evidence for the ingredient itself.
peptides.what_it_is: Cosmetic ingredient, a collagen-inspired signal peptide
peptides.research_at_a_glance: Activity supported mainly by laboratory and manufacturer data
peptides.key_takeaway: Hexapeptide-9 is a synthetic six-amino acid "signal" peptide whose sequence mirrors a short motif found in human collagen. Laboratory work suggests it signals skin cells to build more supporting matrix, which is the basis for its use in products aimed at the appearance of firmness and fewer fine lines. As of 2026, independent human evidence for the standard ingredient is limited, with the one controlled human study testing a chemically modified version rather than hexapeptide-9 itself.
peptides.mechanism: Laboratory studies describe hexapeptide-9 as a matrikine, a peptide fragment that acts as a signal to skin cells. The proposed mechanism is that it tells dermal fibroblasts and surface keratinocytes to increase production of extracellular matrix components such as collagen, as well as to strengthen the junction between the upper and lower layers of skin. The idea is that healthier-looking matrix supports the appearance of firmer, smoother skin. These are laboratory and manufacturer findings about how the peptide behaves in cell models. In finished cosmetics the benefit is described in appearance terms, such as the look of firmness and reduced fine lines, rather than as a claim to rebuild collagen.
peptides.human_study_findings: The direct human evidence is limited: - According to PubMed, a randomized, controlled trial reported wrinkle improvements, but it tested a cyclized derivative of the molecule rather than standard hexapeptide-9, and it was industry-sponsored. - Other studies use the peptide inside delivery systems or combination products, so the ingredient's individual effect is hard to isolate. - There is no independent, well-controlled human trial of standard hexapeptide-9 on its own, and supplier efficacy claims are largely unpublished.
peptides.side_effects_safety: Hexapeptide-9 is generally considered well tolerated on the skin, with low irritation potential at cosmetic use levels. As with any new skincare ingredient, a patch test is sensible for sensitive or reactive skin, since individual responses vary.

detail.sections:
title: What is hexapeptide-9?
text: Hexapeptide-9 is a peptide of six amino acids whose sequence mirrors a short motif found in human collagen, the protein that gives skin its structure. In skincare it is used as a "signal" or messenger peptide, meant to prompt skin cells rather than to add collagen directly. It is sold under trade names such as Collaxyl and is a cosmetic ingredient, not a drug.
title: How does it work?
text: Laboratory studies describe hexapeptide-9 as a matrikine, a peptide fragment that acts as a signal to skin cells. The proposed mechanism is that it tells dermal fibroblasts and surface keratinocytes to increase production of extracellular matrix components such as collagen, as well as to strengthen the junction between the upper and lower layers of skin. The idea is that healthier-looking matrix supports the appearance of firmer, smoother skin.
These are laboratory and manufacturer findings about how the peptide behaves in cell models. In finished cosmetics the benefit is described in appearance terms, such as the look of firmness and reduced fine lines, rather than as a claim to rebuild collagen.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No, and it does not need to be. The FDA does not pre-approve cosmetic ingredients. A cosmetic may describe how it affects the look and feel of skin, while a claim to change the body's structure would make a product a drug. Hexapeptide-9 is used within the cosmetic boundary, for the appearance of the skin.
title: What is it used for?
text: Hexapeptide-9 is used in "anti-aging" and firming serums and creams. The appearance goals are the look of firmer skin, improved texture and tone, and a reduction in the appearance of fine lines. It is often paired with other peptides and hydrating ingredients.
title: What does the research show?
text: The direct human evidence is limited:
- According to PubMed, a randomized, controlled trial reported wrinkle improvements, but it tested a cyclized derivative of the molecule rather than standard hexapeptide-9, and it was industry-sponsored.
- Other studies use the peptide inside delivery systems or combination products, so the ingredient's individual effect is hard to isolate.
- There is no independent, well-controlled human trial of standard hexapeptide-9 on its own, and supplier efficacy claims are largely unpublished.
title: What are the side effects?
text: Hexapeptide-9 is generally considered well tolerated on the skin, with low irritation potential at cosmetic use levels. As with any new skincare ingredient, a patch test is sensible for sensitive or reactive skin, since individual responses vary.
detail.sources_note: Sources: a randomized controlled trial of a cyclized hexapeptide-9 derivative (Chang et al., Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology, 2025, DOI: 10.1111/jocd.70290), indexed on PubMed; and cosmetic ingredient reference data on hexapeptide-9. This document is educational and does not constitute medical advice.

Human data are limited to short studies of growth hormone release, with no controlled trials supporting the marketed benefits, and repeated use appears to blunt its own effect. As of 2026 it is not FDA-approved and is banned in sport.
peptides.mechanism: Three features of its proposed mechanism stand out: - It activates the growth hormone secretagogue (ghrelin) receptor on the pituitary to drive growth hormone pulses. - It also binds a receptor called CD36 in cardiovascular tissue, which underlies preclinical interest in effects on the heart that may be separate from growth hormone. - Studies report partial desensitization, in which the growth hormone response can diminish with repeated exposure. The marketed benefits are extrapolated from the growth hormone rise. This describes the proposed mechanism, separate from proven outcomes.
peptides.human_study_findings: The human evidence is short pharmacology. According to PubMed, a study in healthy men found hexarelin produced a larger growth hormone rise than GHRH and acted in synergy with it, a hormone-level result rather than a clinical outcome. Its cardiovascular effects are described mainly in experimental models and reviews. No controlled human trials support the marketed muscle, recovery, or anti-aging uses.

detail.sections:
title: What is hexarelin?
text: Hexarelin, with the generic name examorelin, is a synthetic six-amino acid peptide, structurally a methylated relative of GHRP-6. It is among the more potent growth hormone-releasing peptides for triggering growth hormone release. It is sold through wellness and "research peptide" channels and promoted for recovery and body composition, and it was never marketed as an approved drug.
title: How does it work?
text: Three features of its proposed mechanism stand out:
- It activates the growth hormone secretagogue (ghrelin) receptor on the pituitary to drive growth hormone pulses.
- It also binds a receptor called CD36 in cardiovascular tissue, which underlies preclinical interest in effects on the heart that may be separate from growth hormone.
- Studies report partial desensitization, in which the growth hormone response can diminish with repeated exposure.
The marketed benefits are extrapolated from the growth hormone rise. This describes the proposed mechanism, separate from proven outcomes.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No. Hexarelin is not approved by the FDA and never reached market as a drug. It has been treated as not eligible for routine 503A compounding in the U.S. and is not approved for performance or anti-aging. In sport, growth hormone-releasing peptides including hexarelin (examorelin) are prohibited at all times under the WADA list.
title: What does the research show?
text: The human evidence is short pharmacology. According to PubMed, a study in healthy men found hexarelin produced a larger growth hormone rise than GHRH and acted in synergy with it, a hormone-level result rather than a clinical outcome. Its cardiovascular effects are described mainly in experimental models and reviews. No controlled human trials support the marketed muscle, recovery, or anti-aging uses.
detail.sources_note: Sources: a growth hormone pharmacology study (Arvat et al., Neuroendocrinology, 1995, DOI: 10.1159/000126827) and a review of growth hormone secretagogues (Cao et al., Trends in Endocrinology & Metabolism, 2005, DOI: 10.1016/j.tem.2005.11.004), both indexed on PubMed; and the WADA Prohibited List. This document is educational, is not medical advice or a health claim, and is not an offer to sell any product.

peptides.what_it_is: A GnRH (LHRH) receptor agonist peptide delivered as a 12-month subdermal implant
peptides.key_takeaway: Histrelin (histrelin acetate, sold as Supprelin LA and formerly as Vantas) is a synthetic nonapeptide agonist of gonadotropin-releasing hormone delivered as a small implant that releases drug for about a year. It suppresses the pituitary and the sex hormones it controls, and is used for central precocious puberty in children; a second implant for advanced prostate cancer in adults was discontinued in 2021. The implant products have been FDA-approved in the U.S. since the mid-2000s, and one implant lasts roughly 12 months.
peptides.mechanism: Histrelin binds the GnRH receptor on the pituitary. As with other agonists in its class, an initial dose briefly stimulates the gland, producing a short rise in luteinizing hormone and sex steroids, the flare. Because the implant then delivers the drug continuously, the receptors downregulate and desensitize, and gonadotropin output falls. Sex-hormone levels drop to prepubertal levels in children or castrate levels in men. In central precocious puberty, that suppression stops the premature pubertal cascade, pausing bone maturation and breast or testicular development until a more appropriate age; in advanced prostate cancer, it removes the testosterone that hormone-sensitive tumors rely on. In the pivotal pediatric study, a single subdermal implant lowered peak stimulated luteinizing hormone from about 28 to under 1 mIU/mL and maintained suppression of luteinizing hormone and sex steroids for a full year.
peptides.side_effects_safety: According to the Supprelin LA label, the most common side effect is a reaction at the implant site, reported in about half of children in clinical trials: - Pain, bruising, soreness, or swelling where the implant is placed More serious considerations include: - Implant breakage or difficult removal - A brief rise in sex hormones in the first week, which can temporarily worsen symptoms - Mood and behavior changes such as irritability, crying, anger, or aggression - Convulsions - Raised pressure around the brain (pseudotumor cerebri), with symptoms such as headache and vision changes - Severe skin reactions

detail.sections:
title: What is histrelin?
text: Histrelin, known generically as histrelin acetate and sold under the brand Supprelin LA and formerly as Vantas, is a synthetic nine-amino-acid analog of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH, also called LHRH). It is one of the more potent GnRH agonists and is delivered from a flexible implant that sits under the skin and releases drug steadily for about 12 months, so a child or patient needs only one placement per year rather than repeated injections. Earlier forms of histrelin were given as daily injections; the modern products are implants.
title: How does histrelin work?
text: Histrelin binds the GnRH receptor on the pituitary. As with other agonists in its class, an initial dose briefly stimulates the gland, producing a short rise in luteinizing hormone and sex steroids, the flare. Because the implant then delivers the drug continuously, the receptors downregulate and desensitize, and gonadotropin output falls. Sex-hormone levels drop to prepubertal levels in children or castrate levels in men.
In central precocious puberty, that suppression stops the premature pubertal cascade, pausing bone maturation and breast or testicular development until a more appropriate age; in advanced prostate cancer, it removes the testosterone that hormone-sensitive tumors rely on. In the pivotal pediatric study, a single subdermal implant lowered peak stimulated luteinizing hormone from about 28 to under 1 mIU/mL and maintained suppression of luteinizing hormone and sex steroids for a full year.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: Yes. Histrelin's U.S. approval and market history:
Year | Event
Early 1990s | An earlier daily-injection form of histrelin was approved
2004 | Vantas implant approved for advanced prostate cancer
2007 | Supprelin LA implant approved for central precocious puberty
2021 | Vantas discontinued by its manufacturer
Supprelin LA is now the only histrelin implant sold in the U.S. Each implant is designed to deliver drug for about 12 months and is then removed and replaced.
title: What is histrelin prescribed for?
text: Histrelin is prescribed for central precocious puberty in children (Supprelin LA). It was also used as palliative treatment of advanced prostate cancer in adults (Vantas) until that implant was discontinued. The implant is placed and removed in a brief in-office procedure.
title: What are the side effects?
text: According to the Supprelin LA label, the most common side effect is a reaction at the implant site, reported in about half of children in clinical trials:
- Pain, bruising, soreness, or swelling where the implant is placed
More serious considerations include:
- Implant breakage or difficult removal
- A brief rise in sex hormones in the first week, which can temporarily worsen symptoms
- Mood and behavior changes such as irritability, crying, anger, or aggression
- Convulsions
- Raised pressure around the brain (pseudotumor cerebri), with symptoms such as headache and vision changes
- Severe skin reactions
detail.sources_note: Sources: FDA prescribing information for Supprelin LA; KFF Health News reporting on the discontinuation of Vantas; the pediatric implant trial (Eugster et al., Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism, 2007, DOI: 10.1210/jc.2006-2479), indexed on PubMed. This document is educational and does not constitute medical advice.

peptides.name: Human chorionic gonadotropin
peptides.fda_status: Yes, for its hormonal indications. The injectable hCG products have been FDA-approved for decades for ovulation induction, male hypogonadism, and cryptorchidism. The agency has separately warned that over-the-counter "homeopathic" hCG weight-loss products are not approved and that prescription hCG is not approved for weight loss.
peptides.evidence_note: Human chorionic gonadotropin is FDA-approved for ovulation induction, male hypogonadism, and cryptorchidism, with established clinical use. It is not approved for weight loss, and the FDA says it has not been shown to be effective for that use.
peptides.what_it_is: A gonadotropin hormone that mimics luteinizing hormone at its receptor
peptides.key_takeaway: Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG; FDA-approved injectable brands include Pregnyl and Novarel) is a placental hormone that acts like luteinizing hormone, triggering ovulation in women and testosterone production in men. It is used in fertility treatment, in male hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and for undescended testicles in boys, and it is not approved for weight loss. In a Cochrane review of seven trials with 1,136 women, recombinant and urinary hCG gave similar ongoing pregnancy or live-birth rates (odds ratio 1.15, 95% confidence interval 0.89 to 1.49).
peptides.mechanism: hCG binds the same receptor as luteinizing hormone (the LH/CG receptor) and mimics the natural mid-cycle luteinizing hormone surge. In women undergoing fertility treatment, a dose of hCG triggers the final maturation and release of the egg after the follicles have been grown with other hormones. In men, hCG stimulates the Leydig cells of the testes to produce testosterone and supports sperm production, which is why it is used in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. In boys with non-anatomical undescended testicles, the testosterone it stimulates can promote testicular descent. In a Cochrane review, urinary-derived and recombinant hCG gave similar ongoing pregnancy or live-birth rates for triggering final egg maturation (odds ratio 1.15, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.49; seven trials, 1,136 women). The FDA has specifically stated that hCG has not been shown to be effective for weight loss and is not approved for that use, despite its promotion in some commercial diet programs.
peptides.side_effects_safety: According to the prescribing information, common side effects include: - Injection-site pain - Headache - Fluid retention or edema - Breast tenderness or gynecomastia (in males) - Irritability, restlessness, and depression More serious considerations include: - Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome and multiple pregnancy in fertility use - Signs of early puberty in boys treated for cryptorchidism - Rare arterial thromboembolism

detail.sections:
title: What is human chorionic gonadotropin?
text: Human chorionic gonadotropin, abbreviated hCG, is a glycoprotein hormone normally produced by the placenta in pregnancy. The FDA-approved injectable products, such as Pregnyl and Novarel, are purified from the urine of pregnant women; a separate recombinant version, choriogonadotropin alfa (Ovidrel), is made in the laboratory. hCG shares its structure and action closely with luteinizing hormone, one of the pituitary hormones that controls the ovaries and testes.
title: How does human chorionic gonadotropin work?
text: hCG binds the same receptor as luteinizing hormone (the LH/CG receptor) and mimics the natural mid-cycle luteinizing hormone surge. In women undergoing fertility treatment, a dose of hCG triggers the final maturation and release of the egg after the follicles have been grown with other hormones. In men, hCG stimulates the Leydig cells of the testes to produce testosterone and supports sperm production, which is why it is used in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. In boys with non-anatomical undescended testicles, the testosterone it stimulates can promote testicular descent.
In a Cochrane review, urinary-derived and recombinant hCG gave similar ongoing pregnancy or live-birth rates for triggering final egg maturation (odds ratio 1.15, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.49; seven trials, 1,136 women). The FDA has specifically stated that hCG has not been shown to be effective for weight loss and is not approved for that use, despite its promotion in some commercial diet programs.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: Yes, for its hormonal indications. The injectable hCG products have been FDA-approved for decades for ovulation induction, male hypogonadism, and cryptorchidism. The agency has separately warned that over-the-counter "homeopathic" hCG weight-loss products are not approved and that prescription hCG is not approved for weight loss.
title: What is human chorionic gonadotropin prescribed for?
text: In women, hCG is prescribed to induce ovulation and pregnancy in carefully selected cases of infertility, after the follicles have been developed with follicle-stimulating hormone or menotropins. In men, it is used for hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and in prepubertal boys for undescended testicles not caused by an anatomical blockage.
Evidence in men comes from small or short studies, summarized below:
Study | Participants | Finding
2021 systematic review pooling 5 hCG trials | 196 men | Mean total testosterone rose from 284.5 to 565.6 ng/dL
2018 randomized trial of clomiphene, hCG, or both | 282 men with hypogonadism who wanted to preserve fertility | Testosterone rose in all 3 arms
title: What are the side effects?
text: According to the prescribing information, common side effects include:
- Injection-site pain
- Headache
- Fluid retention or edema
- Breast tenderness or gynecomastia (in males)
- Irritability, restlessness, and depression
More serious considerations include:
- Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome and multiple pregnancy in fertility use
- Signs of early puberty in boys treated for cryptorchidism
- Rare arterial thromboembolism
detail.sources_note: Sources: FDA prescribing information for Pregnyl and Novarel and FDA statements on hCG weight-loss products; a Cochrane review of recombinant versus urinary hCG for triggering egg maturation (Youssef et al., 2016, DOI: 10.1002/14651858.CD003719.pub4), indexed on PubMed. This document is educational and does not constitute medical advice.

detail.faq:
q: Is humanin FDA-approved?
a: No. Humanin is not FDA-approved for any human indication. No NDA or BLA for humanin has been approved as of September 2026. It has no established compounding pathway and is not legally marketed for human use in the United States.
q: Is humanin legal in the United States?
a: Humanin is not an approved drug and is not a controlled substance. However, it has no legal pathway for human therapeutic use. Products sold online as humanin are marketed as "research use only," which means they fall outside FDA pharmaceutical regulation. Purchasing them for personal use exists in a legal gray zone that does not confer safety assurances.
q: Can a doctor prescribe humanin?
a: No. Humanin is not FDA-approved and has no established 503A or 503B compounding classification, meaning it cannot be prescribed or compounded by a licensed pharmacy for patient use in the United States. No legal prescribing pathway exists as of September 2026.
q: What is the difference between humanin and MOTS-c?
a: Both are mitochondrial-derived peptides (MDPs) encoded within mitochondrial DNA, but they have distinct sequences, mechanisms, and research foci. Humanin is a 24-amino-acid peptide studied primarily for cytoprotection, neuroprotection, and the IGF-1/IGFBP-3 signaling axis. MOTS-c is a 16-amino-acid peptide studied primarily for metabolic effects, particularly glucose regulation and exercise adaptation. They share the MDP classification and a relationship to aging biology but are pharmacologically distinct compounds with separate evidence bases. This comparison is for scientific context only; these compounds have fundamentally different research profiles and neither has an approved human therapeutic indication.
q: What does the human data on humanin actually show?
a: Human data on humanin is observational only, and the findings are mixed. Some studies report a decline with age, while a cohort of 693 people aged 21 to 113 found higher plasma humanin in older age, with the highest levels in centenarians. A later study found lower humanin in Alzheimer's disease but not in type 2 diabetes, and a genetic variant linked to lower circulating humanin was associated with faster cognitive aging. These correlations are hypothesis-generating; they do not establish causality or support therapeutic use.
q: What is the S14G-humanin (HNG) analog?
a: HNG is a synthetic analog of native humanin in which the amino acid at position 14 is changed from serine to glycine. Laboratory research reports that this substitution produces approximately 1,000-fold greater potency in neuroprotection assays compared to the native sequence. HNG and native humanin are distinct compounds with different potency profiles and potentially different safety considerations, though neither has human safety data.
q: Did FDA's April 2026 peptide list change affect humanin?
a: No. In April 2026, FDA removed a group of peptides from its Category 2 list after the nominators withdrew their nominations, which was not a finding that those substances are safe. Humanin is not on any FDA category list, so its status is unchanged: no FDA-approved formulation exists, and no compounding pathway has been established.
q: Are peptides legal in 2026?
a: The legality of specific peptides varies by compound. Some peptides (such as bremelanotide and tesamorelin) have FDA-approved indications. Others, including humanin, have no approved therapeutic use and no compounding classification. FDA's April 2026 changes to its Category 2 list do not create a legal pathway for compounds like humanin that are not on any FDA category list. Consulting a licensed healthcare provider is the appropriate step for any questions about specific compounds.

peptides.key_takeaway: Icatibant (sold as Firazyr) is a peptide that blocks the bradykinin B2 receptor, used to treat acute attacks of hereditary angioedema, a condition of sudden, severe swelling. peptides.mechanism: Icatibant targets bradykinin, the molecule responsible for the swelling in hereditary angioedema. Icatibant is a selective competitive antagonist at the B2 receptor, so it blocks bradykinin from acting there and allows the attack to subside. Because it acts directly at the receptor regardless of the upstream cause, it works in HAE attacks driven by bradykinin and can be given by the patient at the first sign of an attack. In the FAST-3 trial, icatibant shortened the median time to meaningful symptom relief to about 2 hours, compared with roughly 20 hours on placebo.

detail.sections:
title: What is icatibant?
text: Icatibant, sold under the brand Firazyr, is a synthetic ten-amino-acid peptide that blocks the bradykinin B2 receptor. It is used for acute attacks of hereditary angioedema (HAE), a genetic disorder in which episodes of severe swelling affect the skin, abdomen, and sometimes the airway. It was developed under the code HOE 140 and approved in the United States in 2011.
title: How does icatibant work?
text: Icatibant targets bradykinin, the molecule responsible for the swelling in hereditary angioedema. In HAE, a deficiency or dysfunction of the C1 inhibitor protein leads to overproduction of bradykinin, which binds B2 receptors on blood vessels and makes them dilate and leak fluid into tissues, producing the characteristic swelling and pain. Icatibant is a selective competitive antagonist at the B2 receptor, so it blocks bradykinin from acting there and allows the attack to subside.
Because it acts directly at the receptor regardless of the upstream cause, it works in HAE attacks driven by bradykinin and can be given by the patient at the first sign of an attack. In the FAST-3 trial, icatibant shortened the median time to meaningful symptom relief to about 2 hours, compared with roughly 20 hours on placebo.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: Yes. Icatibant was approved by the FDA in 2011 for acute attacks of hereditary angioedema in adults, and generic versions are also available. It is formulated for subcutaneous self-injection.
title: What is icatibant prescribed for?
text: Icatibant is prescribed to treat acute attacks of hereditary angioedema in adults. Patients are typically trained to self-inject at the onset of an attack. Attacks involving the airway still warrant medical attention, even after treatment.

- Injection-site reactions such as redness, swelling, pain, and itching, which are nearly universal

- Hives, reported after approval

peptides.fda_status: Non-FDA-approved IGF-1 analog sold as a research chemical / performance drug
peptides.evidence_note: There is no human efficacy evidence; the muscle-growth rationale rests entirely on animal and cell studies.
peptides.what_it_is: Truncated, more potent version of IGF-1
peptides.research_at_a_glance: Evidence is animal and cell-based only; there are no human efficacy trials
peptides.key_takeaway: IGF-1 DES is a shortened, more potent laboratory analog of insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), sold on the "research peptide" and performance market for muscle growth. Its evidence is entirely animal and cell-based, with no human trials, and it is a known performance-enhancing drug. As of 2026 it is not FDA-approved and is banned in sport.
peptides.mechanism: IGF-1 DES acts on the IGF-1 receptor, the pathway that drives muscle protein synthesis and tissue growth. Because it is less bound by carrier proteins, it is proposed to have higher local activity than natural IGF-1. In rodents it improved nitrogen balance and reduced muscle protein breakdown, and it is used in cell culture as a high-potency growth stimulus. These are animal and laboratory findings. This describes the proposed mechanism, separate from proven outcomes in people. (A different, full-length IGF-1 product, mecasermin, is an approved drug for a rare growth disorder; IGF-1 DES is a separate, unapproved analog.)
peptides.human_study_findings: The evidence is preclinical. According to PubMed, an animal study reported improved nitrogen balance and reduced protein breakdown, and the peptide is a standard high-potency reagent in cell-growth assays. There are no human clinical trials supporting muscle or performance use, so its marketed benefit is unproven in people.

title: What is IGF-1 DES?
text: IGF-1 DES (short for DES(1-3) IGF-1) is a modified version of insulin-like growth factor-1, missing its first three amino acids. peptides.mechanism: IGF-1 LR3 activates the IGF-1 receptor, driving the growth signaling that promotes muscle protein synthesis in cell and animal models. Its modifications are proposed to prolong its activity in the body. In laboratory work it increased muscle-cell differentiation, and in a mouse model of cancer-related muscle wasting it limited muscle loss, but at the cost of accelerated tumor growth, illustrating the mitogenic (growth-promoting) concern that comes with strong IGF signaling. These are animal and cell findings. This describes the proposed mechanism, separate from proven outcomes in people.
peptides.human_study_findings: The evidence is preclinical. According to PubMed, a mouse study found IGF-1 LR3 limited muscle loss in cancer cachexia but accelerated tumor growth, and laboratory assays show it stimulates muscle-cell growth. There are no human clinical trials supporting muscle or performance use, and the tumor-growth signal is a specific preclinical concern. Its marketed benefit is unproven in people.
