peptides.name: Insulin analogs
peptides.fda_status: Yes. Insulin analogs have been FDA-approved since 1996, starting with lispro, followed by glargine in 2000 and others including aspart, glulisine, detemir, and degludec. They are approved to improve blood-sugar control in adults and, for many products, children with diabetes.
peptides.evidence_note: Insulin analogs are FDA-approved for type 1 and type 2 diabetes, supported by extensive randomized evidence including trials such as Treat-to-Target.
peptides.what_it_is: Engineered insulin peptide hormones with altered onset and duration
peptides.key_takeaway: Insulin analogs are laboratory-engineered versions of the hormone insulin, redesigned to act faster or last longer than natural insulin, and they are prescribed for type 1 diabetes and for type 2 diabetes when other treatments are not enough. Rapid-acting analogs cover meals and long-acting (basal) analogs provide steady background coverage. Insulin analogs have been FDA-approved in the U.S. since the 1990s and are given by subcutaneous injection or pump.
peptides.mechanism:
Insulin analogs bind the insulin receptor on muscle, fat, and liver cells, just as natural insulin does. Activating the receptor prompts cells to take up glucose from the blood (through the GLUT4 transporter), stimulates storage of glucose, fat, and protein, and suppresses the liver's production of glucose, all of which lower blood sugar. The amino-acid changes in the analogs do not alter this core action; they change the pharmacokinetics, how fast the insulin is absorbed and how long it lingers.
Rapid-acting analogs are engineered so their molecules separate and absorb quickly after injection, matching the glucose rise from a meal, while basal analogs are designed to precipitate or to bind albumin so they release slowly and provide flat, all-day coverage. Combining the two reproduces the body's natural pattern more closely than older insulins. In the Treat-to-Target trial, adding a basal analog to oral drugs let a larger share of patients reach their HbA1c goal without documented nighttime low blood sugar, compared with older NPH insulin.
peptides.side_effects_safety: According to product labels such as the Humalog prescribing information, the most common and important side effect is: - Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia), which can be severe Other effects include: - Weight gain - Injection-site reactions or fatty lumps (lipodystrophy) - Low potassium More serious considerations include: - Severe hypoglycemia, which can cause seizures or loss of consciousness - Fluid retention and heart failure when combined with certain diabetes pills (thiazolidinediones) Insulin pens must never be shared between people, even if the needle is changed.
peptides.summary_es: Familia de insulinas utilizadas para controlar glucosa en diabetes; las diferencias de acción y concentración son críticas para evitar errores.

Activating the receptor prompts cells to take up glucose from the blood (through the GLUT4 transporter), stimulates storage of glucose, fat, and protein, and suppresses the liver's production of glucose, all of which lower blood sugar. The amino-acid changes in the analogs do not alter this core action; they change the pharmacokinetics, how fast the insulin is absorbed and how long it lingers.
Rapid-acting analogs are engineered so their molecules separate and absorb quickly after injection, matching the glucose rise from a meal, while basal analogs are designed to precipitate or to bind albumin so they release slowly and provide flat, all-day coverage. Combining the two reproduces the body's natural pattern more closely than older insulins. In the Treat-to-Target trial, adding a basal analog to oral drugs let a larger share of patients reach their HbA1c goal without documented nighttime low blood sugar, compared with older NPH insulin.
detail.safety_side_effects:
According to product labels such as the Humalog prescribing information, the most common and important side effect is:
- Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia), which can be severe
Other effects include:
- Weight gain
- Injection-site reactions or fatty lumps (lipodystrophy)
- Low potassium
More serious considerations include:
- Severe hypoglycemia, which can cause seizures or loss of consciousness
- Fluid retention and heart failure when combined with certain diabetes pills (thiazolidinediones)
Insulin pens must never be shared between people, even if the needle is changed.
detail.sections:
title: What are insulin analogs?
text: Insulin analogs are modified forms of human insulin, the peptide hormone (two chains totaling 51 amino acids) that lowers blood sugar. By changing a few amino acids or adding a fatty-acid chain, chemists adjusted how quickly insulin is absorbed and how long it lasts, without changing what it does at the receptor. The main analogs fall into two groups:
Analog | Brand | Type
Lispro | Humalog | Rapid-acting
Aspart | NovoLog | Rapid-acting
Glulisine | Apidra | Rapid-acting
Glargine | Lantus | Long-acting basal
Degludec | Tresiba | Long-acting basal
Detemir | Levemir | Long-acting basal
Detemir was discontinued in the U.S. at the end of 2024. The first analog, lispro, was approved in the United States in 1996.
title: The history of insulin analogs
text: Insulin itself was one of the great medical breakthroughs of the twentieth century, first used to treat diabetes in the early 1920s and transforming a fatal disease into a manageable one. For decades, patients used animal-derived and later recombinant human insulin, but these did not match the body's natural pattern well: regular insulin acted too slowly for meals, and intermediate insulin produced peaks and troughs overnight. The analogs, beginning with lispro in 1996 and glargine in 2000, were engineered specifically to fix those mismatches, giving faster mealtime insulins and flatter, longer basal insulins.
title: How do insulin analogs work?
text: Insulin analogs bind the insulin receptor on muscle, fat, and liver cells, just as natural insulin does. Activating the receptor prompts cells to take up glucose from the blood (through the GLUT4 transporter), stimulates storage of glucose, fat, and protein, and suppresses the liver's production of glucose, all of which lower blood sugar. The amino-acid changes in the analogs do not alter this core action; they change the pharmacokinetics, how fast the insulin is absorbed and how long it lingers.
Rapid-acting analogs are engineered so their molecules separate and absorb quickly after injection, matching the glucose rise from a meal, while basal analogs are designed to precipitate or to bind albumin so they release slowly and provide flat, all-day coverage. Combining the two reproduces the body's natural pattern more closely than older insulins. In the Treat-to-Target trial, adding a basal analog to oral drugs let a larger share of patients reach their HbA1c goal without documented nighttime low blood sugar, compared with older NPH insulin.
title: Are they FDA-approved?
text: Yes. Insulin analogs have been FDA-approved since 1996, starting with lispro, followed by glargine in 2000 and others including aspart, glulisine, detemir, and degludec. They are approved to improve blood-sugar control in adults and, for many products, children with diabetes.
title: What are insulin analogs prescribed for?
text: Insulin analogs are prescribed for type 1 diabetes, where insulin is essential, and for type 2 diabetes when other treatments are not enough. Treatment is individualized, often combining a basal analog for background coverage with a rapid-acting analog at meals, delivered by pen, syringe, or pump.
title: What are the side effects?
text: According to product labels such as the Humalog prescribing information, the most common and important side effect is:
- Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia), which can be severe
Other effects include:
- Weight gain
- Injection-site reactions or fatty lumps (lipodystrophy)
- Low potassium
More serious considerations include:
- Severe hypoglycemia, which can cause seizures or loss of consciousness
- Fluid retention and heart failure when combined with certain diabetes pills (thiazolidinediones)
Insulin pens must never be shared between people, even if the needle is changed.

This document is educational and does not constitute medical advice.

peptides.what_it_is: Selective ghrelin-receptor agonist ("growth hormone secretagogue")
peptides.research_at_a_glance: Human data are limited to short pharmacology studies; benefit for recovery or body composition is unproven
peptides.key_takeaway: Ipamorelin is a synthetic peptide that mimics ghrelin to prompt the body to release more of its own growth hormone, and it is sold on the wellness and "research peptide" market. In a phase 2 trial of 114 bowel-resection patients (Beck, 2014), intravenous ipamorelin brought a median first tolerated meal at 25.3 hours versus 32.6 hours on placebo, a difference that was not significant (p = 0.15). Other human data show only that it raises growth hormone. As of 2026 it is not FDA-approved, it is not eligible for routine pharmacy compounding, and it is banned in sport.
peptides.mechanism: Ipamorelin activates the growth hormone secretagogue receptor, the same receptor the hunger hormone ghrelin uses, which triggers the pituitary to release growth hormone in pulses. In laboratory work it is described as relatively "selective," raising growth hormone with comparatively little effect on other hormones such as cortisol and prolactin. In conscious swine, it released GH without raising ACTH or cortisol, while GHRP-6 and GHRP-2 raised both. Because growth hormone and GHRH signaling act together, ghrelin-mimic peptides are often combined with GHRH analogs. No published human randomized controlled trial tests ipamorelin with CJC-1295 as of September 2026. The marketed benefits are extrapolated from this growth-hormone effect. This describes the proposed mechanism, separate from proven outcomes.

detail.faq:
q: Is ipamorelin FDA-approved?
a: No. Ipamorelin has never been FDA-approved for any human therapeutic indication. In a Phase 2 trial for postoperative ileus, ipamorelin showed no significant difference from placebo on the key efficacy endpoint, and clinical development did not produce an approved product. Ipamorelin has not undergone the Phase 3 trials required for FDA approval.
q: Is ipamorelin legal in the United States?
a: Ipamorelin's 503A nomination was withdrawn after it had been placed in Category 2, and FDA now lists it among bulk drug substances nominated but withdrawn. As of September 2026, ipamorelin is not eligible for compounding under Section 503A, so it cannot be legally used in 503A compounded medications for human administration. Products sold online as ipamorelin are not regulated and do not have a legal pathway to human use in the United States.
q: Can a doctor prescribe ipamorelin?
a: Not in any way that can be lawfully filled in the United States under current regulations. Ipamorelin is not eligible for 503A compounding and remains on FDA's 503B Category 2 list, so no compounded preparation for human use is lawful. There is no FDA-approved manufactured form of ipamorelin to prescribe. Any product available online falls outside the regulated pharmaceutical supply chain.
q: What changed in the FDA peptide category list, and how does it affect ipamorelin?
a: The FDA's Section 503A bulk drug substance review process evaluates whether specific compounds may be used in compounded medications. Ipamorelin had been on the 503A Category 2 list, which removed the legal pathway that let compounding pharmacies prepare and dispense it under physician prescription. Its 503A nomination was later withdrawn, and FDA now lists it among substances nominated but withdrawn, a step that was not a finding that it is safe. Ipamorelin was already off 503A Category 2 before April 2026, when FDA moved a group of other peptides, such as BPC-157, to that list. Withdrawal did not restore compounding eligibility: a withdrawn substance is not eligible for 503A compounding unless FDA adds it to the 503A bulks list or places it in Category 1, and ipamorelin remains on FDA's 503B Category 2 list.
q: What is the difference between ipamorelin and sermorelin?
a: Ipamorelin is a GHS-R1a agonist that mimics ghrelin at its receptor. Sermorelin is a GHRH analog that activates the GHRH receptor. Both ultimately stimulate GH release from the pituitary, but through different receptor pathways with different regulatory inputs. In studies of the growth-hormone-releasing peptide class, not ipamorelin itself, somatostatin only blunted their effect but nearly abolished GHRH's.
q: What is the difference between ipamorelin and GHRP-2 or GHRP-6?
a: The primary distinction is hormonal selectivity. In swine, ipamorelin released GH without significantly raising ACTH or cortisol, while GHRP-2 and GHRP-6 raised both. In healthy adults, GHRP-2 and hexarelin also raised prolactin, ACTH, and cortisol alongside GH. GHRP-2 and GHRP-6 sit in FDA's Category 3 for 503A compounding.
q: Is ipamorelin prohibited in sport?
a: Yes. As of the 2026 WADA Prohibited List, ipamorelin is prohibited under category S2 (peptide hormones, growth factors, related substances, and mimetics), both in- and out-of-competition. Detection methodology in urine has been validated. Athletes subject to WADA or USADA jurisdiction who use ipamorelin risk anti-doping rule violations.

peptides.name: Kisspeptin-10
peptides.fda_status: Non-FDA-approved peptide; remains investigational
peptides.evidence_note: There is real, peer-reviewed, placebo-controlled human investigational data with a well-characterized reproductive-axis mechanism, but the trials are small, use surrogate endpoints, often used a longer form of the peptide, and no approved efficacy exists.
peptides.what_it_is: Fragment of kisspeptin, which triggers the reproductive hormone axis
peptides.research_at_a_glance: Real, peer-reviewed human investigational studies, though small and often using a longer form (kisspeptin-54)
peptides.key_takeaway: Kisspeptin-10 is a fragment of a natural reproductive hormone, sold on the "research peptide" market and not FDA-approved. The one human trial of kisspeptin-10 itself was small. In a 2013 proof-of-concept study by George and colleagues, five men with type 2 diabetes and low testosterone took part. An 11-hour infusion in four of them raised luteinizing hormone (LH) from 3.9 to 20.7 IU/L (p = 0.03) and testosterone from 8.5 to 11.4 nmol/L (p = 0.002) against their own baseline, with no placebo group. Much other human work used the longer kisspeptin-54, and the peptide remains investigational.
peptides.mechanism: Kisspeptin acts on receptors on the brain's GnRH neurons, stimulating the release of GnRH, which in turn drives the pituitary hormones LH and FSH that regulate the gonads. This reproductive-axis role is well established in humans and animals. Additional effects on brain regions involved in sexual and emotional processing are an emerging, investigational area. This describes the mechanism, separate from any approved treatment use.
peptides.human_study_findings: There is genuine, peer-reviewed human investigational data, with limits. According to PubMed, controlled studies from academic groups have reported that kisspeptin modulates brain processing of sexual and emotional cues in healthy men (here and here) and in women with low sexual desire (here), alongside its well-characterized stimulation of reproductive hormones (review). These studies have limits: - They are small, early-phase studies. - They often use brain-imaging rather than clinical endpoints. - Much of the sexual-behavior work used the longer kisspeptin-54. The work is investigational and does not amount to an approved, proven treatment. The only trial of kisspeptin-10 itself was small. In 2013, George and colleagues found that a single intravenous dose raised LH in five men with type 2 diabetes and low testosterone, plus seven healthy men. In four of the men with diabetes, an 11-hour infusion raised LH and testosterone. Hormone | Before infusion | After infusion | p-value LH | 3.9 IU/L | 20.7 IU/L | 0.03 Testosterone | 8.5 nmol/L | 11.4 nmol/L | 0.002 The trial had no placebo arm, so it shows feasibility rather than benefit. The women's trial enrolled 32 premenopausal women with hypoactive sexual desire disorder in a crossover design using kisspeptin-54. Brain scans showed deactivation of the left inferior frontal gyrus, an imaging finding rather than a clinical outcome.

detail.sections:
title: What is kisspeptin-10?
text: Kisspeptin-10 is a ten-amino acid fragment of kisspeptin, a natural hormone that acts as a master switch for the reproductive system. It is studied for reproductive and sexual function and sold through "research peptide" channels. A closely related longer natural form, kisspeptin-54, is used in much of the human research. It is not an approved medicine.
title: How does it work?
text: Kisspeptin acts on receptors on the brain's GnRH neurons, stimulating the release of GnRH, which in turn drives the pituitary hormones LH and FSH that regulate the gonads. This reproductive-axis role is well established in humans and animals. Additional effects on brain regions involved in sexual and emotional processing are an emerging, investigational area. This describes the mechanism, separate from any approved treatment use.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No. There is no FDA-approved kisspeptin product for any indication, and it remains investigational. It was not among the peptides reviewed favorably at the 2026 FDA compounding advisory meetings.
The WADA 2026 Prohibited List bans kisspeptin and its agonist analogues in male athletes.
title: What does the research show?
text: There is genuine, peer-reviewed human investigational data, with limits. According to PubMed, controlled studies from academic groups have reported that kisspeptin modulates brain processing of sexual and emotional cues in healthy men (here and here) and in women with low sexual desire (here), alongside its well-characterized stimulation of reproductive hormones (review). These studies have limits:
- They are small, early-phase studies.
- They often use brain-imaging rather than clinical endpoints.
- Much of the sexual-behavior work used the longer kisspeptin-54.
The work is investigational and does not amount to an approved, proven treatment.
The only trial of kisspeptin-10 itself was small. In 2013, George and colleagues found that a single intravenous dose raised LH in five men with type 2 diabetes and low testosterone, plus seven healthy men. In four of the men with diabetes, an 11-hour infusion raised LH and testosterone.
Hormone | Before infusion | After infusion | p-value
LH | 3.9 IU/L | 20.7 IU/L | 0.03
Testosterone | 8.5 nmol/L | 11.4 nmol/L | 0.002
The trial had no placebo arm, so it shows feasibility rather than benefit.
The women's trial enrolled 32 premenopausal women with hypoactive sexual desire disorder in a crossover design using kisspeptin-54. Brain scans showed deactivation of the left inferior frontal gyrus, an imaging finding rather than a clinical outcome.

Much other human work used the longer kisspeptin-54, and the peptide remains investigational.

detail.sections:
title: What is KPV?
text: KPV is a tripeptide (lysine-proline-valine) corresponding to the tail end of alpha-MSH, a hormone with anti-inflammatory properties. It is sold through wellness and "research peptide" channels for gut inflammation, inflammatory bowel conditions, and skin, and it is not an approved medicine.
title: How does it work?
text: KPV retains much of alpha-MSH's anti-inflammatory activity. In laboratory models it is taken up into gut and immune cells, where it is proposed to reduce pro-inflammatory signaling, including the NF-kB pathway and downstream inflammatory messengers such as TNF-alpha. Notably, some of its anti-inflammatory activity appears independent of the MC1R receptor. These are cell and animal findings. This describes the proposed mechanism, separate from demonstrated benefit in people.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No. KPV is not approved by the FDA. In July 2026 the FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee gave KPV a non-binding favorable vote toward the 503A compounding list. Because that vote is only a recommendation and the FDA has not completed rulemaking, KPV is not currently on the list and cannot be legally compounded on that basis.
title: What does the research show?
text: The evidence is preclinical. According to PubMed, two mouse studies of colitis reported these results:
Form tested | Model | Finding
KPV | Mouse models of colitis | Reduced inflammation, partly independent of MC1R (here)
Nanoparticle-delivered KPV | Mice with colitis | Eased colitis, with mucosal healing and reduced TNF-alpha (here)
Its anti-inflammatory basis is reviewed here. There are no controlled human trials establishing KPV for gut or skin use, so its marketed benefit is unproven in people.

This document is educational, is not medical advice or a health claim, and is not an offer to sell any product.

peptides.what_it_is: A long-acting somatostatin analog peptide
peptides.key_takeaway: Lanreotide (sold as Somatuline Depot) is a long-acting somatostatin analog that suppresses growth hormone and gut hormones and slows the growth of certain neuroendocrine tumors. It is used for acromegaly and for gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, and in the CLARINET trial it significantly delayed tumor progression. It has been FDA-approved in the U.S. since 2007 and is given as a deep subcutaneous injection about once a month.
peptides.mechanism: Lanreotide binds somatostatin receptors, primarily subtypes 2 and 5, on hormone-secreting and tumor cells. Activating those receptors suppresses growth hormone and insulin-like growth factor 1 and reduces the release of gut hormones. Beyond controlling hormone excess, somatostatin-receptor activation has an antiproliferative effect on well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumors, slowing their growth. In acromegaly, that suppression lowers growth hormone and IGF-1 and improves symptoms; in neuroendocrine tumors, it both controls hormone-related symptoms and delays progression. In the CLARINET trial, lanreotide significantly prolonged progression-free survival compared with placebo in people with metastatic enteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors: Group | Median progression-free survival Lanreotide | Not reached Placebo | 18 months The depot formulation is injected deeply under the skin about once a month.

title: What is lanreotide?
text: Lanreotide, sold under the brand Somatuline Depot (Somatuline Autogel outside the U.S.), is a synthetic cyclic octapeptide analog of somatostatin. Like octreotide it mimics the body's natural "off switch" for growth hormone and several gut hormones, but it is supplied as a long-acting gel in a prefilled syringe that maintains drug levels for weeks. It was developed under the code BIM-23014 and approved in the United States in 2007.

peptides.fda_status: Investigational peptide, not approved by the FDA
peptides.evidence_note: Its pivotal Phase 3 was stopped for futility and pooled trial data show no effect on the permeability endpoint, so there is no sound human evidence that it works.
peptides.what_it_is: Larazotide acetate is an experimental peptide of eight amino acids, taken by mouth, studied as an adjunct to the gluten-free diet in celiac disease, an autoimmune reaction to gluten that damages the small intestine. It was most recently developed by 9 Meters Biopharma under the code AT-1001. It is investigational, is not approved, and its lead development program has been discontinued.
peptides.key_takeaway: Larazotide acetate is an investigational oral peptide that was studied as an add-on to the gluten-free diet for celiac disease, intended to tighten the junctions between intestinal cells. Its pivotal Phase 3 trial was stopped for futility, and pooled trial data did not show an effect on a key measure of intestinal permeability. As of 2026, it is not approved and its lead program has been halted.
peptides.mechanism: Larazotide was designed to act as a "tight-junction regulator." The intestinal lining has junctions between cells that control what passes through; in celiac disease these are thought to loosen, letting gluten fragments cross and trigger inflammation. Larazotide was proposed to counter the hormone zonulin and promote closure of these junctions, reducing the leakage. This is the proposed mechanism; as the trials below show, it did not translate into a confirmed clinical benefit.

Overall, the human evidence does not support a benefit.

peptides.name: Leuprolide
peptides.fda_status: Yes. Leuprolide was first approved by the FDA in 1985 as a daily subcutaneous injection, with the long-acting Lupron Depot following in 1989. Over the following decades the FDA cleared additional depot strengths, new indications, and several brands, including Eligard, the Fensolvi pediatric depot, and the ready-to-use Camcevi.
peptides.evidence_note: Leuprolide is FDA-approved for prostate cancer, endometriosis, uterine fibroids, and central precocious puberty, supported by decades of controlled trials and depot registration studies.
peptides.what_it_is: A GnRH (LHRH) receptor agonist peptide that suppresses sex-hormone production
peptides.key_takeaway: Leuprolide (leuprolide acetate; brands include Lupron, Eligard, and Fensolvi) is a synthetic nonapeptide agonist of gonadotropin-releasing hormone that, given continuously, suppresses the pituitary and shuts down testosterone and estrogen production. It is prescribed for prostate cancer, endometriosis, and precocious puberty, lowering testosterone to castrate levels within two to four weeks. It has been FDA-approved in the U.S. since 1985 and comes in depot formulations lasting from one to six months.
peptides.mechanism:
Leuprolide binds the GnRH receptor on the pituitary, and its effect depends on how it is delivered. A first dose actually stimulates the pituitary, producing a short-lived surge in LH, FSH, and testosterone known as the "flare." Because leuprolide then occupies the receptor continuously rather than in natural pulses, the pituitary gonadotrophs downregulate and desensitize. Within about two to four weeks LH and FSH fall, and testosterone in men, or estrogen in women, drops to castrate or postmenopausal levels.
That sustained suppression is the therapeutic goal, and the table below shows what it does in each condition.
Condition | What hormone suppression does
Prostate cancer | Removing testosterone starves hormone-sensitive tumor cells
Endometriosis and fibroids | Lowering estrogen shrinks hormone-driven tissue
Central precocious puberty | Switching off the premature hormone signal halts early sexual development and helps preserve adult height
The flare is why men with advanced prostate cancer are often given an anti-androgen in the first weeks, to blunt any transient worsening. Depot formulations release the drug slowly so a single injection maintains suppression for one, three, four, or six months. In the pediatric registration program, a three-month depot kept stimulated LH suppressed in 78 to 95% of treated children.
peptides.side_effects_safety: According to the prescribing information, common side effects reflect low sex-hormone levels and the injection itself: - Hot flashes and sweating - Injection-site pain or reactions - Decreased libido and erectile dysfunction - Fatigue and mood changes - Bone-density loss with long-term use More serious considerations include: - Transient tumor "flare" symptoms in the first weeks of prostate-cancer treatment - Increased risk of hyperglycemia, diabetes, and cardiovascular events with long-term androgen deprivation - Rare seizures - Severe skin reactions - In children treated for precocious puberty, mood and behavior changes and raised pressure around the brain (pseudotumor cerebri), per the pediatric label

detail.sections:
title: What is leuprolide?
text: Leuprolide, known generically as leuprolide acetate (INN leuprorelin) and sold as Lupron, Lupron Depot, Eligard, Fensolvi, and Camcevi, is a synthetic nine-amino-acid analog of gonadotropin-releasing hormone. The natural hormone is released in pulses by the hypothalamus and tells the pituitary to make luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), which in turn drive the testes and ovaries to produce testosterone and estrogen. Leuprolide is a far more potent and longer-lasting version of that signal, first developed under the code TAP-144 and approved in the United States in 1985.
title: The history of leuprolide
text: Leuprolide grew directly out of the discovery of GnRH itself. Andrew Schally and Roger Guillemin shared the 1977 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for isolating and sequencing the hypothalamic releasing hormones, including GnRH. Once the ten-amino-acid structure was known, chemists built analogs that resisted breakdown and bound the receptor more tightly. Leuprolide, with a single amino-acid substitution and an ethylamide tail, was among the first of these "superagonists" to reach the clinic, and its approval in 1985 helped establish medical castration as an alternative to surgical removal of the testes for prostate cancer.
title: How does leuprolide work?
text: Leuprolide binds the GnRH receptor on the pituitary, and its effect depends on how it is delivered. A first dose actually stimulates the pituitary, producing a short-lived surge in LH, FSH, and testosterone known as the "flare." Because leuprolide then occupies the receptor continuously rather than in natural pulses, the pituitary gonadotrophs downregulate and desensitize. Within about two to four weeks LH and FSH fall, and testosterone in men, or estrogen in women, drops to castrate or postmenopausal levels.
That sustained suppression is the therapeutic goal, and the table below shows what it does in each condition.
Condition | What hormone suppression does
Prostate cancer | Removing testosterone starves hormone-sensitive tumor cells
Endometriosis and fibroids | Lowering estrogen shrinks hormone-driven tissue
Central precocious puberty | Switching off the premature hormone signal halts early sexual development and helps preserve adult height
The flare is why men with advanced prostate cancer are often given an anti-androgen in the first weeks, to blunt any transient worsening. Depot formulations release the drug slowly so a single injection maintains suppression for one, three, four, or six months. In the pediatric registration program, a three-month depot kept stimulated LH suppressed in 78 to 95% of treated children.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: Yes. Leuprolide was first approved by the FDA in 1985 as a daily subcutaneous injection, with the long-acting Lupron Depot following in 1989. Over the following decades the FDA cleared additional depot strengths, new indications, and several brands, including Eligard, the Fensolvi pediatric depot, and the ready-to-use Camcevi.
title: What is leuprolide prescribed for?
text: Leuprolide is prescribed for:
- Advanced or metastatic prostate cancer, as palliative hormone therapy
- Endometriosis
- Uterine fibroids with associated anemia, usually before surgery and combined with iron
- Central precocious puberty in children
Because it works by suppressing sex hormones, it is contraindicated in pregnancy; the gynecologic and pediatric uses are often time-limited in part to protect bone density.
title: What are the side effects?
text: According to the prescribing information, common side effects reflect low sex-hormone levels and the injection itself:
- Hot flashes and sweating
- Injection-site pain or reactions
- Decreased libido and erectile dysfunction
- Fatigue and mood changes
- Bone-density loss with long-term use
More serious considerations include:
- Transient tumor "flare" symptoms in the first weeks of prostate-cancer treatment
- Increased risk of hyperglycemia, diabetes, and cardiovascular events with long-term androgen deprivation
- Rare seizures
- Severe skin reactions
- In children treated for precocious puberty, mood and behavior changes and raised pressure around the brain (pseudotumor cerebri), per the pediatric label
detail.sources_note: Sources: FDA prescribing information for Lupron Depot, Eligard, and Fensolvi; a trial of the three-month pediatric depot (Lee et al., Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism, 2012, DOI: 10.1210/jc.2011-2704), indexed on PubMed; and background on the Nobel-recognized discovery of GnRH. This document is educational and does not constitute medical advice.

peptides.key_takeaway: Linaclotide (sold as Linzess) is a minimally absorbed peptide that works inside the gut to draw in fluid and ease abdominal pain, used for constipation-predominant irritable bowel syndrome and chronic constipation. It activates a receptor on the intestinal lining that increases fluid secretion and speeds transit. It has been FDA-approved in the U.S. since 2012, is taken as a daily capsule, and carries a boxed warning against use in very young children.
peptides.mechanism: Linaclotide activates guanylate cyclase-C, a receptor on the surface of the cells lining the intestine. Switching on this receptor raises cyclic GMP inside and around those cells, which opens chloride and bicarbonate channels and drives secretion of fluid into the intestinal lumen. The added fluid softens stool and speeds its passage, relieving constipation. The elevated cyclic GMP outside the cells is also thought to reduce the sensitivity of the pain-sensing nerves in the gut wall, which may explain the reduction in abdominal pain seen in IBS-C. Because linaclotide stays in the gut and is not meaningfully absorbed, its effects are local. In the phase 3 IBS-C program, roughly a third of patients met the FDA combined responder endpoint versus about 14 percent on placebo.

title: What is linaclotide?
text: Linaclotide, sold under the brand Linzess (Constella in some regions), is a 14-amino-acid peptide taken by mouth that acts almost entirely within the intestine, since it is barely absorbed into the bloodstream. It is used for chronic constipation and for irritable bowel syndrome with constipation (IBS-C), conditions where slow transit and abdominal discomfort go together. It was developed under the code MD-1100 and approved in the United States in 2012.
title: How does linaclotide work?
text: Linaclotide activates guanylate cyclase-C, a receptor on the surface of the cells lining the intestine. Switching on this receptor raises cyclic GMP inside and around those cells, which opens chloride and bicarbonate channels and drives secretion of fluid into the intestinal lumen. The added fluid softens stool and speeds its passage, relieving constipation.
The elevated cyclic GMP outside the cells is also thought to reduce the sensitivity of the pain-sensing nerves in the gut wall, which may explain the reduction in abdominal pain seen in IBS-C. Because linaclotide stays in the gut and is not meaningfully absorbed, its effects are local. In the phase 3 IBS-C program, roughly a third of patients met the FDA combined responder endpoint versus about 14 percent on placebo.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: Yes. Linaclotide was approved by the FDA in stages, starting with adults and later extending to children.

text: Linaclotide is prescribed for irritable bowel syndrome with constipation in adults and children 7 and older, chronic idiopathic constipation in adults, and functional constipation in children 2 and older. It is taken once daily on an empty stomach, and it must not be used in children under 2.

peptides.fda_status: Yes. Victoza was first approved in 2010 for type 2 diabetes, and later to reduce cardiovascular risk in people with type 2 diabetes and heart disease. Saxenda was approved in 2014 for weight management, and both have since been approved for use in adolescents.
peptides.evidence_note: It is approved by the FDA for type 2 diabetes, chronic weight management, and cardiovascular risk reduction in type 2 diabetes, backed by the large LEAD, SCALE, and LEADER randomized controlled trial programs.
peptides.what_it_is: FDA-approved GLP-1 peptide, sold as Victoza for type 2 diabetes and Saxenda for weight management
peptides.key_takeaway: Liraglutide is a once-daily GLP-1 receptor agonist and the first of its kind, engineered from human GLP-1 with a fatty-acid chain that binds albumin to extend its action. Sold as Victoza for type 2 diabetes and Saxenda for weight management, it produced about 8% average weight loss in the SCALE trial and became the first GLP-1 shown to reduce cardiovascular events in LEADER. Its albumin-binding design paved the way for once-weekly semaglutide.
peptides.mechanism:
Liraglutide activates the GLP-1 receptor, mimicking a natural gut hormone the body releases after eating. Through that receptor it prompts the pancreas to release insulin when blood sugar is high. Because this effect is glucose-dependent, meaning it works mainly when blood sugar is already elevated, liraglutide on its own carries a low risk of causing hypoglycemia. It also reduces the release of glucagon (a hormone that raises blood sugar) and slows the rate at which the stomach empties, which blunts the rise in blood sugar after a meal and helps a person feel full for longer.
Beyond the gut and pancreas, liraglutide acts on appetite centers in the brain, where it increases feelings of fullness and reduces hunger and how much a person eats. This appetite effect is a large part of why it produces weight loss, not just better blood sugar control.
Native GLP-1 breaks down within minutes, so liraglutide is engineered with a fatty-acid chain that binds to albumin in the blood. This extends its half-life to about 13 hours and allows once-daily dosing. In the SCALE weight-management trial, adults on the 3.0 mg dose lost about 8% of their body weight over 56 weeks, compared with about 2.6% on placebo.

detail.sections:
title: What is liraglutide?
text: Liraglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist, a peptide that closely mimics the natural gut hormone GLP-1. It shares about 97% of its structure with human GLP-1 and has a fatty-acid chain added so it binds to proteins in the blood and lasts long enough to be dosed once a day.
It is made by Novo Nordisk and sold under two brand names, Victoza for type 2 diabetes and Saxenda for weight management, and a generic version is now available. Both branded forms are once-daily subcutaneous injections.
title: The history of liraglutide
text: Liraglutide's history includes three U.S. milestones:
Year | Milestone
2010 | Reached the U.S. market as Victoza, the first once-daily GLP-1 drug
2014 | A higher-dose version called Saxenda became one of the first GLP-1 drugs approved specifically for weight management
2016 | The LEADER trial made liraglutide the first GLP-1 shown to reduce cardiovascular events
Victoza improved on the earlier exenatide, which had to be injected twice a day. Its key engineering step, attaching a fatty-acid chain so the peptide clings to albumin and survives longer in the body, is the same approach Novo Nordisk later used to create once-weekly semaglutide.
In that sense, liraglutide paved the way for the current generation of GLP-1 medicines, including semaglutide and tirzepatide.
title: How does it work?
text: Liraglutide activates the GLP-1 receptor, mimicking a natural gut hormone the body releases after eating. Through that receptor it prompts the pancreas to release insulin when blood sugar is high. Because this effect is glucose-dependent, meaning it works mainly when blood sugar is already elevated, liraglutide on its own carries a low risk of causing hypoglycemia. It also reduces the release of glucagon (a hormone that raises blood sugar) and slows the rate at which the stomach empties, which blunts the rise in blood sugar after a meal and helps a person feel full for longer.
Beyond the gut and pancreas, liraglutide acts on appetite centers in the brain, where it increases feelings of fullness and reduces hunger and how much a person eats. This appetite effect is a large part of why it produces weight loss, not just better blood sugar control.
Native GLP-1 breaks down within minutes, so liraglutide is engineered with a fatty-acid chain that binds to albumin in the blood. This extends its half-life to about 13 hours and allows once-daily dosing. In the SCALE weight-management trial, adults on the 3.0 mg dose lost about 8% of their body weight over 56 weeks, compared with about 2.6% on placebo.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: Yes. Victoza was first approved in 2010 for type 2 diabetes, and later to reduce cardiovascular risk in people with type 2 diabetes and heart disease. Saxenda was approved in 2014 for weight management, and both have since been approved for use in adolescents.
title: What is liraglutide prescribed for?
text: For type 2 diabetes, Victoza is prescribed to improve blood sugar control alongside diet and exercise. For weight management, Saxenda is approved for adults with obesity (a BMI of 30 or higher) or overweight (a BMI of 27 or higher) plus a weight-related condition such as high blood pressure or high cholesterol, and for adolescents aged 12 and older with obesity.
It should not be used by people with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2, or by anyone with a known allergy to liraglutide.
title: What are the side effects?
text: The most common side effects are gastrointestinal, and they are usually strongest when the dose is increased:
- Nausea
- Diarrhea
- Vomiting
- Constipation
- Decreased appetite
- Headache
- Fatigue
Less common but more serious risks include:
- Thyroid C-cell tumors: liraglutide carries a boxed warning based on rodent studies. It is not known whether this happens in humans.
- Pancreatitis, or inflammation of the pancreas
- Gallbladder problems, including gallstones
- Acute kidney injury, usually from dehydration caused by vomiting or diarrhea
- Low blood sugar, especially when combined with insulin or a sulfonylurea
- Increased heart rate
detail.sources_note: Sources: FDA prescribing information for Victoza and Saxenda (liraglutide); the SCALE weight-management trial (Pi-Sunyer et al., 2015, DOI: 10.1056/NEJMoa1411892) and the LEADER cardiovascular outcomes trial (Marso et al., 2016, DOI: 10.1056/NEJMoa1603827) in the New England Journal of Medicine, both indexed on PubMed; and a review of the history of GLP-1 receptor agonists. This document is educational and does not constitute medical advice.

title: What is lixisenatide?

It is made by Sanofi and was sold on its own as Adlyxin, and it is also available combined with insulin glargine in a product called Soliqua. It is given as a subcutaneous injection.
title: How does it work?

- Lowers glucagon
- Markedly slows the rate at which the stomach empties
Because it is short-acting, its strongest effect is blunting the post-meal blood sugar spike rather than providing round-the-clock coverage, which is why it is taken before a meal. In the ELIXA trial, in people who had recently had acute coronary syndrome, lixisenatide was shown to be cardiovascular-safe, one of the first cardiovascular outcome trials for a GLP-1 drug.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: Yes. Lixisenatide was approved in the U.S. in 2016 for type 2 diabetes. Sanofi discontinued the standalone Adlyxin product in the U.S. in 2023 for business reasons, though lixisenatide remains available in the combination product Soliqua.
title: What is lixisenatide prescribed for?
text: Lixisenatide is prescribed to improve blood sugar control in adults with type 2 diabetes, alongside diet and exercise, with a particular effect on after-meal blood sugar. It is not a treatment for type 1 diabetes. Unlike the long-acting GLP-1 drugs, this short-acting exendin-based agent does not carry a thyroid C-cell tumor boxed warning.
title: What are the side effects?
text: The most common side effects are gastrointestinal:
- Nausea
- Vomiting
- Diarrhea
- Headache
- Dizziness
Less common but more serious risks include:
- Pancreatitis, or inflammation of the pancreas
- Severe allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis
- Acute kidney injury, usually from dehydration caused by vomiting or diarrhea
- Low blood sugar, especially when combined with insulin or a sulfonylurea

This document is educational and does not constitute medical advice.

detail.faq:
q: Is LL-37 FDA-approved?
a: No. LL-37 is not FDA-approved for any indication, and as of September 2026 it is not eligible for 503A compounding: FDA removed it from Category 2 in April 2026 after the nomination was withdrawn, but it is not on the 503A bulks list or in FDA's Category 1. FDA has announced an advisory committee meeting, to be held before the end of February 2027, that will discuss LL-37.
q: What does LL-37 do in the body naturally?
a: LL-37 is an endogenous antimicrobial peptide produced by neutrophils and various epithelial cells, including skin cells. In neutrophils, its precursor protein hCAP-18 is cleaved by proteinase 3 after release from the cell, freeing the active peptide. It kills bacteria, viruses, and fungi directly through membrane disruption; recruits neutrophils, monocytes, and T cells to infection sites via FPRL1 receptor signaling; and supports wound healing through skin re-epithelialization and new blood-vessel formation.
q: How does vitamin D affect LL-37 levels?
a: Vitamin D receptor activation by 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D drives transcription of the CAMP gene, which encodes hCAP-18 (the LL-37 precursor). In laboratory studies of human immune cells, serum with low 25-hydroxyvitamin D was less able to support cathelicidin induction.
q: Can LL-37 make autoimmune conditions worse?
a: Potentially, yes. LL-37 has been identified as a psoriasis T-cell autoantigen, and it can bind self-DNA to activate plasmacytoid dendritic cells via TLR9, triggering an interferon response that may drive autoimmunity in psoriasis. It is also implicated in rosacea as an inflammatory mediator when abnormally processed by elevated serine proteases.
q: What is the difference between LL-37 and defensins?
a: LL-37 is a cathelicidin, while defensins are a structurally distinct family of antimicrobial peptides. LL-37 takes on a helical shape in membrane-like environments and kills through amphipathic membrane disruption; defensins contain six cysteine residues linked by three disulfide bonds into a beta-sheet structure. Both are components of the human innate immune system.
q: What has the human clinical research examined?
a: The most advanced human clinical evidence for LL-37 comes from topical wound-healing research. A multicenter phase IIb randomized trial of topical LL-37 in 148 patients with hard-to-heal venous leg ulcers found no significant benefit across the full cohort, with a signal in larger ulcers on post-hoc analysis. A 2023 randomized trial in diabetic foot ulcers reported consistently greater granulation in the LL-37 group. This is the research application with the most human trial data, but the evidence does not meet the threshold for an FDA-approved indication.
q: Who should not use LL-37?
a: Based on LL-37's dual-edged biology, the populations of greatest concern include individuals with active or history of psoriasis (LL-37 is a psoriasis autoantigen and, bound to self-DNA, activates plasmacytoid dendritic cells through TLR9), rosacea or rosacea-prone skin (abnormal cathelicidin processing is implicated in rosacea), active malignancy (LL-37 is upregulated in ovarian, breast, and lung tumors, and FDA notes nonclinical findings that it can be protumorigenic in some tissues), systemic autoimmune conditions involving innate immune dysregulation, pregnancy or breastfeeding (no safety data), and known hypersensitivity to LL-37. These are illustrative mechanistic concerns, not a formal contraindication checklist.
detail.sections:
title: What is LL-37?
text: LL-37 is the active 37-amino acid fragment of the only human cathelicidin, a natural host-defense (antimicrobial) peptide produced by immune and skin cells. It is a well-studied part of the body's innate immune system. It is sold through wellness and "research peptide" channels for antimicrobial and immune support, and it is not an approved medicine.
title: How does it work?
text: LL-37 has two broad actions. Its positively charged, membrane-active structure can directly disrupt the membranes of microbes, and it also modulates the immune system, influencing immune-cell recruitment, inflammation, and wound healing, and binding some microbial factors. These roles are documented in a large laboratory and animal literature. Importantly, its effects are context-dependent: it can be either pro- or anti-inflammatory and has been implicated in some inflammatory skin diseases. This describes its biology, separate from demonstrated benefit from giving it as a therapy.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No. There is no FDA-approved exogenous LL-37 therapeutic, and gray-market versions are unapproved. It was not among the peptides reviewed favorably at the 2026 FDA compounding advisory meetings.
title: What does the research show?
text: The evidence is preclinical for any injected wellness use. LL-37's biology in innate immunity, wound healing, and skin disease is documented in humans and in extensive laboratory work, including studies of how it disrupts microbes and binds microbial factors (example).
However, there are no controlled human trials establishing efficacy or safety of self-administered LL-37 for antimicrobial, immune, or healing wellness uses, and its context-dependent, sometimes pro-inflammatory, behavior argues against simple benefit claims.

peptides.evidence_note: There is real but limited positive human evidence from an early-phase, uncontrolled trial, with no randomized efficacy data and later results resting partly on company reports.
peptides.what_it_is: Oncolytic peptide injected directly into tumors (intratumorally)
peptides.research_at_a_glance: Early-phase human data show injected-tumor shrinkage and immune activation
peptides.key_takeaway: LTX-315 is an investigational "oncolytic" peptide that is injected directly into tumors to break tumor cells apart and provoke an immune response, developed by Lytix Biopharma. In an early-phase trial it shrank injected tumors and triggered immune cell infiltration, and the company has described plans toward a registrational trial in melanoma. As of 2026, it is not approved and its efficacy has not been tested in controlled trials.
peptides.mechanism: LTX-315 inserts into and disrupts cell membranes, causing tumor cells to rupture in a way that releases tumor antigens and "danger signals." This form of cell death is intended to alert the immune system, drawing in cancer-fighting T-cells and potentially producing responses even in tumors that were not injected (an "abscopal" effect). The approach is being combined with immune-checkpoint drugs on the theory that releasing tumor antigens makes the immune response stronger. This describes the proposed mechanism, separate from the outcomes below.
peptides.human_study_findings: The human evidence is early-phase and uncontrolled. According to PubMed, a Phase 1 dose-ranging trial in advanced solid tumors reported: - Tumor necrosis - Infiltration of cancer-fighting T-cells - At least 30% shrinkage of injected tumors in some patients - Signs of a systemic immune response However, standard objective responses to the drug alone were not seen. Later Phase 2 and combination data have been reported mainly via company releases. There are no controlled efficacy trials yet, so the benefit is suggested but not established.

detail.sections:
title: What is LTX-315?
text: LTX-315 (also known as oncopore and ruxotemitide) is an experimental peptide of nine amino acids that is injected directly into a tumor to destroy tumor cells and stimulate the immune system. It is developed by Lytix Biopharma and studied alone and in combination with immunotherapy for solid tumors such as melanoma. It is investigational and not approved.
title: How does it work?
text: LTX-315 inserts into and disrupts cell membranes, causing tumor cells to rupture in a way that releases tumor antigens and "danger signals." This form of cell death is intended to alert the immune system, drawing in cancer-fighting T-cells and potentially producing responses even in tumors that were not injected (an "abscopal" effect). The approach is being combined with immune-checkpoint drugs on the theory that releasing tumor antigens makes the immune response stronger. This describes the proposed mechanism, separate from the outcomes below.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No. LTX-315 is investigational and not approved. Its two development programs sit at different stages:
Program | Developer | Indication | Regulatory stage
LTX-315 | Lytix Biopharma | High-risk resectable melanoma | According to the company, FDA feedback supports a path toward a registrational Phase 3 trial, but no such trial has been completed
VP-315 (licensed LTX-315) | Verrica Pharmaceuticals | Basal cell carcinoma | The FDA accepted the investigational new drug (IND) application for that program in 2021, which is clearance to begin a Phase 2 clinical trial, not a marketing approval
title: What does the research show?
text: The human evidence is early-phase and uncontrolled. According to PubMed, a Phase 1 dose-ranging trial in advanced solid tumors reported:
- Tumor necrosis
- Infiltration of cancer-fighting T-cells
- At least 30% shrinkage of injected tumors in some patients
- Signs of a systemic immune response
However, standard objective responses to the drug alone were not seen.
Later Phase 2 and combination data have been reported mainly via company releases. There are no controlled efficacy trials yet, so the benefit is suggested but not established.

peptides.fda_status: Yes. Lutetium Lu-177 dotatate (Lutathera) was approved by the FDA in 2018 for somatostatin-receptor-positive gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors in adults, with later expansion to adolescents. It is given as four intravenous infusions about eight weeks apart.

peptides.what_it_is: A lutetium-177-labeled somatostatin analog delivering targeted radiation (peptide receptor radionuclide therapy)
peptides.key_takeaway: Lutetium Lu-177 dotatate (sold as Lutathera) is a targeted radiation therapy that attaches a radioactive isotope to a somatostatin analog to deliver radiation directly to neuroendocrine tumors. It was the first peptide receptor radionuclide therapy approved in the United States. It has been FDA-approved in the U.S. since 2018 and is given as a series of intravenous infusions.
peptides.mechanism: The dotatate peptide binds somatostatin receptor subtype 2 on neuroendocrine tumor cells and is taken inside them. Attached to it is lutetium-177, which emits beta particles, a short-range form of radiation. Because the tracer concentrates in receptor-rich tumor cells, the radiation is delivered largely where it is needed, damaging the DNA of the tumor cells and the cells immediately around them while sparing much of the healthy tissue. This targeted delivery is the principle of PRRT, often described as a "theranostic" pairing with the gallium-68 imaging agent: the scan confirms the target before the therapy is given. In the NETTER-1 trial in advanced midgut neuroendocrine tumors, lutetium-177 dotatate markedly improved progression-free survival compared with high-dose octreotide. An amino-acid solution is infused alongside it to protect the kidneys.
peptides.side_effects_safety: According to the prescribing information, common side effects include: - Nausea and vomiting, partly from the protective amino-acid infusion - Fatigue - Low blood counts More serious considerations include: - Bone-marrow suppression and a risk of secondary myelodysplastic syndrome or leukemia - Kidney and liver toxicity - A temporary surge of tumor hormones (neuroendocrine hormonal crisis) - Allergic reactions, including swelling of the face or throat (angioedema) - Radiation exposure and effects on fertility

detail.faq:
q: Is mazdutide FDA-approved?
a: No. As of September 2026, mazdutide has received regulatory approval from China's National Medical Products Administration (NMPA) for obesity and, since September 2025, for glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes, but it has not been approved by the FDA for any indication. Eli Lilly has completed US-based Phase 2 trials, but no US Phase 3 trial is registered.
q: How is mazdutide different from tirzepatide?
a: Both are dual receptor co-agonists that include GLP-1R activation, but they pair it with different second targets. Tirzepatide activates the GIP receptor (GIPR), which stimulates insulin secretion. Mazdutide activates the glucagon receptor (GCGR), which is intended to increase energy expenditure and reduce liver fat. These are mechanistically distinct second targets. No head-to-head trial between the two compounds has been completed as of September 2026, so direct efficacy comparisons are not supported by published evidence.
q: Is mazdutide better than semaglutide for weight loss?
a: No peer-reviewed head-to-head comparison has been published as of September 2026. Network meta-analyses provide indirect comparisons, but these are hypothesis-generating, not definitive. The Phase 3 dataset for mazdutide comes from Chinese trial populations; whether results would be comparable in US or European populations with different baseline characteristics has not been established in Phase 3 trials.
q: Can a doctor in the United States prescribe mazdutide?
a: No. Mazdutide has no FDA-approved indication and no approved labeling in the United States, where it remains investigational.
q: What is the difference between mazdutide and a GLP-1 agonist like semaglutide?
a: Semaglutide is a selective GLP-1R agonist: it targets one receptor and produces its effects primarily through appetite suppression, slowed gastric emptying, and glucose-dependent insulin secretion. Mazdutide adds GCGR agonism to those effects, which is proposed to increase energy expenditure and to reduce liver fat. The pharmacological distinction is at the receptor level; whether this translates to a clinically meaningful advantage across diverse populations requires additional trial data, and no Phase 3 data yet exist for mazdutide in US or European patients.
q: What are the side effects of mazdutide?
a: The safety profile reported in Phase 2 and Phase 3 trials is mainly gastrointestinal: vomiting, nausea, and diarrhea were the most common adverse events in the 60-week GLORY-2 trial in China, and most were mild to moderate. A 2024 meta-analysis of randomized trials in people with and without diabetes likewise found a higher risk of transient, mild or moderate gastrointestinal side effects. As of September 2026, published US safety data come only from Phase 1 and Phase 2 trials.
q: What does the GLORY-1 trial show?
a: GLORY-1 was a Phase 3 randomized controlled trial of once-weekly mazdutide 4 mg or 6 mg versus placebo over 48 weeks in Chinese adults with obesity or overweight with comorbidities. Published by Ji and colleagues in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2025, the trial demonstrated clinically meaningful weight loss at both doses, supporting NMPA approval for obesity. The trial enrolled Chinese participants only; results may not generalize to other populations without additional evidence.
q: Is mazdutide approved for type 2 diabetes?
a: In China, yes, but not in the United States. As of September 2026, China's NMPA has approved mazdutide for glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes, approved in September 2025. That adds to its earlier NMPA approval for chronic weight management. Mazdutide is not FDA-approved for type 2 diabetes or any other indication.

title: What is mazdutide?
text: Mazdutide is a dual-receptor agonist that activates both the GLP-1 receptor and the glucagon receptor in one molecule, based on an analog of the natural hormone oxyntomodulin. It is developed by Innovent Biologics under license from Eli Lilly, with Innovent holding rights in China. It is given as a once-weekly injection for weight management and type 2 diabetes.

title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: Not in the United States. Mazdutide is investigational in the U.S. and has not been approved by the FDA. It was approved in China by the NMPA in 2025 for chronic weight management, reported as the first glucagon/GLP-1 dual agonist approved for weight loss, and in September 2025 it was also approved there for type 2 diabetes. Those approvals apply in China and not in the United States.

In GLORY-2, gastrointestinal effects were the most common side effects. A systematic review summarized consistent results across studies in predominantly Chinese populations. These are positive, replicated Phase 3 results underpinning the China approval, though not an FDA approval.

detail.sections:
title: What is mecasermin?
text: Mecasermin, sold under the brand Increlex, is a laboratory-made copy of insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), the hormone that actually carries out much of growth hormone's work in the body. Growth hormone stimulates the liver to make IGF-1, and IGF-1 then drives tissue growth. Children who cannot make IGF-1, or who cannot respond to growth hormone, do not grow normally; mecasermin provides the IGF-1 directly. It was approved in the United States in 2005.

peptides.name: Mechano growth factor
peptides.fda_status: Non-FDA-approved peptide sold as a research chemical / performance drug
peptides.evidence_note: The muscle-repair rationale rests on laboratory and cell studies, there is no human efficacy evidence, and the pegylated form sold on the market is uncharacterized.
peptides.what_it_is: Muscle-produced splice variant of IGF-1; a pegylated form (PEG-MGF) is also sold
peptides.research_at_a_glance: Laboratory and cell-based only; no human efficacy trials
peptides.key_takeaway: Mechano growth factor (MGF) is a muscle-made splice variant of IGF-1, sold on the research-peptide market and often pegylated as PEG-MGF. Its strongest human evidence is observational. In a 2003 biopsy study, one bout of leg exercise raised MGF mRNA significantly in eight men aged 25 to 36 but not in seven men aged 70 to 82. There are no controlled human trials of MGF, and it is not FDA-approved and is banned in sport.
peptides.mechanism: MGF is proposed to act on muscle stem cells (satellite cells), activating them and helping them multiply and delay aging, which would support muscle repair and growth. This is attributed to its unique tail region, thought to work somewhat differently from the classic IGF-1 growth signal. In human muscle-cell cultures, the MGF peptide enhanced satellite-cell activation and fusion, and laboratory versions promoted cell growth and migration. These are cell and laboratory findings. detail.sections:
title: What is mechano growth factor?
text: Mechano growth factor (MGF, also called IGF-1Ec) is a variant of the IGF-1 gene produced in muscle that has been mechanically loaded or damaged. It has a unique tail region distinct from the IGF-1 that circulates in the blood. In the performance market it is sold as a muscle-repair peptide, frequently as a pegylated version (PEG-MGF) claimed to last longer. It is not an approved medicine.
title: How does it work?
text: MGF is proposed to act on muscle stem cells (satellite cells), activating them and helping them multiply and delay aging, which would support muscle repair and growth. This is attributed to its unique tail region, thought to work somewhat differently from the classic IGF-1 growth signal.
In human muscle-cell cultures, the MGF peptide enhanced satellite-cell activation and fusion, and laboratory versions promoted cell growth and migration. These are cell and laboratory findings. The pegylated form sold on the market is a modification that has not been characterized as a pharmaceutical. This describes the proposed mechanism, separate from proven outcomes in people.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No. MGF and PEG-MGF are not approved by the FDA; they are research chemicals and performance-enhancing drugs with no approved compounding status. In sport, mechano growth factors are prohibited at all times under the WADA list.

peptides.key_takeaway: Melanotan I is a synthetic peptide that darkens skin by activating a pigment receptor, sold on the gray market as an injectable "tanning peptide." The same molecule, as the approved drug afamelanotide (Scenesse), is used for a rare light-sensitivity disorder. In two placebo-controlled trials of the approved implant in 168 adults with EPP, U.S. patients logged a median 69.4 pain-free hours in direct sunlight versus 40.8 on placebo (P = 0.04). No controlled trial supports the gray-market tanning product, which is not FDA-approved as of 2026.
peptides.mechanism: Melanotan I activates MC1R on pigment-producing skin cells, which raises production of the dark pigment eumelanin, darkening the skin independently of UV exposure. The receptor pharmacology is well characterized. This describes how it produces pigmentation, separate from whether unregulated self-injection for tanning is effective or safe. In a placebo-controlled study of 65 fair-skinned volunteers, epidermal melanin density rose an average of 41% in low-MED, burn-prone skin and 12% in high-MED skin. That result shows the molecule's pigment effect, not the quality or safety of gray-market vials.
peptides.human_study_findings: The rigorous human data belong to the approved drug and a different use. Afamelanotide has clinical trial evidence for reducing phototoxicity in the rare disorder it treats, not for cosmetic tanning. There are no controlled human trials supporting unregulated self-injected Melanotan I for tanning, so its cosmetic benefit and safety as sold are unestablished. Two placebo-controlled trials of the approved implant, reported in 2015, enrolled 168 adults with EPP, split by trial as shown below. Trial | Adults with EPP | Median pain-free hours in direct sunlight, afamelanotide versus placebo | P value United States | 94 | 69.4 versus 40.8 | 0.04 European Union | 74 | 6.0 versus 0.8 | 0.005 In the EU trial, patients also had 77 phototoxic reactions versus 146 (P = 0.04). The most common adverse events were headache, nausea, nasopharyngitis, and back pain, with mild implant-site hyperpigmentation in about one third of treated patients. These figures come from a medical implant used for EPP, so they say nothing about tanning vials.

detail.sections:
title: What is Melanotan I?
text: Melanotan I is a synthetic analog of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH), a potent activator of the skin's MC1R pigment receptor. Chemically it is the same molecule as afamelanotide, the approved drug sold as Scenesse. The distinction is the product and the use: gray-market "Melanotan I" is an unregulated, self-injected tanning product, not the approved, quality-controlled implant. It is not an approved medicine in that form.
title: How does it work?
text: Melanotan I activates MC1R on pigment-producing skin cells, which raises production of the dark pigment eumelanin, darkening the skin independently of UV exposure. The receptor pharmacology is well characterized. This describes how it produces pigmentation, separate from whether unregulated self-injection for tanning is effective or safe.
In a placebo-controlled study of 65 fair-skinned volunteers, epidermal melanin density rose an average of 41% in low-MED, burn-prone skin and 12% in high-MED skin. That result shows the molecule's pigment effect, not the quality or safety of gray-market vials.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No, not as a tanning product. The identical molecule is FDA-approved as afamelanotide (Scenesse), a controlled-release implant for erythropoietic protoporphyria, a rare light-sensitivity disorder, given under medical supervision. Gray-market Melanotan I vials sold for cosmetic tanning are not Scenesse, carry none of its manufacturing or quality controls, and are not approved.
title: What does the research show?
text: The rigorous human data belong to the approved drug and a different use. Afamelanotide has clinical trial evidence for reducing phototoxicity in the rare disorder it treats, not for cosmetic tanning. There are no controlled human trials supporting unregulated self-injected Melanotan I for tanning, so its cosmetic benefit and safety as sold are unestablished.
Two placebo-controlled trials of the approved implant, reported in 2015, enrolled 168 adults with EPP, split by trial as shown below.
Trial | Adults with EPP | Median pain-free hours in direct sunlight, afamelanotide versus placebo | P value
United States | 94 | 69.4 versus 40.8 | 0.04
European Union | 74 | 6.0 versus 0.8 | 0.005
In the EU trial, patients also had 77 phototoxic reactions versus 146 (P = 0.04). The most common adverse events were headache, nausea, nasopharyngitis, and back pain, with mild implant-site hyperpigmentation in about one third of treated patients. These figures come from a medical implant used for EPP, so they say nothing about tanning vials.

detail.sections:
title: What is Melanotan II?
text: Melanotan II is a synthetic cyclic peptide that activates several melanocortin receptors (MC1R, MC3R, MC4R, and MC5R), sometimes nicknamed "the Barbie drug." It is the structural parent from which the approved drug bremelanotide was derived. It is sold through gray-market channels as an injectable for tanning and sexual arousal, and it is not an approved medicine.
title: How does it work?
text: Melanotan II is proposed to work through two receptor effects: activating MC1R on skin cells to drive pigmentation and tanning, and activating MC4R in the brain, which is linked to sexual arousal and appetite. The sexual and appetite effects come largely from animal and early pharmacology work. This describes the proposed mechanism, separate from whether unregulated use for these purposes is effective or safe.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No. Melanotan II is not approved by the FDA and is an unapproved drug; the FDA has previously issued warning letters targeting injectable tanning products containing melanotan. Its compounding nomination was withdrawn, so FDA removed it from its Category 2 list in April 2026 and lists it as nominated but withdrawn. The approved melanocortin drugs Scenesse (for a rare light disorder) and Vyleesi (for low sexual desire in certain women) are distinct, regulated products that Melanotan II is not.
title: What does the research show?
text: There are no controlled human trials supporting tanning or libido use. The published clinical literature consists mainly of case reports and clinician warnings. Reports have described new or changing moles and darkening of pigmented lesions after use of melanocortin tanning injections (example and example), and poison-center and dermatology sources describe nausea, flushing, and other effects. These are reports and warnings, not controlled trials, and unregulated product quality adds further uncertainty.
The first human data came from a 1996 pilot study in three healthy men, which reported:
Finding | Result
Increased pigmentation | 2 of the 3 men
Spontaneous erections | Lasted 1 to 5 hours
Mild nausea | Appeared at most dose levels
Grade II somnolence and fatigue | 1 of 2 men escalated to the highest dose
It was a small drug-development study, not evidence that gray-market use is safe. The most serious skin report followed later: in one case report, a 20-year-old woman with fair skin developed melanoma after using it with a tanning bed.

peptides.name: MK-677 (ibutamoren)
peptides.fda_status: Non-FDA-approved, investigational drug; a small molecule, not a peptide
peptides.evidence_note: It has genuine multi-year human trials showing it raises growth hormone, IGF-1, and lean mass, but efficacy for meaningful functional outcomes is unproven, there are negative trials and metabolic safety signals, and it is not approved.
peptides.what_it_is: Orally active ghrelin-mimic growth hormone secretagogue
peptides.research_at_a_glance: Human trials show it raises growth hormone, IGF-1, and lean mass, but not strength or function, with metabolic signals
peptides.key_takeaway: MK-677 (ibutamoren) is an orally active, non-peptide drug that mimics the hunger hormone ghrelin to raise the body's own growth hormone, sold on the wellness market for muscle, sleep, and appetite. In a randomized trial of 65 healthy adults aged 60 to 81 (Nass 2008), fat-free mass rose 1.1 kg on MK-677 versus a 0.5 kg loss on placebo over 12 months (P < 0.001), yet strength and function did not improve and fasting glucose rose. A large Alzheimer's trial failed. As of 2026 it is not FDA-approved and is banned in sport.
peptides.mechanism: MK-677 activates the growth hormone secretagogue (ghrelin) receptor, prompting the pituitary to release growth hormone in pulses, which raises IGF-1. Its distinguishing feature is that it is orally bioavailable, unlike the injectable peptide secretagogues. This describes the mechanism; the human trials below show what it does and does not achieve.
peptides.human_study_findings: It has real human trials with a mixed picture. According to PubMed, two trials define it: Trial | Participants | Duration | Main finding Nass 2008, randomized trial | 65 healthy adults aged 60 to 81 | 2 years | MK-677 raised growth hormone and IGF-1 Sevigny 2008, trial | 563 people with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease | 12 months | Raised IGF-1 but found no significant difference from placebo on any of 4 clinical scales In the Nass trial's first year, fat-free mass rose 1.1 kg on MK-677 and fell 0.5 kg on placebo (P < 0.001), but strength and function did not improve. Body weight rose 2.7 kg versus 0.8 kg on placebo, and fasting glucose rose 5 mg/dL. MK-677 was also associated with: - Increased appetite - Weight gain - Mild fluid retention - Higher fasting glucose - Reduced insulin sensitivity So it reliably raises growth hormone and lean mass, but without demonstrated functional benefit, with metabolic concerns, and with negative results for disease.
peptides.dosing_info: 8 kg on placebo, and fasting glucose rose 5 mg/dL.

peptides.key_takeaway: Motixafortide (sold as Aphexda) is a peptide that blocks the CXCR4 receptor to pull stem cells out of the bone marrow into the blood, where they can be collected for a transplant in people with multiple myeloma. peptides.mechanism: Blood-forming stem cells are normally held in the bone marrow by the interaction between the CXCR4 receptor on the stem cells and a marrow signal called CXCL12 (also known as SDF-1). Motixafortide is a high-affinity, long-acting CXCR4 antagonist that interrupts this anchoring signal, releasing stem cells from the marrow into the bloodstream, where they can be collected by apheresis. It is used together with filgrastim, a growth factor that also mobilizes stem cells, and the two work synergistically to raise the yield. Collecting enough stem cells in as few sessions as possible matters for the success and efficiency of an autologous transplant. In the phase 3 GENESIS trial, far more patients reached the target collection of CD34-positive cells in up to two apheresis sessions with motixafortide plus filgrastim than with filgrastim alone.

title: What is motixafortide?
text: Motixafortide, sold under the brand Aphexda, is a synthetic cyclic peptide that blocks the CXCR4 receptor. It is used in stem-cell transplantation for multiple myeloma, specifically to help collect enough of a patient's own blood-forming stem cells before a transplant. It was developed under the codes BL-8040 and BKT140 and approved in the United States in 2023.
title: How does motixafortide work?
text: Blood-forming stem cells are normally held in the bone marrow by the interaction between the CXCR4 receptor on the stem cells and a marrow signal called CXCL12 (also known as SDF-1). Motixafortide is a high-affinity, long-acting CXCR4 antagonist that interrupts this anchoring signal, releasing stem cells from the marrow into the bloodstream, where they can be collected by apheresis.
It is used together with filgrastim, a growth factor that also mobilizes stem cells, and the two work synergistically to raise the yield. Collecting enough stem cells in as few sessions as possible matters for the success and efficiency of an autologous transplant. In the phase 3 GENESIS trial, far more patients reached the target collection of CD34-positive cells in up to two apheresis sessions with motixafortide plus filgrastim than with filgrastim alone.

title: What is motixafortide prescribed for?
text: Motixafortide is prescribed, alongside filgrastim, to mobilize blood-forming stem cells into the circulation so they can be collected for an autologous (self) stem-cell transplant in people with multiple myeloma. Patients receive an antihistamine and other premedication before dosing.

- Injection-site reactions such as pain, redness, and itching
- Flushing
