detail.faq:
q: What is MOTS-c and what does it do?
a: MOTS-c is a 16-amino-acid peptide encoded in the mitochondrial genome, identified in a 2015 paper by Lee and colleagues in Cell Metabolism. In cell culture and mouse models, it activates AMPK through folate-cycle pathway inhibition, increases GLUT4 expression and glucose uptake in skeletal muscle, and translocates to the nucleus during metabolic stress to regulate antioxidant response genes. In humans, endogenous MOTS-c rises substantially with exercise. Whether injectable MOTS-c produces equivalent biological effects in humans has not been established in controlled clinical trials.
q: Is MOTS-c a mitochondrial peptide?
a: Yes. MOTS-c is encoded within the 12S ribosomal RNA gene of the mitochondrial genome ,  making it part of a family of molecules called mitochondrial-derived peptides (MDPs). This is a biologically unusual feature: most circulating signaling peptides are encoded in the nuclear genome. The mitochondrial origin of MOTS-c is central to its proposed biology as a retrograde stress signal that communicates mitochondrial metabolic state to the nucleus and other tissues.
q: Is MOTS-c FDA-approved?
a: No. As of September 2026, MOTS-c is not FDA-approved for any indication. It is not legally marketed for human therapeutic use in the United States. There is no completed Phase 2 or Phase 3 human efficacy trial in the published literature. Products sold online as injectable MOTS-c are not regulated for quality, purity, or sterility.
q: Is MOTS-c legal in the United States?
a: MOTS-c is not FDA-approved and is not legally marketed as a therapeutic product. As of September 2026, it is not on the FDA's 503A bulks list or in Category 1, and FDA removed it from Category 2 in April 2026, so no approved compounding pathway exists. Products sourced from online vendors are sold as research chemicals and fall outside pharmaceutical regulatory oversight. For competitive athletes, MOTS-c is explicitly prohibited at all times under the 2026 WADA Prohibited List (Section S4.4.1, AMPK activators).
q: What does the research show about MOTS-c and exercise physiology?
a: In mouse models, MOTS-c injections increased running capacity; the Reynolds et al. 2021 Nature Communications study reported improved physical capacity metrics in late-life rodent dosing experiments. In humans, endogenous MOTS-c in skeletal muscle rises approximately 12-fold with an acute bout of exercise, consistent with a role as an exercise-response signaling molecule. Whether exogenous MOTS-c administration replicates these preclinical findings in humans has not been tested in any published controlled human trial.
q: What are the side effects of MOTS-c?
a: No peer-reviewed human safety data exists, and FDA has identified no human exposure data for drug products containing MOTS-c. Long-term safety in humans is entirely unknown.
q: Can a doctor prescribe MOTS-c?
a: No. MOTS-c is not FDA-approved for any indication and does not have a legal compounding pathway under 503A as of September 2026. It cannot be prescribed and dispensed through a licensed pharmacy. Any product sold as MOTS-c exists outside the regulated pharmaceutical system.
q: What is the difference between MOTS-c and humanin?
a: Both are mitochondrial-derived peptides encoded in the mitochondrial genome, but in different regions: MOTS-c is encoded in the 12S rRNA gene, while humanin is encoded in the 16S rRNA gene. Their proposed mechanisms differ as well ,  MOTS-c is primarily studied for metabolic and exercise-related effects through AMPK activation, while humanin has been more extensively studied for neuroprotective and cytoprotective effects. Both show age-related changes in circulating levels, and both belong to the MDP family described in the 2022 Miller et al. review in the Journal of Clinical Investigation. This comparison is for scientific context only; neither compound is FDA-approved for human therapeutic use.

peptides.what_it_is: Murepavadin is an experimental antibiotic built as a protegrin-derived peptidomimetic, a cyclized peptide-like molecule. It was developed by Polyphor (later Spexis) specifically against Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a bacterium that causes serious hospital and lung infections and is often resistant to other drugs. It was studied intravenously for hospital- and ventilator-associated pneumonia and later explored as an inhaled formulation. It is investigational and not approved.
peptides.key_takeaway: Murepavadin is an investigational antimicrobial peptidomimetic that targets a protein unique to Pseudomonas aeruginosa, developed by Polyphor for serious lung infections. Its intravenous Phase 3 program was halted after an unexpected rate of kidney injury, and later inhaled development did not mature. As of 2026 it is not approved.
peptides.mechanism: Murepavadin acts through a species-specific, non-lytic mechanism. It targets LptD, an outer-membrane protein that Pseudomonas aeruginosa needs to transport and assemble lipopolysaccharide, a building block of its outer membrane. Disrupting LptD impairs the bacterium's outer-membrane construction and kills it. In the laboratory, it was active against multidrug-resistant and even colistin-resistant strains. This describes the mechanism, separate from the safety outcome below.
peptides.human_study_findings: The pivotal program was stopped for safety. There is no positive confirmatory efficacy trial, and the IV program ended on a safety signal.

detail.sections:
title: What is nafarelin?
text: Nafarelin, known generically as nafarelin acetate and sold under the brand Synarel, is a synthetic ten-amino-acid analog of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH, also called LHRH). It is distinctive in its class for being absorbed through the lining of the nose rather than injected, which makes it convenient but means absorption can be reduced by nasal congestion or decongestant sprays. It was developed under the code RS-94991 and approved in the United States in 1990.
title: How does nafarelin work?
text: Nafarelin binds the GnRH receptor on the pituitary. Repeated dosing first stimulates the gland, then, through continuous rather than pulsatile exposure, downregulates and desensitizes the receptors so that luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone output falls. In women this lowers ovarian estrogen to produce a reversible, menopause-like low-estrogen state.
That hypoestrogenic state is what treats endometriosis: estrogen-dependent lesions regress and the associated pain eases while treatment continues. In central precocious puberty, higher divided daily dosing suppresses the premature hormone signal and halts early sexual development. In a multicenter double-blind trial, intranasal nafarelin reduced laparoscopic endometriosis scores about as effectively as oral danazol, with most patients improving, while avoiding danazol's unfavorable effects on blood lipids. Because the low-estrogen state causes bone loss, treatment for endometriosis is generally limited to about six months.
title: Is it FDA-approved?

title: What is nafarelin prescribed for?
text: Nafarelin is prescribed for the management of endometriosis, including pain relief and reduction of lesions, and for central precocious puberty in children. It is contraindicated in pregnancy, and patients are usually advised to avoid nasal decongestants around dosing because they can lower absorption.

- Hot flashes and sweating

- Acne and emotional lability

peptides.key_takeaway: Nangibotide is an investigational peptide that inhibits the inflammatory receptor TREM-1, developed by Inotrem as an intravenous treatment for septic shock. Its Phase 2b trial did not meet its primary endpoint, though a signal appeared in a subgroup of patients with high levels of a related biomarker. As of 2026 it is not approved.
peptides.mechanism: Nangibotide acts as a decoy that interferes with TREM-1 (Triggering Receptor Expressed on Myeloid cells-1). TREM-1 normally amplifies the immune system's inflammatory response, and in septic shock this amplification can become harmful. By blocking TREM-1 engagement, nangibotide is intended to dampen the excessive release of inflammatory signals. A related marker, soluble TREM-1, is used to identify patients whose TREM-1 pathway is most activated. This describes the mechanism, separate from the trial outcome below.
peptides.human_study_findings: The controlled evidence did not meet its goal. detail.sections:
title: What is nangibotide?
text: Nangibotide (also known as LR12 or Motrem) is an experimental peptide of twelve amino acids that inhibits TREM-1, a receptor that amplifies inflammation. It is developed by Inotrem and given by intravenous infusion, studied for septic shock, a life-threatening condition in which infection triggers a dangerous drop in blood pressure and organ dysfunction. It is investigational and not approved.
title: How does it work?
text: Nangibotide acts as a decoy that interferes with TREM-1 (Triggering Receptor Expressed on Myeloid cells-1). TREM-1 normally amplifies the immune system's inflammatory response, and in septic shock this amplification can become harmful. By blocking TREM-1 engagement, nangibotide is intended to dampen the excessive release of inflammatory signals. A related marker, soluble TREM-1, is used to identify patients whose TREM-1 pathway is most activated. This describes the mechanism, separate from the trial outcome below.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No. Nangibotide is investigational and not approved. Development has continued toward a possible Phase 3 using a biomarker-enrichment strategy to select patients.

It was approved in the United States in 2001 and has since been largely withdrawn from the market for commercial reasons.

peptides.what_it_is: Oral analog of cyclic glycine-proline, related to the IGF-1 system
peptides.research_at_a_glance: Published human data from an open-label Phase 2; a placebo-controlled Phase 3 is ongoing
peptides.key_takeaway: NNZ-2591 is an investigational oral peptide related to a natural fragment of IGF-1, developed by Neuren Pharmaceuticals for several rare genetic neurodevelopmental disorders including Phelan-McDermid, Rett, and Angelman syndromes. Its published human evidence is an open-label (uncontrolled) Phase 2 trial reporting broad improvement, and a placebo-controlled Phase 3 is under way. As of 2026 it is not approved.
peptides.mechanism: As an analog of cyclic glycine-proline, NNZ-2591 is proposed to modulate the IGF-1 signaling system, including helping to normalize the availability of IGF-1, which supports the formation and function of connections between nerve cells. The rationale is that correcting IGF-1-related signaling could help the brain circuits affected in these developmental disorders. This describes the proposed mechanism; the human efficacy data so far are uncontrolled.
peptides.human_study_findings: The published human evidence is open-label. According to PubMed, a single-group, open-label Phase 2 trial in children and adolescents with Phelan-McDermid syndrome reported that the drug was generally well tolerated and that most efficacy measures improved from baseline over 13 weeks. Because this study had no placebo group, improvement cannot be separated from natural variation or expectation effects. Results in Rett, Angelman, and Pitt-Hopkins syndromes have been reported mainly through company announcements. A placebo-controlled Phase 3 is intended to test efficacy properly; until then, the benefit is promising but unproven.

title: What is NNZ-2591?
text: NNZ-2591 is an experimental drug based on cyclic glycine-proline, a naturally occurring breakdown product of insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1). It is developed by Neuren Pharmaceuticals, taken by mouth, and studied across several genetic neurodevelopmental disorders, including Phelan-McDermid, Rett, Angelman, and Pitt-Hopkins syndromes. It is investigational and not approved.
title: How does it work?
text: As an analog of cyclic glycine-proline, NNZ-2591 is proposed to modulate the IGF-1 signaling system, including helping to normalize the availability of IGF-1, which supports the formation and function of connections between nerve cells. The rationale is that correcting IGF-1-related signaling could help the brain circuits affected in these developmental disorders. This describes the proposed mechanism; the human efficacy data so far are uncontrolled.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No. NNZ-2591 is investigational and not approved. Phase 2 trials have been completed in several indications, and a placebo-controlled Phase 3 trial in Phelan-McDermid syndrome is enrolling.
title: What does the research show?
text: The published human evidence is open-label. According to PubMed, a single-group, open-label Phase 2 trial in children and adolescents with Phelan-McDermid syndrome reported that the drug was generally well tolerated and that most efficacy measures improved from baseline over 13 weeks. Because this study had no placebo group, improvement cannot be separated from natural variation or expectation effects.
Results in Rett, Angelman, and Pitt-Hopkins syndromes have been reported mainly through company announcements. A placebo-controlled Phase 3 is intended to test efficacy properly; until then, the benefit is promising but unproven.
detail.sources_note: Sources: the open-label Phase 2 trial in Phelan-McDermid syndrome (Neumeyer et al., Neurology Genetics, 2025, DOI: 10.1212/NXG.0000000000200338; erratum DOI: 10.1212/NXG.0000000000200405), indexed on PubMed; and Neuren Pharmaceuticals development updates. This document is educational, is not medical advice or a health claim, and is not an offer to sell any product.

peptides.what_it_is: Cosmetic ingredient, a peptide used for skin brightening
peptides.research_at_a_glance: Activity supported by laboratory data and manufacturer claims; human trials are lacking
peptides.key_takeaway: Nonapeptide-1 is a synthetic nine-amino acid peptide, sold as Melanostatine, used in skincare as a brightening ingredient. Laboratory work suggests it blocks a hormone signal that tells pigment cells to make melanin, which is the basis for its use in products aimed at the appearance of dark spots and uneven tone. As of 2026, the evidence is essentially laboratory data and manufacturer claims, with no published human trial of the ingredient.
peptides.mechanism: Laboratory studies describe nonapeptide-1 as a blocker of a specific pigment signal. Pigment-producing cells, called melanocytes, make more melanin when a hormone known as alpha-MSH binds to a receptor on their surface called MC1R. Nonapeptide-1 is designed to compete with alpha-MSH for that receptor, so the downstream signal to switch on melanin-making enzymes is dampened. In cell studies, it has been used as a reference antagonist that reduces melanin production. The practical idea is prevention more than correction: By quieting the signal that drives new pigment, it is positioned to limit the appearance of future dark spots rather than to strip away existing ones. These are laboratory findings, and in finished products the benefit is described in appearance terms, such as a brighter, more even-looking complexion.
peptides.human_study_findings: The evidence is thin and mostly laboratory-based. According to PubMed, nonapeptide-1 appears in a cell study where it served as a known alpha-MSH blocker used for comparison, confirming anti-pigment activity in the lab. The manufacturer reports brightening activity in skin, but no corresponding independent, peer-reviewed human trial of the ingredient was found. So the brightening rationale is supported in principle by laboratory work but not by published human appearance trials.
peptides.side_effects_safety: Nonapeptide-1 is generally reported as well tolerated and non-irritating at cosmetic use levels, and it is positioned as a gentler alternative to some older brightening agents. Independent human safety data are limited, so a patch test is reasonable for sensitive skin.

detail.sections:
title: What is nonapeptide-1?
text: Nonapeptide-1 is a synthetic peptide of nine amino acids, marketed in skincare under the name Melanostatine (for example, Melanostatine-5). It is used as a brightening ingredient, intended to help with the appearance of dark spots and uneven skin tone rather than to bleach the skin. It is a cosmetic ingredient, not a drug.
title: How does it work?
text: Laboratory studies describe nonapeptide-1 as a blocker of a specific pigment signal. Pigment-producing cells, called melanocytes, make more melanin when a hormone known as alpha-MSH binds to a receptor on their surface called MC1R. Nonapeptide-1 is designed to compete with alpha-MSH for that receptor, so the downstream signal to switch on melanin-making enzymes is dampened. In cell studies, it has been used as a reference antagonist that reduces melanin production.
The practical idea is prevention more than correction: By quieting the signal that drives new pigment, it is positioned to limit the appearance of future dark spots rather than to strip away existing ones. These are laboratory findings, and in finished products the benefit is described in appearance terms, such as a brighter, more even-looking complexion.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No, and it does not need to be. The FDA does not pre-approve cosmetic ingredients. A cosmetic may describe effects on the look of skin tone, while a claim to treat a pigmentation disorder would make a product a drug. Nonapeptide-1 is used as a cosmetic ingredient, for the appearance of the skin.
title: What is it used for?
text: Nonapeptide-1 is used in brightening serums and creams aimed at the look of dark spots, hyperpigmentation, and overall radiance. It is commonly combined with other brightening ingredients such as niacinamide or vitamin C and, in practice, is used alongside daily sun protection, since UV exposure drives pigmentation.
title: What does the research show?
text: The evidence is thin and mostly laboratory-based. According to PubMed, nonapeptide-1 appears in a cell study where it served as a known alpha-MSH blocker used for comparison, confirming anti-pigment activity in the lab. The manufacturer reports brightening activity in skin, but no corresponding independent, peer-reviewed human trial of the ingredient was found. So the brightening rationale is supported in principle by laboratory work but not by published human appearance trials.
title: What are the side effects?
text: Nonapeptide-1 is generally reported as well tolerated and non-irritating at cosmetic use levels, and it is positioned as a gentler alternative to some older brightening agents. Independent human safety data are limited, so a patch test is reasonable for sensitive skin.
detail.sources_note: Sources: a cell study using nonapeptide-1 as an alpha-MSH antagonist reference (Chen et al., Advances in Dermatology and Allergology, 2022, DOI: 10.5114/ada.2022.115890), indexed on PubMed; and manufacturer and cosmetic ingredient reference data on Melanostatine. This document is educational and does not constitute medical advice.

peptides.fda_status: Yes. Octreotide was approved by the FDA in 1988 as the short-acting Sandostatin injection, with the monthly Sandostatin LAR Depot following about a decade later and the oral Mycapssa capsule approved in 2020 for maintenance in acromegaly.
peptides.evidence_note: Octreotide is FDA-approved for acromegaly and hormone-secreting tumors, with randomized evidence including the PROMID trial showing delayed tumor progression.
peptides.what_it_is: A somatostatin analog peptide that suppresses growth hormone and gut hormones
peptides.key_takeaway: Octreotide (sold as Sandostatin and, as an oral capsule, Mycapssa) is a synthetic analog of the hormone somatostatin that suppresses growth hormone and a range of gut hormones. It is used to control acromegaly and the symptoms of certain hormone-secreting tumors, including carcinoid syndrome. It has been FDA-approved in the U.S. since 1988 and is available as short-acting injections, a monthly depot, and an oral form.
peptides.mechanism:
Octreotide binds somatostatin receptors, chiefly the subtype 2 receptor, on hormone-secreting cells. Activating those receptors suppresses the release of growth hormone and insulin-like growth factor 1, as well as gut hormones such as serotonin, vasoactive intestinal peptide, and gastrin. By damping that hormone output, octreotide controls the symptoms and biochemistry of conditions driven by hormone excess.
Its effect differs by condition:
Condition | Effect of octreotide
Acromegaly | Suppressing growth hormone and IGF-1 improves symptoms and can shrink pituitary tumors
Carcinoid syndrome | Reducing serotonin and related mediators eases flushing and diarrhea
VIPoma | Reduces the severe secretory diarrhea
Somatostatin analogs also have an antiproliferative effect on some neuroendocrine tumors. In the PROMID trial, the long-acting depot lengthened the median time to tumor progression to 14.3 months versus 6.0 months with placebo in metastatic midgut neuroendocrine tumors. Depot and oral formulations allow steady control without multiple daily injections.
peptides.side_effects_safety: According to the prescribing information, common side effects include: - Diarrhea, abdominal pain, nausea, and flatulence - Injection-site pain - Gallstones or biliary sludge - High or low blood sugar More serious considerations include: - Gallbladder disease with long-term use - Changes in blood glucose and thyroid function - Slowed heart rate and cardiac conduction effects

detail.sections:
title: What is octreotide?
text: Octreotide, sold as Sandostatin, Sandostatin LAR Depot, and the oral capsule Mycapssa, is a synthetic cyclic octapeptide that mimics somatostatin, the body's own hormone that puts the brakes on several endocrine systems. Natural somatostatin is broken down within minutes; octreotide is engineered to last far longer, which makes it practical as a medicine. It was developed under the code SMS 201-995 and approved in the United States in 1988.
title: How does octreotide work?
text: Octreotide binds somatostatin receptors, chiefly the subtype 2 receptor, on hormone-secreting cells. Activating those receptors suppresses the release of growth hormone and insulin-like growth factor 1, as well as gut hormones such as serotonin, vasoactive intestinal peptide, and gastrin. By damping that hormone output, octreotide controls the symptoms and biochemistry of conditions driven by hormone excess.
Its effect differs by condition:
Condition | Effect of octreotide
Acromegaly | Suppressing growth hormone and IGF-1 improves symptoms and can shrink pituitary tumors
Carcinoid syndrome | Reducing serotonin and related mediators eases flushing and diarrhea
VIPoma | Reduces the severe secretory diarrhea
Somatostatin analogs also have an antiproliferative effect on some neuroendocrine tumors. In the PROMID trial, the long-acting depot lengthened the median time to tumor progression to 14.3 months versus 6.0 months with placebo in metastatic midgut neuroendocrine tumors. Depot and oral formulations allow steady control without multiple daily injections.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: Yes. Octreotide was approved by the FDA in 1988 as the short-acting Sandostatin injection, with the monthly Sandostatin LAR Depot following about a decade later and the oral Mycapssa capsule approved in 2020 for maintenance in acromegaly.
title: What is octreotide prescribed for?
text: Octreotide is prescribed for acromegaly, for the flushing and diarrhea of carcinoid syndrome, and for the profuse diarrhea of VIPoma. The oral form is used for long-term maintenance in people with acromegaly who have already responded to and tolerated injectable somatostatin analogs.
title: What are the side effects?
text: According to the prescribing information, common side effects include:
- Diarrhea, abdominal pain, nausea, and flatulence
- Injection-site pain
- Gallstones or biliary sludge
- High or low blood sugar
More serious considerations include:
- Gallbladder disease with long-term use
- Changes in blood glucose and thyroid function
- Slowed heart rate and cardiac conduction effects

peptides.name: Oligopeptide-1
peptides.fda_status: Does not require FDA approval, as a cosmetic ingredient rather than a drug
peptides.evidence_note: Several small human studies, including a pilot randomized trial, point toward texture and firmness benefits, but they are small, short, frequently industry-linked, and sometimes test EGF within multi-ingredient products, so the human evidence is real but limited.
peptides.what_it_is: Cosmetic ingredient, a form of epidermal growth factor (EGF) made by recombinant technology
peptides.research_at_a_glance: Small human studies suggest texture and firmness benefits, but they are limited and often industry-linked
peptides.key_takeaway: Oligopeptide-1 is the cosmetic name for human epidermal growth factor (EGF), a 53-amino acid protein that the body uses to drive skin cell growth and repair. Laboratory work shows it binds a receptor that stimulates skin cells to multiply and renew, which is the basis for its use in products aimed at the appearance of smoother, firmer skin and post-procedure recovery. As of 2026, several small human studies point toward texture and firmness benefits, but they are mostly small, short, and industry-linked, with a real open question about how well such a large protein penetrates intact skin.
peptides.mechanism: Laboratory studies show epidermal growth factor works by switching on a cellular growth signal. It binds to the epidermal growth factor receptor on skin cells, which prompts keratinocytes and fibroblasts to multiply, migrate, and renew, the same cascade the body uses during wound healing. In the process, it supports production of collagen, elastin, and other matrix components that influence how firm and smooth skin looks. One genuine caveat belongs in any honest description: Epidermal growth factor is a relatively large protein, and how much of it can pass through intact outer skin is debated, which is why delivery is a recognized challenge for these products. In finished cosmetics, the goal is described in appearance terms, the look of renewed, smoother, firmer skin.
peptides.human_study_findings: Several small human studies point in a positive direction, with important limits. According to PubMed, a small pilot randomized trial comparing a recombinant EGF (oligopeptide-1) serum with another EGF serum found investigator-rated improvements in texture and firmness, though wrinkle change was minimal and the study was small and short. Other work tests EGF inside multi-component regimens, where its individual effect cannot be isolated. There is no large independent trial or meta-analysis supporting standalone topical EGF for wrinkles, so the evidence is suggestive but not robust.
peptides.side_effects_safety: Epidermal growth factor products are reported as well tolerated in the small studies available. Because it is a protein that drives cell growth, some caution is reasonable when using it on compromised skin or for people with a personal history of skin cancer; cosmetic topical studies have not shown adverse growth effects, but the data are limited. A patch test is sensible for sensitive skin.

detail.sections:
title: What is oligopeptide-1?
text: Oligopeptide-1, often labeled sh-oligopeptide-1, is the cosmetic ingredient name for epidermal growth factor, a natural human protein of 53 amino acids. The "sh-" prefix means "synthetic human," indicating it is produced by recombinant technology in microbes, yeast, or plants rather than extracted from people. It is a true growth-factor protein, larger than most skincare peptides, and it is a cosmetic ingredient, not a drug.
title: How does it work?
text: Laboratory studies show epidermal growth factor works by switching on a cellular growth signal. It binds to the epidermal growth factor receptor on skin cells, which prompts keratinocytes and fibroblasts to multiply, migrate, and renew, the same cascade the body uses during wound healing. In the process, it supports production of collagen, elastin, and other matrix components that influence how firm and smooth skin looks.
One genuine caveat belongs in any honest description: Epidermal growth factor is a relatively large protein, and how much of it can pass through intact outer skin is debated, which is why delivery is a recognized challenge for these products. In finished cosmetics, the goal is described in appearance terms, the look of renewed, smoother, firmer skin.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No, and it does not need to be. The FDA does not pre-approve cosmetic ingredients. A cosmetic may describe effects on the appearance of skin, while a claim to heal wounds or change the body's structure would make a product a drug. Oligopeptide-1 is used as a cosmetic ingredient, for the appearance of the skin.
title: What is it used for?
text: Oligopeptide-1 is used in "regenerating" or "repair" serums and in post-procedure skincare. The appearance goals are the look of fine lines and improved texture, firmer and more elastic-looking skin, and support for recovery and comfort after cosmetic procedures. It is often combined with other actives.
title: What does the research show?
text: Several small human studies point in a positive direction, with important limits. According to PubMed, a small pilot randomized trial comparing a recombinant EGF (oligopeptide-1) serum with another EGF serum found investigator-rated improvements in texture and firmness, though wrinkle change was minimal and the study was small and short. Other work tests EGF inside multi-component regimens, where its individual effect cannot be isolated. There is no large independent trial or meta-analysis supporting standalone topical EGF for wrinkles, so the evidence is suggestive but not robust.
title: What are the side effects?
text: Epidermal growth factor products are reported as well tolerated in the small studies available. Because it is a protein that drives cell growth, some caution is reasonable when using it on compromised skin or for people with a personal history of skin cancer; cosmetic topical studies have not shown adverse growth effects, but the data are limited. A patch test is sensible for sensitive skin.
detail.sources_note: Sources: a pilot randomized trial of recombinant EGF serum (Abud et al., Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology, 2026, DOI: 10.1111/jocd.70927); and a study of EGF within a multi-component regimen (Dayan et al., Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology, 2019, DOI: 10.1111/jocd.12977), both indexed on PubMed. This document is educational and does not constitute medical advice.

peptides.name: Oxytocin
peptides.fda_status: Yes. Synthetic oxytocin (Pitocin) is approved by the FDA and has been a standard obstetric drug for decades. Its label carries a boxed warning that it is not indicated for elective induction of labor, meaning induction with no medical reason, because the available data are inadequate to weigh the benefits against the risks.
peptides.evidence_note: Oxytocin is FDA-approved for labor induction and augmentation and postpartum bleeding, supported by extensive clinical use and comparative dosing trials.
peptides.what_it_is: A nonapeptide hormone (uterotonic) that stimulates uterine contractions
peptides.key_takeaway: Oxytocin (sold as Pitocin) is a nine-amino-acid pituitary hormone that makes the uterus contract, used to start or strengthen labor and to control bleeding after delivery. It was the first peptide hormone to be chemically synthesized, work that earned a Nobel Prize, and it remains a mainstay of obstetric care. Synthetic oxytocin has been in U.S. clinical use for decades and is given by controlled intravenous infusion for labor.
peptides.mechanism: Oxytocin binds oxytocin receptors on uterine smooth muscle, raising intracellular calcium and increasing the force and frequency of contractions. The uterus becomes markedly more sensitive to oxytocin as pregnancy reaches term, which is why carefully titrated doses can establish an effective labor pattern. Oxytocin also acts on the myoepithelial cells around the mammary glands to produce milk let-down. Because the dose-response is steep and varies between women, oxytocin for labor is given as a dilute intravenous infusion that is titrated slowly against the contraction pattern and the baby's heart rate. For postpartum bleeding, oxytocin causes the emptied uterus to clamp down, reducing blood loss.

detail.faq:
q: How does oxytocin work in the brain beyond childbirth?
a: Beyond its peripheral obstetric role, oxytocin functions as a central neuromodulator, synthesized in hypothalamic paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei, with oxytocin neurons projecting widely through the central nervous system. Besides release from the posterior pituitary into the bloodstream, oxytocin can be released from axonal projections to forebrain regions, which is thought to contribute to its behavioral effects. One proposed mechanism includes dampening amygdala reactivity, and one trial in people with anxiety found reduced amygdala hyper-reactivity after intranasal oxytocin.
q: What does the research show about oxytocin and anxiety?
a: Clinical trials of intranasal oxytocin for anxiety and depressive disorders have shown mixed results. A 2019 systematic review of 15 RCTs across social anxiety, phobia, major depression, and postnatal depression, mostly testing a single dose, found no significant effects on core symptoms. A meta-analysis of 18 laboratory studies found that oxytocin's overall effect on cortisol responses was modest and not statistically significant, though it was larger during tasks that strongly activated the stress response. However, the magnitude of anxiolytic effects varies and is not uniform across populations or anxiety subtypes.
q: What does the research show about oxytocin and PTSD?
a: Oxytocin has shown promise in PTSD research by normalizing disrupted amygdala connectivity patterns, though evidence is mixed and sample sizes are generally small. A neuroimaging RCT in police officers, 37 with PTSD and 40 trauma-exposed controls, found that a single 40 IU intranasal dose restored right centromedial amygdala to vmPFC connectivity in male PTSD patients and dampened right basolateral amygdala to bilateral dACC connectivity in female PTSD patients. An RCT in 107 emergency department patients who started 40 IU oxytocin within 12 days of trauma found no significant overall group difference, though participants with high baseline symptoms who received oxytocin had lower CAPS scores across 1.5, 3, and 6-month follow-ups. A 2020 systematic review of 14 studies offered tentative evidence of safety but mixed efficacy results, suggesting the evidence remains promising rather than conclusive.
q: Can oxytocin help with pain?
a: Clinical research suggests oxytocin may be associated with modest reductions in pain intensity and threshold, though pooled evidence remains nonsignificant and individual response varies. In a 2014 crossover study of 37 pain-free adults, 40 IU intranasal oxytocin versus placebo significantly reduced pain intensity (50.6 vs 56.7, p=0.047), pain unpleasantness (47.0 vs 55.8, p=0.033), and increased pain threshold (p=0.040) during cold pressor testing. A 2020 study of 22 men with chronic low back pain and 22 healthy controls found that oxytocin attenuated heat pain intensity ratings in the chronic pain group versus controls but did not reduce spontaneous chronic pain. However, a 2023 review of 14 studies covering 1,504 people living with pain reported a nonsignificant pooled effect in the 3 studies amenable to meta-analysis (n=95; Hedges' g=0.31; 95% CI −0.10 to 0.73).
q: Is intranasal oxytocin FDA-approved for anxiety, PTSD, or pain?
a: Compounded intranasal oxytocin is not FDA-approved for anxiety, PTSD, or pain. The only FDA-approved oxytocin products on the market are injections, such as Pitocin, indicated for labor induction, labor augmentation, management of incomplete or inevitable abortion, and control of postpartum hemorrhage. The safety and efficacy of compounded nasal spray and sublingual forms for anxiety, PTSD, or pain have not been established through adequate, well-controlled FDA-reviewed clinical trials. Additionally, nose-to-brain pharmacokinetics in humans remain an active research question.
q: What is the research on oxytocin and social cognition?
a: Clinical research suggests oxytocin administration can modulate social cognition and prosocial behavior, though results vary. A 2021 review of human and animal research found converging evidence for functionally relevant effects of intranasal oxytocin, while noting ongoing debate over how much reaches the brain through the nose and unresolved questions about dosage. A review of oxytocin and prosocial behavior emphasized that the peptide's effects are susceptible to diverse factors that produce heterogeneous outcomes.
q: What role does oxytocin play in sexual function and intimacy?
a: Oxytocin levels rise during orgasm and ejaculation in most studies that have measured them, and research suggests a role in affiliative behavior. A 2021 systematic review of 13 studies found that most detected higher systemic oxytocin during orgasm or ejaculation, though many relied on subjective reports of arousal and orgasm. However, evidence remains preliminary.
detail.sections:
title: What is oxytocin?
text: Oxytocin, sold under the brand Pitocin, is a synthetic copy of a nine-amino-acid hormone made in the hypothalamus and released by the posterior pituitary. In the body it drives uterine contractions during labor and the "let-down" of milk during breastfeeding. The pharmaceutical form is used chiefly in obstetrics to influence the timing and strength of labor and to reduce bleeding after birth.
title: The history of oxytocin
text: Oxytocin has a notable place in the history of biochemistry. In 1953 the chemist Vincent du Vigneaud determined its structure and synthesized it, making oxytocin the first polypeptide hormone to be chemically made in the laboratory. That achievement earned him the 1955 Nobel Prize in Chemistry and opened the door to synthetic peptide drugs more broadly. Synthetic oxytocin replaced earlier pituitary extracts and has been a standard obstetric medication ever since.
title: How does oxytocin work?
text: Oxytocin binds oxytocin receptors on uterine smooth muscle, raising intracellular calcium and increasing the force and frequency of contractions. The uterus becomes markedly more sensitive to oxytocin as pregnancy reaches term, which is why carefully titrated doses can establish an effective labor pattern. Oxytocin also acts on the myoepithelial cells around the mammary glands to produce milk let-down.
Because the dose-response is steep and varies between women, oxytocin for labor is given as a dilute intravenous infusion that is titrated slowly against the contraction pattern and the baby's heart rate. Comparative trials show that higher-dose regimens increase the chance of uterine hyperstimulation without clearly shortening labor, so monitoring is essential. For postpartum bleeding, oxytocin causes the emptied uterus to clamp down, reducing blood loss.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: Yes. Synthetic oxytocin (Pitocin) is approved by the FDA and has been a standard obstetric drug for decades. Its label carries a boxed warning that it is not indicated for elective induction of labor, meaning induction with no medical reason, because the available data are inadequate to weigh the benefits against the risks.
title: What is oxytocin prescribed for?
text: Oxytocin is used:
- To initiate or improve uterine contractions when there is a medical reason to induce or augment labor
- To help manage incomplete or inevitable abortion
- After delivery, to control uterine bleeding and atony
It is administered by clinicians in a monitored setting.
title: What are the side effects?
text: Common and dose-related effects include:
- Nausea
- Faster or stronger uterine contractions
- Transient changes in maternal blood pressure or heart rate
More serious considerations include:
- Uterine hyperstimulation or tetanic contractions, which can cause fetal distress or, rarely, uterine rupture
- Water intoxication and low blood sodium with prolonged high-dose infusion, because oxytocin has a mild antidiuretic effect

peptides.key_takeaway: Palmitoyl hexapeptide-12 is a fat-attached "signal" peptide based on a fragment of elastin, the protein that gives skin its stretch, sold as Biopeptide CL. Laboratory work suggests it signals skin cells to make more structural proteins and can help reinforce the skin barrier, which is the basis for its use in products aimed at the appearance of firm, supple skin. As of 2026, the human data are limited to mechanistic and safety studies, with no independent trial showing an appearance benefit.
peptides.mechanism: Laboratory studies describe palmitoyl hexapeptide-12 as an elastin-derived matrikine, a fragment that signals skin cells. In cell models it is reported to prompt fibroblasts to make more elastin, glycosaminoglycans, and collagen, and to lower an inflammatory messenger, interleukin-6. More recent laboratory work on human skin samples also shows the peptide can self-assemble, penetrate the outer layers, and help reinforce a weakened skin barrier. One nuance belongs in an honest description: Elastin-derived fragments have a mixed biology, and at some levels they can actually promote inflammation, so a benefit should not be assumed from the mechanism alone. In finished cosmetics, the goal is described in appearance terms for the look of firmer, smoother, more resilient skin.

No independent human study measuring wrinkle or firmness outcomes was found, so efficacy claims rest on manufacturer and laboratory data.

detail.sections:
title: What is palmitoyl hexapeptide-12?
text: Palmitoyl hexapeptide-12 is a peptide of six amino acids joined to palmitic acid to help it penetrate the skin. Its peptide core is a fragment sequence derived from elastin, the protein that lets skin stretch and recoil, which places it among the signal peptides that aim to influence the skin's support structure. It is made by Sederma (Croda Beauty Actives) under the name Biopeptide EL and is a cosmetic ingredient, not a drug. On some labels it can be cross-listed with "palmitoyl oligopeptide," so naming is occasionally ambiguous.
title: How does it work?
text: Laboratory studies describe palmitoyl hexapeptide-12 as an elastin-derived matrikine, a fragment that signals skin cells. In cell models it is reported to prompt fibroblasts to make more elastin, glycosaminoglycans, and collagen, and to lower an inflammatory messenger, interleukin-6. More recent laboratory work on human skin samples also shows the peptide can self-assemble, penetrate the outer layers, and help reinforce a weakened skin barrier.
One nuance belongs in an honest description: Elastin-derived fragments have a mixed biology, and at some levels they can actually promote inflammation, so a benefit should not be assumed from the mechanism alone. In finished cosmetics, the goal is described in appearance terms for the look of firmer, smoother, more resilient skin.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No, and it does not need to be. The FDA does not pre-approve cosmetic ingredients. A cosmetic may describe effects on the look and feel of skin, while a claim to rebuild the body's elastin would make a product a drug. Palmitoyl hexapeptide-12 is used as a cosmetic ingredient, for the appearance of the skin.
title: What is it used for?
text: Palmitoyl hexapeptide-12 is used in "anti-aging" and barrier-support serums and moisturizers. The appearance goals are the look of firmness and elasticity, smoother texture, and a reduction in the appearance of fine lines.
title: What does the research show?
text: The human evidence is limited to mechanism and safety rather than appearance outcomes. According to PubMed, two studies address it:
Study | Evidence type | Finding
Ex-vivo human skin study | Mechanism | The peptide penetrates skin and can help repair a stripped barrier
Cosmetic-peptide safety analysis | Safety | No toxicity or allergy flags for it
Neither is an efficacy trial. No independent human study measuring wrinkle or firmness outcomes was found, so efficacy claims rest on manufacturer and laboratory data.
title: What are the side effects?
text: Palmitoyl hexapeptide-12 is considered low-irritation and safe at cosmetic use levels, and bioinformatic screening found no allergen or toxin flags. Independent clinical safety data are limited, so a patch test is reasonable for sensitive skin.
detail.sources_note: Sources: an ex-vivo human skin study of penetration and barrier repair (Ligorio et al., ACS Applied Bio Materials, 2025, DOI: 10.1021/acsabm.4c01816); and a cosmetic-peptide safety analysis (Bjerke et al., Current Research in Toxicology, 2026, DOI: 10.1016/j.crtox.2026.100291), both indexed on PubMed. This document is educational and does not constitute medical advice.

detail.sections:
title: What is palmitoyl pentapeptide-4?
text: Palmitoyl pentapeptide-4, often written pal-KTTKS, is a synthetic peptide designed as a topical skincare agent. Its active core, KTTKS, is a five amino acid sequence (lysine-threonine-threonine-lysine-serine) taken from the propeptide of type I collagen. A palmitic acid chain is attached to that core to create the palmitoylated form, pal-KTTKS, which is the version used on skin.
It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient under trade names such as Matrixyl, and it is included in serums and moisturizers for skin conditioning, smoothing, and anti-aging purposes.
title: How does it work?
text: KTTKS is a fragment released when type I collagen is processed in the skin, and in laboratory studies, it stimulates fibroblasts to produce type I collagen, type III collagen, and fibronectin, the main components of the skin's supportive matrix. Researchers proposed that this fragment acts as a feedback signal, with the released collagen piece prompting cells to make more matrix.
The plain KTTKS peptide is not well suited to topical use on its own, so a palmitic acid group is attached to create pal-KTTKS, the form developed as a topical agent to stimulate collagen production for an anti-wrinkle benefit. Applied to the skin, it is used to support the appearance of firmer skin and reduce the look of fine lines and wrinkles.
title: Is palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 FDA-approved?
text: No, and it does not need to be. The FDA does not approve cosmetics or most cosmetic ingredients before they go on the market. Cosmetics are regulated and must be safe when used as directed and properly labeled, but there is no pre-market approval step the way there is for drugs, so no anti-aging peptide in a serum is "FDA-approved."
The line that actually matters for an ingredient like this is the difference between a cosmetic and a drug. A product is a cosmetic when it is intended to improve appearance, but if it claims to change the structure or function of the skin, the FDA can regulate it as an unapproved drug. This is why skincare claims are usually written around the appearance of the skin rather than a promised physiological change.
title: What is it used for?
text: Palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 is used almost entirely in topical anti-aging products, where it is included for skin conditioning, smoothing, and soothing. In its main clinical study, it was tested for improving the appearance of fine lines and wrinkles in photoaged facial skin.
title: What does the research show?
text: The main controlled evidence is a trial, and the rationale for its effect traces to earlier laboratory work.

The evidence base is real but limited:
- The key trial was conducted by researchers at Procter & Gamble.

detail.sections:
title: What is palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7?
text: Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 is a peptide of four amino acids (glycine, glutamine, proline, and arginine) joined to palmitic acid to help it penetrate the skin. Its peptide sequence derives from a fragment of immunoglobulin, an immune protein, which is why it is grouped with signal peptides that influence the skin's response rather than ones that directly build collagen. It is made by Sederma under the name Rigin and is the companion peptide to palmitoyl tripeptide-1 in Matrixyl 3000. It is a cosmetic ingredient, not a drug.
title: How does it work?
text: Laboratory studies describe palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 as a signal that reduces inflammatory activity in skin. In cell models it is reported to lower interleukin-6, a messenger involved in inflammation. The rationale is that chronic low-grade inflammation, sometimes called "inflammaging," drives the enzymes that break down collagen, so calming that signaling may help skin keep the appearance of firmness.
These are laboratory and manufacturer findings about the peptide's behavior, not a proven clinical outcome. In finished cosmetics the benefit is framed in appearance terms, such as a calmer, firmer, smoother look.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No, and it does not need to be. The FDA does not pre-approve cosmetic ingredients. A cosmetic may describe how it affects the look and feel of skin, while a claim to treat inflammation or change the body's structure would make a product a drug. Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 is used as a cosmetic ingredient, for the appearance of the skin.
title: What is it used for?
text: Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 is used in soothing and "anti-aging" serums and creams, typically paired with palmitoyl tripeptide-1 as Matrixyl 3000. The appearance goals are the look of calmer, less red skin and a reduction in the appearance of fine lines, and it is often chosen for sensitive-skin formulas.
title: What does the research show?
text: The direct human evidence is limited, for several reasons:
- According to PubMed, the peptide appears in a human study of a multi-peptide serum, but its effect cannot be separated from the other active ingredients.
- The specific efficacy data come largely from manufacturer in-use panels.
- An independent review notes that peptides of this type penetrate skin poorly, a practical limit on real-world performance.
- No independent single-ingredient human trial was found.
title: What are the side effects?

peptides.name: Palopegteriparatide
peptides.fda_status: Yes. Palopegteriparatide was approved by the FDA in 2024 as Yorvipath for hypoparathyroidism in adults, following earlier approval in Europe. Its label warns of a potential risk of osteosarcoma, based on rat studies of parathyroid hormone analogs, and it is not recommended for people at increased risk of that cancer. It is given as a once-daily subcutaneous injection.
peptides.evidence_note: Palopegteriparatide is FDA-approved for hypoparathyroidism, supported by the phase 3 PaTHway trial showing normal calcium and independence from conventional therapy.
peptides.what_it_is: A long-acting prodrug of parathyroid hormone, PTH(1-34)
peptides.key_takeaway: Palopegteriparatide (sold as Yorvipath) is a long-acting form of parathyroid hormone designed to release the hormone steadily over 24 hours, used to treat hypoparathyroidism in adults. Its sustained delivery aims to mimic the body's natural, around-the-clock parathyroid hormone levels more closely than earlier products. It has been FDA-approved in the U.S. since 2024 and is given as a once-daily injection.
peptides.mechanism: Palopegteriparatide is an inactive prodrug that gradually releases active PTH(1-34) after injection, producing steady hormone levels across 24 hours rather than the sharp peak and rapid fall of standard teriparatide. The released hormone binds the PTH-1 receptor and restores calcium balance through the kidney, vitamin D activation, and bone, replacing the hormone that is deficient in hypoparathyroidism. The continuous exposure is the point: in hypoparathyroidism, steady parathyroid hormone keeps blood calcium normal while reducing reliance on high-dose calcium and active vitamin D. In the phase 3 PaTHway trial, most patients on the drug met a composite goal of normal calcium with independence from conventional therapy at 26 weeks, and the large majority became independent of calcium and active vitamin D.
peptides.side_effects_safety: According to the prescribing information, common side effects include: - Injection-site reactions - Flushing, lightheadedness, or a drop in blood pressure on standing - Headache - Back pain - Diarrhea - High blood calcium - Sore throat More serious considerations include: - A potential risk of osteosarcoma, based on rat studies of parathyroid hormone analogs - High or low blood calcium, particularly when doses are adjusted - Hypersensitivity reactions
peptides.summary_es: Terapia de reemplazo de PTH utilizada en adultos con hipoparatiroidismo; requiere control de calcio y seguimiento específico.

A notable trade-off is that pasireotide raises blood glucose more than other somatostatin analogs, because its receptor activity reduces insulin secretion.

title: What is pegvisomant?
text: Pegvisomant, sold under the brand Somavert, is a genetically engineered analog of human growth hormone that has been chemically altered and attached to polyethylene glycol (PEG). Unlike the somatostatin analogs that lower growth hormone output from the pituitary, pegvisomant acts at the target: it blocks growth hormone from signaling at its receptor. It was developed from a mutated growth hormone molecule known as B2036 and approved in the United States in 2003.
title: How does pegvisomant work?
text: Pegvisomant binds the growth hormone receptor but, because of its engineered substitutions, prevents the receptor from changing shape in the way needed to transmit a signal. Growth hormone normally works by bringing two receptor subunits together; pegvisomant occupies the receptor and blocks that functional pairing, so the downstream production of insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) in the liver falls. The PEG attachment extends its half-life to allow once-daily dosing. In a controlled trial, pegvisomant normalized IGF-1 in about 90 percent of patients at the 20 mg daily dose, with symptom improvement.

text: Yes. Pegvisomant was approved by the FDA in 2003 for acromegaly. It is given as a daily subcutaneous injection, usually starting with a loading dose and then a daily maintenance dose titrated to IGF-1 levels.
title: What is pegvisomant prescribed for?
text: Pegvisomant is prescribed for acromegaly in people who have not responded adequately to surgery, radiation, or other medical therapy, or for whom those options are not appropriate. Because it lowers IGF-1 without shrinking the tumor, patients are monitored with periodic pituitary imaging.

- Injection-site reactions, including fatty lumps (lipohypertrophy)
- Infections, such as cold symptoms
- Pain
- Nausea and diarrhea
- Flu-like symptoms

peptides.key_takeaway: Pemvidutide is an investigational GLP-1 and glucagon dual-receptor agonist, developed by Altimmune as a once-weekly injection for liver disease (MASH) and obesity. In Phase 2 trials it reduced liver fat and body weight, and a Phase 3 program in MASH is being planned. As of 2026 it is not approved anywhere.
peptides.mechanism: Pemvidutide combines two hormone actions. The GLP-1 arm reduces appetite and supports weight loss, while the glucagon arm acts directly on the liver to stimulate fat burning and reduce fat production. The rationale for pairing them is to combine weight loss with a direct effect on liver fat, which is relevant to MASH. This describes the proposed mechanism, separate from patient outcomes.

detail.sections:
title: What is pemvidutide?
text: Pemvidutide is an experimental dual-receptor agonist that activates the GLP-1 and glucagon receptors, developed by Altimmune under the code ALT-801. It is given as a once-weekly injection and is being developed primarily for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), a form of fatty liver disease, as well as for obesity. It is investigational and not approved.
title: How does it work?
text: Pemvidutide combines two hormone actions. The GLP-1 arm reduces appetite and supports weight loss, while the glucagon arm acts directly on the liver to stimulate fat burning and reduce fat production. The rationale for pairing them is to combine weight loss with a direct effect on liver fat, which is relevant to MASH. This describes the proposed mechanism, separate from patient outcomes.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No. Pemvidutide is investigational and not approved. According to Altimmune, the lead focus is MASH, with a Phase 3 program being planned following positive Phase 2b results, and an obesity Phase 2 program has also been completed.
title: What does the research show?
text: The evidence is from Phase 2 studies, two of them indexed on PubMed:
Trial | Population | Result
Phase 2b IMPACT trial | Biopsy-confirmed MASH | Positive results on liver endpoints at 24 weeks of an ongoing trial
Phase 1b/2a study | Fatty liver | Large relative reductions in liver fat along with weight loss over 24 weeks
Phase 2 obesity trial, reported by the company (not yet peer-reviewed) | Obesity | Meaningful weight loss at the top dose
These are positive Phase 2 findings; no Phase 3 trial has been completed, so efficacy is not yet established at the confirmatory level.
detail.sources_note: Sources: the Phase 2b IMPACT trial (Noureddin et al., The Lancet, 2025, DOI: 10.1016/S0140-6736(25)02114-2) and a Phase 1b/2a fatty-liver study (Browne et al., JHEP Reports, 2025, DOI: 10.1016/j.jhepr.2025.101483), both indexed on PubMed; and Altimmune development updates. peptides.name: Pentapeptide-18
peptides.fda_status: Does not require FDA approval, as a cosmetic ingredient rather than a drug
peptides.evidence_note: The peptide-specific evidence is computational and laboratory-based, and the human data come only from combination formulas, so there is no sound human evidence for the ingredient on its own.
peptides.what_it_is: Cosmetic ingredient, a neuro-inspired "expression line" peptide (sold as Leuphasyl)
peptides.research_at_a_glance: Activity rests on laboratory and manufacturer data; human evidence comes from combination formulas
peptides.key_takeaway: Pentapeptide-18 is a synthetic five-amino acid peptide, sold as Leuphasyl, used in skincare to target expression lines. Laboratory work suggests it mimics a natural "calming" messenger that reduces the release of the neurotransmitter that triggers muscle contraction, which is the basis for its use in products aimed at the look of dynamic wrinkles. As of 2026, the support is laboratory and manufacturer data, with human testing done only inside combination formulas rather than on the peptide alone.
peptides.mechanism: Laboratory studies describe pentapeptide-18 as a peptide that quiets the signal driving muscle contraction, but at an earlier step than some related peptides. The proposed mechanism runs in steps: - As an enkephalin mimic, it binds receptors on the nerve ending. - Those receptors in turn reduce the inflow of calcium. - Because calcium is needed to release acetylcholine, the neurotransmitter that tells muscle to contract, less acetylcholine is released. - The small muscles that form expression lines contract less. It is marketed as working in tandem with Argireline, which acts at a different point in the same release pathway. These are laboratory and manufacturer findings, and a topical cosmetic does not reach or paralyze muscle the way an injection does. In finished products the benefit is described in appearance terms, the look of softer, smoother expression lines.
peptides.human_study_findings: The direct evidence for the isolated peptide is limited. According to PubMed, the peptide-specific research is largely computational and laboratory work, such as a modeling study of how it interacts with its target. Where it has been tested on people, it has been combined with other actives, for example within retinol-loaded formulations, so the effect cannot be attributed to pentapeptide-18 alone. No independent human trial of the ingredient by itself was found.
peptides.side_effects_safety: Pentapeptide-18 is generally reported as well tolerated on the skin, with low irritation potential at cosmetic use levels, and topical use is not known to produce a systemic nerve or muscle effect. Independent safety data are limited, so a patch test is reasonable for sensitive skin.
peptides.summary_es: Ingrediente cosmético estudiado para líneas de expresión, a menudo en mezclas; no equivale a toxina botulínica.

detail.sections:
title: What is pentapeptide-18?
text: Pentapeptide-18 is a synthetic peptide of five amino acids, modeled on enkephalin, one of the body's natural signaling peptides. It is made by Lipotec under the trade name Leuphasyl and is used in skincare aimed at the appearance of expression lines. It is a cosmetic ingredient, not a drug, and is often paired with other "expression line" peptides.
title: How does it work?
text: Laboratory studies describe pentapeptide-18 as a peptide that quiets the signal driving muscle contraction, but at an earlier step than some related peptides. The proposed mechanism runs in steps:
- As an enkephalin mimic, it binds receptors on the nerve ending.
- Those receptors in turn reduce the inflow of calcium.
- Because calcium is needed to release acetylcholine, the neurotransmitter that tells muscle to contract, less acetylcholine is released.
- The small muscles that form expression lines contract less.
It is marketed as working in tandem with Argireline, which acts at a different point in the same release pathway.
These are laboratory and manufacturer findings, and a topical cosmetic does not reach or paralyze muscle the way an injection does. In finished products the benefit is described in appearance terms, the look of softer, smoother expression lines.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No, and it does not need to be. The FDA does not pre-approve cosmetic ingredients. A cosmetic may describe effects on the appearance of skin, while a claim to relax muscles or change the body's function would make a product a drug. Pentapeptide-18 is used as a cosmetic ingredient, for the appearance of the skin.
title: What is it used for?
text: Pentapeptide-18 is used in "anti-aging" serums and creams aimed at dynamic or expression lines, such as forehead lines and crow's-feet. The appearance goal is smoother-looking skin and a reduction in the look of movement-related lines. It is frequently combined with acetyl hexapeptide-8 (Argireline) and other actives.
title: What does the research show?
text: The direct evidence for the isolated peptide is limited. According to PubMed, the peptide-specific research is largely computational and laboratory work, such as a modeling study of how it interacts with its target. Where it has been tested on people, it has been combined with other actives, for example within retinol-loaded formulations, so the effect cannot be attributed to pentapeptide-18 alone. No independent human trial of the ingredient by itself was found.
title: What are the side effects?
text: Pentapeptide-18 is generally reported as well tolerated on the skin, with low irritation potential at cosmetic use levels, and topical use is not known to produce a systemic nerve or muscle effect. Independent safety data are limited, so a patch test is reasonable for sensitive skin.
detail.sources_note: Sources: a molecular modeling study of pentapeptide-18 (Akhan et al., Computational Biology and Chemistry, 2026, DOI: 10.1016/j.compbiolchem.2026.108952); and a study of retinol-and-peptide formulations tested on volunteers (Pawłowska et al., Life, 2024, DOI: 10.3390/life14101212), both indexed on PubMed. This document is educational and does not constitute medical advice.

This is associated with three effects that together lower food intake: - Reduced appetite - Slower gastric emptying - Suppression of glucagon Because amylin signaling is a different pathway from the GLP-1 and GIP incretin systems, petrelintide is also being explored in combination with incretin drugs. This describes the proposed mechanism, separate from whether it improves outcomes.

According to PubMed, the ZUPREME-1 trial in people with obesity without diabetes reported mean weight loss at two timepoints: Timepoint | Mean weight loss 28 weeks | Roughly 9 to 10% 42 weeks | Continuing to around 11% Mild nausea was the main side effect, and overall gastrointestinal tolerability was similar to placebo. This is one positive, placebo-controlled Phase 2 study; Phase 3 trials have not yet been completed, so longer-term efficacy and safety remain to be established.

detail.sections:
title: What is petrelintide?
text: Petrelintide is an experimental drug that mimics amylin, the pancreatic hormone that signals fullness. It was engineered by Zealand Pharma under the development code ZP8396 for stability and a long half-life suitable for once-weekly injection. It is being developed in collaboration with Roche, including a planned combination study with a separate incretin drug. It is investigational and not approved for any use.
title: How does it work?
text: Petrelintide activates amylin receptors, reproducing the satiety signaling of the natural hormone amylin. This is associated with three effects that together lower food intake:
- Reduced appetite
- Slower gastric emptying
- Suppression of glucagon
Because amylin signaling is a different pathway from the GLP-1 and GIP incretin systems, petrelintide is also being explored in combination with incretin drugs. This describes the proposed mechanism, separate from whether it improves outcomes.
title: Is it FDA-approved?

peptides.what_it_is: Oral α4β7 integrin antagonist studied for ulcerative colitis
peptides.research_at_a_glance: First controlled trial missed its primary endpoint
peptides.key_takeaway: PN-943 is an investigational oral peptide that blocks the α4β7 integrin, the same gut-homing target as the antibody vedolizumab, developed by Protagonist Therapeutics for ulcerative colitis. Its earliest controlled trial missed its primary endpoint, and a later Phase 2 reported only a partial, internally inconsistent signal. As of 2026 it is not approved and the program is inactive.
peptides.mechanism: PN-943 blocks the α4β7 integrin on immune cells (lymphocytes), preventing it from binding its partner MAdCAM-1 on blood vessels in the gut. That interaction is how certain inflammatory T-cells "home" to the intestinal lining, so blocking it is intended to reduce the gut inflammation that drives ulcerative colitis. Delivering this as a gut-targeted oral peptide is the distinguishing idea. This describes the mechanism, separate from the trial outcomes below.

detail.sections:
title: What is PN-943?
text: PN-943 is an experimental peptide taken by mouth, designed to act locally in the gut, developed by Protagonist Therapeutics for moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis, an inflammatory bowel disease. It blocks the α4β7 integrin, the same pathway targeted by the approved injectable antibody vedolizumab, but as an oral peptide. It is investigational and not approved.
title: How does it work?
text: PN-943 blocks the α4β7 integrin on immune cells (lymphocytes), preventing it from binding its partner MAdCAM-1 on blood vessels in the gut. That interaction is how certain inflammatory T-cells "home" to the intestinal lining, so blocking it is intended to reduce the gut inflammation that drives ulcerative colitis. Delivering this as a gut-targeted oral peptide is the distinguishing idea. This describes the mechanism, separate from the trial outcomes below.

- Protagonist indicated the drug would need an external partner to advance
- No Phase 3 has started
- The company's focus shifted to other programs

peptides.what_it_is: Polymyxin cyclic lipopeptide antibiotics active against Gram-negative bacteria
peptides.key_takeaway: Polymyxin B and colistin (colistin is also called polymyxin E) are older cyclic lipopeptide antibiotics that have returned to use as last-resort treatments for multidrug-resistant Gram-negative infections. They punch holes in the bacterial outer membrane but carry meaningful kidney and nerve toxicity. Both have long been FDA-approved in the U.S. and are reserved for serious infections with few other options.
peptides.mechanism: Polymyxins act like a detergent on the Gram-negative outer membrane. Their positively charged ring binds the lipid A portion of lipopolysaccharide, the molecule that forms the outer surface of Gram-negative bacteria, and displaces the stabilizing magnesium and calcium ions. This disrupts and permeabilizes both the outer and inner membranes, so the cell's contents leak out and it dies. Polymyxins also bind and neutralize circulating lipopolysaccharide (endotoxin). Because their target is unique to Gram-negative bacteria, polymyxins are used specifically against those organisms, often when nothing else is active. Their use is limited by toxicity, and the best way to use them is still debated: in the AIDA trial, adding a carbapenem to colistin did not improve outcomes over colistin alone for serious carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative infections. Dosing is a careful balance between efficacy and kidney injury.
peptides.side_effects_safety: Common and dose-related effects include: - Kidney injury, the main dose-limiting toxicity - Numbness, tingling, and dizziness (neurotoxicity) More serious considerations include: - Acute kidney injury, which can be significant - Neuromuscular blockade that can impair breathing, especially with other such drugs

detail.sections:
title: What are polymyxin B and colistin?
text: Polymyxin B and colistin are polymyxins, a class of cyclic lipopeptide antibiotics discovered in the 1940s. They fell out of favor decades ago because of toxicity, but the rise of highly resistant Gram-negative bacteria such as carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter, Pseudomonas, and Klebsiella has brought them back as drugs of last resort. Colistin is also known as polymyxin E, and it is given as an inactive prodrug, colistimethate, that converts to active colistin in the body. Both have been FDA-approved for many years.
title: How do they work?
text: Polymyxins act like a detergent on the Gram-negative outer membrane. Their positively charged ring binds the lipid A portion of lipopolysaccharide, the molecule that forms the outer surface of Gram-negative bacteria, and displaces the stabilizing magnesium and calcium ions. This disrupts and permeabilizes both the outer and inner membranes, so the cell's contents leak out and it dies. Polymyxins also bind and neutralize circulating lipopolysaccharide (endotoxin).
Because their target is unique to Gram-negative bacteria, polymyxins are used specifically against those organisms, often when nothing else is active. Their use is limited by toxicity, and the best way to use them is still debated: in the AIDA trial, adding a carbapenem to colistin did not improve outcomes over colistin alone for serious carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative infections. Dosing is a careful balance between efficacy and kidney injury.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: Yes. Both polymyxin B and colistin (as colistimethate) were approved by the FDA decades ago for serious Gram-negative infections. The table below compares how their labels warn about toxicity.
Product | Label warning
Injectable polymyxin B | Boxed warning about kidney toxicity and neurotoxicity, including the risk of respiratory paralysis from neuromuscular blockade
Colistimethate | Warnings about the same risks, though not in boxed form
title: What are they prescribed for?
text: Polymyxin B and colistin are prescribed for serious infections caused by susceptible Gram-negative bacteria, particularly multidrug-resistant organisms for which few other antibiotics remain effective. Polymyxin B is also widely used topically and in eye preparations, often in combination products. They are generally reserved for situations where safer agents cannot be used.
title: What are the side effects?
text: Common and dose-related effects include:
- Kidney injury, the main dose-limiting toxicity
- Numbness, tingling, and dizziness (neurotoxicity)
More serious considerations include:
- Acute kidney injury, which can be significant
- Neuromuscular blockade that can impair breathing, especially with other such drugs

peptides.name: Pramlintide
peptides.fda_status: FDA-approved peptide, sold as Symlin, used alongside insulin at mealtimes
peptides.evidence_note: It is approved by the FDA as an add-on to mealtime insulin for type 1 and type 2 diabetes, supported by its randomized controlled trial program.
peptides.what_it_is: Synthetic version of amylin, a hormone the pancreas releases with insulin, and not a GLP-1 drug
peptides.key_takeaway: Pramlintide is a synthetic analog of amylin, the hormone the pancreas releases alongside insulin, and it is not a GLP-1 drug. Injected before meals, it slows gastric emptying, suppresses glucagon, and increases fullness, and it is approved as an add-on to mealtime insulin for adults with type 1 or type 2 diabetes. Approved in 2005 and still marketed as Symlin, it carries a boxed warning for severe insulin-induced hypoglycemia.
peptides.mechanism: Pramlintide lowers after-meal blood sugar by replacing amylin, the hormone that normally works alongside insulin to control how fast glucose enters the blood. It acts in three ways: - It slows stomach emptying so glucose is absorbed more gradually. - It suppresses the release of glucagon after meals, something insulin alone does not fully control. - It acts on the brain to increase fullness and reduce food intake. Because insulin handles glucose entering the cells while amylin controls the rate and timing of glucose appearing in the blood, pramlintide is used as an add-on to mealtime insulin rather than a replacement for it. It typically produces small reductions in A1c along with modest weight loss.
peptides.side_effects_safety: According to the prescribing information, the most common side effects are: - Nausea - Vomiting - Decreased appetite - Headache - Low blood sugar The most serious risk is severe low blood sugar. Pramlintide carries a boxed warning that, when added to insulin, it can cause severe insulin-induced hypoglycemia, usually within three hours of injection. Because of this, insulin doses are reduced when starting pramlintide, and it is used carefully in people at high risk of low blood sugar.

detail.sections:
title: What is pramlintide?
text: Pramlintide is a synthetic analog of amylin, a hormone that the pancreas releases together with insulin after meals. It is not a GLP-1 drug, which sets it apart from most of the injectable diabetes peptides.
Natural human amylin tends to clump together and is difficult to formulate as a medicine, so pramlintide was designed with three amino acid substitutions that keep it soluble and stable while preserving its activity. It is made by AstraZeneca and sold as Symlin (SymlinPen), given as a subcutaneous injection before meals.

text: Pramlintide lowers after-meal blood sugar by replacing amylin, the hormone that normally works alongside insulin to control how fast glucose enters the blood. It acts in three ways:
- It slows stomach emptying so glucose is absorbed more gradually.
- It suppresses the release of glucagon after meals, something insulin alone does not fully control.
- It acts on the brain to increase fullness and reduce food intake.
Because insulin handles glucose entering the cells while amylin controls the rate and timing of glucose appearing in the blood, pramlintide is used as an add-on to mealtime insulin rather than a replacement for it. It typically produces small reductions in A1c along with modest weight loss.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: Yes. Pramlintide was approved in 2005 and remains on the market as Symlin. It is approved as an add-on to mealtime insulin for adults with type 1 or type 2 diabetes who use insulin but have not reached their blood sugar goals.
title: What is pramlintide prescribed for?
text: Pramlintide is prescribed alongside mealtime insulin for adults with type 1 or type 2 diabetes who are already using insulin but still have high after-meal blood sugar. It is added to insulin, not used on its own. It is contraindicated in people who have trouble sensing low blood sugar (hypoglycemia unawareness) or who have gastroparesis, a condition of very slow stomach emptying.
title: What are the side effects?
text: According to the prescribing information, the most common side effects are:
- Nausea
- Vomiting
- Decreased appetite
- Headache
- Low blood sugar
The most serious risk is severe low blood sugar. Pramlintide carries a boxed warning that, when added to insulin, it can cause severe insulin-induced hypoglycemia, usually within three hours of injection. Because of this, insulin doses are reduced when starting pramlintide, and it is used carefully in people at high risk of low blood sugar.
