detail.title: Tesamorelin: What It Is and How It Reduces Abdominal Fat
detail.evidence_note: Tesamorelin is FDA-approved for HIV-associated lipodystrophy, supported by randomized trials showing reductions in visceral abdominal fat.
detail.fda_status: Yes. Tesamorelin was approved by the FDA in 2010 as Egrifta, with later formulations marketed as Egrifta SV and Egrifta WR. It is given as a daily subcutaneous injection.
detail.description: Tesamorelin (Egrifta) is an FDA-approved growth hormone-releasing hormone analog that reduces excess abdominal fat in people with HIV-associated lipodystrophy.

One of growth hormone's effects is lipolysis, the breakdown of fat, and visceral (intra-abdominal) fat is particularly responsive. By boosting the body's own growth hormone rather than supplying growth hormone directly, tesamorelin reduces that deep abdominal fat.
The table below shows how visceral adipose tissue changed in the HIV lipodystrophy trials.
Group | Change in visceral adipose tissue
Tesamorelin, at 6 months | Reduced by roughly 11 percent
Tesamorelin, with continued treatment | Reduction approaching 18 percent
Placebo | Changed little

- Joint, muscle, and limb pain
- Swelling from fluid retention
More serious considerations include:
- Higher blood sugar and glucose intolerance
- Fluid retention
- An increased risk of new tumors, so any existing cancer should be inactive and fully treated before starting

- Allergic reactions

The most commonly reported side effects in Phase III trials were injection-site reactions (erythema, pruritus, pain), arthralgia, pain in the extremities, myalgia, peripheral edema, and paresthesia. These are broadly consistent with GH-class effects and local subcutaneous injection reactions. Injection-site reactions were the most frequently reported individual adverse event. detail.faq:
q: What is tesamorelin used for?
a: Tesamorelin (Egrifta SV) is FDA-approved for the reduction of excess abdominal fat in adults with HIV-associated lipodystrophy. Researchers have also studied tesamorelin in non-HIV populations with visceral adiposity and HIV-associated non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, but these uses are not FDA-approved indications. Any prescribing outside the approved indication is the independent clinical judgment of the provider.
q: How long does it take for tesamorelin to reduce visceral fat?
a: In the pivotal Phase III trials, statistically significant and clinically meaningful visceral fat reductions were documented at 26 weeks of treatment compared to placebo. One trial in 412 adults with HIV reported a 15.2% VAT reduction with tesamorelin versus a 5.0% increase with placebo (p < 0.001), and a pooled analysis of 806 adults reported a treatment effect of approximately -15.4% at 26 weeks. Extension trial data confirmed that visceral fat returns toward baseline after discontinuation, so continued use is associated with sustained effect.
q: Does tesamorelin affect blood sugar?
a: Growth hormone has counter-regulatory effects on insulin sensitivity, meaning it can raise fasting glucose and reduce insulin sensitivity at elevated GH levels. In pooled pivotal trials of 806 adults with HIV, tesamorelin was generally well tolerated, with no clinically meaningful between-group differences in glucose parameters. A 12-week randomized trial in 53 adults with type 2 diabetes found no significant differences in fasting glucose or insulin response between tesamorelin and placebo arms. Across the clinical trials, though, an HbA1c of 6.5% or higher by week 26 was more common with tesamorelin than placebo (5% vs 1%). Providers evaluate glucose before starting tesamorelin and monitor it periodically during therapy.
q: What is the difference between tesamorelin and sermorelin?
a: Tesamorelin is a full-length GHRH(1-44) analog stabilized with a trans-3-hexenoyl modification at the N-terminus, giving it resistance to DPP-IV degradation. It is FDA-approved for HIV-associated lipodystrophy with multiple Phase III RCTs demonstrating visceral fat reduction. Sermorelin is a shorter GHRH(1-29) fragment comprising the minimum active sequence without N-terminal stabilization. Sermorelin is not currently FDA-approved (its earlier approval as Geref ended after discontinuation) and has a substantially smaller clinical evidence base. No head-to-head trial comparing the two compounds has been published.
q: Who should not take tesamorelin?
a: Contraindications include disruption of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis (hypopituitarism, pituitary tumor, prior head irradiation, head trauma), active malignancy, pregnancy, and known hypersensitivity to tesamorelin or its components. A provider will conduct a complete clinical evaluation before prescribing.
q: Does tesamorelin cause side effects?
a: The most commonly reported side effects in Phase III trials were injection-site reactions (erythema, pruritus, pain), arthralgia, pain in the extremities, myalgia, peripheral edema, and paresthesia. These are broadly consistent with GH-class effects and local subcutaneous injection reactions. Injection-site reactions were the most frequently reported individual adverse event. Glucose dysregulation and IGF-1 elevation above the reference range are metabolic effects requiring monitoring. Hypersensitivity reactions occurred in 4% of trial patients and warrant prompt provider contact.
q: How long does tesamorelin need to be taken for the effect to persist?
a: A 12-month trial with an extension phase found that visceral fat reduction is sustained with continued tesamorelin use and that visceral adipose tissue returns toward baseline values after discontinuation. This indicates that the medication requires continued use to maintain the visceral fat reduction effect. Providers assess the risk-benefit balance of long-term use on an individual basis, taking into account metabolic monitoring results, IGF-1 levels, and overall clinical response.

peptides.name: Thymosin alpha-1
peptides.fda_status: Not FDA-approved in the U.S.; approved as thymalfasin (Zadaxin) in many other countries
peptides.evidence_note: It has multiple independent human trials and meta-analyses in its studied immune and antiviral uses and is approved outside the United States, but results are mixed, the key recent sepsis trial was negative, and there is no evidence for the general wellness use.
peptides.what_it_is: Immune-modulating peptide originally from thymus extract
peptides.research_at_a_glance: Real human trials in hepatitis and sepsis, but results are mixed and a key recent trial was negative
peptides.key_takeaway: Thymosin alpha-1 is an immune-modulating peptide approved as thymalfasin (Zadaxin) in many countries but not in the United States. In the 2025 TESTS trial of 1,089 patients with sepsis, found 28-day mortality of 23.4% on thymosin alpha-1 versus 24.1% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.27, p = 0.93). Hepatitis B trials are more encouraging, results are mixed overall, and none of it supports a general wellness use.
peptides.mechanism: Thymosin alpha-1 modulates the immune system in several ways: - Influencing the maturation and function of T-cells - Boosting signals such as interferon-gamma and interleukin-2 - Enhancing natural killer-cell activity, partly through Toll-like receptor pathways This mechanism is supported by laboratory and clinical immune data, such as improved immune-cell markers in sepsis studies. This describes how it acts on the immune system, separate from whether it improves outcomes in a given condition.
peptides.human_study_findings: It has real human trials, with mixed results, in specific immune conditions, not general wellness. Three trials report outcome figures. Condition and trial | Patients | Result Chronic hepatitis B, randomized trial comparing thymosin alpha-1 with no treatment | 98 | Complete virological response reached 40.6% after a 26-week course versus 9.4% in controls (p = 0.004); a 52-week course was not significantly better than control Sepsis, earlier multicenter trial | 361 | Borderline mortality benefit suggested: 26.0% versus 35.0% at 28 days (p = 0.062) Sepsis, larger double-blind Phase 3 TESTS trial | 1,089 | No mortality benefit: 28-day mortality 23.4% on thymosin alpha-1 versus 24.1% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.27, p = 0.93) In chronic hepatitis B, a separate trial reported modest effects on viral and liver markers. In sepsis, a 2025 meta-analysis found the apparent benefit disappeared in higher-quality studies. So real human efficacy exists for some immune and antiviral uses but is mixed, and none of it supports a general wellness or longevity use.

detail.faq:
q: Is thymosin alpha-1 FDA-approved?
a: No. As of September 2026, thymosin alpha-1 is not FDA-approved for any indication in the United States. It is approved internationally as Zadaxin in more than 35 countries, including for chronic hepatitis B. In the US, it is not eligible for 503A compounding as of September 2026: FDA lists its Category 2 nomination as withdrawn, and it is not on the 503A bulks list or in Category 1.
q: What is the difference between thymosin alpha-1 and thymosin beta-4?
a: Thymosin alpha-1 and thymosin beta-4 were both first isolated from thymosin fraction 5, a calf thymus extract, but they have distinct structures and mechanisms. Thymosin alpha-1 is a 28-amino-acid N-acetylated peptide that acts on dendritic cells and T-cell maturation, partly through TLR9 signaling. Thymosin beta-4 is a 43-amino-acid peptide that acts primarily on actin polymerization, tissue repair, and anti-inflammatory pathways at injury sites. Their clinical applications are largely non-overlapping: Tα1 is studied for immune-modulating effects in infection and oncology; thymosin beta-4 is studied for wound healing and tissue regeneration.
q: How long does thymosin alpha-1 take to work?
a: Response kinetics depend on the indication. In hepatitis B trials, the characteristic response pattern includes a delayed peak effect: a meta-analysis published in Alimentary Pharmacology and Therapeutics in 2001 found that the virological response grew after treatment stopped and was clearest about 12 months after therapy ended, rather than during the treatment period itself.
q: What are the side effects of thymosin alpha-1?
a: Thymosin alpha-1 has a low reported adverse-event burden in clinical trials. In a hepatitis B trial, all adverse drug reactions were mild, and most involved fluctuating liver enzymes. In the phase 3 TESTS sepsis trial, no safety outcome differed significantly from placebo.
q: What happened to thymosin alpha-1 on FDA's compounding list?
a: FDA lists thymosin alpha-1 among bulk substances that were previously in its 503A Category 2 list and whose nominations were withdrawn by the nominators. That was not a finding that it is safe, and thymosin alpha-1 is not on the 503A bulks list or in Category 1, so it is not eligible for 503A compounding as of September 2026. This does not affect thymosin alpha-1's international approval status as Zadaxin, which remains unchanged in the more than 35 countries where it holds regulatory approval.
q: Are peptides legal in 2026?
a: The legality of specific peptides in the United States depends on their individual regulatory status. Some peptides are FDA-approved drugs, available by prescription through standard pharmacy channels. Others are available through licensed 503A compounding pharmacies by prescription, which requires a patient-specific prescription from a licensed provider. As of September 2026, thymosin alpha-1 is not in that group: FDA lists its Category 2 nomination as withdrawn, and it is not eligible for 503A compounding. No peptide in this class is available over the counter in the United States.
q: Can you get thymosin alpha-1 without a prescription?
a: No. Thymosin alpha-1 is not available over the counter in any legally recognized formulation in the United States. As of September 2026, it is also not eligible for 503A compounding, so no licensed compounding pharmacy can legally prepare it. Any product marketed as thymosin alpha-1 in the US is operating outside the legal framework and should be approached with caution.
q: What did the 2025 TESTS trial find about thymosin alpha-1 in sepsis?
a: The TESTS trial, published in the BMJ in 2025 by Wu, Pei, and colleagues, was a multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 RCT that enrolled 1,106 adults with sepsis (1,089 analyzed) across 22 Chinese medical centers. Patients received subcutaneous Tα1 every 12 hours for seven days or placebo. Twenty-eight-day all-cause mortality was 23.4% in the Tα1 group versus 24.1% in the placebo group (hazard ratio 0.99; 95% CI 0.77-1.27; p = 0.93). No secondary or safety outcome differed significantly. The authors concluded there was no clear evidence that Tα1 reduces 28-day mortality in sepsis.

detail.faq:
q: What is the difference between thymosin beta-4 and TB-500?
a: Thymosin beta-4 is the full endogenous 43-amino-acid peptide found in most mammalian cells. TB-500 is a synthetic 7-amino-acid acetylated fragment (Ac-LKKTETQ) corresponding to residues 17 through 23 of that sequence, which researchers describe as the active site for actin binding and cell migration. The clinical trial data, including the Phase II and Phase III ophthalmic trials and the 2025 cardiac RCT, all involve full-length Tβ4. TB-500 has no comparable human trial program as of September 2026, and FDA has identified no human exposure data for it.
q: Is thymosin beta-4 FDA-approved?
a: No. As of September 2026, thymosin beta-4 is not FDA-approved for any indication. The RGN-259 ophthalmic program (0.1% Tβ4 eye drops developed by ReGenTree) has completed Phase III trials in dry eye and has a Phase III trial in neurotrophic keratopathy listed as recruiting, but no FDA marketing approval has been granted.
q: What are the side effects of thymosin beta-4?
a: The available human safety data from two Phase I studies, published in the Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences in 2010 by Ruff and colleagues and in the Journal of Cellular and Molecular Medicine in 2021 by Wang and colleagues, reported Tβ4 as well tolerated in healthy volunteers across single and multiple doses up to 1,260 mg intravenously. In a Phase III eye-drop trial in neurotrophic keratopathy, no significant adverse effects were observed. Long-term safety data for chronic subcutaneous use are limited.
q: Can you get thymosin beta-4 without a prescription?
a: No. Thymosin beta-4 is not legally available over the counter in the United States. Products marketed online are unregulated and may not contain what they claim.
q: How does thymosin beta-4 work for wound healing?
a: In preclinical models, Tβ4 has been studied for its effects on wound healing primarily through two mechanisms: it sequesters G-actin monomers, which helps cells such as keratinocytes reorganize their cytoskeletons and migrate toward the wound edge; and it promotes angiogenesis, the new blood-vessel growth that supplies healing tissue. A proposed anti-inflammatory effect may also modulate the inflammatory environment that can slow repair. The foundational preclinical data from Malinda and colleagues in 1999 demonstrated a 42% increase in reepithelialization at day 4 (up to 61% at day 7) in a rat full-thickness wound model. No large-scale human wound-healing RCTs have been completed as of September 2026.
q: Are peptides legal in 2026?
a: Legality depends on the specific compound, its regulatory status, and the context of use. Thymosin beta-4 is not FDA-approved and is not approved for OTC sale. As of September 2026, its fragment TB-500 is not eligible for 503A compounding: FDA removed it from Category 2 in April 2026 after the nomination was withdrawn, but it is not on the 503A bulks list or in Category 1. For athletes, Tβ4 is prohibited under the 2026 WADA Prohibited List (Section S2). Consult a qualified provider or regulatory expert for guidance specific to your situation.
q: What changed on FDA's peptide compounding list in 2026?
a: FDA announced on April 15, 2026 that its advisers would review compounding restrictions on 12 peptides, and by April 22 it had moved TB-500 off its Category 2 list after nominators withdrew their nominations. That was not a finding that the peptides are safe, and TB-500 (the thymosin beta-4 fragment) is not on the 503A bulks list or in Category 1. On July 23, 2026, an FDA advisory committee voted 8-6 to recommend TB-500 for wound healing for the bulks list, a non-binding vote that still requires FDA rulemaking. Consult a qualified provider for guidance specific to your situation.
q: Is thymosin beta-4 prohibited in sport?
a: Yes. As of the 2026 WADA Prohibited List, thymosin beta-4 is classified as a prohibited substance under Section S2 (Peptide Hormones, Growth Factors, Related Substances, and Mimetics). This prohibition applies both in competition and out of competition. TB-500 is equally prohibited under the same section. Athletes subject to anti-doping rules governed by WADA or their sport's governing body should not use thymosin beta-4 or TB-500, regardless of source, and should consult their sport's anti-doping authority before using any related peptide.

detail.sections:
title: What is thymulin?
text: Thymulin is a nine-amino acid peptide produced by the thymus gland, where immune cells mature. It is unusual in that it is only biologically active when coupled to zinc. It has historically been studied as a thymic immune hormone, and it is sold through wellness and "research peptide" channels for immune support. It is not an approved medicine.
title: How does it work?
text: Thymulin is involved in the development and differentiation of T-cells, the immune system's coordinating cells, and has been reported in animal work to have anti-inflammatory and pain-modulating effects. A notable feature of its biology is the zinc link: zinc deficiency lowers active thymulin levels and shifts the immune response. These mechanisms come largely from animal and physiological studies. This describes the proposed mechanism, separate from demonstrated benefit from giving the peptide.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No. Thymulin is not approved by the FDA or any regulator as a therapy. It is not on FDA compounding lists and was not among the peptides reviewed at the 2026 FDA compounding advisory meetings.
title: What does the research show?
text: The evidence is largely preclinical and physiological. According to PubMed, the main human-relevant observations are that thymulin activity tracks zinc status and thymic function, summarized in reviews of its biology and of zinc and immunity. detail.faq:
q: How does tirzepatide work, and what makes it different from GLP-1 agonists?
a: Tirzepatide is a dual agonist, it activates both GIP and GLP-1 receptors simultaneously, which affects appetite, gastric emptying, and insulin secretion. Unlike semaglutide (GLP-1 only), tirzepatide is a first-in-class medication, and it has also been shown to reduce LDL cholesterol and triglycerides. A network meta-analysis of 28 RCTs with 23,622 adults with type 2 diabetes found that, compared with placebo, tirzepatide 15 mg reduced HbA1c by 1.96 percentage points versus 1.59 percentage points for semaglutide 2.0 mg (a difference the analysis rated comparable), and bodyweight by 9.57 kg versus 4.97 kg.
q: What did the SURMOUNT-1 trial show about tirzepatide for weight loss?
a: SURMOUNT-1 is the landmark weight trial for tirzepatide, demonstrating dose-dependent average weight reductions of 15.0% to 20.9% over 72 weeks in adults without type 2 diabetes. The trial enrolled 2,539 adults with obesity, or overweight with at least one weight-related complication; placebo produced 3.1% weight loss, and individual results varied. SURMOUNT-4 further demonstrated weight maintenance benefits: after participants achieved 20.9% mean weight loss during a 36-week open-label run-in phase, the 670 who were randomized showed that continued tirzepatide led to a further 5.5% loss while those switched to placebo regained 14.0% (a difference of 19.4 percentage points), for total weight loss of 25.3% versus 9.9% from the start.
q: Does tirzepatide work for people who have type 2 diabetes and obesity?
a: Yes, tirzepatide works for people with both type 2 diabetes and obesity. SURMOUNT-2 evaluated tirzepatide specifically in adults with both conditions (N=938; 72 weeks), showing weight reductions of 12.8% with the 10 mg dose and 14.7% with the 15 mg dose, compared to 3.2% with placebo (treatment differences of 9.6 and 11.6 percentage points, respectively). While these results demonstrate meaningful weight reduction, the magnitude was smaller than in SURMOUNT-1, which excluded people with diabetes.
q: What is tirzepatide's FDA-approved status?
a: Tirzepatide has five FDA-approved uses across two brand names. Mounjaro was FDA-approved in May 2022 for type 2 diabetes, and its label now also covers pediatric patients 10 years and older and cardiovascular risk reduction in high-risk adults with type 2 diabetes, while Zepbound received approval in November 2023 for chronic weight management in adults with obesity or overweight with at least one weight-related comorbidity, and in December 2024 for moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity. Compounded tirzepatide is not FDA-approved and has not been evaluated by the FDA for safety, effectiveness, or quality.
q: What does the research show about tirzepatide and sleep apnea?
a: The SURMOUNT-OSA trials demonstrated that tirzepatide at the maximum tolerated dose reduced the apnea-hypopnea index by 25.3 events per hour in adults with moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea and obesity not using positive airway pressure (PAP) therapy. That 52-week trial, one of two that together enrolled 469 participants, showed a treatment difference of 20.0 events per hour versus placebo (95% CI 14.2-25.8), with benefit tied to weight reduction. These findings formed the basis for the FDA indication granted in December 2024.
q: Can tirzepatide reduce the risk of developing type 2 diabetes?
a: Yes, tirzepatide is associated with a markedly lower rate of type 2 diabetes development in adults with obesity and prediabetes. A 176-week analysis of SURMOUNT-1 participants with prediabetes found that type 2 diabetes developed in only 1.3% of tirzepatide-treated participants compared to 13.3% with placebo (hazard ratio 0.07; 95% CI 0.0-0.1), alongside mean weight reductions of 12.3% (5 mg), 18.7% (10 mg), and 19.7% (15 mg) versus 1.3% with placebo among 1,032 participants with obesity and prediabetes.
q: How does tirzepatide compare to semaglutide for weight loss?
a: Comparative evidence shows tirzepatide produces greater weight reduction than semaglutide, though both increase gastrointestinal adverse events, particularly at higher tirzepatide doses. A 2025 meta-analysis of 7 direct comparative studies (N=28,980; five observational, two randomized) found tirzepatide was associated with significantly higher odds of achieving ≥10% weight loss versus semaglutide, with a standardized mean difference in weight loss of 0.75 (95% CI 0.52-0.92), though heterogeneity across studies was high. Similarly, a 2024 network meta-analysis covering 28 RCTs with 23,622 adults with type 2 diabetes found that, compared with placebo, tirzepatide 15 mg reduced bodyweight by 9.57 kg compared to 4.97 kg for semaglutide 2.0 mg.

The rationale is that aged skin has fragmented decorin, so supplying a decorin-like signal may help the appearance of smooth, well-structured skin. These are laboratory findings. In finished cosmetics the benefit is described in appearance terms, such as the look of smoother texture and firmer skin.

detail.sections:
title: What is tripeptide-10 citrulline?
text: Tripeptide-10 citrulline is a short synthetic peptide built around three amino acids with an added citrulline group. It is designed to mimic decorin, a small protein in skin that attaches to collagen fibers and helps control how they are organized. It is made by Lubrizol under the trade name Decorinyl, with roots in research at Lipotec, and is a cosmetic ingredient, not a drug.
title: How does it work?
text: Laboratory studies describe tripeptide-10 citrulline as a decorin mimic that influences the assembly of collagen. Rather than trying to make more collagen, it is proposed to copy decorin's role in guiding collagen fibers to form at a more uniform diameter and spacing. In an in-vitro study of collagen fiber formation, the peptide regulated fiber diameter, which is the basis for the claim that it supports better-organized, healthier-looking collagen. The rationale is that aged skin has fragmented decorin, so supplying a decorin-like signal may help the appearance of smooth, well-structured skin.
These are laboratory findings. In finished cosmetics the benefit is described in appearance terms, such as the look of smoother texture and firmer skin.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: No, and it does not need to be. The FDA does not pre-approve cosmetic ingredients. A cosmetic may describe effects on the appearance of skin, while a claim to reorganize the body's collagen would make a product a drug. Tripeptide-10 citrulline is used as a cosmetic ingredient, for the appearance of the skin.
title: What is it used for?
text: Tripeptide-10 citrulline is used in "anti-aging" serums and creams aimed at the look of smoother texture, suppleness, and firmness. It is often positioned around "collagen quality" and combined with other peptides and hydrating ingredients.
title: What does the research show?
text: The evidence is thin:
Source | Type | What it shows
Founding study, according to PubMed | Laboratory and tissue-culture experiment, not a clinical appearance trial | The peptide can regulate collagen fiber formation
A frequently cited figure | Manufacturer data rather than an independently published trial | A low-concentration cream improved skin suppleness in a small group
No independent human efficacy study was found.
title: What are the side effects?
text: Tripeptide-10 citrulline is generally reported as well tolerated at the low concentrations used in cosmetics, with low irritation potential for this class of peptide. Independent safety data are limited, so a patch test is reasonable for sensitive skin.
detail.sources_note: Sources: a laboratory and tissue-culture study of the decorin-like peptide and collagen fiber organization (Puig et al., International Journal of Cosmetic Science, 2008, DOI: 10.1111/j.1468-2494.2008.00429.x), indexed on PubMed; and manufacturer and cosmetic ingredient reference data on Decorinyl. This document is educational and does not constitute medical advice.

Cosmetic ingredient, a decorin-inspired signal peptide (sold as Decorinyl) Signal peptide Skin & aging Tripeptide-10 citrulline is a short "signal" peptide, sold as Decorinyl, designed to imitate decorin, a natural protein that organizes how collagen fibers assemble in skin. Laboratory work suggests it helps collagen form into more uniform, orderly fibers, targeting the quality of collagen rather than the quantity, which is the basis for its use in products aimed at the appearance of smoother, firmer skin. As of 2026, the support is a single laboratory study plus manufacturer claims, with no independent human trial.

title: What is triptorelin?
text: Triptorelin, known generically as triptorelin pamoate (also triptorelin acetate or embonate) and sold as Trelstar and Triptodur, is a synthetic ten-amino-acid analog of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH, also called LHRH). It is sometimes referred to in the research literature as D-Trp6-LHRH, after the substitution that distinguishes it. It is formulated as a microsphere depot that releases drug over weeks to months. Triptorelin was developed by Debiopharm and approved in the United States in 2000; it is marketed in Europe and elsewhere as Decapeptyl.
title: How does triptorelin work?
text: Triptorelin binds the GnRH receptor on the pituitary. A first dose transiently stimulates the gland, briefly raising luteinizing hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone, and testosterone, the flare. Because the depot then exposes the receptor continuously, the pituitary gonadotrophs downregulate and desensitize, and gonadotropin output falls, driving testosterone in men to castrate levels.
In advanced prostate cancer, removing testosterone starves hormone-sensitive tumor cells, which is the basis of treatment; in central precocious puberty, suppressing the premature hormone signal halts early sexual development. It is available in 1-, 3-, and 6-month depot strengths.

text: Triptorelin is prescribed for the palliative treatment of advanced prostate cancer in men and for central precocious puberty in children. It is given by a healthcare professional as an intramuscular injection on the schedule matched to the depot strength.

peptides.fda_status: FDA-approved as DAYBUE for Rett syndrome; other (predecessor) programs are investigational
peptides.evidence_note: For the investigational predecessor programs, the Fragile X evidence is a single short exploratory Phase 2 reporting only a preliminary signal that was never confirmed, and the traumatic brain injury program did not succeed. (The separate Rett syndrome use is FDA-approved.)
peptides.what_it_is: Oral peptide analog of a fragment of IGF-1
peptides.key_takeaway: Trofinetide is an IGF-1-derived peptide that is FDA-approved as DAYBUE for Rett syndrome, but its earlier "predecessor" programs, chiefly Fragile X syndrome and traumatic brain injury, were investigational and did not lead to approval. In Fragile X, a short exploratory trial reported only a preliminary signal that was never confirmed. This entry covers those investigational predecessor uses, not the approved Rett indication.
peptides.mechanism: As an IGF-1-related peptide, trofinetide is proposed to support synaptic maturation and to reduce neuroinflammation and dysfunction in the brain's support cells (glia). This mechanism underpins its development across several neurodevelopmental conditions. This describes the proposed mechanism; for the predecessor programs, the human outcomes did not support approval.
peptides.human_study_findings: For Fragile X, the evidence is a short exploratory trial. According to PubMed, a double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 2 study in adolescent and adult males with Fragile X syndrome reported that the higher dose met prespecified exploratory efficacy criteria on several Fragile X-specific measures over a brief 28-day period, which the authors framed as a preliminary signal. This program was not advanced to a successful registration trial, and trofinetide is not approved for Fragile X. Earlier work in traumatic brain injury likewise did not yield an approved indication. The predecessor-program evidence is limited and unconfirmed.

detail.sections:
title: What is trofinetide?
text: Trofinetide is a synthetic analog of a small fragment of insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), taken by mouth, originated by Neuren Pharmaceuticals. It is approved by the FDA as DAYBUE for Rett syndrome, a rare neurodevelopmental disorder. Before that approval, it was also studied in other conditions, principally Fragile X syndrome and traumatic brain injury, and those earlier "predecessor" programs, the focus of this entry, remained investigational and did not reach approval.
title: How does it work?
text: As an IGF-1-related peptide, trofinetide is proposed to support synaptic maturation and to reduce neuroinflammation and dysfunction in the brain's support cells (glia). This mechanism underpins its development across several neurodevelopmental conditions. This describes the proposed mechanism; for the predecessor programs, the human outcomes did not support approval.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: For Rett syndrome, yes. For the investigational predecessor uses, no. Status by program:
Program | FDA status
Rett syndrome | Approved, as DAYBUE
Fragile X syndrome | No approved indication
Traumatic brain injury | Not approved; the program did not succeed
This entry concerns those unapproved uses; the approved Rett syndrome product is separate.
title: What does the research show?
text: For Fragile X, the evidence is a short exploratory trial. According to PubMed, a double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 2 study in adolescent and adult males with Fragile X syndrome reported that the higher dose met prespecified exploratory efficacy criteria on several Fragile X-specific measures over a brief 28-day period, which the authors framed as a preliminary signal.
This program was not advanced to a successful registration trial, and trofinetide is not approved for Fragile X. Earlier work in traumatic brain injury likewise did not yield an approved indication. The predecessor-program evidence is limited and unconfirmed.
detail.sources_note: Sources: the Phase 2 Fragile X syndrome trial (Berry-Kravis et al., Pediatric Neurology, 2020, DOI: 10.1016/j.pediatrneurol.2020.04.019), indexed on PubMed; and the FDA approval of DAYBUE (trofinetide) for Rett syndrome. This document is educational, is not medical advice or a health claim, and is not an offer to sell any product.

peptides.name: Trofinetide
peptides.fda_status: Yes. Trofinetide (DAYBUE) was approved by the FDA in 2023 for the treatment of Rett syndrome in adults and children 2 years and older. It was the first approved treatment for the condition. DAYBUE Stix, a powder that is mixed into a solution, appears in the current prescribing information, revised in December 2025.
peptides.evidence_note: Trofinetide is FDA-approved for Rett syndrome, supported by the phase 3 LAVENDER trial showing improvement on caregiver and clinician measures.
peptides.what_it_is: A synthetic analog of the IGF-1-derived tripeptide glycine-proline-glutamate (GPE)
peptides.key_takeaway: Trofinetide (sold as DAYBUE and DAYBUE Stix) is a synthetic analog of a small fragment of insulin-like growth factor 1, and the first drug the FDA approved for Rett syndrome, a rare genetic disorder, in 2023. In the 12-week LAVENDER phase 3 trial of 187 females, scores on the caregiver-rated Rett Syndrome Behaviour Questionnaire fell 4.9 points on trofinetide versus 1.7 on placebo (P = 0.0175). Clinician global impression also improved significantly on trofinetide versus placebo.
peptides.mechanism:
The precise way trofinetide helps in Rett syndrome is not fully established, which the labeling acknowledges. Based on preclinical work, it is thought to act on several of the processes disturbed in the condition:
- Reducing neuroinflammation by modulating the brain's immune cells (microglia and astrocytes)
- Supporting the formation and maturation of synapses and dendrites
- Normalizing signaling related to IGF-1 in the central nervous system
The aim is to improve the function of brain circuits affected by the loss of the MECP2 gene that causes Rett syndrome.
Because Rett syndrome had no approved drug treatment before it, trofinetide's benefit is measured on scales of behavior and overall clinical impression rather than a single biomarker. In the phase 3 LAVENDER trial, trofinetide significantly improved both the caregiver-rated Rett Syndrome Behaviour Questionnaire and a clinician's global impression compared with placebo. The trial randomized 187 females for 12 weeks (P = 0.0175 for the questionnaire difference):
Arm | Females randomized | Questionnaire score change
Trofinetide | 93 | Fell 4.9 points
Placebo | 94 | Fell 1.7 points
The most common effects of trofinetide are gastrointestinal.

detail.sections:
title: What is trofinetide?
text: Trofinetide, sold under the brands DAYBUE and DAYBUE Stix, is a synthetic analog of glycine-proline-glutamate (GPE), a three-amino-acid fragment naturally cleaved from insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) in the brain. It is the first medication approved specifically for Rett syndrome, a rare genetic disorder, almost always in girls, that causes loss of acquired skills, movement problems, and impaired communication. It was approved in the United States in 2023.
title: How does trofinetide work?
text: The precise way trofinetide helps in Rett syndrome is not fully established, which the labeling acknowledges. Based on preclinical work, it is thought to act on several of the processes disturbed in the condition:
- Reducing neuroinflammation by modulating the brain's immune cells (microglia and astrocytes)
- Supporting the formation and maturation of synapses and dendrites
- Normalizing signaling related to IGF-1 in the central nervous system
The aim is to improve the function of brain circuits affected by the loss of the MECP2 gene that causes Rett syndrome.
Because Rett syndrome had no approved drug treatment before it, trofinetide's benefit is measured on scales of behavior and overall clinical impression rather than a single biomarker. In the phase 3 LAVENDER trial, trofinetide significantly improved both the caregiver-rated Rett Syndrome Behaviour Questionnaire and a clinician's global impression compared with placebo. The trial randomized 187 females for 12 weeks (P = 0.0175 for the questionnaire difference):
Arm | Females randomized | Questionnaire score change
Trofinetide | 93 | Fell 4.9 points
Placebo | 94 | Fell 1.7 points
The most common effects of trofinetide are gastrointestinal.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: Yes. Trofinetide (DAYBUE) was approved by the FDA in 2023 for the treatment of Rett syndrome in adults and children 2 years and older. It was the first approved treatment for the condition. DAYBUE Stix, a powder that is mixed into a solution, appears in the current prescribing information, revised in December 2025.
title: What is trofinetide prescribed for?
text: Trofinetide is prescribed for Rett syndrome in people 2 years and older. Because diarrhea is common, medicines that can worsen diarrhea or dehydration are used carefully alongside it.
title: What are the side effects?
text: According to the prescribing information, common side effects include:
- Diarrhea, which most patients experience
- Vomiting
- Fever
- Decreased appetite and fatigue
- Anxiety
- Seizure
- Cold symptoms
More serious considerations include:
- Diarrhea and dehydration, which may require managing fluids and adjusting other medicines
- Severe vomiting, which can lead to aspiration of stomach contents

peptides.name: Vancomycin
peptides.fda_status: Yes. Vancomycin has been FDA-approved since 1958 and is available as intravenous formulations and an oral form. Its approved uses span serious Gram-positive infections systemically and C. difficile infection and staphylococcal enterocolitis when given orally.
peptides.evidence_note: Vancomycin is FDA-approved for serious Gram-positive infections and C. difficile infection, with decades of clinical use establishing it as a standard of care.
peptides.what_it_is: A glycopeptide antibiotic active against Gram-positive bacteria
peptides.key_takeaway: Vancomycin (sold as a generic injection and, for oral use, as Vancocin and Firvanq) is a glycopeptide antibiotic that has been a mainstay against serious Gram-positive infections, including MRSA, for decades. It kills bacteria by blocking construction of their cell wall, and the same drug, taken by mouth, treats intestinal C. difficile infection. It has been FDA-approved in the U.S. since 1958 and is given intravenously for most infections or orally for gut infections.
peptides.mechanism:
Vancomycin blocks bacterial cell-wall synthesis. It binds tightly to the building blocks of peptidoglycan, the mesh that gives the bacterial wall its strength, specifically the D-alanyl-D-alanine end of those precursors. By capping that site, it prevents the cross-linking that would complete the wall, so the growing bacterium cannot maintain its structure and dies. This is a different target from the penicillins, which is why vancomycin works against many penicillin-resistant organisms.
Where it acts depends on the form given:
Form | Where it acts | Infections treated
Intravenous | Distributes through the body | Bloodstream, bone, skin, and other serious Gram-positive infections
Oral | Barely absorbed, so it acts locally in the intestine | C. difficile, where local action is exactly what is wanted
Dosing is guided by blood levels, because too little risks treatment failure and resistance while too much raises the risk of kidney injury. Vancomycin is established enough that newer drugs are tested against it. In a 2006 trial in Staphylococcus aureus bloodstream infection, daptomycin was compared with standard therapy that included vancomycin.

title: What is vancomycin?
text: Vancomycin, sold as a generic injection and as the oral products Vancocin (capsules) and Firvanq (oral solution), is a glycopeptide antibiotic, a large, complex molecule that bacteria have found relatively hard to resist. It is used for serious infections caused by Gram-positive bacteria, especially methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), and it has a distinct second role: taken orally, where it stays in the gut, it treats Clostridioides difficile infection. It was approved in the United States in 1958.
title: The history of vancomycin
text: Vancomycin came from a soil bacterium collected in the 1950s, at a time when penicillin resistance in staphylococci was becoming a serious problem. The earliest preparations were impure and brown, earning the nickname "Mississippi mud," and early formulations were associated with more side effects than the purified drug used today. For years it was held in reserve, but with the spread of MRSA it became one of the most important last-resort antibiotics in the hospital, a role it still holds more than six decades after approval.
title: How does vancomycin work?
text: Vancomycin blocks bacterial cell-wall synthesis. It binds tightly to the building blocks of peptidoglycan, the mesh that gives the bacterial wall its strength, specifically the D-alanyl-D-alanine end of those precursors. By capping that site, it prevents the cross-linking that would complete the wall, so the growing bacterium cannot maintain its structure and dies. This is a different target from the penicillins, which is why vancomycin works against many penicillin-resistant organisms.
Where it acts depends on the form given:
Form | Where it acts | Infections treated
Intravenous | Distributes through the body | Bloodstream, bone, skin, and other serious Gram-positive infections
Oral | Barely absorbed, so it acts locally in the intestine | C. difficile, where local action is exactly what is wanted
Dosing is guided by blood levels, because too little risks treatment failure and resistance while too much raises the risk of kidney injury. Vancomycin is established enough that newer drugs are tested against it. In a 2006 trial in Staphylococcus aureus bloodstream infection, daptomycin was compared with standard therapy that included vancomycin.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: Yes. Vancomycin has been FDA-approved since 1958 and is available as intravenous formulations and an oral form. Its approved uses span serious Gram-positive infections systemically and C. difficile infection and staphylococcal enterocolitis when given orally.
title: What is vancomycin prescribed for?
text: Intravenous vancomycin is prescribed for serious Gram-positive infections such as MRSA bloodstream infections, endocarditis, bone and joint infections, skin and soft-tissue infections, and pneumonia. Oral vancomycin is prescribed for C. difficile-associated diarrhea, where it acts within the gut.
title: What are the side effects?
text: According to the prescribing information, common side effects of intravenous vancomycin include:
- Kidney injury
- Hearing loss
- Low white-cell counts
- Allergic reactions

- Nausea

peptides.key_takeaway: Vasopressin (sold as Vasostrict) is a synthetic copy of the body's antidiuretic hormone, used in intensive care to raise blood pressure in patients whose blood vessels have lost tone despite other treatment. It tightens blood vessels through a pathway independent of the usual catecholamine drugs. The formally approved product has been FDA-approved in the U.S. since 2014 and is given as a continuous intravenous infusion.
peptides.mechanism:
Vasopressin raises blood pressure mainly through V1a receptors on the smooth muscle of blood vessels, and it also acts at the kidney's V2 receptors. The table below compares the two.
Receptor | Where it sits | Effect of activation
V1a | Smooth muscle of blood vessels | Triggers the vessel wall to contract, increasing systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure
V2 | Kidney | Promotes water reabsorption, its antidiuretic effect
Importantly, this blood-pressure action works through a different signaling pathway than the catecholamine vasopressors such as norepinephrine, so vasopressin can add blood-pressure support when those drugs alone are not enough, including in states where their receptors have become less responsive.
In vasodilatory shock, such as septic shock, the blood vessels are pathologically relaxed, and vasopressin helps restore tone. The evidence shows it supports blood pressure but does not necessarily improve survival: in the VASST trial, adding low-dose vasopressin to norepinephrine did not reduce 28-day mortality compared with norepinephrine alone, though a subgroup with less severe shock showed possible benefit. It is used to maintain pressure and reduce the dose of other vasopressors.
peptides.side_effects_safety: According to the prescribing information, common side effects include: - Decreased cardiac output - Slowed heart rate or arrhythmia More serious considerations include: - Reduced blood flow to the heart, gut, fingers, toes, or skin, which can cause tissue damage - Low blood sodium - Tissue injury if the infusion leaks out of the vein

title: What is vasopressin?

Although vasopressin had been used clinically for many years under older marketing arrangements, Vasostrict became the first fully FDA-approved vasopressin injection in 2014.

Receptor | Where it sits | Effect of activation
V1a | Smooth muscle of blood vessels | Triggers the vessel wall to contract, increasing systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure
V2 | Kidney | Promotes water reabsorption, its antidiuretic effect
Importantly, this blood-pressure action works through a different signaling pathway than the catecholamine vasopressors such as norepinephrine, so vasopressin can add blood-pressure support when those drugs alone are not enough, including in states where their receptors have become less responsive.

It is used to maintain pressure and reduce the dose of other vasopressors.

title: What is vasopressin prescribed for?
text: Vasopressin is used to increase blood pressure in adults with vasodilatory shock, such as septic or post-cardiotomy shock, who are not responding adequately to fluid resuscitation and catecholamine vasopressors. It is an intensive-care medication, not an outpatient treatment.
title: What are the side effects?
text: According to the prescribing information, common side effects include:
- Decreased cardiac output
- Slowed heart rate or arrhythmia

- Reduced blood flow to the heart, gut, fingers, toes, or skin, which can cause tissue damage
- Low blood sodium
- Tissue injury if the infusion leaks out of the vein

A known effect is a transient drop in blood pressure, so children are given food and fluid before dosing.

More serious considerations include: - Low blood pressure, which is managed by ensuring the child has eaten and had fluids before the dose

peptides.what_it_is: A synthetic cone snail peptide that blocks N-type calcium channels (a non-opioid analgesic)
peptides.key_takeaway: Ziconotide (sold as Prialt) is a synthetic copy of a cone snail venom peptide, used as a non-opioid painkiller delivered directly into the spinal fluid for severe, treatment-resistant chronic pain. It blocks a specific calcium channel on pain-signaling nerves in the spinal cord. It has been FDA-approved in the U.S. since 2004, is given only by intrathecal pump, and carries a boxed warning for serious psychiatric and neurological effects.
peptides.mechanism: Ziconotide selectively blocks N-type voltage-gated calcium channels found on the pain-sensing nerves that terminate in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord. Those channels control the release of neurotransmitters that pass pain signals up to the brain. By blocking them, ziconotide prevents the release of these pain-signaling chemicals, interrupting transmission of the pain message at the level of the spinal cord. Because it is a peptide that does not cross readily into the brain from the bloodstream, it has to be infused directly into the spinal fluid through a pump, and it must never be given intravenously. Its mechanism is entirely different from opioids, so it does not cause respiratory depression or the same tolerance, which is part of its appeal for intractable pain. In a controlled trial in refractory cancer and AIDS pain, ziconotide reduced pain scores substantially more than placebo. It has a narrow therapeutic window, so dosing is cautious and slow.
peptides.side_effects_safety: According to the prescribing information, common side effects include: - Dizziness and nausea - Confusion and memory problems - Abnormal gait, drowsiness, and involuntary eye movements More serious considerations include: - A boxed warning for severe psychiatric symptoms (including depression and suicidal thoughts, hallucinations) and neurological impairment, so patients are monitored closely - The need to stop the drug if serious neurological or psychiatric signs develop - Meningitis or other infections if the pump or catheter becomes contaminated

title: What is ziconotide?
text: Ziconotide, sold under the brand Prialt, is a synthetic version of a peptide found in the venom of a marine cone snail, Conus magus. It is a potent non-opioid painkiller used for severe chronic pain, delivered directly into the cerebrospinal fluid around the spinal cord. It was developed under the code SNX-111 (its natural counterpart is omega-conotoxin MVIIA) and approved in the United States in 2004.
title: How does ziconotide work?
text: Ziconotide selectively blocks N-type voltage-gated calcium channels found on the pain-sensing nerves that terminate in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord. Those channels control the release of neurotransmitters that pass pain signals up to the brain. By blocking them, ziconotide prevents the release of these pain-signaling chemicals, interrupting transmission of the pain message at the level of the spinal cord.
Because it is a peptide that does not cross readily into the brain from the bloodstream, it has to be infused directly into the spinal fluid through a pump, and it must never be given intravenously. Its mechanism is entirely different from opioids, so it does not cause respiratory depression or the same tolerance, which is part of its appeal for intractable pain. In a controlled trial in refractory cancer and AIDS pain, ziconotide reduced pain scores substantially more than placebo. It has a narrow therapeutic window, so dosing is cautious and slow.
title: Is it FDA-approved?
text: Yes. Ziconotide (Prialt) was approved by the FDA in 2004 for the management of severe chronic pain in patients for whom intrathecal therapy is warranted and who are intolerant of or refractory to other treatments. It carries a boxed warning for severe psychiatric symptoms and neurological impairment and is contraindicated in people with a history of psychosis.
title: What is ziconotide prescribed for?
text: Ziconotide is prescribed for severe chronic pain in carefully selected patients who need intrathecal (spinal) drug delivery and have not responded to or cannot tolerate other therapies, including intrathecal morphine. It is managed by pain specialists using an implanted or external microinfusion pump.
title: What are the side effects?
text: According to the prescribing information, common side effects include:
- Dizziness and nausea
- Confusion and memory problems
- Abnormal gait, drowsiness, and involuntary eye movements
More serious considerations include:
- A boxed warning for severe psychiatric symptoms (including depression and suicidal thoughts, hallucinations) and neurological impairment, so patients are monitored closely
- The need to stop the drug if serious neurological or psychiatric signs develop
- Meningitis or other infections if the pump or catheter becomes contaminated

title: What is zilucoplan?
text: Zilucoplan, sold under the brand Zilbrysq, is a synthetic macrocyclic (ring-shaped) peptide that inhibits complement component C5. It treats generalized myasthenia gravis (gMG), an autoimmune disease in which antibodies attack the connection between nerve and muscle, causing weakness. It is used specifically in patients whose disease is driven by antibodies to the acetylcholine receptor. It was developed under the code RA101495 and approved in the United States in 2023.

text: Zilucoplan binds complement protein C5 and blocks its cleavage into the fragments C5a and C5b, which prevents assembly of the membrane attack complex, the complement structure that punches holes in cell membranes. By blocking C5, zilucoplan protects that junction from complement damage.
As a small peptide, it can be given as a simple once-daily subcutaneous injection that patients administer themselves, which is a practical contrast to intravenous complement therapies.
